title: The birth of Islam
description: In 622, a merchant from Mecca named Muhammad fled his city for Medina. That departure, the Hijra, marks year 1 of Islam and the start of a world civilization.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What was the Hijra in 622?
quiz.explanation: The Hijra is Muhammad leaving Mecca, where his life was under threat, for the oasis of Medina. From then on, that year is year 1 of the Muslim calendar.
options: Muhammad's departure from Mecca to Medina
The first revelation received by Muhammad
The capture of Mecca by the Muslims
The death of Muhammad in Medina

quiz.question: Who controlled trade around the Kaaba before Islam?
quiz.explanation: The Quraysh, the dominant tribe of Mecca, drew their power from pilgrimage and trade around the polytheist Kaaba.

quiz.question: True or false: after taking Mecca in 630, Muhammad massacred his former persecutors.
quiz.explanation: Muhammad, on the contrary, grants a general pardon, which facilitates the rallying of Arab tribes to Islam.

quiz.question: In what year did Muhammad die, leaving Arabia unified under one authority?
quiz.explanation: Muhammad died in 632, only ten years after the Hijra, when almost all of Arabia was unified.

quiz.question: Put these events in Muhammad's life in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four dates (622, 624, 630, 632) mark the twenty years in which Muhammad went from threatened prophet to head of a state unifying Arabia.
items: The Hijra: departure to Medina
The Battle of Badr
The capture of Mecca
The death of Muhammad

quiz.question: What is the Dhimma established by the Muslim conquerors?
quiz.explanation: Dhimma is the protected status that lets “people of the Book” keep their religion if they pay the jizya.
options: The status that lets Christians and Jews keep their religion in exchange for a tax
The name of the Muslim calendar
The court charged with judging infidels

quiz.question: Which two great empires were exhausted by their wars around Arabia in the 7th century?
quiz.explanation: Endless wars between Byzantium (the Eastern Roman Empire) and the Sasanian Persians left a geopolitical vacuum that Muhammad's new message could fill.

quiz.question: What is the Umma, founded by Muhammad in Medina?
quiz.explanation: The Umma replaces old tribal loyalties with a community built on shared faith.
options: The community of believers, which goes beyond blood and clan ties
The name of the Muslim calendar

title: Urban II's call and the First Crusade
description: In November 1095, at Clermont, Pope Urban II made a call that sent tens of thousands of Europeans toward Jerusalem. The Crusades were born.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What event occurred at the Council of Clermont in November 1095?
quiz.explanation: At the Council of Clermont, on November 27, 1095, Urban II called on Western Christians to go and liberate Jerusalem, in exchange for forgiveness of their sins.
options: Pope Urban II calls for crusade to liberate Jerusalem
The Crusaders found the Latin States of the East

quiz.question: What event pushed the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Comnenus to ask the pope for help?
quiz.explanation: In 1071, in Mantzikert, the Seljuk Turks crushed the Byzantine army and opened Anatolia, pushing Alexios I Comnenus to petition Rome.
options: The defeat of Mantzikert against the Seljuk Turks
The capture of Jerusalem by the Muslims

quiz.question: True or false: the “poor people's crusade” led by Peter the Hermit was a disciplined army that reached Jerusalem without difficulty.
quiz.explanation: Without discipline or supplies, this troop of poor people plundered in their path and was decimated in Anatolia before reaching Jerusalem.

quiz.question: What does Urban II promise to those who go on crusade?
quiz.explanation: Urban II promises a plenary indulgence: total forgiveness of sins for those who take the cross.
options: Full forgiveness of the penalties due to their sins
Land guaranteed in the Holy Land
A salary paid by the Church

quiz.question: True or false: after the capture of Jerusalem, Godfrey of Bouillon proclaimed himself king of the city.
quiz.explanation: Godfrey of Bouillon refused the title of king and preferred to be called Avowed of the Holy Sepulchre, protector of the tomb of Christ.

quiz.question: Put these events in the history of the Crusades in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones range from 1071 to 1187: the Byzantine defeat precedes the pope's appeal, which precedes the capture and then recapture of Jerusalem.
items: Byzantine defeat of Mantzikert against the Seljuk Turks
Call to crusade at the Council of Clermont
Capture of Jerusalem by the Crusaders
Resumption of Jerusalem by Saladin

quiz.question: In what year did the Crusaders capture Jerusalem?
quiz.explanation: Jerusalem fell on July 15, 1099, after the expedition left in 1096 and the siege of Antioch.

quiz.question: Which Muslim sultan recaptures Jerusalem in 1187?
quiz.explanation: In 1187, Sultan Saladin recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders, restarting the cycle of the Crusades.

quiz.question: In what year did Saint-Jean-d'Acre, the last bastion of the Latin States of the East, fall?
quiz.explanation: The fall of Saint-Jean-d'Acre in 1291 marks the end of the Latin presence in the Holy Land.

title: The sack of Rome by the Visigoths
description: In August 410, Alaric's Visigoths looted Rome for three days. For the first time in eight centuries, an enemy army walked into the Eternal City.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Who led the Visigoths during the capture of Rome in 410?
quiz.explanation: King Alaric, a former officer in the Roman army, led the Visigoths who forced the gates of Rome in August 410.

quiz.question: True or false: Before 410, no enemy army had entered Rome for about eight centuries.
quiz.explanation: The last capture of Rome by an enemy dates back to the Gallic sack of 390 BC. BC, almost 800 years before the arrival of Alaric.

quiz.question: Why did Emperor Honorius leave Rome for Ravenna in 402?
quiz.explanation: Ravenna is a city in Italy protected by its marshes, making it a safer refuge for the emperor than Rome.
options: Ravenna, protected by its marshes, is easier to defend
Rome had just been destroyed by fire
The Roman Senate had expelled him from the city
He wanted to get closer to Constantinople

quiz.question: What is the Roman foedus mentioned in the course?
quiz.explanation: To hold its borders despite the lack of soldiers, the Empire settled Germanic peoples on its soil in exchange for their military service.
options: A treaty by which “barbarian” peoples settled on Roman territory in exchange for military service
A tax paid by the provinces to Rome
A peace treaty signed with the Persians
A law prohibiting Germans from serving in the Roman army

quiz.question: True or false: Alaric was a former officer in the Roman army before becoming king of the Visigoths.
quiz.explanation: Alaric served in the Roman army before becoming leader of the Visigoths, which explains his knowledge of Roman institutions.

quiz.question: What work did Saint Augustine write to respond to the shock caused by the sack of Rome?
quiz.explanation: Faced with the pagans who accuse Christianity of having weakened Rome, Augustine responds in The City of God that earthly empires pass away, but that the Church remains.

quiz.question: Put these events from the fall of the Western Roman Empire in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These stages range from 402 to 476: the withdrawal to Ravenna precedes the Visigoth sack, then the more destructive Vandal sack, until the end of the Western Empire.
items: Honorius abandons Rome for Ravenna
Sack of Rome by Alaric and the Visigoths
Sack of Rome by the Vandals
Deposition of the last Western emperor

quiz.question: In what year did Alaric and the Visigoths pillage Rome?
quiz.explanation: The sack of Rome by the Visigoths took place in August 410, a shock to the entire ancient world.

quiz.question: In what year was the last Western Roman emperor deposed?
quiz.explanation: In 476, the leader Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, ending the Western Roman Empire.

title: The coronation of Charlemagne
description: On Christmas Day 800, in Rome, Pope Leo III placed a crown on Charlemagne's head. The West had an emperor again, and Europe had a model that would last.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Who crowned Charlemagne “Emperor of the Romans” on Christmas Day 800?
quiz.explanation: On December 25, 800, in Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, Pope Leo III placed the imperial crown on the head of Charlemagne.

quiz.question: What empire does the coronation of 800 claim to restore?
quiz.explanation: Leo III's gesture purports to restore the Western Roman Empire, which had disappeared since the deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476.
options: The Western Roman Empire, disappeared since 476

quiz.question: True or false: Charlemagne led about thirty years of war against the Saxons.
quiz.explanation: Charlemagne fought the Saxons for three decades, notably imposing their forced conversion to Christianity.

quiz.question: What are the missi dominici instituted by Charlemagne?
quiz.explanation: The missi dominici are inspectors sent in pairs to the provinces to verify the action of local counts.
options: Inspectors sent in pairs to control the provinces
Monks responsible for copying ancient texts
Soldiers guarding the borders of the empire

quiz.question: True or false: in Constantinople, Charlemagne's coronation was hailed as a just recognition of his power.
quiz.explanation: For the Byzantines, there was only one legitimate Roman emperor: Charlemagne's coronation was seen as a usurpation.

quiz.question: What writing did Charlemagne adopt to standardize the texts copied in the empire?
quiz.explanation: The palace school of Aix-la-Chapelle spread the Caroline script, readable throughout the empire.

quiz.question: Put these events in Charlemagne's life in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones go from 768 to 843: from the accession of Charlemagne to the Lombard conquest, then to the coronation, until the division of the empire between his grandsons.
items: Advent of the Frankish kingdom
Conquest of the Lombard kingdom of Northern Italy
Imperial coronation in Rome
Treaty of Verdun dividing the empire

quiz.question: In what year was Charlemagne crowned emperor in Rome?
quiz.explanation: The coronation took place on December 25, 800, in Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome.

quiz.question: In what year did the Treaty of Verdun divide the empire between Charlemagne's grandsons?
quiz.explanation: In 843, the Treaty of Verdun divided the Carolingian Empire into three kingdoms, foreshadowing France and Germany.

title: Magna Carta
description: In June 1215, John Lackland set his seal to a charter forced on him by his barons. Over the centuries, a feudal text became the symbol of law standing above the king.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Why did the English barons impose the Magna Carta on King John Lackland in 1215?
quiz.explanation: Faced with taxes, hostages and arbitrary fines imposed by John Lackland to reconquer his lands, the barons rebel and impose a text limiting his power.
options: To limit royal arbitrariness: taxes, hostages and abusive fines
To finance a new crusade in the Holy Land
To elect a new king in John's place

quiz.question: True or false: before 1215, John Lackland lost Normandy to the French king Philip II Augustus.
quiz.explanation: In 1204, John Lackland lost Normandy to Philip II Augustus, a setback which weakened him permanently.

quiz.question: What does Clause 39 of Magna Carta say?
quiz.explanation: Clause 39 establishes the principle that no free man can be arrested or imprisoned without due trial of his peers.
options: No free man can be arrested without a judgment of his peers
The king must be elected by the barons

quiz.question: True or false: The Magna Carta of 1215 granted equal rights to all inhabitants of the kingdom, including serfs.
quiz.explanation: The text of 1215 is mainly addressed to “free men”; the serfs, peasants tied to the land, do not benefit directly.

quiz.question: What happened in August 1215, shortly after the signing of Magna Carta?
quiz.explanation: John obtained the annulment of the text by the Pope in August 1215, which reignited the conflict with the barons.
options: John Lackland has the text annulled by the Pope and the civil war resumes
The king is deposed by the barons
The charter is immediately applied throughout the kingdom
John Lackland goes into exile in France

quiz.question: What military defeat in 1214 definitively isolated John Lackland before Magna Carta?
quiz.explanation: In 1214, the defeat of Bouvines, where Philippe Auguste defeated a coalition including England, isolated John Lackland.
options: The sack of London by the barons
The revolt of the northern barons

quiz.question: Put these events from the reign of John Lackland in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These stages go from 1204 to 1216: the loss of Normandy precedes the defeat of Bouvines, then the signing of the charter and its reissue by Henry III.
items: Loss of Normandy against Philippe Auguste
Defeat of Bouvines
Signing of the Magna Carta at Runnymede
Reissue of the charter by Henry III

quiz.question: In what year was Magna Carta sealed at Runnymede?
quiz.explanation: King John Lackland placed his seal on the Magna Carta in June 1215, in Runnymede Meadow.

quiz.question: How many clauses are in the text of the Magna Carta of 1215?
quiz.explanation: The document drawn up under the influence of Archbishop Stephen Langton has 63 clauses.

title: The Black Death in Europe
description: Between 1347 and 1353, bubonic plague killed 30 to 60% of Europeans. A health catastrophe that shook medieval society and sped up the shift into a new world.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What bacteria caused the Black Death?
quiz.explanation: The Black Death is caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis, transmitted to humans by rat fleas.

quiz.question: By what route does the plague travel from Central Asia to the Mediterranean?
quiz.explanation: The Pax Mongolica secures the Silk Road, providing the bacteria with a rapid route of travel between Central Asia and the Mediterranean.
options: The Silk Road, secured by the Pax Mongolica

quiz.question: True or false: According to legend, at the siege of Caffa, the Golden Horde catapulted infected corpses over the city walls.
quiz.explanation: The Golden Horde's siege of Caffa is often cited as one of the earliest examples of biological warfare, with infected corpses catapulted into the city.

quiz.question: What is the real vector of the plague, which doctors of the time were unable to identify?
quiz.explanation: Doctors believe in the theory of miasma, corrupted air, when the real vector is the rat flea, Xenopsylla cheopis.

quiz.question: True or false: the pneumonic form of the plague, which is transmitted from human to human, kills in just 24 to 48 hours.
quiz.explanation: The pneumonic form is the most devastating: transmitted directly between humans, it kills within 24 to 48 hours.

quiz.question: Why did pogroms target Jewish communities between 1348 and 1349?
quiz.explanation: In the absence of a rational explanation for the epidemic, Jewish communities were accused of poisoning wells and massacred in several regions.
options: They are accused of having poisoned the wells
They refuse to pay royal tax
They are accused of having introduced the plague from Asia
They refuse to welcome the flagellants

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Black Death in Europe in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These stages span from 1346 to 1353: from the arrival in Caffa until the epidemic subsides after having ravaged all of Europe.
items: The plague reaches the Genoese trading post of Caffa, in Crimea
Genoese galleys introduce the scourge into Sicily
The epidemic spreads to France, England and the Empire
The pandemic is ebbing in Europe

quiz.question: In what year did the Genoese galleys introduce the plague to Europe, to Messina?
quiz.explanation: In October 1347, Genoese galleys fleeing Caffa docked at Messina, Sicily, introducing the plague to Europe.

quiz.question: According to the estimates given in the course, what is the maximum share of the European population lost by the Black Death between 1347 and 1353?
quiz.explanation: The course estimates that the Black Death killed between 30 and 60% of the European population, or 25 to 50 million people.

title: Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War
description: In 1429, a 17-year-old peasant girl persuaded the Dauphin to hand her an army. Within months, Joan of Arc turned around a war France seemed to have lost.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: How old was Joan of Arc when she joined the dauphin Charles in 1429?
quiz.explanation: Jeanne was 17 when she left Domrémy to convince the dauphin to entrust her with an army.

quiz.question: Where did Joan of Arc come from?
quiz.explanation: Jeanne is a peasant girl from Domrémy, in Lorraine.

quiz.question: True or false: the Hundred Years' War pitted the kings of France against the kings of Spain.
quiz.explanation: The Hundred Years' War pitted the kings of England, the Plantagenets, against the kings of France, the Valois, not Spain.

quiz.question: What does the Treaty of Troyes of 1420 provide?
quiz.explanation: The Treaty of Troyes disinherits the Dauphin Charles in favor of the King of England, whose reign is proclaimed in Paris.
options: The dauphin is disinherited in favor of the King of England
Joan of Arc is made a knight
The immediate coronation of Charles VII in Reims

quiz.question: What mission does Jeanne say she received from her voices?
quiz.explanation: His voices order him to lift the siege of Orléans, then to lead the dauphin to the coronation of Reims, the only rite which makes a true king.
options: Lift the siege of Orléans then lead the dauphin to the coronation of Reims
Driving the Burgundians out of Paris

quiz.question: In what year did Joan of Arc raise the siege of Orléans?
quiz.explanation: Joan broke the siege of Orléans in May 1429, in just nine days.

quiz.question: True or false: Joan of Arc killed many enemies with her own hand during battle.
quiz.explanation: Jeanne has never killed an enemy with her own hand; she preferred to carry her banner to lead without shedding blood herself.

quiz.question: Put these events in the life of Joan of Arc in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones go from 1420 to 1431: the treaty of Troyes, then Orléans and Reims in 1429, the capture in 1430 and the execution in 1431.
items: The Treaty of Troyes disinherits the dauphin
Joan lifts the siege of Orléans
The coronation of Charles VII in Reims
The capture of Jeanne at Compiègne
The pyre of Rouen

title: The Fall of Constantinople
description: On May 29, 1453, after 53 days of siege, the Ottomans forced the walls of Constantinople. The New Rome fell, and the Middle Ages tipped into a new age.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: In what year did Constantinople fall to the Ottomans?
quiz.explanation: Constantinople fell on May 29, 1453, after 53 days of siege.

quiz.question: Who led the siege and capture of Constantinople in 1453?
quiz.explanation: It was the young Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II who led the siege and capture of the city.

quiz.question: True or false: before 1453, the Theodosian walls had never been forced by the earth for a thousand years.
quiz.explanation: This triple rampart from the 5th century had resisted all land assaults for a millennium, until the Ottoman artillery of 1453.

quiz.question: What lastingly weakened the Byzantine Empire before 1453?
quiz.explanation: Christian crusaders from the West had sacked the city in 1204, leaving the Byzantine Empire bloodless.
options: The sack of Constantinople by the 4th Crusade in 1204

quiz.question: What is the name of the giant cannon made by the founder Urban for Mehmed II?
quiz.explanation: Urban forges for Mehmed II an 8 meter cannon called the Basilica, capable of firing 600 kg cannonballs.

quiz.question: How many defenders did the last Byzantine emperor Constantine XI line up against the Ottomans?
quiz.explanation: Faced with tens of thousands of Ottomans, Constantine XI only had around 7,000 defenders.

quiz.question: Put these events of the fall of Constantinople in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four stages go from 1204 to 1453: the weakening of Byzantium, the coming to power of Mehmed II, the siege, then the fall.
items: The sack of the city by the 4th Crusade
The accession of Mehmed II as sultan
The beginning of the Ottoman siege
The capture of the city and its conversion into an Ottoman capital

quiz.question: What happened to the Hagia Sophia after the city was taken?
quiz.explanation: Mehmed II converted the great Hagia Sophia into a mosque after the conquest.

quiz.question: What is one of the European consequences of the fall of Constantinople?
quiz.explanation: By heavily taxing the Eastern routes, the Ottomans pushed Portugal and Spain to seek the Atlantic, opening the way to the Great Discoveries.
options: With routes to the East blocked, Europe seeks other routes to Asia
The Pope moves his capital to Constantinople
The Western Roman Empire is reborn

title: The Aztec Empire
description: In less than two centuries, the Aztecs built a capital of 200,000 people on a lake. Their empire, founded on tribute and sacrifice, collapsed in two years once the Spanish arrived.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: In what year did the Mexica found Tenochtitlán?
quiz.explanation: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlán in 1325, on an islet in Lake Texcoco.

quiz.question: What sign are the Mexica looking for to found their capital, according to their god Huitzilopochtli?
quiz.explanation: The Mexica found this sign on an islet in Lake Texcoco, where they founded Tenochtitlán in 1325.
options: An eagle devouring a snake on a cactus

quiz.question: What are chinampas, perfected by the Aztecs?
quiz.explanation: These ultra-fertile artificial islands help feed the lake capital of Tenochtitlán.
options: Fertile artificial islands made of mud and plants

quiz.question: True or false: The Aztecs used horses and oxen to transport the stones of their pyramids.
quiz.explanation: The Aztecs had neither a wheel for transport nor a beast of burden; yet they moved millions of tons of stone.

quiz.question: What is the Triple Alliance, formed in 1428?
quiz.explanation: In 1428, Tenochtitlán allied itself with Texcoco and Tlacopan, forming the Triple Alliance which soon dominated the region.
options: The union of Tenochtitlán, Texcoco and Tlacopan
An alliance between Aztecs and Spaniards
A peace treaty with the Tlaxcaltecs

quiz.question: According to the Cosmogony of the Five Suns, why did the Aztecs practice human sacrifices?
quiz.explanation: This myth says that the sun only survives nourished by human blood, making sacrifices necessary for the continuity of the world.
options: To feed the sun with blood and keep the world going
To punish the criminals of the empire

quiz.question: What was the main factor in the rapid fall of the Aztec Empire to the Spanish?
quiz.explanation: The real killer is smallpox, a European disease unknown to local populations, which decimates the Aztecs much more than the Spanish weapons.
options: Smallpox, a disease against which the Aztecs had no immunity
The absence of a fortified capital
The refusal of the Aztecs to fight

quiz.question: How many days did the final siege of Tenochtitlán last in 1521?
quiz.explanation: Tenochtitlán fell in 1521 after 80 days of siege, starving and ravaged by disease.

quiz.question: Put these stages of Aztec history in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four milestones go from 1325 to 1521: the founding of the capital, the imperial expansion, the arrival of the Spanish, then the final fall.
items: The founding of Tenochtitlán on Lake Texcoco
The formation of the Triple Alliance
Cortés' arrival in Mexico
The fall of Tenochtitlán

title: The discovery of America
description: On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus reached an island in the Bahamas that he believed was Japan. One navigational error opened the age of globalization.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: In what year did Christopher Columbus reach the Bahamas?
quiz.explanation: Columbus landed on October 12, 1492 on an island in the Bahamas that he named San Salvador.

quiz.question: What was the true economic purpose of Columbus' westward expedition?
quiz.explanation: Columbus seeks a western route to Asia to circumvent the Ottomans, who control the trade routes of the Orient.
options: Reach spices and silk without passing through Ottoman-controlled routes
Prove that the Earth is round
Finding gold to finance a crusade

quiz.question: True or false: Christopher Columbus sought above all to prove that the Earth was round, an idea unknown before him.
quiz.explanation: The sphericity of the Earth was already calculated by the Greek scholar Eratosthenes in the 3rd century BC. AD; Columbus' goal was economic.

quiz.question: What are the three ships of the 1492 expedition?
quiz.explanation: These three ships left Palos, Spain, on August 3, 1492, with a crew of approximately 90 men.
options: La Pinta, la Niña and la Santa María
The Santa Fe, the Reina and the Isabela

quiz.question: How many days does it take to cross the Atlantic to San Salvador?
quiz.explanation: The crossing lasts approximately 70 days, from early August to mid-October 1492.

quiz.question: What did Columbus call the indigenous inhabitants he encountered, convinced they were in Asia?
quiz.explanation: Convinced of having reached the Indies, Columbus calls the Tainos he meets “Indians”.

quiz.question: What is the Colombian Exchange?
quiz.explanation: This transfer brings potatoes and tomatoes to Europe, and wheat, horses or cattle to America, changing both worlds forever.
options: A massive transfer of plants, animals and diseases between Europe and America
A peace treaty between Spain and Portugal
The slave trade between Africa and the West Indies
The exchange of prisoners of war between Columbus and the Tainos

quiz.question: What share of indigenous populations die from diseases imported from Europe in a century?
quiz.explanation: Smallpox, measles and influenza kill between 50 and 90% of indigenous populations in a century, depending on the region.

quiz.question: In 1507, which cartographer gave the continent the name America?
quiz.explanation: In 1507, the cartographer Waldseemüller named the continent America, in homage to the navigator Amerigo Vespucci.

quiz.question: Put these stages of Columbus' expedition in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four stages go from August 1492 to 1507: departure, arrival in the Bahamas, the Treaty of Tordesillas, then the name given to the continent.
items: The departure of the three ships from Palos
Arrival on an island in the Bahamas
Sharing the world between Spain and Portugal
The baptism of the American continent by Waldseemüller

title: The storming of the Bastille
description: On July 14, 1789, a Paris crowd stormed a fortress that held only **7 prisoners**. That act became the symbol of the French Revolution.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What were the Parisians seeking above all when they took the Bastille on July 14, 1789?
quiz.explanation: The Bastille contained only 7 prisoners; the attackers were mainly looking for the powder stored in the fortress.
options: The release of thousands of prisoners

quiz.question: True or false: the Bastille housed thousands of political prisoners on July 14, 1789.
quiz.explanation: That day, the Bastille contained only 7 prisoners: 4 forgers, 2 men deemed insane and an aristocrat.

quiz.question: Why did Louis XVI convene the Estates General in May 1789?
quiz.explanation: The kingdom is ruined, notably by the costly support given to the American colonies, and the king seeks new taxes.
options: To raise new taxes because the kingdom was bankrupt
To organize the coronation of his son

quiz.question: What did the Third Estate do on June 17, 1789, faced with the blockage of the Estates General?
quiz.explanation: Blocked by the system of three orders, the Third Estate proclaimed itself National Assembly on June 17.

quiz.question: What event precipitated the panic in Paris on July 11, 1789?
quiz.explanation: The dismissal of Necker, a very popular minister, triggered panic and pushed Parisians to arm themselves.
options: The dismissal of Jacques Necker, popular Minister of Finance
The arrest of the Third Estate

quiz.question: How many rifles did the crowd seize at Les Invalides on the morning of July 14?
quiz.explanation: The crowd seized around 32,000 rifles from Les Invalides, but they still lacked the powder.

quiz.question: What is a lettre de cachet that makes the Bastille so hated?
quiz.explanation: The lettre de cachet allows someone to be locked up without trial, which embodies royal arbitrariness in the eyes of Parisians.
options: An order of confinement without trial

quiz.question: True or false: when the king was told of the storming of the Bastille, he replied that it was a simple revolt.
quiz.explanation: On the contrary, he was told “No Sire, it’s a revolution”, even though the king had noted “Nothing” in his hunting diary on the 14th.

quiz.question: Put these events of the summer of 1789 in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four stages go from May to August 1789: the royal summons, the oath of deputies, the storming of the Bastille, then the abolition of privileges.
items: The convocation of the Estates General
The Oath of the Palm Game
The Storming of the Bastille
The abolition of privileges

quiz.question: What happened in the countryside after the storming of the Bastille, under the effect of the Great Fear?
quiz.explanation: Fearing revenge from the nobles, the peasants burned the papers of their seigneurial rights, precipitating the abolition of privileges.
options: The peasants burn the papers of seigneurial rights
Peasants rise up against the National Assembly
The campaigns remain indifferent to the events in Paris
The peasants demand the return of the absolute king

title: Napoleon's strategy at Ulm
description: In October 1805, Napoleon surrounded and captured **60,000 Austrians** in two weeks, with almost no major battle. Ulm showed the power of speed.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: In what year did the Ulm campaign take place?
quiz.explanation: The Ulm campaign took place in October 1805, a few weeks before the victory at Austerlitz.

quiz.question: Who commands the Austrian army pushed to Ulm?
quiz.explanation: General Karl Mack commands the Austrian army, which he believes is sheltered behind the walls of Ulm.

quiz.question: True or false: Austria is waiting for Russian reinforcements to arrive before committing its troops to Ulm.
quiz.explanation: Austria does not wait for the Russians: it alone pushes around 70,000 men to Ulm, an error which isolates Mack.

quiz.question: What is the Napoleonic Army Corps, a key asset of the campaign?
quiz.explanation: Each army corps is an autonomous force capable of maneuvering alone, allowing seven corps to march in parallel towards Ulm.
options: A small autonomous army with its infantry, cavalry and cannons

quiz.question: What role does Marshal Murat play in the encirclement maneuver?
quiz.explanation: Murat occupied Mack from the west while other marshals bypassed Ulm from the north to cut off his route to Vienna.
options: He focuses Mack's attention to the west while other corps circle around Ulm

quiz.question: How many Austrian soldiers surrendered during the capitulation of Ulm on October 17, 1805?
quiz.explanation: On October 17, 1805, 27,000 Austrian soldiers laid down their arms on site in Ulm.

quiz.question: What happened to the French fleet the same week as the capitulation of Ulm?
quiz.explanation: The same month, at Trafalgar, Admiral Nelson destroyed the Franco-Spanish fleet, leaving England in control of the seas.
options: It is destroyed by Nelson at Trafalgar
It blocks the port of Vienna

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Ulm and Austerlitz campaigns in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four stages go from the end of September to December 1805: the pivot towards Germany, the encirclement, the surrender of Mack, then the decisive victory of Austerlitz.
items: The crossing of the Rhine by the Grande Armée
The crossing of the Danube behind Mack
The capitulation of Ulm
The victory of Austerlitz

quiz.question: What did General Mack say to Napoleon during their meeting after the capitulation?
quiz.explanation: Mack thus presents himself before Napoleon, who nevertheless gives him back his sword during a dinner between officers.

title: The Battle of Waterloo
description: On **June 18, 1815**, in a single rainy day in Belgium, Napoleon's empire collapsed. Waterloo closed the Hundred Days and opened a century of monarchical order in Europe.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: In what year did the Battle of Waterloo take place?
quiz.explanation: The Battle of Waterloo took place on June 18, 1815, in Belgium.

quiz.question: Who were the two commanders who faced Napoleon at Waterloo?
quiz.explanation: Napoleon faces both the Duke of Wellington and the Prussian Marshal Blücher.

quiz.question: What was Napoleon's initial plan before the battle, called the Central Position?
quiz.explanation: Napoleon wants to place himself between the two enemy armies and defeat them one after the other, before they join together.
options: Place yourself between Wellington and Blücher to beat them separately

quiz.question: True or false: Napoleon sent Marshal Grouchy to pursue the Prussians after Ligny, thinking he had put them out of action.
quiz.explanation: Napoleon thought the Prussians were finished after Ligny and sent Grouchy after them with 33,000 men — a costly mistake.

quiz.question: Why did Napoleon wait until 11:30 a.m. on the morning of June 18 to attack?
quiz.explanation: After a night of rain, Napoleon waited for the ground to dry before moving his artillery, which gave Blücher time to arrive.
options: He wants the ground to dry to move his Grand Battery of cannons
He is waiting for reinforcements from Grouchy
He negotiates a truce with Wellington

quiz.question: What event triggered the panic and rout of the French army at Waterloo?
quiz.explanation: Launched as a last resort, the Imperial Guard retreats for the first time, and the cry “The Guard retreats!” » transforms retreat into rout.
options: The retreat of the Imperial Guard
The destruction of the Great Battery

quiz.question: Where was Napoleon exiled after his final defeat at Waterloo?
quiz.explanation: After his abdication on June 22, 1815, Napoleon was exiled to Saint Helena, an isolated island in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.

quiz.question: Put these events of the Hundred Days in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four stages go from March 1 to June 22, 1815: the return from the island of Elba, the partial victory of Ligny, the defeat of Waterloo, then the abdication.
items: Napoleon's landing near Antibes
The Battle of Ligny
The Battle of Waterloo
Napoleon's final abdication

quiz.question: What did the Congress of Vienna decide after the final fall of Napoleon?
quiz.explanation: The Congress of Vienna imposes the principle of Legitimacy, restoring the royal dynasties to frame a Concert of Europe which maintains peace until 1914.
options: Putting the royal dynasties back on their thrones, Legitimacy
Give the crown of France to Wellington

title: The Paris Commune
description: From March 18 to May 28, 1871, Paris governed itself for **72 days**. The experiment ended in the Bloody Week, a crackdown that left a lasting mark on French memory.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: How many days did the Paris Commune last, from March 18 to May 28, 1871?
quiz.explanation: The Commune governed Paris for 72 days, from March 18 to May 28, 1871.

quiz.question: What event directly triggered the uprising of March 18, 1871?
quiz.explanation: On March 18, Thiers wanted to seize the cannons stored in Montmartre, but the crowd fraternized with the soldiers and Thiers had to evacuate Paris.
options: Thiers' attempt to seize the National Guard's cannons in Montmartre
The arrival of Prussian troops in Paris

quiz.question: True or false: the Paris Commune was born directly after the French defeat in the Franco-Prussian War.
quiz.explanation: The capture of Napoleon III at Sedan and the starving siege of Paris created the context of rupture which led to the Commune.

quiz.question: Who leads the majority monarchist Assembly withdrawn to Versailles?
quiz.explanation: Adolphe Thiers heads this conservative Assembly, in open conflict with insurgent Paris.

quiz.question: What social measures did the Commune put in place during its existence?
quiz.explanation: The Municipal Council legislates urgently, with social measures such as rent remission.
options: Remission of rents and abolition of night work for bakers
The creation of an income tax

quiz.question: Which symbol of the Empire is the Commune tearing down?
quiz.explanation: The Vendôme column, symbol of the First Empire, was demolished by the Commune.

quiz.question: True or false: during the Commune, the tricolor flag remained the official emblem of Paris.
quiz.explanation: The red flag became the official emblem of Paris during the Commune, replacing the tricolor deemed too linked to the powers which had capitulated.

quiz.question: What is the name of the final repression which puts an end to the Commune?
quiz.explanation: From May 21 to 28, 1871, the troops of Versailles crushed the insurrection during Bloody Week.
options: The Night of the Long Knives

quiz.question: Put these events of the Paris Commune in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four stages go from March to May 1871: the uprising, the proclamation of the Commune, then its crushing during Bloody Week.
items: The attempt to seize the cannons at Montmartre
The proclamation of the Commune
The start of Bloody Week
The last battles at Père-Lachaise

quiz.question: Approximately how many people die during Bloody Week?
quiz.explanation: The death toll from Bloody Week is between 10,000 and 30,000 deaths, according to estimates.

title: The Belle Époque
description: Between the end of the war of 1870 and August 1914, Europe believed in progress. Electricity, world's fairs, brand-new art movements, and the cracks that led to catastrophe.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What does the Belle Époque mean, between 1871 and 1914?
quiz.explanation: The Belle Époque goes from the end of the Franco-Prussian War (1871) to the outbreak of the First World War (1914), a period when people believed in science and progress.
options: A period of relative peace marked by faith in progress
The years of reconstruction after World War II
The personal reign of Napoleon III
The decade of the French Revolution

quiz.question: True or false: the expression “Belle Époque” is used by people who lived through it, before 1914.
quiz.explanation: The name only appeared after 1914: it was the survivors of the trenches who invented this lost paradise, with the hindsight of the war.

quiz.question: What affair tore the French Republic apart during the Belle Époque, around a Jewish officer wrongly convicted of espionage?
quiz.explanation: Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish officer, is wrongly convicted of espionage: the affair reveals virulent anti-Semitism and lastingly divides France.

quiz.question: What scientific discovery by Albert Einstein, published in 1905, revolutionized the conception of space and time?
quiz.explanation: Einstein published the theory of Relativity in 1905, challenging classical notions of space and time.

quiz.question: In what year does the Universal Exhibition open in Paris, which attracts 50 million visitors?
quiz.explanation: The Universal Exhibition of 1900 attracted 50 million visitors and made Paris a global showcase of progress.

quiz.question: What event in June 1914 triggered the spiral that ended the Belle Époque?
quiz.explanation: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, triggered the game of alliances which led to the First World War.
options: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo
The fall of the French government
The fire at the Eiffel Tower
The signing of a Franco-German treaty

quiz.question: How many hours per day did workers often work during the Belle Époque?
quiz.explanation: Behind the windows of progress, workers often work 10 to 12 hours a day, without real social protection.

quiz.question: Put these events of the Belle Époque in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones span from 1871 to 1914 and trace the rise and then the brutal end of the Belle Époque.
items: End of the Franco-Prussian War
Construction of the Eiffel Tower
Paris Universal Exhibition
Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand

title: The Battle of Verdun
description: For **299 days**, French and German armies tore each other apart around Verdun. **700,000** casualties for almost no ground gained: the symbol of the horror of the trenches.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What is the code name given by the Germans to their offensive against Verdun in 1916?
quiz.explanation: The operation bears the name Gericht, “the tribunal”, chosen by General Falkenhayn.

quiz.question: Why did German General Falkenhayn choose Verdun precisely for his offensive?
quiz.explanation: Falkenhayn wants to “bleed France dry” by drawing it into a battle of attrition on a place that it cannot give up defending.
options: Because France cannot abandon it without losing face, which allows it to bleed dry
Because Verdun is the military capital of France
Because Verdun is the least defended city on the front
Because the British are stationed there

quiz.question: For how many days did the Battle of Verdun last, from February 21 to December 18, 1916?
quiz.explanation: The battle lasted 299 days, one of the longest of the First World War.

quiz.question: True or false: Fort Douaumont, key to French defense, fell after heroic resistance lasting several weeks.
quiz.explanation: Fort Douaumont fell on February 25, 1916, almost without a fight, only four days after the start of the German offensive.

quiz.question: What is the role of the Sacred Way during the Battle of Verdun?
quiz.explanation: The Voie Sacrée connects Bar-le-Duc to Verdun: nearly 6,000 trucks travel there every day to maintain supplies.
options: Supply Verdun with men and equipment from Bar-le-Duc
Connect Verdun to the Maginot line
Transporting German prisoners to the rear

quiz.question: What does the troop rotation system, the Noria, put in place by Pétain allow?
quiz.explanation: Thanks to the Noria, the divisions are relieved regularly, so that around 70% of the French army fights at Verdun at one time or another.
options: Rotate divisions quickly to limit time spent at the front
Replace French soldiers with colonial troops only
Concentrate a single division during the entire battle

quiz.question: Approximately how many men, French and Germans combined, were killed or wounded during the Battle of Verdun?
quiz.explanation: The battle caused around 700,000 casualties in total, around 370,000 French and 330,000 Germans.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Battle of Verdun and its memory in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones range from the opening of the German offensive in February 1916 to the Franco-German reconciliation of 1984.
items: Opening of the German bombardment
Fall of Fort Douaumont
The Allied Somme offensive relieves Verdun
End of the Battle of Verdun
Handshake between French and German leaders in front of the ossuary

quiz.question: What does the handshake between François Mitterrand and Helmut Kohl in Verdun in 1984 symbolize?
quiz.explanation: This gesture in front of the Douaumont ossuary makes Verdun a symbol of peace between France and Germany.
options: The signing of a new military treaty
The inauguration of the European Union

title: The Russian Revolution
description: In less than eight months, Russia went from the rule of the tsars to the rule of the Bolsheviks. 1917 invented a model that would divide the world for decades.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What sparked the February 1917 revolution in Russia?
quiz.explanation: The February revolution started with demonstrations for bread in Petrograd; the workers take to the streets and the garrison fraternizes with them.
options: Protests linked to bread shortages in Petrograd
A military coup organized by Lenin
The total defeat of the Russian army against Germany
An attack against Tsar Nicholas II

quiz.question: How many years had the Romanov dynasty reigned when Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917?
quiz.explanation: The abdication of Nicholas II on March 2, 1917, put an end to 300 years of reign of the Romanov dynasty.

quiz.question: True or false: after the abdication of Nicholas II, a single power clearly rules Russia.
quiz.explanation: A “double power” was established: the Provisional Government on one side, the Petrograd Soviet, a council of workers and soldiers, on the other.

quiz.question: What slogan summarizes the program that Lenin launched in his April Theses?
quiz.explanation: Upon his return in April 1917, Lenin called for “Peace, Bread, Land”, a program which directly responded to popular expectations.

quiz.question: How did Lenin manage to return to Russia in 1917?
quiz.explanation: Germany, which wants to weaken its Russian enemy, organizes Lenin's return from exile in a “leaded train”.
options: In a sealed train organized by Germany, which hopes to weaken Russia
By a secret agreement with the Tsar

quiz.question: Who organized, alongside Lenin, the Bolshevik insurrection of October 1917?
quiz.explanation: Leon Trotsky, an outstanding organizer, prepared with Lenin the insurrection which overthrew the Provisional Government.

quiz.question: Put these events of the Russian Revolution in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones range from the fall of Tsarism in February 1917 to the founding of the USSR in 1922.
items: Abdication of Nicholas II
April Theses of Lenin
Capture of the Winter Palace
Peace of Brest-Litovsk
Birth of the USSR

quiz.question: What is the Cheka, the Bolshevik political police, putting in place?
quiz.explanation: The Cheka launched terror against opponents of the new power, particularly after the Bolshevik takeover.
options: A policy of terror against opponents

quiz.question: What ideology founded the USSR, born in 1922?
quiz.explanation: The USSR is the first state built on Marxism-Leninism, which combines the ideas of Marx and the method of Lenin.

title: The Great Depression
description: On **October 24, 1929**, Wall Street collapses. Within three years **25%** of Americans are out of work, and the crisis opens the way for political extremism in Europe.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: On what day in 1929 did the New York Stock Exchange crash, triggering the Great Depression?
quiz.explanation: On October 24, 1929, nicknamed Black Thursday, the New York Stock Exchange collapsed and triggered the Great Depression.

quiz.question: What share of Americans were unemployed at the height of the Great Depression?
quiz.explanation: About 25% of Americans find themselves unemployed during the crisis.

quiz.question: What mechanism fueled the speculative bubble of the Roaring Twenties before the crash?
quiz.explanation: We borrow to buy shares by betting on their rise: this system of purchasing on margin multiplies losses when the market collapses.
options: Buying stocks on margin, borrowing to buy securities
Mass printing of money by the state
The continued decline in agricultural prices

quiz.question: True or false: between 1929 and 1932, the American stock market lost nearly 90% of its value.
quiz.explanation: The American stock market lost approximately 89% of its value between 1929 and 1932.

quiz.question: What are the “bank runs” that hit American banks after the crash?
quiz.explanation: Panicked customers rush to withdraw their money, causing around 9,000 US banks to fail.
options: Waves of customers withdrawing their money in panic
Mandatory audits imposed by the State

quiz.question: Put these events of the Great Depression in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: The crash of October 1929 led to a chain of bank failures, then the crisis paved the way for Hitler and the New Deal response, both in early 1933.
items: Black Thursday on Wall Street
A wave of bank failures in the United States
Hitler's rise to power in Germany
Roosevelt's launch of the New Deal

quiz.question: Which monetary system is propagating the American economic crisis to Europe?
quiz.explanation: To maintain their gold reserves, European central banks raise their interest rates, which further worsens the recession.
options: The gold standard, which pushes central banks to raise their interest rates
The gold franc, the single European currency

quiz.question: Who took advantage of massive unemployment in Germany to come to power in January 1933?
quiz.explanation: With 30% unemployment in Germany, Hitler exploited popular despair against the fragile Weimar Republic.

quiz.question: What policy did Franklin D. Roosevelt launch to respond to the crisis?
quiz.explanation: Elected in 1932, Roosevelt launched the New Deal: major works, banking regulation and the start of social protection, to revive the economy.
options: The New Deal, which puts an end to laissez-faire and revives the economy through the State

title: The Battle of Stalingrad
description: From the summer of 1942 to February 1943, Germans and Soviets killed each other in the ruins of a city on the Volga. Stalingrad became the turning point of the Second World War.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What was the initial objective of the German “Case Blue” offensive, launched in 1942?
quiz.explanation: Case Blue first targets Caucasian oil; Stalingrad is initially just a secondary objective on the road.

quiz.question: Who commanded the 6th German Army engaged in the Battle of Stalingrad?
quiz.explanation: The 6th Army, diverted to Stalingrad, is commanded by General Friedrich Paulus.

quiz.question: What tactics did Soviet General Chuikov impose on his troops in the ruins of Stalingrad?
quiz.explanation: By remaining in very close contact with the enemy, the Soviets prevented German artillery and aircraft from striking without hitting their own troops.
options: Stay within 30 meters of the enemy to prevent German artillery from striking without risk
Systematically retreat to the other side of the Volga
Negotiate local truces with the Germans

quiz.question: For how many days did Pavlov House, held by a handful of Soviet soldiers, resist German assaults?
quiz.explanation: The Pavlov House resisted German attacks for 58 days, becoming a symbol of Soviet resistance.

quiz.question: True or false: Stalin's Order 227 authorizes Soviet soldiers to withdraw freely in the face of the enemy.
quiz.explanation: Order 227, on the contrary, imposes “Not a step back”, prohibiting any withdrawal without an order.

quiz.question: What Soviet operation, prepared by Marshal Zhukov, surrounded the German 6th Army in November 1942?
quiz.explanation: On November 19, 1942, Operation Uranus closed its grip on the poorly defended German flanks and surrounded around 300,000 men.

quiz.question: Approximately how many men were surrounded at Stalingrad during Operation Uranus on November 19, 1942?
quiz.explanation: Operation Uranus encircles around 300,000 German and allied troops in the Stalingrad pocket.

quiz.question: Who promised, without success, an airlift to supply the German troops surrounded in Stalingrad?
quiz.explanation: Hermann Göring, head of the Luftwaffe, promised an airlift which failed, leaving the surrounded troops to die of hunger and cold.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Battle of Stalingrad in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the summer of 1942 to February 2, 1943, the battle went from a triumphant German offensive to the complete annihilation of the 6th Army.
items: Launch of the German Case Blue offensive
Close-quarters combat in the city ruins
Encirclement of the 6th Army during Operation Uranus
Capitulation of General Paulus

title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
description: On **August 6, 1945**, an atomic bomb flattened Hiroshima. Three days later, Nagasaki. The Second World War ended, and the nuclear age began.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Which American project, launched in 1942, developed the first atomic bomb?
quiz.explanation: The Manhattan Project, launched in 1942, mobilized approximately 130,000 people and $2 billion to develop the atomic bomb.

quiz.question: Which test, carried out on July 16, 1945 in the New Mexico desert, validated the atomic bomb for the first time?
quiz.explanation: The Trinity test, on July 16, 1945, was the first nuclear explosion in history and confirmed that the bomb worked.

quiz.question: Which bomber dropped the “Little Boy” bomb on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945?
quiz.explanation: The Enola Gay dropped Little Boy on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, at 8:15 a.m.

quiz.question: True or false: Nagasaki was the target planned from the start for the second atomic bomb.
quiz.explanation: The Bockscar initially aimed for the town of Kokura, but clouds prevented it from dropping its bomb, sending it back to Nagasaki.

quiz.question: Which country entered war against Japan on the same day as the bombing of Nagasaki, August 9, 1945?
quiz.explanation: The Soviet entry into war against Japan on August 9, 1945 destroyed the hope of mediation by Moscow.

quiz.question: How many days separate the bombing of Hiroshima from that of Nagasaki?
quiz.explanation: Hiroshima was bombed on August 6, 1945, Nagasaki three days later, on August 9.

quiz.question: Who announced the surrender of Japan on the radio on August 15, 1945?
quiz.explanation: In a historic speech, Emperor Hirohito announced Japan's surrender on August 15, 1945.

quiz.question: What are Japanese survivors of the atomic bombings called?
quiz.explanation: The Hibakusha, the survivors, bear physical aftereffects and an ethical debate which still lasts today.

quiz.question: Put these events of 1945 in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: In one month, humanity goes from the first successful nuclear test to the end of World War II in Asia.
items: Successful Trinity nuclear test
Bombing of Hiroshima
Bombing of Nagasaki and entry into the war of the USSR
Japanese surrender announced by Hirohito

title: Rosa Parks and Montgomery
description: On **December 1, 1955**, a seamstress refused to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery. Her arrest launched a **381-day** boycott and changed the civil rights movement.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What did Rosa Parks do on December 1, 1955, in Montgomery, which triggered the bus boycott?
quiz.explanation: Rosa Parks refuses to get up to give up her seat to a white passenger, which leads to her arrest and then a boycott of the buses.
options: She refuses to give up her seat to a white passenger on a bus
She organizes a demonstration in front of the Alabama Capitol
She files a complaint against her employer
She refuses to pay her bus ticket

quiz.question: What laws imposed racial separation in the American South at the time?
quiz.explanation: Jim Crow laws enforced racial separation in the South's schools, hospitals, drinking fountains, and transportation.

quiz.question: True or false: Rosa Parks is the first person to refuse to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus.
quiz.explanation: Nine months earlier, high school student Claudette Colvin, 15, had already refused to give up her place, but the activists had not put her forward.

quiz.question: Why do activists choose Rosa Parks, rather than Claudette Colvin, as the public face of the movement?
quiz.explanation: An NAACP activist trained in nonviolent resistance, Rosa Parks was considered more respectable than Colvin, then pregnant and single, to bring the fight to public opinion.
options: Her calm and respectability as a trained activist make her an ideal figure for public opinion.
She is the only one to have been arrested
She is the president of the NAACP
She is the younger of the two

quiz.question: Who is leading the Montgomery Improvement Association to organize the boycott?
quiz.explanation: Martin Luther King Jr., a young 26-year-old pastor, took the helm of the Montgomery Improvement Association and became the face of the movement.
options: Martin Luther King Jr., pastor of 26 years

quiz.question: How many days does the Montgomery bus boycott last?
quiz.explanation: The boycott lasted 381 days, from December 5, 1955 to December 21, 1956.

quiz.question: What share of Montgomery bus riders are black?
quiz.explanation: Black people make up about 75% of bus riders, which explains the massive economic impact of the boycott.

quiz.question: Which decision legally ends segregation on Alabama buses?
quiz.explanation: On November 13, 1956, the Supreme Court upheld that bus segregation in Alabama was unconstitutional.
options: A decision of the Supreme Court of November 13, 1956
An executive order from President Eisenhower
A vote by the US Congress
An agreement between King and the bus company

quiz.question: Put these events of the Montgomery boycott in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the arrest of Rosa Parks to the end of the boycott, 381 days passed between December 1955 and December 1956.
items: Arrest of Rosa Parks
Start of bus boycott
Supreme Court ruling against bus segregation
Official end of the boycott

title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
description: In October **1962**, the world spent **13 days** a hair away from nuclear war. Missiles in Cuba, fleets on alert: the Cold War reached its peak.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Why did the USSR secretly install nuclear missiles in Cuba in 1962?
quiz.explanation: Khrushchev wants to compensate for the Jupiter missiles that the Americans have installed in Italy and Turkey, very close to the USSR.
options: To restore balance in the face of American missiles already installed in Italy and Turkey
To help Cuba defend itself against an imminent invasion by the United States
To test its missiles in a tropical climate
To obtain a permanent naval base in the Caribbean

quiz.question: How did the Americans discover the Soviet missiles installed in Cuba?
quiz.explanation: On October 14, 1962, an American U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet missile ramps on Cuban soil.
options: Thanks to photos of a U-2 spy plane, October 14, 1962
Thanks to a high-ranking Soviet defector
Thanks to rumors broadcast by Radio Moscow
Thanks to a public statement by Fidel Castro

quiz.question: What solution did Kennedy choose rather than an immediate strike or an invasion of Cuba?
quiz.explanation: Kennedy chose a middle path: a naval blockade which he called "quarantine" to avoid the word "blockade", which is equivalent to a declaration of war in international law.
options: A naval blockade, which he calls “quarantine”
An immediate nuclear ultimatum to Moscow
The unilateral withdrawal of American troops from Europe

quiz.question: True or false: October 27, 1962, nicknamed “Black Saturday,” was the calmest moment of the entire crisis.
quiz.explanation: Black Saturday, on the contrary, is the most dangerous day: a U-2 is shot down and a Soviet submarine is almost ready to launch a nuclear torpedo.

quiz.question: Who refuses, on board the Soviet submarine B-59, to validate a nuclear torpedo shot?
quiz.explanation: Vasili Arkhipov, political officer aboard the B-59, said no even though two other officers had agreed to the shot.

quiz.question: How many days did the Cuban Missile Crisis last in October 1962?
quiz.explanation: The crisis lasted 13 days, from October 14 to 28, 1962, before Khrushchev announced the withdrawal of the missiles.

quiz.question: What secret clause accompanies the official resolution of the Cuban Missile Crisis?
quiz.explanation: In exchange for the withdrawal of Soviet missiles from Cuba, the Americans secretly agreed to withdraw their own missiles from Türkiye.
options: The later withdrawal of American missiles installed in Türkiye
Official recognition of the Castro regime by the United States
The immediate lifting of the American embargo on Cuba

quiz.question: What doctrine prevails after the crisis, according to which no one can win a nuclear war?
quiz.explanation: The doctrine of mutually assured destruction is required: since no one can win a nuclear war, no one should start one.

quiz.question: Put these events of the Cuban Missile Crisis in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the failure of the Bay of Pigs in 1961 to the withdrawal of the missiles in October 1962, these milestones trace the rise and then the resolution of the crisis.
items: Failed landing at the Bay of Pigs
Discovery of Soviet missiles in Cuba
Kennedy's televised speech announcing quarantine
Black Saturday: U-2 shot down and submarine about to fire
Announcement of the withdrawal of Soviet missiles

title: The Algerian War
description: For **eight years**, France fought a war of independence on land it insisted was its own. The Algerian War brought down the Fourth Republic and left lasting scars.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Why has France considered Algeria as part of its own territory for a long time?
quiz.explanation: Conquered from 1830, Algeria was divided into French departments in 1848: leaving it, for many, amounted to amputating the national territory.
options: Because it was divided into French departments in 1848
Because it gained its independence in 1848
Because it is populated only by French citizens
Because it has belonged to the UN since 1945

quiz.question: What movement triggered the insurrection on November 1, 1954, “All Saints’ Day”?
quiz.explanation: On November 1, 1954, the FLN launched around sixty attacks, marking the start of the insurrection.
options: The OAS, Organization of the Secret Army

quiz.question: True or false: France officially recognized the term “war” to designate the Algerian conflict since the 1960s.
quiz.explanation: Until 1999, the French state legally refused the word “war” and spoke of “law and order” operations.

quiz.question: What do the “special powers” ​​voted by the French Parliament in 1956 allow?
quiz.explanation: The special powers give the army police powers, with nearly 400,000 soldiers deployed to face the FLN guerrillas.
options: The army receives police powers to fight the FLN
Settlers win voting rights for Muslims
The FLN obtains a seat at the UN

quiz.question: Who led the paratroopers who dismantled the FLN networks during the Battle of Algiers in 1957?
quiz.explanation: General Jacques Massu commands the paratroopers who dismantle the networks of FLN bombers in Algiers.

quiz.question: True or false: the Battle of Algiers, in 1957, was a French military victory which caused no controversy in mainland France.
quiz.explanation: It is a military victory but a moral defeat: torture becomes a common tool, and the scandal grows in mainland France.

quiz.question: What event in May 1958 brought Charles de Gaulle back to power?
quiz.explanation: On May 13, 1958, Algiers rebelled to keep French Algeria, which provoked the return of De Gaulle and the founding of the Fifth Republic.
options: The Algiers insurrection to keep “French Algeria”

quiz.question: What did the OAS do after the failure of the generals' putsch of April 1961?
quiz.explanation: After the failure of the putsch, the OAS, Organization of the Secret Army, increased attacks to prevent any negotiations towards independence.
options: It multiplies attacks to block all negotiations
She negotiated directly with de Gaulle

quiz.question: Approximately how many pieds-noirs fled to the metropolis after Algeria's independence?
quiz.explanation: Nearly a million pied-noirs fled to the metropolis after independence, abandoning their lives in Algeria.

quiz.question: Put these events of the Algerian War in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the FLN insurrection in 1954 to the Evian Accords in 1962, these milestones retrace the eight years of the Algerian War.
items: All Saints' Day, start of the FLN insurrection
The Battle of Algiers
Charles de Gaulle's return to power
The Evian Accords

title: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu
description: From **March 13** to **May 7, 1954**, a French army besieged in a valley in northern Vietnam surrendered to the Viet Minh. The defeat ended French Indochina.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Who led the Viet Minh forces during the Battle of Dien Bien Phu?
quiz.explanation: General Võ Nguyên Giáp, a former history professor, leads the Viet-Minh forces and defeats the French army.

quiz.question: True or false: General Giáp trained at a prestigious military school before becoming a strategist.
quiz.explanation: Giáp never attended military school; he said he learned strategy by reading Napoleon's campaigns in the Hanoi library.

quiz.question: What is the name of the French operation which established the air-land base in Diên Bien Phu in November 1953?
quiz.explanation: Operation Castor installed the French air-land base in the Diên Bien Phu basin by parachute in November 1953.

quiz.question: True or false: the French general staff believed that the Viet-Minh would never be able to hoist heavy artillery in the jungle surrounding Diên Bien Phu.
quiz.explanation: This was the French calculation, but tens of thousands of porters carried cannons and ammunition on their backs to the ridges overlooking the camp.

quiz.question: Which French officer commits suicide after promising to silence the Viet Minh artillery?
quiz.explanation: Colonel Charles Piroth, in charge of the French artillery, committed suicide in the first days of the siege after the failure of his promise.

quiz.question: How many days did the siege of Dien Bien Phu last, from March 13 to May 7, 1954?
quiz.explanation: The siege lasted 55 days, from March 13 to May 7, 1954, before the French capitulation.

quiz.question: Which country refuses a massive air intervention to save the French entrenched camp?
quiz.explanation: The United States refused a massive air intervention, allowing French forces to capitulate on May 7, 1954.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Battle of Dien Bien Phu in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: Operation Castor (November 1953), the offensive of March 13, 1954, the capitulation of May 7, then the Geneva Accords (July 1954) marked the end of the Indochina War.
items: Installation of the French air-land base
Destruction of the airstrip by Viet-Minh artillery
Capitulation of the French entrenched camp
Signature of the Geneva agreements

title: The Armenian Genocide
description: Between **1915** and **1916**, the Ottoman government organized the deportation and systematic killing of much of the empire's Armenian population.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Which empire organized the extermination of a large part of its Armenian population between 1915 and 1916?
quiz.explanation: The government of the Ottoman Empire orchestrated the deportation and extermination of a large part of its Armenian population.

quiz.question: True or false: the Hamidian massacres of 1894-1896 were judged and punished by the Ottoman authorities.
quiz.explanation: These massacres, which caused 100,000 to 300,000 deaths under Sultan Abdülhamid II, remained unpunished.

quiz.question: What event of April 24, 1915, in Constantinople, marks the symbolic beginning of the genocide?
quiz.explanation: That date, now the worldwide day of commemoration, marks the arrest and then the execution of the Armenian elites of the capital.
options: The arrest then execution of more than 200 Armenian intellectuals and notables
The proclamation of the deportation law

quiz.question: What did the deportation law passed in May 1915 allow?
quiz.explanation: This law provides a legal framework for forced expulsions to the deserts of Mesopotamia, where convoys are decimated.
options: A legal framework for expulsions to the deserts of Mesopotamia
The creation of an Armenian army
The return of the Armenian exiles

quiz.question: True or false: American diplomat Henry Morgenthau described the events of 1915 as “race murder.”
quiz.explanation: Henry Morgenthau, a neutral diplomat stationed in the Ottoman Empire, used this expression to describe the massacres.

quiz.question: Who coined the word “genocide”, explicitly thinking of the Armenians?
quiz.explanation: Polish jurist Raphael Lemkin invented the legal concept of genocide with the fate of the Armenians in mind; the UN enshrined it in law in 1948.

quiz.question: What proportion of Armenians in the Ottoman Empire perished between 1915 and 1916?
quiz.explanation: About two-thirds of the empire's Armenians died during this period, depending on the course.

quiz.question: What position does present-day Turkey adopt regarding the events of 1915-1916?
quiz.explanation: Turkey recognizes suffering and massacres in the chaos of the war, but rejects the term genocide, unlike France (2001) or the United States (2021).
options: She recognizes massacres but rejects the term genocide
She denies any violence against Armenians
She issued a formal apology in 1915

quiz.question: Put these milestones of the Armenian genocide and its recognition in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four milestones range from the impunity of the first massacres (1894-1896) to the late recognition of the genocide by certain States (2001 for France).
items: Hamidian massacres under Sultan Abdülhamid II
Arrest of Armenian intellectuals in Constantinople
Deportations and mass massacres in Anatolia
Official recognition of the genocide by France

title: The creation of the UN
description: On **June 26, 1945**, **51** countries signed the Charter of the United Nations in San Francisco. Born from the ashes of the Second World War, the UN set out to spare the world the scourge of war.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: How many countries signed the United Nations Charter in San Francisco on June 26, 1945?
quiz.explanation: 51 countries signed the United Nations Charter in San Francisco on June 26, 1945.

quiz.question: Which organization, ancestor of the UN, notably failed to stop the Italian invasion of Ethiopia?
quiz.explanation: The League of Nations, without the United States and without real means of pressure, cannot stop Japan in Manchuria or Italy in Ethiopia.

quiz.question: True or false: The United States joined the League of Nations after World War I.
quiz.explanation: The American Senate, attached to isolationism, refused to join the League of Nations, despite its launch by President Wilson.

quiz.question: What is the veto power in the UN Security Council?
quiz.explanation: Each of the five permanent members of the Security Council can block a resolution using their veto power.
options: The ability of a permanent member to block a resolution
The right to vote of all Member States
The power to dissolve the General Assembly
The right to exclude a state from the UN

quiz.question: Which five countries became permanent members of the Security Council in 1945?
quiz.explanation: The five winners of 1945, the United States, the USSR, the United Kingdom, France and China, became permanent members with the right of veto.
options: United States, USSR, United Kingdom, France, China
United States, Germany, Japan, Italy, China
United Kingdom, France, Spain, Portugal, China

quiz.question: True or false: WHO action enabled the eradication of smallpox in 1980.
quiz.explanation: The World Health Organization, a UN agency, coordinated the effort that led to the eradication of smallpox in 1980.

quiz.question: How many countries are members of the UN today, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: The UN today has 193 members, compared to 51 signatories in 1945.

quiz.question: Which conference in February 1945, between Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin, shaped the structure of the UN?
quiz.explanation: The Yalta Conference, in February 1945, brought together Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin and shaped the future organization of the United Nations.

title: The birth of the EU
description: The European Union grew out of one practical idea: make war between France and Germany physically impossible by tying together coal and steel. Small steps led from **1950** to Maastricht.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What is the objective of the Schuman Declaration in 1950?
quiz.explanation: Jean Monnet and Robert Schuman propose placing Franco-German coal and steel under a common High Authority, to make war materially impossible.
options: Place Franco-German coal and steel production under a common authority
Establish the free movement of people

quiz.question: Which countries join France and Germany in the ECSC, created in 1951?
quiz.explanation: Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg (the Benelux) join France and Germany in the ECSC.

quiz.question: True or false: the ECSC is the first time that States delegate part of their sovereignty to a body that goes beyond them.
quiz.explanation: The ECSC marks a historic first: States accept that a common High Authority decides above them in a key industrial area.

quiz.question: What do the Treaties of Rome, signed on March 25, 1957, create?
quiz.explanation: The Six sign the treaties in Rome which create the European Economic Community (EEC) and Euratom, for the civil atom.
options: The euro and the European Central Bank

quiz.question: Which treaty transformed the EEC into the European Union in 1992?
quiz.explanation: The Treaty of Maastricht (1992) created the European Union, with European citizenship and economic and monetary union.

quiz.question: True or false: euro coins and notes were put into circulation as soon as the Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1992.
quiz.explanation: The euro only became a written reality in 1999, then circulated in coins and notes only from January 1, 2002.

quiz.question: When did the UK, Ireland and Denmark join the EEC?
quiz.explanation: The United Kingdom, Ireland and Denmark joined the EEC in 1973, expanding the initial small industrial circle.

quiz.question: Put these stages of European construction in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the Schuman Declaration (1950) to the ECSC (1951), then from the Treaties of Rome (1957) to Maastricht (1992), European integration advances in stages.
items: Schuman Declaration on coal and steel
Creation of the ECSC
Signing of the Treaties of Rome
Signing of the Maastricht Treaty

title: The Rwandan genocide
description: In **100 days**, between April and July **1994**, hundreds of thousands of Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed in Rwanda. The fastest genocide of the century unfolded in full view of the world.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Who fixed Hutu/Tutsi ethnicity on an identity card in 1933?
quiz.explanation: In 1933, the Belgian administration fixed ethnic affiliation on the identity card, whereas previously it was mainly social and economic.

quiz.question: True or false: before colonization, a Hutu enriched with livestock could become a Tutsi.
quiz.explanation: The distinction between Hutus and Tutsis was mainly social and economic before colonization, and could evolve with wealth in livestock.

quiz.question: What event on April 6, 1994 triggered the start of the genocide?
quiz.explanation: On April 6, 1994, the presidential plane was shot down; within the hour, the dams close and the genocide begins.
options: President Habyarimana's plane is shot down
The independence of Rwanda is proclaimed
Radio des Mille Collines is created

quiz.question: What role did Radio des Mille Collines play before and during the genocide?
quiz.explanation: Radio des Mille Collines broadcasts daily hate propaganda which prepares and accompanies the massacres.
options: She spreads hatred every day and dehumanizes the Tutsis
It is censored by the Habyarimana regime

quiz.question: True or false: the Rwandan genocide of 1994 was an explosion of spontaneous violence, without prior organization.
quiz.explanation: The massacre, carried out by neighbors, colleagues and local authorities, was the result of a planned operation, not a spontaneous explosion.

quiz.question: Why did the United States slow down any intervention in Rwanda in 1994?
quiz.explanation: Traumatized by the failure in Somalia, the United States is slowing down any intervention and even avoiding the word “genocide”.
options: They remain marked by the failure of their intervention in Somalia
They negotiate a trade agreement with Rwanda

quiz.question: Who concretely put an end to the massacres, by taking Kigali on July 4, 1994?
quiz.explanation: It was not the UN but the RPF offensive, led by Paul Kagame, which put an end to the massacres by taking Kigali.
options: The offensive of the Rwandan Patriotic Front, led by Paul Kagame
The UN mission commanded by Roméo Dallaire

quiz.question: How many days did the Rwandan genocide last, between April and July 1994?
quiz.explanation: In just 100 days, between April and July 1994, the genocide left hundreds of thousands dead.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Rwandan genocide in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the ethnic identity card of 1933 to the capture of Kigali on July 4, 1994, these milestones summarize the mechanics of the genocide and its end.
items: Fixation of ethnic identities by the Belgian colonial administration
Attack on presidential plane
Mass massacres throughout the territory
Capture of Kigali by the Rwandan Patriotic Front

title: The fall of the Berlin Wall
description: On the night of **November 9 to 10, 1989**, Berliners tore down with their bare hands the wall that had divided their city for **28 years**. A misunderstanding on live television sped up the end of the Cold War.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: How long did the Berlin Wall divide the city before it fell in 1989?
quiz.explanation: Built in 1961, the wall divided Berlin for 28 years, until its fall on the night of November 9 to 10, 1989.

quiz.question: Why was the Berlin Wall built in 1961?
quiz.explanation: Between 1949 and 1961, more than 3 million East Germans fled to the West; the wall is built to stop this bleeding.
options: To stop the massive flight of Germans from the East to the West
To prevent the arrival of refugees from the West
To protect Berlin from a Soviet invasion
To separate the American and French occupation zones

quiz.question: True or false: the East German regime officially presented the wall as an “anti-fascist protective rampart”.
quiz.explanation: The regime claimed to be keeping spies out, rather than admitting that it was about keeping its citizens out.

quiz.question: Which event of May 1989 constituted the first real breach in the Iron Curtain?
quiz.explanation: In May 1989, Hungary opened its border with Austria, providing the first real breach in the Iron Curtain.
options: The opening of the border between Hungary and Austria
The fall of the Berlin Wall
Bruce Springsteen's concert in East Berlin

quiz.question: What error by spokesperson Günter Schabowski precipitated the opening of the checkpoints on November 9, 1989?
quiz.explanation: Schabowski let go “immediately, without delay” even though the measure was not to apply until the next day, causing the influx of Berliners towards the checkpoints.
