options: It mistakenly announces that the new travel rules apply immediately
He announces the resignation of the East German government
He orders the border guards to open the wall

quiz.question: True or false: Mikhail Gorbachev chose to militarily crush the protest movements in Eastern Europe in 1989, as in 1968 in Prague.
quiz.explanation: Gorbachev, on the contrary, refuses to crush his satellites as in 1968, which allows protest movements to prosper.

quiz.question: How long is the Berlin Wall, in kilometers?
quiz.explanation: The Berlin Wall, built from 1961, extends over 155 km.

quiz.question: Put these stages in the history of the Berlin Wall in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the construction of the wall (1961) to its fall (November 9, 1989), then reunification (October 3, 1990), these milestones cover nearly three decades.
items: Construction of the wall between East and West Berlin
Opening of the border between Hungary and Austria
Fall of the Berlin Wall
Official reunification of Germany

title: Blitzkrieg
description: In **six weeks**, from **May 10** to **June 22, 1940**, the German army conquered France and the Benelux countries. This “lightning war” rewrote the art of war through sheer speed.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Who coined the term “Blitzkrieg” for the German strategy of 1940?
quiz.explanation: Blitzkrieg was never official Wehrmacht vocabulary. The Germans talked about a war of movement; Anglo-American newspapers coined the term.

quiz.question: What German idea means concentrating everything on a narrow point to break the enemy front?
quiz.explanation: Schwerpunkt is the concentration of forces on one precise point — a key idea in German mobile warfare.

quiz.question: True or false: the sirens of German Stukas had a real military use in detecting enemy positions.
quiz.explanation: These sirens, nicknamed “jericho trumpets”, had no real military use: they were only used to terrorize soldiers and civilians.

quiz.question: Which region, considered impassable by the French, was crossed by the bulk of German panzers in May 1940?
quiz.explanation: On the advice of General von Manstein, the Sichelschnitt plan brought the bulk of German panzers across the Ardennes, considered impassable.

quiz.question: How many Franco-British soldiers were evacuated during Operation Dynamo in Dunkirk?
quiz.explanation: Operation Dynamo evacuates 338,000 Franco-British soldiers to England, saving the British army.

quiz.question: True or false: the 1940 armistice was signed in the same carriage as that of the 1918 armistice, in Compiègne.
quiz.explanation: Hitler takes the wagon out of the Compiègne museum to stage his revenge, 22 years after the German capitulation of 1918.

quiz.question: In how many weeks did the German army conquer France and the Benelux in 1940?
quiz.explanation: In just six weeks, from May 10 to June 22, 1940, the German army conquered France, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg.

quiz.question: From which city did General de Gaulle launch his appeal of June 18, 1940?
quiz.explanation: On June 18, 1940, from London, General de Gaulle launched his appeal to the BBC stating that France had lost a battle, not the war.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the 1940 campaign in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the offensive of May 10 to the armistice of June 22, 1940, these stages summarize the lightning defeat of France in six weeks.
items: German offensive in the West
Panzer breakthrough at Sedan
Evacuation of Allied troops at Dunkirk
Signing of the Franco-German armistice

title: The Marshall Plan
description: In **1947** Europe lay in ruins. The United States offered massive aid to rebuild it, and to hold back communism.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Who announced the Marshall Plan in June 1947?
quiz.explanation: In June 1947, American Secretary of State George Marshall announced an unprecedented aid plan to rebuild Europe.
options: US Secretary of State George Marshall

quiz.question: What is the real strategy behind the Marshall Plan, beyond reconstruction?
quiz.explanation: Officially aid for reconstruction, the plan also aims to prevent poverty from pushing Western Europe towards communism, facing the USSR.
options: Preventing poverty from pushing Western Europe towards communism

quiz.question: True or false: Stalin accepts Marshall Plan aid for the USSR and its allied countries.
quiz.explanation: Stalin refuses the offer and forbids Poland and Czechoslovakia from accepting it, cutting the continent in two.

quiz.question: What condition did Marshall pose to the Europeans in his Harvard speech on June 5, 1947?
quiz.explanation: Marshall demanded that Europeans organize themselves around a common plan rather than receiving aid dispersed country by country.
options: They must agree on a common plan, rather than receiving scattered aid
They must repay the aid with interest
They must adopt the dollar as their currency

quiz.question: In what form does American aid mainly arrive in Europe?
quiz.explanation: The aid does not mainly consist of tickets, but of material goods: machines, coal, tractors, food.

quiz.question: True or false: in 1952, industrial production in Western Europe remained below its pre-war level.
quiz.explanation: By 1952, industrial production exceeded pre-war levels by 35%, marking the economic success of the plan.

quiz.question: How many billions of dollars did the United States send to Europe between 1948 and 1952?
quiz.explanation: Between 1948 and 1952, the United States sent approximately 13 billion dollars, or more than 150 billion today.

quiz.question: What organization are the 16 countries of Western Europe creating to distribute American aid?
quiz.explanation: The 16 countries of Western Europe come together in the OEEC, the organization responsible for distributing the funds of the Marshall Plan.

title: The Vietnam War
description: For twenty years the United States poured enormous force into Vietnam to hold back communism. It got bogged down, tore itself apart, and left without winning.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What did the 1954 Geneva Accords decide about Vietnam?
quiz.explanation: The Geneva Accords of 1954 temporarily divided Vietnam in two at the 17th parallel, with Ho Chi Minh in the North and a regime supported by Washington in the South.
options: The division of the country in two at the 17th parallel
The immediate and unified independence of Vietnam
The total withdrawal of French troops without any territorial agreement
The creation of a federation with Laos and Cambodia

quiz.question: What theory pushes Presidents Kennedy then Johnson to intervene in Vietnam?
quiz.explanation: According to this theory, if one country falls under communism, its neighbors would follow in cascade, justifying American intervention.

quiz.question: True or false: the Gulf of Tonkin incident in August 1964 served as a pretext to expand American military commitment.
quiz.explanation: This naval incident, the reality of which was privately contested by Johnson himself, served to justify military escalation from 1965.

quiz.question: What strategy did the Americans adopt without succeeding in cutting off North Vietnamese supplies?
quiz.explanation: This strategy of seeking and then destroying the enemy is not enough to break the Ho Chi Minh Trail, the northern supply route.

quiz.question: In 1969, how many American soldiers were present in Vietnam?
quiz.explanation: In 1969, approximately 543,000 American soldiers were deployed there, without succeeding in breaking North Vietnamese resistance.

quiz.question: How much of South Vietnam's forests are destroyed by defoliants like Agent Orange?
quiz.explanation: More than 80 million liters of herbicides destroyed around 20% of South Vietnam's forests.

quiz.question: What did the Tet offensive in January 1968 change in the perception of the conflict?
quiz.explanation: On the ground, the offensive failed for the North, but its televised scale in the United States contradicted the optimistic announcements from Washington.
options: It shatters the illusion of a near American victory, despite a military failure of the North
It marks the first undisputed American military victory
It provokes China's entry into the war on the side of the South
She immediately ended the fighting with an armistice.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Vietnam War in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones range from the partition of 1954 to the fall of Saigon in 1975, which sealed the reunification of the country under communism.
items: Partition of the country at the 17th parallel
Gulf of Tonkin incident
Tet Offensive
Signing of the Paris agreements
Fall of Saigon

quiz.question: Which massacre committed by American soldiers in 1968 reveals some of the war crimes of the conflict?
quiz.explanation: At My Lai, American soldiers killed Vietnamese civilians in 1968, an episode that shocked already divided American opinion.

title: The Nuremberg trials
description: Between **1945** and **1946**, **24** Nazi leaders stood trial at Nuremberg. For the first time, an international court invented crimes against humanity.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Which line ultimately prevails in judging the Nazi leaders, supported by the American jurist Robert Jackson?
quiz.explanation: Unlike the proposals of Churchill (summary executions) or Stalin (trial with a fixed verdict), the American line imposes a real adversarial trial.
options: A trial with evidence and defense rights
A trial whose verdict is written in advance

quiz.question: What new legal category did the London Statute of 1945 create for the first time?
quiz.explanation: Alongside conspiracy, crimes against peace and war crimes already known, crimes against humanity appear for the first time in international law.

quiz.question: True or false: the Nuremberg trials relied primarily on the Nazi archives themselves as evidence.
quiz.explanation: The lawyer Robert Jackson mainly uses the millions of pages of archives, photos and diaries produced by the Nazi regime itself.

quiz.question: Who dominates the dock with his arrogance, as the former head of the Luftwaffe?
quiz.explanation: Hermann Göring, former head of the German Air Force, stands out for his defiant attitude towards the judges.

quiz.question: How many defendants were tried at the Nuremberg Trials?
quiz.explanation: Twenty-four Nazi leaders representing the regime apparatus are tried before the international tribunal.

quiz.question: What do the Nuremberg Principles say about obeying orders?
quiz.explanation: The court affirms that individual responsibility takes precedence: following orders does not constitute a valid excuse for a crime.
options: Obeying a superior does not absolve you of a crime
Obeying a superior totally exempts you from responsibility
Only heads of state can be judged
Written orders are the only valid proof

quiz.question: True or false: all 24 defendants from the Nuremberg trials were sentenced to death.
quiz.explanation: The verdict distinguishes individual responsibilities: 12 death sentences, 3 life sentences, 4 prison sentences and 3 acquittals.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Nuremberg Trials and its legacy in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the London Statute in August 1945 to the creation of the International Criminal Court in 2002, Nuremberg opens the way to permanent international justice.
items: Signing of the London Statute
Opening of the trial before the international tribunal
Pronouncement of the final verdict
Creation of the International Criminal Court

quiz.question: What limitations have been criticized for the Nuremberg trials, concerning crimes committed by the Allies themselves?
quiz.explanation: The Katyn massacre, where Polish officers were killed by the Soviets in 1940, was never tried, which fueled the idea of ​​variable geometry justice.
options: The lack of judgment on the Katyn massacre, committed by the Soviets
The absence of any documentary evidence
Refusal to appoint an American judge

title: Decolonization: an overview
description: Between **1945** and **1975**, more than **80** countries won their independence. The European empires collapsed and the map of the world changed.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: Which 1941 text, signed by Roosevelt and Churchill, is reinterpreted by independence movements to claim their sovereignty?
quiz.explanation: Although Churchill wanted to limit its scope to Europe, African and Asian leaders seized on this promise of the right of peoples to choose their government.
options: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights

quiz.question: True or false: the United Kingdom generally negotiates the independence of its colonies to maintain influence via the Commonwealth.
quiz.explanation: Unlike France, the United Kingdom favors a negotiated transition while maintaining links via the Commonwealth, a club of former colonies.

quiz.question: Which country became the first British colony in independent sub-Saharan Africa in 1957, under the leadership of Kwame Nkrumah?
quiz.explanation: Kwame Nkrumah gained sovereignty over Ghana in 1957, paving the way for African independence.

quiz.question: Which French colonial war caused the fall of the Fourth Republic in 1958?
quiz.explanation: The Algerian War (1954-1962), particularly violent, caused the political crisis which put an end to the Fourth Republic.

quiz.question: How many French colonies became sovereign in 1960, “the year of Africa”?
quiz.explanation: In 1960, fourteen French colonies gained independence in a single year, an unprecedented movement.

quiz.question: What happens to Patrice Lumumba, first Prime Minister of independent Congo?
quiz.explanation: Belgium's hasty departure from the Congo led to political chaos and the assassination of Lumumba.
options: He is assassinated after a hasty Belgian departure which leads to chaos
He peacefully negotiates the maintenance of Belgium in power
He becomes the first president of the African Union
He founded the non-aligned movement in Bandung

quiz.question: What principle do the 29 countries gathered at the Bandung Conference in 1955 defend?
quiz.explanation: Brought together for the first time, these Asian and African countries advocate non-alignment rather than an automatic choice between Washington and Moscow.
options: Non-alignment, refusing to automatically choose a Cold War side
Collective membership in the Soviet camp
The creation of a common African and Asian currency
The maintenance of colonial empires in a federal form

quiz.question: True or false: the term “Third World” was coined by French demographer Alfred Sauvy in 1952.
quiz.explanation: Alfred Sauvy invented this term in 1952, by analogy with the Third Estate of 1789.

quiz.question: Put these stages of decolonization in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones range from Indian independence in 1947 to the end of the Iberian empires in 1975, which ended the wave of decolonization.
items: Independence of India and Pakistan
Bandung Conference
Wave of French-speaking independence in Africa
End of the Algerian War
Independence of the Portuguese colonies

title: Apartheid and Mandela
description: For **46** years South Africa organized racial segregation by law. **Nelson Mandela**, after **27** years in prison, helped the country leave it behind without a civil war.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What does the word "apartheid" mean in Afrikaans?
quiz.explanation: “Apartheid” means “separation” in Afrikaans, a name which sums up the principle of the system established in 1948.

quiz.question: What role do the Bantustans play in the apartheid system?
quiz.explanation: Supposed to be “national centers”, the bantustans cover only 13% of the territory and mainly serve to strip black people of their South African citizenship.
options: Remove South African citizenship from black people by confining them to small reserves
Offer real economic autonomy to black populations
Guarantee the right to vote for populations classified as Métis
Create free trade zones open to all

quiz.question: True or false: Nelson Mandela first believed in non-violence before joining the armed struggle.
quiz.explanation: Mandela initially adhered to non-violence, before changing strategy after the Sharpeville massacre in 1960.

quiz.question: What happened during the Sharpeville massacre in March 1960?
quiz.explanation: The police opened fire on unarmed demonstrators opposed to the pass system, killing 69 people, which pushed the ANC towards armed struggle.
options: Police shoot unarmed crowd protesting passes
South African army invades neighboring country
Mandela is arrested during a peaceful demonstration

quiz.question: How many years did Nelson Mandela spend in captivity before his release?
quiz.explanation: Arrested in 1962 and sentenced to life in 1964, Mandela was released after 27 years in prison in February 1990.

quiz.question: Which South African president, who came to power in 1989, initiated the end of apartheid?
quiz.explanation: De Klerk understands that the survival of the country requires the end of apartheid and begins negotiations with Mandela.

quiz.question: With what percentage of the votes was Nelson Mandela elected president in April 1994?
quiz.explanation: In the first multiracial elections, the ANC won and Mandela became president with 62.6% of the vote.

quiz.question: What principle does the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, led by Desmond Tutu, propose?
quiz.explanation: This transitional justice offers amnesty in exchange for public confessions, so the truth can come out without tearing the country apart.
options: Amnesty in exchange for public confessions, to learn what happened to the victims
The systematic execution of former apartheid officials
An international trial for all white leaders

quiz.question: Put these stages of apartheid and its fall in chronological order.

Sharpeville Massacre

Multiracial elections and the election of Mandela

title: The Cultural Revolution in China

subject: histoire

quiz.question: What failure pushed Mao to want to regain power by launching the Cultural Revolution?
quiz.explanation: The Great Leap Forward (1958-1962) caused a catastrophic famine which shook the prestige of Mao, sidelined by more pragmatic leaders.
options: The failure of the Great Leap Forward, marked by famine and millions of deaths
The loss of Taiwan to the Nationalists
The failure of the Geneva agreements on Indochina

quiz.question: What does the Dazibao “Bombard the Headquarters”, published by Mao in 1966, denounce?
quiz.explanation: This wall poster marks the launch of the Cultural Revolution: Mao declares war on his own administration.
options: The economic policy of the Western powers
Lack of discipline in the People's Army

quiz.question: What mission did Mao entrust to the Red Guards, made up of millions of high school and university students?

Rebuilding infrastructure destroyed by the civil war

quiz.question: True or false: from 1967, the different Red Guard factions began to clash with each other.

quiz.question: How many young urban people were sent to “re-educate” in the countryside during the Cultural Revolution?

quiz.question: Who made up the “Gang of Four,” a radical group that fought for power at the end of the Cultural Revolution?

quiz.question: What human toll is estimated for the Cultural Revolution?

An assessment that remains completely unknown

Spike in violence between Red Guard factions
Death of Mao and arrest of the Gang of Four
Deng Xiaoping's economic reforms

title: The Holocaust: the mechanics of a genocide
description: Between **1941** and **1945**, the Nazi regime organized the murder of six million Jews. The Holocaust was not a sudden burst of hatred. It was a process run by a state.
subject: histoire

quiz.question: What does the word “Shoah” mean in Hebrew?
quiz.explanation: “Shoah” means “catastrophe” in Hebrew, a term chosen to designate this genocide.

quiz.question: What did the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 do to German Jews?
quiz.explanation: These 1935 laws deprived German Jews of citizenship and prohibited intermarriage, a first legal step toward exclusion.
options: Loss of citizenship and ban on mixed unions
The obligation to wear a yellow star

quiz.question: True or false: After the invasion of Poland in 1939, the Nazis locked Jews in ghettos like those in Warsaw and Łódź.
quiz.explanation: Ghettoization confined Jewish populations in closed neighborhoods, causing famine and epidemics even before the industrial killing.

quiz.question: Which mobile units of the SS murdered communists and Jewish populations after the invasion of the USSR in 1941?
quiz.explanation: These mobile SS commandos followed the advance of the German army and killed nearly 1.5 million people in approximately 18 months.

quiz.question: Why did the Nazi regime seek a system different from mass shootings like at Babi Yar?
quiz.explanation: Mass shootings, like that of Babi Yar where 33,771 Jews were killed in two days, push the regime towards a more anonymous system of extermination.
options: This method is considered too slow, too visible and too demanding for the performers.
The shootings were not killing enough victims at once
The Allies threatened to bomb the shooting sites
The cost of ammunition was becoming too high for the army

quiz.question: What did the Wannsee conference decide in January 1942?
quiz.explanation: The principle of extermination is already established; the conference mainly organizes the logistics of deportation on a continent-wide scale.
options: The logistical organization of the deportation of all the Jews of Europe
The very principle of extermination, decided for the first time
An end to the persecution of the Jews in exchange for a separate peace
The creation of the State of Israel after the war

quiz.question: How many senior Nazi officials attended the Wannsee Conference?
quiz.explanation: Fifteen senior Nazi officials meet near Berlin to coordinate the deportation of Europe's Jews.

quiz.question: What proportion of the pre-war European Jewish population disappeared in the Holocaust?
quiz.explanation: Of approximately 9 million pre-war European Jews, approximately two-thirds disappeared in the Holocaust.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Holocaust in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From legal exclusion in 1935 to the liberation of the camps in 1945, these milestones show a state process that worsens in stages.
items: Adoption of the Nuremberg Laws excluding German Jews
Mass shootings by Einsatzgruppen in the East
Administrative coordination of the deportation to Wannsee
Liberation of the camps by the Allies

quiz.question: How many planes did Al-Qaeda members hijack on September 11, 2001?
quiz.explanation: Nineteen members of Al Qaeda hijack four planes that day, two of which hit the World Trade Center.

quiz.question: Why did Osama bin Laden decide to strike the West after the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan?

quiz.question: What happens to the fourth hijacked plane, United 93?

quiz.question: How many people died in the attacks of September 11, 2001?

quiz.question: Where and when was Osama bin Laden killed?

title: Athenian democracy
description: In the 5th century BC, Athens invented a system where citizens governed directly. Selection by lot, an equal right to speak, and exclusion on a massive scale.

quiz.question: What did Solon, elected in 594 BC, do to open the city of Athens?
quiz.explanation: Solon puts an end to debt slavery and allows access to magistracy according to wealth, rather than by birth alone.
options: He abolishes debt slavery and opens magistrates according to fortune
He establishes the drawing of lots for all magistrates
He creates the Ecclesia, an assembly of all citizens
It proclaims total equality between men and women

quiz.question: What institution did Cleisthenes create around 508-507 BC to break the power of the clans?
quiz.explanation: By creating ten mixed tribes and the Boulé, Cleisthenes weakened traditional clan solidarity in favor of a new civic organization.
options: La Boulé, Council of Five Hundred drawn by lot
The Ecclesia, general assembly of citizens
Ostracism, temporary exile of the powerful

quiz.question: What does Isegoria guarantee in Athenian democracy under Pericles?
quiz.explanation: Isegoria ensures that every citizen has the same right to speak before the assembly, a pillar of direct democracy.
options: The right to vote for women

quiz.question: What is the purpose of Misthos, a daily allowance established in Athens?
quiz.explanation: Without this compensation, poor citizens would not have been able to afford to abandon their work to participate in public life.
options: Allow the poorest citizens to sit in institutions
Paying the soldiers of the Athenian army
Finance the construction of the Parthenon
Rewarding the winners of the Olympic Games

quiz.question: True or false: women, slaves and metics have the right to vote in the Ecclesia.
quiz.explanation: Only male citizens, between 30,000 and 50,000 out of approximately 300,000 inhabitants, have the right to vote.

quiz.question: Approximately how many times a year does the Ecclesia, the assembly of citizens, meet under Pericles?
quiz.explanation: The Ecclesia meets about 40 times a year on Pnyx Hill to vote on laws, war, peace and the budget.

quiz.question: How are the 6,000 jurors of Helia, the Athenian popular court, appointed?

quiz.explanation: Plato, marked by the condemnation of his master Socrates in 399 BC, criticizes a democracy where emotion and opinion can prevail over reason.

He considers it the perfect and untouchable political regime
He proposes to extend it to all Greek cities
He praised it in several public speeches

quiz.question: Put these reforms and events in Athenian democracy in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From Solon to the death of Socrates, these milestones cover nearly two centuries of construction, then questioning, of Athenian democracy.
items: Solon's Reforms
Cleisthenes' reforms
Apogee under Pericles
Death of Socrates

title: The American Civil War

quiz.question: What caused the election of Abraham Lincoln in November 1860?
quiz.explanation: Lincoln, a Republican opposed to the expansion of slavery, was elected without a single Southern vote, triggering the secession of seven states.
options: The secession of seven Southern States which founded the Confederacy
The immediate signing of a peace treaty with the South
The immediate abolition of slavery throughout the country
A military alliance between North and South

quiz.question: What economy was the South primarily based on before the Civil War?
quiz.explanation: The South remained a rural economy, based on the production of cotton by a workforce of 4 million slaves.
options: Cotton produced by around 4 million slaves
The textile industry employing wage workers

quiz.question: True or false: the Battle of Antietam, in September 1862, remains the bloodiest day in American military history.
quiz.explanation: With approximately 23,000 casualties in twelve hours, Antietam remains the deadliest day in United States military history.

quiz.question: What changed in the Emancipation Proclamation signed by Lincoln on January 1, 1863?
quiz.explanation: By freeing the rebel states' slaves, Lincoln transformed the war for the Union into a war for freedom, which closed the door to European support for the South.

She immediately ends the war with an armistice

quiz.question: How many people died in total during the Civil War?
quiz.explanation: The Civil War left more than 620,000 dead, a death toll that remains the heaviest in American military history.

quiz.question: Which Confederate general surrendered at Appomattox on April 9, 1865, marking the end of the fighting?
quiz.explanation: Robert E. Lee, the leading Confederate general, surrenders to Ulysses Grant at Appomattox, ending the war.

quiz.question: True or false: Abraham Lincoln was assassinated before Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox.

quiz.question: What did the 13th Amendment, adopted in December 1865, do?

He grants women the right to vote

Bombing of Fort Sumter
Emancipation Proclamation

title: Why is the sky blue?
description: Looking at a blue sky is so ordinary that we forget to ask why. The answer lies in the light of the Sun and in the air we look through to see it.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Why does the sky seem blue to us?
quiz.explanation: Short waves like blue are much more dispersed by air molecules than long waves like red: this is Rayleigh scattering.
options: Air molecules scatter blue light much more than red light
The Sun only emits blue light
The atmosphere itself is tinged with blue
Our eyes artificially add blue to what we look at

quiz.question: True or false: on the Moon, in broad daylight, the sky appears black.
quiz.explanation: Without air to disperse the light, there is nothing to color the lunar sky: it remains black even in broad daylight.

quiz.question: Approximately how many times more is blue light scattered than red light by the atmosphere?
quiz.explanation: According to Rayleigh scattering, blue is scattered about 9 times more than red by air molecules.

quiz.question: Who mathematically formulated this diffusion phenomenon in 1871?
quiz.explanation: The British physicist Lord Rayleigh described in 1871 how air molecules disperse colors differently depending on their wavelength.

quiz.question: Why isn't the sky purple, even though purple is even more scattered than blue?
quiz.explanation: The Sun sends more blue light than violet, and our eye cones are more sensitive to blue: the brain therefore perceives a blue sky.
options: The Sun emits more blue and our eyes are more sensitive to it
Violet is totally absorbed by ozone
Violet never passes through the atmosphere
There is no purple in the light of the Sun

quiz.question: True or false: at sunset, light passes through a greater thickness of air than at noon.
quiz.explanation: When the Sun is low, its rays pass through a much longer layer of air, which disperses all the blue and allows only red and orange to pass through.

quiz.question: What is the dominant color of the sky on Mars during the day, unlike Earth?
quiz.explanation: On Mars, dust rich in iron oxide disperses light differently than on Earth: the sky is pink during the day, but the sunsets are blue.
options: Black, because Mars has no atmosphere

quiz.question: True or false: it is mainly the nitrogen and oxygen molecules in the air that disperse the Sun's light.
quiz.explanation: The air is filled with tiny gas molecules, especially nitrogen and oxygen, which scatter light in all directions.

title: Why do we dream?
description: Every night you dream for about two hours. Most of those dreams are gone the moment you wake. Here is what science understands about the mystery today.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: During which phase of sleep are most long and narrative dreams born?
quiz.explanation: It is during paradoxical sleep, where the brain is almost as active as it is awake, that long and narrative dreams are especially born.

quiz.question: True or false: During REM sleep, the body is paralyzed while the brain is almost as active as it is awake.
quiz.explanation: REM sleep is a phase where the brain is highly activated while the body remains paralyzed, preventing the dream from physically playing out.

quiz.question: Why do we forget most of our dreams so quickly after waking up?
quiz.explanation: During paradoxical sleep, the level of noradrenaline drops, which leaves the dream in a very fragile memory, quickly overwritten by the stimulations of waking up.
options: Norepinephrine levels drop during REM sleep, which weakens memory
The brain voluntarily erases unnecessary dreams
Dreams are never recorded in memory
We sleep less soundly at the end of the night

quiz.question: Approximately how many hours do we spend dreaming each night?
quiz.explanation: We dream about two hours each night, which represents almost six years of our entire life.

quiz.question: What is the best way to remember a dream?
quiz.explanation: The memory of the dream is very fragile: as soon as we move or expose ourselves to the light and thoughts of the day, it fades, so it must be noted immediately.
options: Write it down right away when you wake up, before even moving
Close your eyes tightly while concentrating
Drink a large glass of water
Wait until the evening to think about it

quiz.question: According to current research ideas, what could dreaming be used for?
quiz.explanation: Three avenues dominate today: sorting out memory, training for danger without real risk, and digesting the strong emotions of the day.
options: Sorting out memory, training for danger and digesting emotions
Coming to a complete rest without any brain activity

quiz.question: What is a lucid dream?
quiz.explanation: In a lucid dream, we become aware that we are dreaming while we are still asleep, which sometimes allows us to influence the dream.
options: A dream where you realize you are dreaming while remaining asleep
A dream that you remember perfectly when you wake up
A dream caused by a sleeping pill
A dream that only lasts a few seconds

quiz.question: Which area of ​​the brain reactivates a little during a lucid dream?
quiz.explanation: The prefrontal cortex, involved in logic and self-reflection, turns back on a little during a lucid dream, allowing one to realize that one is dreaming.
options: The prefrontal cortex, linked to logic and self-reflection

title: Why does ice float?
description: Ice floats on water. It looks perfectly normal, but it is in fact very rare. And lucky for life on Earth.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Why does ice float on liquid water?
quiz.explanation: As it solidifies, water forms a more airy hexagonal network that leaves more space between the molecules, making it less dense than liquid water.
options: It is less dense, because its molecular network leaves more void
The air trapped in the ice makes it lighter
The salt in the water pushes it upwards

quiz.question: True or false: For most substances, the solid is denser than the liquid and sinks.
quiz.explanation: Water is an exception: unlike most substances, its solid, ice, is less dense than its liquid.

quiz.question: What is the shape of the water molecule that explains this particular behavior?
quiz.explanation: The water molecule forms a V shape, which distributes electrical charges unevenly and creates hydrogen bonds between neighboring molecules.
options: A V, with one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms

quiz.question: What can happen if you put a full bottle of water in the freezer?
quiz.explanation: Since ice takes up more volume than liquid water, a full bottle can burst when it freezes.
options: It can burst because ice takes up more volume than liquid water
It becomes lighter without changing volume

quiz.question: At what temperature, in degrees Celsius, does water solidify?
quiz.explanation: Water solidifies around 0°C, forming a hexagonal network that is less dense than liquid water.

quiz.question: Why is it vital that ice floats rather than sinks into lakes?
quiz.explanation: Surface ice insulates the water below, which can stay around 4°C, enough for fish and aquatic plants to survive the winter.
options: It forms an insulating cover that allows the liquid water underneath to remain warm enough for aquatic life
It prevents any evaporation from the lake
It directly heats the bottom of the lake
It blocks the surrounding sea currents

quiz.question: Around what temperature, in degrees Celsius, can liquid water remain under the ice of a frozen lake?
quiz.explanation: Under the insulating ice, liquid water can stay around 4°C, a sufficient temperature for aquatic life to survive.

quiz.question: What is the climatic effect of the melting of the white ice pack?
quiz.explanation: White ice reflects sunlight back into space; if it disappears, the dark ocean absorbs more heat and accelerates warming.
options: Dark ocean absorbs more heat, speeding up warming
This cools the planet because there is more liquid water
It has no effect on the climate
This only increases the amount of salt in the oceans

title: Why is seawater salty?
description: A liter of seawater holds about 35 grams of salt. That salt has been building up for billions of years. Here is where it comes from.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Where does most of the salt in the oceans come from?
quiz.explanation: Slightly acidic rain erodes rocks, and rivers carry dissolved minerals, especially sodium and chlorine, to the sea.
options: From the erosion of rocks on the continents, transported by rivers
Rain that contains salt as soon as it is formed
Spray falling directly into the sea

quiz.question: Why are the rivers that carry salt to the sea not salty themselves?
quiz.explanation: In rivers, the salt remains very diluted and the water is constantly renewed, unlike in the ocean where it accumulates.
options: The salt is very diluted and the water is constantly renewed
They don't actually contain any minerals
Salt settles to the bottom before reaching the sea
Freshwater fish absorb all the salt

quiz.question: Why does salt build up in the ocean over time?
quiz.explanation: Under the influence of the Sun, seawater evaporates, leaving salt behind, which has been accumulating for billions of years.
options: The water evaporates and returns to the sky, but the salt remains
Salt is produced directly by the waves
Salt comes only from underwater volcanoes
Fish release salt into the water

quiz.question: Approximately how many grams of salt are in a liter of sea water?
quiz.explanation: A liter of seawater contains on average around 35 grams of salt.

quiz.question: What happens when surface water freezes at the poles?
quiz.explanation: When surface water freezes, it releases some of its salt into the surrounding liquid water, which becomes denser and sinks to the bottom.
options: The salt is partly released into the surrounding liquid water, which becomes denser and sinks
The salt evaporates with the ice that forms
The surrounding water immediately becomes soft
The salt dissolves completely inside the ice

quiz.question: True or false: this movement of dense salt water sinking at the poles helps drive large ocean currents.
quiz.explanation: Dense salt water that sinks at the poles helps drive the great ocean currents, which carry heat and nutrients around the globe.

quiz.question: Why is salinity not the same everywhere in the oceans?
quiz.explanation: Near the equator, strong evaporation concentrates the salt, while near rivers or melting ice the water is fresher.
options: It depends on local evaporation and fresh water inputs, such as rivers or melting ice.
It only depends on the depth of the water
It is the same everywhere, only the temperature changes
It depends on the color of the water there.

quiz.question: How much of the planet's surface is covered by oceans?
quiz.explanation: Oceans cover more than 70% of the Earth's surface.

title: Why are there seasons?
description: The seasons do not come from Earth being closer to or farther from the Sun. The real cause is the tilt of Earth's axis.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What is the real cause of the seasons?
quiz.explanation: The seasons come from the tilt of the earth's axis, which means that a hemisphere receives sunlight more or less directly depending on the time of year.
options: The tilt of the Earth's axis of rotation
The changing distance between Earth and the Sun
The speed of rotation of the Earth on itself

quiz.question: True or false: it is hotter in summer because the Earth is closer to the Sun.
quiz.explanation: This is false: in January, the Earth is even a little closer to the Sun than in July, even though it is winter in the northern hemisphere.

quiz.question: How many degrees is the Earth's axis tilted relative to its orbit?
quiz.explanation: The Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees from its orbit, which causes the seasons.

quiz.question: Why is it warmer when one hemisphere tilts toward the Sun?
quiz.explanation: When a hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, the days lengthen and the rays strike the ground more directly, which concentrates the energy received.
options: The days are longer and the rays arrive more directly, concentrating the energy
The Sun gets bigger this time of year
The atmosphere becomes finer in this place
The Earth spins faster on its axis

quiz.question: What does the fact that in January the Earth is closer to the Sun than in July prove, even though it is winter in the northern hemisphere?
quiz.explanation: This difference in distance clearly shows that it is not this which determines the seasons, but the inclination of the earth's axis.
options: That the distance from the Sun does not explain the seasons
That the Sun is weaker in January
That the southern hemisphere receives all the heat from the Earth
That the seasons are actually random

quiz.question: What happens near the equator, where the Earth's tilt does little to change day length?
quiz.explanation: Near the equator, day length changes little all year round, giving dry and wet seasons rather than four true seasons.
options: There are not really four seasons, but drier and wetter periods
There is a perpetual summer without any winter
Days last twice as long there as elsewhere
The Sun is never visible there

quiz.question: What would happen if the Earth's axis was not tilted at all?
quiz.explanation: Without tilt, each location would receive a roughly constant amount of sunlight all year round, erasing the seasons.
options: Each place would receive roughly the same amount of sunlight all year round, with no real summer or winter
The seasons would be twice as marked as today
The Earth would no longer revolve around the Sun
Days and nights would disappear completely

quiz.question: At the poles, what is the extreme effect of the Earth's tilt?
quiz.explanation: At the poles, the tilt of the Earth produces an extreme effect: several months of continuous day in summer and several months of night in winter.
options: Several months of continuous day in summer, several months of night in winter
A reversal of the Earth's magnetic field
One identical season all year round

title: How do planes fly?
description: A plane weighing several hundred tons flies. It is not magic: it comes down to the shape of a wing, speed, and forces that balance out.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What are the four main forces that act on an airplane in flight?
quiz.explanation: An airplane in flight experiences four main forces: forward thrust, braking drag, downward weight, and upward lift.

quiz.question: Why does wing shape create lift?
quiz.explanation: The domed profile of the wing accelerates the air passing over it, which lowers its pressure and creates a pressure difference that lifts the wing.
options: The air passes faster above the wing, which lowers the pressure compared to below
The wing is magnetized by the ground
The engine blows air directly under the wing
The wing heats the air passing through it

quiz.question: True or false: an airplane flies because it is lighter than air, like a helium balloon.
quiz.explanation: An airplane is much denser than air: it flies because it forces the air to carry it, thanks to its speed and the shape of its wings.

quiz.question: Why does a plane need a long runway to take off?
quiz.explanation: Without enough speed, the air passing over the wing does not create enough lift; the long runway allows the engines to accelerate the plane sufficiently.
options: You must achieve sufficient speed to create enough lift
To give passengers time to settle in
To cool the engines before flight

quiz.question: How does a plane turn sideways?
quiz.explanation: The ailerons, movable parts of the wings, allow the plane to be tilted sideways to turn it.
options: By tilting the plane using the ailerons, movable parts of the wings
By stopping one of the two engines
By changing the shape of the fuselage

quiz.question: What do the flaps that extend from the wing do when landing?
quiz.explanation: Flaps increase the wing's lift, allowing the plane to stay airborne even when slowing down for landing.
options: They increase lift at low speeds
They directly brake the plane on the runway
They reduce the weight of the plane

quiz.question: What is the main difference between a bird and a plane when it comes to moving through the air?
quiz.explanation: Both the wings of the bird and the plane create lift, but the bird flaps its wings to move forward while the plane uses its engines.
options: The bird flaps its wings to move forward, the plane moves forward thanks to its engines
The bird does not need lift to fly
The plane has no wings at all
The bird always flies faster than a plane

quiz.question: In cruise flight, what happens when the plane moves at an approximately constant speed?
quiz.explanation: When cruising, the lift exactly compensates for the weight and the thrust of the engines compensates for the drag, which maintains a stable speed.
options: Lift balances weight, and thrust balances drag
The weight of the plane becomes zero

title: Why do we yawn?
description: Everyone yawns: humans, dogs, sometimes even unborn babies. It is probably not about running short of oxygen. Here are the strongest leads.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Why do we yawn, according to the most solid current explanations?
quiz.explanation: The strongest idea today is that yawning helps regulate brain temperature, making it somewhat ventilate and cool.
options: To fill the blood with oxygen
To stretch only the neck muscles

quiz.question: True or false: Experiments have shown that increasing oxygen in the air does not prevent yawning.
quiz.explanation: Experiments have shown that neither more oxygen nor less carbon dioxide prevents yawning, ruling out the idea of ​​simple lack of air.

quiz.question: Why is yawning contagious in humans?
quiz.explanation: Seeing or hearing someone yawn activates circuits related to empathy and mirror neurons, which in turn triggers a yawn.
options: It affects empathy and circuits linked to mirror neurons
It is caused by a lack of shared air in the room
It is transmitted only by the sound of breathing
It's not really contagious, it's a coincidence

quiz.question: From approximately what week of pregnancy does a fetus start to yawn?
quiz.explanation: Fetuses yawn from around the eleventh week of pregnancy, long before they breathe air.

quiz.question: Why does the fetus yawn prove that it is not for “lack of oxygen”?
quiz.explanation: The fetus yawns even though its lungs are not yet breathing air, showing that yawning is not related to a lack of oxygen.
options: Because at this point his lungs aren't breathing air yet
Because the fetus does not yet have a brain
Because the fetus sleeps all the time
Because the fetus is not moving yet

quiz.question: True or false: young children are very susceptible to contagious yawning, from birth.
quiz.explanation: Young children yawn little by contagion: this sensitivity arrives later, at the same time as certain social skills.

quiz.question: In what other situations, besides fatigue, do we yawn often?
quiz.explanation: We also yawn just before a test or when we are bored while wanting to stay focused, which could help us stay alert.
options: Right before a test, or while bored while trying to stay focused
Only after eating a large meal

quiz.question: What could help develop yawning in the fetus, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: In the fetus, yawning could contribute to the development of jaw and facial muscles.
options: The muscles of the jaw and face

title: How does memory work?
description: Memory is not a camera. Every recollection is rebuilt. Here is how the brain encodes, stores, and sometimes invents.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: How does the brain act when we remember something?
quiz.explanation: Unlike a hard drive, the brain actively reconstructs a scene with each recall, making memory powerful but fallible.
options: It actively reconstructs a scene, rather than replaying it as an untouched recording
It replays a file stored intact, such as a hard drive
He projects a frozen image from childhood
It copies the memory from another area of ​​the brain without modifying it

quiz.question: What is the difference between working memory and long-term memory?
quiz.explanation: Working memory keeps information in mind for a few seconds, such as a telephone number, while long-term memory retains facts and know-how for a long time.
options: Working memory retains information for a few seconds and is limited, long-term memory retains facts and know-how for a long time
They are both found only in the hippocampus
Working memory lasts a lifetime, unlike long-term memory
There is actually only one type of memory

quiz.question: Which brain structure plays a key role in forming new memories of events?
quiz.explanation: The hippocampus, a deep structure in the brain, helps consolidate new memories of events.

quiz.question: True or false: sleep helps consolidate what we learned during the day.
quiz.explanation: Certain phases of sleep help consolidate the day's learning, making revising and then sleeping often more effective than revising all night.

quiz.question: What does Donald Hebb's rule, “what lights together, sticks together” mean?
quiz.explanation: According to Hebb's rule, when neurons fire at the same time, their connections strengthen, which builds memory.
options: Neurons that fire together tend to connect more strongly
The most recent memories always erase the oldest
The brain can only remember one piece of information at a time
The two hemispheres of the brain never communicate with each other

quiz.question: What happens when we recall a memory?
quiz.explanation: Recalling a memory makes it temporarily malleable: details from the present can slip into it before it is stored again.
options: It becomes temporarily malleable and can be modified with details of the present
It remains perfectly frozen and intact, like the first time
It is automatically removed from the brain
It becomes impossible to find a second time

quiz.question: True or false: we can have false memories, that is to say scenes that we believe to be true but which never took place as we tell them.
quiz.explanation: The brain can create false memories, scenes that are believed to be true but which never happened, or not exactly as they are told.

quiz.question: Why is forgetting not always a failure?
quiz.explanation: Without forgetting, we would be saturated with useless details: forgetting, on the contrary, helps to generalize, decide and keep the essentials.
options: It helps to generalize, decide and keep the essential rather than being saturated with unnecessary details
It consistently proves that the brain is damaged

title: Why do we get chills?
description: Cold, fear, music: chills have several causes. They all run through the nervous system, but not for the same reasons.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Which area of ​​the brain acts as a thermostat when the skin detects cold?
quiz.explanation: When the skin detects cold, it alerts the hypothalamus, an area of ​​the brain that acts as a body thermostat.

quiz.question: Why do cold shivers produce heat?
quiz.explanation: Shivering comes from rapid, repeated muscle contractions, which produce heat to warm the body.
options: Muscles contract very quickly and repeatedly
The skin directly absorbs heat from the air
The heart stops for a few seconds

quiz.question: True or false: goosebumps come from an old reflex which served to raise the hairs to better insulate from the cold.
quiz.explanation: Goosebumps are an old reflex that raises the hairs to better insulate the body, even if it no longer serves much purpose in humans with little hair.

quiz.question: What substance does the sympathetic nervous system release when faced with a threat?
quiz.explanation: When faced with a threat, the sympathetic nervous system releases adrenaline, which tenses the muscles and accelerates the heart.

quiz.question: Why can you get goosebumps while watching a horror film, cozy on your couch?
quiz.explanation: The sympathetic nervous system reacts to the fear felt while watching the film, even without real danger, which triggers goosebumps.
options: The alert nervous system reacts to fear, as if there were a real threat
The room temperature always drops during a scary movie
This is only a reaction to the loud noise in the film
The body chemically confuses film and reality

quiz.question: What pleasure-related substance is associated with the thrills felt while listening to upsetting music?
quiz.explanation: Musical thrills activate the brain's reward circuit, with dopamine, a substance linked to pleasure.

quiz.question: True or false: the shivers of cold, fear and music all go through the same mechanism, with the same goal.
quiz.explanation: These shivers share the word but not the mechanism: cold produces heat, fear prepares us to react, music touches emotional pleasure.

quiz.question: When should chills cause concern and merit medical advice?
quiz.explanation: Chills accompanied by high fever, or constant chills without a clear cause, may signal a problem and merit medical attention.
options: Chills with a high fever, or constant chills for no clear reason
Every time we shiver while listening to music
Every time we feel cold in winter
As soon as we watch a moving film

title: How does soap kill viruses?
description: Soap is not magic. It attacks the fatty shell of certain viruses and pulls them off your skin. Here is why 20 seconds matter.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Why is soap particularly effective against viruses like coronaviruses or the flu?
quiz.explanation: Coronaviruses and the flu virus have an envelope made of fat, which soap is particularly effective at destroying.
options: These viruses have a fatty envelope that soap destroys
Soap is acidic and directly burns the virus
Soap stops the virus from breathing

quiz.question: What are soap molecules called “surfactants”?
quiz.explanation: Soap surfactants have a head that likes water and a tail that clings to grease, allowing them to tear apart the coating of viruses.
options: Molecules with a water-loving head and a fat-loving tail
Molecules that repel both water and fat

quiz.question: True or false: “naked” viruses, without a fatty envelope, are more resistant to soap than enveloped viruses.
quiz.explanation: Without a fatty envelope to attack, naked viruses are more resistant to soap and alcohol than enveloped viruses.

quiz.question: How does soap actually deactivate an enveloped virus?
quiz.explanation: The fatty tail of the soap molecules dig into the virus's coat and tear it apart, deactivating it before the water washes away the debris.
options: Its fatty tail sinks into the virus envelope and tears it
It changes the color of the virus
It only neutralizes its genetic material

quiz.question: How many seconds of scrubbing are generally recommended for effective hand washing?
quiz.explanation: About 20 seconds of rubbing is recommended to let the soap reach all the creases of the hands.

quiz.question: Why is friction important when washing hands?
quiz.explanation: Rubbing allows the soap to reach every corner of the hands, where viruses can hide.
options: It takes time for the soap to reach all the creases, like between the fingers and under the nails
It heats the water to kill viruses
It creates foam which alone kills viruses
It actually has no particular effect

quiz.question: What minimum percentage of alcohol should a hydroalcoholic gel contain to effectively destroy many enveloped viruses?
quiz.explanation: A hydroalcoholic gel must contain at least 60% alcohol to effectively destroy many enveloped viruses.

quiz.question: In which case are soap and water preferable to hydroalcoholic gel?
quiz.explanation: Faced with visible dirt or grease, hydroalcoholic gel is less effective, because this dirt acts as a screen: soap and water then remain the best choice.
options: When there is visible dirt or grease on the hands
When hands are already perfectly clean
When we are short of time

title: The discovery of penicillin
description: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold had killed the bacteria on a culture dish. That accident produced the first great antibiotic.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What did Alexander Fleming notice in 1928 on one of his forgotten culture boxes?
quiz.explanation: When Fleming returned from vacation, he observed that mold had grown on a culture dish and that the bacteria around it had died.
options: A mold had killed the bacteria around it
All the bacteria had survived without any change
The box was completely empty of all life
An unknown fungus made bacteria more resistant

quiz.question: When did Alexander Fleming discover penicillin?
quiz.explanation: Fleming discovered penicillin by chance in 1928, in London.

quiz.question: What genus does the mold discovered by Fleming belong to?
quiz.explanation: The mold observed by Fleming belongs to the genus Penicillium, hence the name given to the substance: penicillin.

quiz.question: True or false: Fleming alone succeeded in purifying penicillin sufficiently to treat the sick.
quiz.explanation: Fleming was unable to purify penicillin sufficiently to treat patients: this work would later fall to Florey and Chain.

quiz.question: Who took up and transformed Fleming's discovery into a real medicine in the early 1940s?
quiz.explanation: At Oxford, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain isolated, concentrated and tested penicillin, transforming it into a real medicine.
options: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, in Oxford

quiz.question: Why did World War II accelerate the development of penicillin?
quiz.explanation: The war made it urgent to be able to treat infected soldiers, which pushed penicillin from the laboratory towards a strategic issue.
options: Infected soldiers had to be treated urgently
The civilian laboratories had all closed
Scientists were looking for a chemical weapon
The government wanted to sell it to enemy countries

quiz.question: How was penicillin produced in sufficient quantities to treat millions of people?
quiz.explanation: During the war, the United States industrialized the production of penicillin in giant vats, like for beer.
options: The United States industrialized its production in giant vats during the war
Each hospital grew its own mold separately
It was chemically synthesized without any mold
It was imported in large quantities from Asia

quiz.question: Put these steps in the history of penicillin in order.
quiz.explanation: Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, Florey and Chain developed it in the early 1940s, production became industrialized during the war, then the three researchers received the Nobel Prize in 1945.
items: Fleming observes mold that killed bacteria on a culture dish
Florey and Chain isolate and test penicillin at Oxford
The United States industrialized the production of penicillin during the war
Fleming, Florey and Chain receive Nobel Prize

quiz.question: What risk did Fleming already anticipate regarding antibiotics?
quiz.explanation: Fleming had already warned that bacteria could become resistant to misused antibiotics, a risk that has become very real today.
options: That certain bacteria could become resistant if antibiotics were misused
That penicillin would become toxic over time
That the price of the drug would become far too high

title: The discovery of electricity
description: Electricity was not invented in one stroke. It was first observed, then understood, then tamed. Here are the key steps.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What did Benjamin Franklin demonstrate with his kite flying experiment?
quiz.explanation: Franklin showed that lightning and electricity produced by friction are the same force, a seminal idea despite the danger of the experiment.
options: That lightning is an electrical phenomenon
That electricity comes directly from the Sun
That the clouds are only loaded with water

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the lightning rod invented following Franklin's work?
quiz.explanation: The lightning rod is a metal rod that guides lightning to the ground without damage, bringing electricity into the engineering.
options: Providing lightning a safe path to the ground
Cool the air during a thunderstorm

quiz.question: What did Michael Faraday discover that made it possible to produce electric current?
quiz.explanation: This is induction: a magnet moving near a wire generates an electric current, the principle at the basis of all modern dynamos and power stations.
options: That a magnet moving near a wire creates a current
That the friction of two metals produces light
That water conducts electricity better than metal
That lightning can be stored in a bottle

quiz.question: True or false: Michael Faraday began his career as a university professor before becoming a scientist.
quiz.explanation: Faraday came from a humble background and started as a bookbinder, learning science by reading what he bound.

quiz.question: In the rivalry of the end of the 19th century, what type of movement did Nikola Tesla defend?
quiz.explanation: Tesla, with the Westinghouse company, defended alternating current against Edison's direct current.

quiz.question: Why did alternating current win out for city power grids?
quiz.explanation: Alternating current is easier to send over long distances, which is why it won out for powering cities.
options: It is easier to transport over long distances
It does not require any power plant

quiz.question: True or false: it was Thomas Edison who defended direct current against Tesla.
quiz.explanation: Edison pushed direct current, while Tesla and Westinghouse championed alternating current.

quiz.question: Today, what is the main challenge around electricity, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: The challenge is no longer just to produce electricity, but to do it cleanly and reliably for a fully connected world.
options: Figuring out how to store it in the air
Invent a new type of atom

title: The discovery of X-rays
description: In 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen discovered an invisible radiation that passes straight through matter. Within months, medicine saw a revolution in it.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: In what year did Wilhelm Röntgen discover X-rays?
quiz.explanation: It was on November 8, 1895, in Würzburg, that Röntgen made this discovery.

quiz.question: What does Röntgen notice that puts him on the X-ray trail?
quiz.explanation: Röntgen notices that a fluorescent screen shines from a distance even though it is not affected by visible light: invisible radiation passes through the room.
options: A fluorescent screen that glows without being affected by visible light
A burning smell in his laboratory
An electric shock on his hand
An unusual noise coming from the tube

quiz.question: What does the “X” in “X-rays” mean?
quiz.explanation: Röntgen calls this radiation “X-rays”, the X meaning “unknown”.

quiz.question: What did Röntgen photograph in a few weeks to demonstrate his discovery?
quiz.explanation: Röntgen photographed the bones of his wife's hand, including the wedding ring: this was the birth of radiology.
options: The skull of a patient in the hospital

quiz.question: True or false: Röntgen filed a patent on X-rays to profit from them.
quiz.explanation: Röntgen never filed a patent, he wanted all of science to be able to use his discovery freely.

quiz.question: Before X-rays, what was often required to “see” a fracture or a bullet in the body?
quiz.explanation: Before X-rays, to see the inside of the body, you often had to operate; with them, you get an image without cutting.
options: Usually had to be opened surgically
You had to wait for natural healing
We were already using an ultrasound

quiz.question: True or false: In the beginning, the dangers of X-rays were well known and avoided.
quiz.explanation: The risks were initially ignored: operators took x-rays for hours, until they developed burns and then cancer.

quiz.question: What did X-rays also contribute to, later useful for the study of DNA?
quiz.explanation: X-rays made it possible to study the structure of crystals, a technique that was later used to observe the structure of DNA.
options: The study of the structure of crystals

title: The discovery of the microwave oven
description: In 1945, an engineer noticed that the chocolate bar in his pocket had melted next to a radar set. That observation gave us the microwave oven.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: In what year did Percy Spencer notice that his candy bar had melted near a radar?
quiz.explanation: It was in 1945 that Spencer, while working on radar, made this accidental discovery.

quiz.question: What does Percy Spencer notice while working on radar?
quiz.explanation: Spencer notices that the candy bar in his pocket has melted, not from body heat but from radar waves.
options: A candy bar in his pocket melted
Radar breaks down for no reason
His hands become hot upon contact with the metal

quiz.question: What does Spencer test next to confirm his hunch?
quiz.explanation: Spencer tests with corn: the popcorn pops, confirming that microwaves can heat food.
options: Water, which starts to boil instantly

quiz.question: Before being used for cooking, what were microwaves mainly used for during the war?
quiz.explanation: During the war, microwaves were mainly used for radar to detect planes and ships.
options: Radars, to detect planes and boats

quiz.question: Around what year was the first commercial microwave oven, the Radarange, released?
quiz.explanation: The Radarange was released around 1947, but it was huge and expensive.

quiz.question: True or false: The first commercial microwave oven was small and inexpensive, intended for home use.
quiz.explanation: The Radarange was huge and expensive, intended more for restaurants or boats; it will take decades to make it affordable.

quiz.question: True or false: Microwaves make food radioactive.
quiz.explanation: This is a common misconception: microwaves heat food, they do not make it radioactive.

quiz.question: What do microwaves mainly do to heat food?
quiz.explanation: Microwaves mainly vibrate water molecules, and a little fats and sugars, creating heat inside the food.
options: They burn the surface on direct contact
They ionize the air around the dish

quiz.question: Why can a thick dish be hot on the outside and lukewarm in the center after microwaving?
quiz.explanation: The waves do not penetrate the food indefinitely, which explains why a thick dish heats up mainly on the surface.
options: The waves do not penetrate infinitely deep into the food
The oven distributes heat poorly due to a manufacturing defect
The center is protected by humidity
The dish turns too quickly in the oven

title: The theory of gravitation
description: In 1687, Newton published a simple and enormous idea: the same force makes an apple fall and keeps the Moon in its orbit. Here is what it changed.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: In what year did Isaac Newton publish the Principia and his theory of universal gravitation?
quiz.explanation: Newton published the Principia in 1687, asserting that gravitation is universal.

quiz.question: According to Newton, what explains why the Moon remains in orbit around the Earth?
quiz.explanation: Newton responds with an attraction: the Earth attracts the Moon, as the Sun attracts the Earth.
options: A force of attraction between the two bodies
A void that pushes the Moon outwards
A constant push from the Sun

quiz.question: How does the gravitational force change when we move two bodies apart?
quiz.explanation: The force increases with the mass of bodies and decreases with the square of the distance separating them.
options: It decreases with the square of the distance
It remains constant whatever the distance
It suddenly disappears beyond a certain threshold

quiz.question: True or false: depending on the course, the story of the apple falling on Newton's head is a well-documented historical fact.
quiz.explanation: The story of the apple is above all an often fictionalized story; the idea it illustrates is very real.

quiz.question: Why doesn't the Moon crash into the Earth, even though it is constantly "falling" towards it?
quiz.explanation: The Moon is constantly falling towards the Earth, but its high lateral speed makes it rotate around instead of crashing: this is the orbit.
options: She also has great sideways speed which makes her spin around instead of crashing.
She is repelled by the Sun at the same time
Her atmosphere slows her down just enough
The Earth actually has no attraction on it.

quiz.question: What does Newton's third law of motion say?
quiz.explanation: Newton's third law states that every action produces an opposite reaction of equal intensity.
options: Every action has an opposite reaction
An object accelerates without any force acting on it
The mass of an object changes depending on its speed
Forces only apply to celestial objects

quiz.question: True or false: depending on the course, Einstein's theory completely invalidated Newton's, which is no longer useful today.
quiz.explanation: Einstein corrects Newton for extreme cases, but Newton's theory remains excellent for launching a rocket or understanding tides.

quiz.question: Which scientists had already laid important foundations before Newton's synthesis?
quiz.explanation: Kepler had described the orbits of the planets and Galileo had studied the fall of bodies, before Newton linked the two.

title: The discovery of radioactivity
description: With Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, Marie Curie opened the chapter of radioactivity. Two Nobel Prizes, a crushing workload, and an immense legacy.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What is unique about Marie Curie among all Nobel Prize winners?
quiz.explanation: Marie Curie is the only person to have received two Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: physics, then chemistry.
options: She is the only person to have received two Nobel Prizes in two different sciences
She is the only woman to ever receive a Nobel Prize
She received the Nobel Prize three times
She received the Nobel Prize for Peace and Physics

quiz.question: Why did Marie Curie go to study in Paris rather than Poland?
quiz.explanation: Born in Poland, she went to study in Paris because local universities closed many doors to women.
options: Local universities closed many doors to women
She wanted to escape the war
There was no university in Poland
His family already lived in Paris

quiz.question: In what year did Henri Becquerel notice that uranium veils photographic plates without light?
quiz.explanation: It was in 1896 that Becquerel made this observation, which pushed Marie Curie to study the phenomenon in detail.

quiz.question: What word did Marie Curie invent to describe this phenomenon?
quiz.explanation: Marie Curie invented the word “radioactivity” to describe this spontaneous radiation of atoms.

quiz.question: What two chemical elements did Marie and Pierre Curie discover together?
quiz.explanation: Together they discovered polonium, named after Poland, and radium.

quiz.question: True or false: to isolate polonium and radium, it was necessary to process enormous quantities of ore (pitchblende).
quiz.explanation: Tons of pitchblende had to be processed to isolate just a few grams of these elements.

quiz.question: In what year did Marie Curie receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone?
quiz.explanation: In 1911, after having already received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903, she alone received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

quiz.question: Put these stages in the history of radioactivity in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: This timeline goes from 1896 to 1911, between Becquerel's initial discovery and Marie Curie's second Nobel.
items: Henri Becquerel observes that uranium veils photographic plates
Marie and Pierre Curie discover polonium and radium
The Nobel Prize in Physics rewards Becquerel and the Curies
Pierre Curie dies accidentally
Marie Curie alone receives the Nobel Prize in Chemistry

quiz.question: What did Marie Curie do during the First World War?
quiz.explanation: She organizes mobile x-ray units, exposing herself to doses that today we would know are unacceptable.
options: She organizes mobile x-ray units to treat the injured
She gives up research to devote herself to her family
She leaves France for the United States
She discovers a new radioactive element

title: The invention of the Internet
description: The Internet has no single inventor. It is a long chain: a military network, a common language, then the Web for human beings.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Why is the US military funding the project that will become ARPANET?
quiz.explanation: In the midst of the Cold War, the objective is to connect computers which continue to communicate even if part of the network is destroyed.
options: So that computers continue to communicate even if part of the network is destroyed
To create a military video game
To replace the telephone in offices

quiz.question: How do messages travel on ARPANET?
quiz.explanation: Messages are split into small packets that take different paths: if one route fails, another takes over.
options: Cut into small packages that take different paths
Sent as a single unit via a single cable

quiz.question: What are Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn developing?
quiz.explanation: Cerf and Kahn designed the TCP/IP protocol, which tells how to cut, address and recompose data.
options: The TCP/IP protocol, a common language for networks

quiz.question: In what year did ARPANET officially switch to TCP/IP?
quiz.explanation: On January 1, 1983, ARPANET officially adopted TCP/IP, a date often considered the technical birth of the Internet.

quiz.question: Who invented the World Wide Web at CERN?
quiz.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN in the early 1990s.

quiz.question: True or false: without the Web, the Internet would have remained primarily a tool reserved for experts.
quiz.explanation: The Web provides the easy layer (pages, links, browsers) that makes the Internet accessible to everyone, not just experts.

quiz.question: Put these three major stages in the history of the Internet in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: ARPANET was born at the end of the 1960s, TCP/IP took hold in 1983, then the Web arrived at the beginning of the 1990s.
items: The creation of the ARPANET network by the American army
Adoption of the common TCP/IP protocol
The invention of the World Wide Web by Tim Berners-Lee

quiz.question: According to the course, what new problems has the Internet also created?
quiz.explanation: The Internet has also created new problems: disinformation, surveillance, the digital divide.
options: The total disappearance of postal mail

title: The structure of DNA
description: In 1953, Watson and Crick described the double helix of DNA. Behind that glory stands the crucial work of Rosalind Franklin.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: In what year did Watson and Crick publish their model of the DNA double helix?
quiz.explanation: The double helix model was published in 1953.

quiz.question: What does DNA mean?
quiz.explanation: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid, the long molecule that contains the genetic code.

quiz.question: What were scientists missing in the 1940s and 1950s to understand how DNA is duplicated?
quiz.explanation: Without knowing the 3D shape of DNA, it was difficult to understand how this code could duplicate itself with each cell division.
options: Knowledge of its basic chemical composition
A microscope powerful enough to see cells
Evidence that parents pass on traits to their children

quiz.question: Which famous image obtained by Rosalind Franklin reveals clear evidence of a helical structure?
quiz.explanation: Rosalind Franklin's famous X-ray Photo 51 shows clear evidence of a propeller.

quiz.question: True or false: Rosalind Franklin received the Nobel Prize in 1962 with Watson and Crick for the discovery of the structure of DNA.
quiz.explanation: Franklin died in 1958; the 1962 Nobel went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins, not to her.

quiz.question: In the structure of DNA, how are the two strands organized?
quiz.explanation: Two complementary strands coil together, their chemical letters facing each other in pairs.
options: They wrap around each other and their letters face each other in pairs
They are completely independent and never touch each other
They form a rigid cube with no possibility of separation
They merge into one single strand

quiz.question: Why does the double helix shape help us understand the copy of DNA?
quiz.explanation: When the two strands separate, each serves as a template to reconstruct the other, making heredity chemically understandable.
options: When the strands separate, each can serve as a model to rebuild the other
Because it prevents any genetic mutation
Because it directly links DNA to the brain

quiz.question: On what other subject did Rosalind Franklin also carry out major work?
quiz.explanation: Franklin also did major work on viruses, a role long underappreciated in popular accounts.

title: The discovery of anesthesia
description: Before 1846, patients were often awake and in extreme pain while surgeons worked. Anesthesia turned an operation into treatment instead of torture.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: In what year was the first public demonstration of ether anesthesia in Boston?
quiz.explanation: On October 16, 1846, in Boston, the first convincing public demonstration of anesthesia took place.

quiz.question: Before anesthesia, what were surgeons primarily judged on?
quiz.explanation: Without anesthesia, surgeons were judged on their speed, to limit the patient's suffering.
options: The number of successful operations without anesthetic
Their ability to make the patient speak

quiz.question: What product did William Morton have a patient inhale during the 1846 demonstration?
quiz.explanation: Dentist William Morton makes the patient inhale ether before the operation.

quiz.question: Who is the surgeon operating on the neck tumor during this demonstration?
quiz.explanation: Surgeon John Warren operates on a neck tumor while the patient is on ether.

quiz.question: True or false: During the 1846 demonstration, the patient screamed in pain during the entire operation.
quiz.explanation: The patient does not scream thanks to the ether, which astonishes the entire room.

quiz.question: What other anesthetic product then became popular, particularly in Great Britain?
quiz.explanation: Chloroform then became popular, particularly in Great Britain, alongside ether.

quiz.question: What problem remains to be solved after the discovery of ether, giving birth to a new medical specialty?
quiz.explanation: We must learn to dose, monitor breathing and the heart: this is the birth of anesthesiology.
options: Dose anesthesia without killing the patient, by monitoring breathing and heart
Find a completely painless product for the anesthesiologist
Convince patients to accept the operation

quiz.question: True or false: today, anesthesia can only put the entire body to sleep, never just one area.
quiz.explanation: Today, we can put the whole body or just an area to sleep, using local or regional anesthesia.

title: Darwin's theory of evolution
