description: In 1859, Darwin published On the Origin of Species. The core idea: living things change over time through natural selection.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: In what year did Charles Darwin publish “On the Origin of Species”?
quiz.explanation: Darwin published his major work in 1859.

quiz.question: On which ship did Darwin travel for years to observe plants, fossils and birds?
quiz.explanation: Darwin boarded the ship the Beagle and spent years observing nature around the world.

quiz.question: What did Darwin observe in the birds of the Galapagos Islands?
quiz.explanation: In the Galapagos, Darwin noticed that nearby birds had different beaks depending on their diet, a strong clue.
options: Different beaks depending on their food
Always the same size whatever the bird

quiz.question: What did Darwin call the mechanism by which traits useful for survival spread through a population?
quiz.explanation: Darwin calls this mechanism natural selection: the environment instead keeps what helps to survive and reproduce.

quiz.question: True or false: according to Darwin, individuals “want” to evolve to adapt to their environment.
quiz.explanation: It is not a will: it is a filter, the environment rather keeps the traits that work, without the intention of the individuals.

quiz.question: What other naturalist comes up with ideas close to those of Darwin, which pushes him to publish his book?
quiz.explanation: Alfred Russel Wallace came up with similar ideas, which pushed Darwin to finally release his book.

quiz.question: Why did Darwin's ideas shock 19th century society?
quiz.explanation: Saying that species change, and that humans share a history with other animals, shakes up the religion and society of the time.
options: They challenge the idea that species were created as they are, and bring humans closer to other animals
They prove that the Earth is younger than we thought
They announce the end of traditional agriculture
They call into question the existence of fossils

quiz.question: According to the course, what current example illustrates “live” evolution?
quiz.explanation: The fight against antibiotic-resistant bacteria is an example of evolution that can be observed directly.
options: The complete disappearance of the dinosaurs

title: The Big Bang
description: 13.8 billion years ago, the universe started to expand. This is not a bomb going off in a void: space itself is what grows.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What is the Big Bang, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: The Big Bang is not an explosion in a pre-existing void: it is space itself which begins to grow, taking matter with it.
options: The expansion of space itself, not an explosion into a void already there
A classic explosion that threw matter into an already existing space
The collision of two giant stars
A phenomenon that still occurs today at the center of each galaxy

quiz.question: How many billion years ago did the Big Bang take place?
quiz.explanation: Scientists date the Big Bang to around 13.8 billion years ago.

quiz.question: Who invented the term “Big Bang” in 1949, actually wanting to make fun of it?
quiz.explanation: British astrophysicist Fred Hoyle coined the term in 1949 to mock the idea, but the nickname stuck.

quiz.question: In what year did Edwin Hubble observe that galaxies move away the faster they are?
quiz.explanation: In 1929, Hubble showed that the universe is not static: it is growing.

quiz.question: What did Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson capture in 1965, major proof of the Big Bang?
quiz.explanation: Penzias and Wilson capture the cosmic microwave background, a thermal echo of the young universe coming from all directions.
options: The cosmic microwave background, a radio crackle coming from everywhere
The direct light of the first stars
A radio signal sent by another civilization

quiz.question: Approximately what proportion of hydrogen was formed in the first minutes of the universe?
quiz.explanation: Calculations and observations indicate approximately 75% hydrogen and 25% helium formed during primordial nucleosynthesis.

quiz.question: Put these major stages in the history of the universe in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: This timeline goes from initial inflation to the formation of the Sun 4.6 billion years ago, through the first cores around 3 minutes and the diffuse background around 380,000 years ago.
items: The inflation phase, just after the beginning of the universe
The formation of the first atomic nuclei
The release of light, at the origin of the cosmic microwave background
The appearance of the first stars
The formation of the Sun

quiz.question: True or false: In the expanding universe, there is a precise central point from which everything moves away.
quiz.explanation: Like a balloon being inflated, no point in the universe is the center: all the points move away from each other.

quiz.question: According to the course, how much of the content of the universe is dark energy?
quiz.explanation: Dark energy represents about 68% of the content of the universe, compared to about 5% for ordinary matter.

quiz.question: What did we observe in 1998 thanks to distant supernovas?
quiz.explanation: In 1998, the observation of distant supernovas showed that the expansion of the universe was accelerating, attributed to a mysterious dark energy.
options: May the expansion of the universe accelerate
That the universe has stopped expanding
That the universe will soon contract
That there is another galaxy identical to ours

title: Why do volcanoes erupt?
description: A volcano is an opening in the Earth's crust. Magma under pressure rises through it and becomes lava. Here is why the Earth “spits.”
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What happens to the magma once it reaches the open air?
quiz.explanation: Once in the open air, the magma that rises to the surface of a volcano becomes lava.

quiz.question: What causes magma to form in a subduction zone?
quiz.explanation: In a subduction zone, the sinking plate carries water that lowers the melting point of rocks, forming magma.
options: Water driven by the plunging plate, which lowers the melting point of rocks
The sudden cooling of the plate which plunges
The total disappearance of the oceanic crust
A sudden drop in atmospheric pressure

quiz.question: True or false: Fluid magma, like that of Hawaii, generally produces explosive eruptions.
quiz.explanation: A fluid magma lets gases escape easily: the eruption is effusive, the lava flows, like in Hawaii or at Piton de la Fournaise.

quiz.question: What determines whether an eruption is more effusive or more explosive?
quiz.explanation: A fluid magma lets the gases escape and flows (effusive eruption), while a sticky magma traps the gases until it explodes (explosive eruption).

quiz.question: How much of the world's volcanic activity takes place beneath the oceans, far from our eyes?
quiz.explanation: About 80% of the world's volcanic activity occurs beneath the oceans, particularly near ridges.

quiz.question: Which 1815 volcanic eruption in Indonesia cooled the global climate and caused “the year without a summer” in 1816?
quiz.explanation: The Tambora eruption in 1815 was so powerful that it cooled the global climate, causing disastrous harvests in 1816.

quiz.question: What are the “black smokers” found near underwater ridges?
quiz.explanation: Black smokers are underwater chimneys that spew hot mineral-rich fluids, around which lightless ecosystems live.
options: Chimneys that emit burning fluids rich in minerals
Ice geysers specific to polar regions
Clouds of volcanic ash on the surface

quiz.question: Which ancient city was buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD? AD?
quiz.explanation: In 79 AD BC, the eruption of Vesuvius, near Naples, buried the city of Pompeii in ashes.

title: How do earthquakes happen?
description: Every year the Earth records hundreds of thousands of earthquakes. Most go unnoticed. A few change whole cities.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What is a fault that causes an earthquake?
quiz.explanation: An earthquake occurs along a fault, a fracture between two blocks of rock that end up sliding suddenly.
options: A fracture between two blocks of rock
A layer of the Earth's atmosphere

quiz.question: Why don't tectonic plates slide continuously, despite their constant movement?
quiz.explanation: At the boundaries of the plates, the friction of the rocks hinders sliding: the energy then accumulates silently until rupture.
options: The friction of rocks blocks their sliding at the borders
They are held together by the Earth's magnetic field
The Earth's mantle is completely solid and immobile

quiz.question: What is the difference between the focus and the epicenter of an earthquake?
quiz.explanation: Focus refers to the breaking point at depth, while epicenter is the point on the surface just above where the effects are often strongest.
options: The focus is the breaking point at depth, the epicenter is the point on the surface just above
The focus is on the surface, the epicenter is deep
These are two different names for exactly the same point.
Focus measures magnitude, epicenter measures duration

quiz.question: True or false: Each additional degree on the magnitude scale multiplies the energy released by approximately 32.
quiz.explanation: The magnitude scale is logarithmic: each degree multiplies the energy by about 32, so that a magnitude 8 earthquake releases about 1,000 times more energy than a magnitude 6 earthquake.

quiz.question: What is the approximate length of the San Andreas Fault in California, in kilometers?
quiz.explanation: The San Andreas Fault stretches approximately 800 miles along California.

quiz.question: What disaster followed the 9.1 magnitude earthquake near Sumatra in 2004?
quiz.explanation: The 2004 earthquake near Sumatra raised the seabed and triggered a tsunami that struck 14 countries, killing an estimated 227,000 people.
options: A tsunami that hit 14 countries and killed around 227,000 people
A major volcanic eruption in Indonesia
An electrical blackout across the entire Asian continent
Extreme cold snap in Southeast Asia

quiz.question: Put in the order of arrival the different types of seismic waves after the rupture of a fault.
quiz.explanation: After rupture, P waves arrive first, followed by S waves and then surface waves, which cause the most visible oscillations in the ground.
items: P waves, which compress the rock like an accordion
S waves, slower and often more destructive
Surface waves, which cause the ground to oscillate very visibly

quiz.question: What is earthquake engineering used for?
quiz.explanation: Seismic engineering designs buildings with mobile foundations or shock absorbers, capable of withstanding tremors.
options: To design buildings capable of absorbing the energy of tremors
To predict the exact day of a future earthquake
To prevent tectonic plates from moving
To measure the magnitude of an earthquake after the fact

quiz.question: True or false: today we know how to accurately predict the exact day of a major earthquake.
quiz.explanation: We do not yet know how to predict the exact day of a major earthquake; we can only map the risk areas.

title: The Chernobyl disaster (1986)
description: On April 26, 1986, reactor No. 4 at Chernobyl exploded. It is the worst civil nuclear accident in history. Here is what happened, without the sensationalism.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What test was the night shift of reactor no. 4 carrying out before the explosion?
quiz.explanation: Engineers were testing whether the still-spinning turbines could power the cooling pumps in the event of a power outage, before the diesel generators started up.
options: A safety test on the power supply to the cooling pumps in the event of a power outage
A seismic resistance test of the building
A test of the water quality of the nearby river

quiz.question: What type of reactor, known for its instability at low power, was used in Chernobyl?
quiz.explanation: The water-cooled, graphite-moderated RBMK reactor became very unstable at low power, which contributed to the accident.

quiz.question: True or false: in Chernobyl, the activation of the control rods immediately stopped the chain reaction.
quiz.explanation: Because of their design, the control rods first caused a brief surge before they could stop the reaction, precipitating the explosion.

quiz.question: Approximately how many inhabitants did Pripyat have at the time of its evacuation?
quiz.explanation: Pripyat had around 50,000 inhabitants, evacuated in a few hours on April 27, 1986.

quiz.question: What level does the Chernobyl disaster reach on the INES scale, which ranks nuclear accidents from 1 to 7?
quiz.explanation: Chernobyl reached level 7, the maximum on the INES scale, like Fukushima in 2011.
options: Level 7, the maximum of the scale
There is no scale for this accident

quiz.question: What do we call the hundreds of thousands of people mobilized by the USSR to contain the disaster?
quiz.explanation: Nearly 600,000 people, called liquidators, were mobilized to contain the disaster: pilots, workers, soldiers.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Chernobyl disaster in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: The explosion occurred on April 26, 1986, Pripyat was evacuated the next day, a first sarcophagus was built in 1986, then replaced by a new arch in 2016.
items: A safety test on reactor No. 4 goes wrong and causes an explosion
The town of Pripyat is urgently evacuated
A first concrete sarcophagus isolates the damaged reactor
A huge steel arch covers the entire site

quiz.question: True or false: the exclusion zone around Chernobyl is now home to abundant wildlife.
quiz.explanation: Without agriculture or towns for decades, the exclusion zone sees abundant wildlife developing there: wolves, elk, Przewalski's horses.

quiz.question: Why did a new steel arch cover the site in 2016?
quiz.explanation: The concrete sarcophagus built in 1986 having weakened, it was covered in 2016 by a new arch designed to last around 100 years.
options: The first concrete sarcophagus built in 1986 had weakened
The first sarcophagus was never finished
A new radioactive leak had just been discovered
The Ukrainian government wanted to reopen the plant

title: Why doesn't the Moon fall to Earth?
description: The Moon is falling toward the Earth all the time. It simply misses, every single time. That is exactly what an orbit is.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Why doesn't the Moon crash into the Earth, even though gravity is constantly pulling it?
quiz.explanation: The Moon is indeed falling towards the Earth, but its lateral speed causes it to continually miss the Earth: this is what we call an orbit.
options: It has a lateral speed which makes it miss the Earth at every moment: it is a permanent free fall
It is held by an invisible magnetic field
Earth's gravity does not act beyond the atmosphere
The Moon does not experience any gravitational pull

quiz.question: What did Isaac Newton imagine to explain the principle of the orbit?
quiz.explanation: Newton imagines a cannon firing a ball horizontally: at a sufficient speed, the ball falls without ever touching the ground, because the Earth curves under it at the same rate.
options: A cannon firing a cannonball from a mountain high enough to escape the atmosphere
A pendulum swinging endlessly in the void
An experiment with two opposing magnets
A balloon filled with helium released at altitude

quiz.question: How far does the Moon orbit the Earth on average, in kilometers?
quiz.explanation: The Moon orbits approximately 384,000 km from Earth.

quiz.question: True or false: if gravity suddenly disappeared, the Moon would travel in a straight line into space.
quiz.explanation: According to the principle of inertia, a body maintains its speed if it is not slowed down: without gravity to hold it back, the Moon would go straight.

quiz.question: What creates tidal forces between the Earth and the Moon?
quiz.explanation: The Moon's gravity pulls harder on the side of the Earth facing it, which deforms the oceans and creates a bulge of water: tides.
options: The Moon attracts the side of the Earth facing it more strongly than the opposite side
The rotation of the Earth on itself
The heat of the earth's core
The solar wind that hits the atmosphere

quiz.question: How many centimeters does the Moon move away from Earth each year?
quiz.explanation: Due to tidal forces, the Moon moves away about 1.5 inches per year.

quiz.question: Why are total solar eclipses possible today?
quiz.explanation: By geometric coincidence, the Sun is both 400 times larger and 400 times farther away than the Moon, giving them the same apparent size in the sky.
options: The Sun is about 400 times larger than the Moon, but also 400 times farther away: both have the same apparent size
The Moon is actually larger than the Sun
The Sun is getting closer and closer to the Earth
The Moon is stationary relative to the Sun

quiz.question: True or false: in the distant future, the Moon will move away to the point where it will no longer be able to cause total solar eclipses.
quiz.explanation: In about 600 million years, the Moon will be too far away to completely hide the Sun: only annular eclipses will remain.

title: Is there life elsewhere in the Universe?
description: Trillions of planets, and yet total radio silence. Science looks for life elsewhere without promising little green men.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What is the Fermi paradox?
quiz.explanation: The Fermi paradox refers to the contradiction between the immense number of possible planets and the absence, to date, of any confirmed extraterrestrial contact.
options: The contradiction between the immense number of possible planets and the absence of any confirmed extraterrestrial contact
A theory that proves there is no life anywhere else in the universe
A mathematical paradox unrelated to astronomy
Proof that aliens have already contacted us

quiz.question: On what two ingredients is known terrestrial life based, the basis of the search for life elsewhere?
quiz.explanation: Life on Earth relies primarily on the chemistry of carbon and liquid water, which allows chemical reactions to take place.

quiz.question: True or false: more than 5,000 exoplanets have been discovered since the 1990s.
quiz.explanation: Since the 1990s, more than 5,500 exoplanets have been discovered around other stars.

quiz.question: What is the Drake equation, proposed in 1961?
quiz.explanation: In 1961, astronomer Frank Drake proposed a formula multiplying several factors to estimate the number of civilizations capable of communicating in our galaxy.
options: A formula that multiplies several factors to estimate the number of communicating civilizations in the Milky Way
A formula that calculates the exact distance between two galaxies
A calculation that proves the existence of life on Mars
An equation used to measure the speed of light

quiz.question: How would the moon Europa, around Jupiter, manage to maintain a liquid ocean under its icy crust?
quiz.explanation: Jupiter's enormous pull distorts Europa and heats its interior through friction, which would allow an ocean to remain liquid beneath the ice.
options: Jupiter's tidal forces heat its interior through friction
A very dense atmosphere protects it from the cold
It is heated by its own active volcanism on the surface
It receives intense sunlight despite the distance

quiz.question: What did the Cassini probe reveal about Saturn's moon Enceladus?
quiz.explanation: The Cassini probe detected geysers and evidence of hydrothermal activity on the ocean floor of Enceladus, a source of chemical energy capable of feeding microbes.
options: Evidence of hydrothermal activity at the bottom of its ocean
The presence of a breathable atmosphere
Traces of vegetation on its surface
A magnetic field identical to that of the Earth

quiz.question: What is the “Great Filter” hypothesis?
quiz.explanation: The Great Filter is a nearly impossible step in evolution — one we may already have passed, or one still waiting for us.
options: An almost impossible step to take in the evolution towards an advanced technological civilization
A natural shield that protects Earth from asteroids
A filter used by radio telescopes to capture signals
The maximum speed limit that a rocket can reach

quiz.question: In what year did Frank Drake propose his equation estimating the number of communicating civilizations?
quiz.explanation: Frank Drake proposed his equation in 1961.

quiz.question: True or false: the Voyager probes have been carrying golden discs with sounds and images of the Earth since 1977.
quiz.explanation: Since 1977, Voyager probes have carried gold discs intended for a possible extraterrestrial civilization, even if the probability of interception is almost zero.

title: What is a black hole?
description: A black hole is not a cosmic vacuum cleaner. It is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: How do you define a black hole?
quiz.explanation: A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity is so intense that the speed needed to escape exceeds that of light.
options: A region where gravity is so intense that not even light can escape
A tunnel that connects two distant points in the universe
A particularly cold and dark star
A total void devoid of any matter

quiz.question: How is a stellar black hole usually born?
quiz.explanation: A stellar black hole is often born from the collapse of the core of a massive star, at least 20 to 25 times the mass of the Sun, once its fuel has been exhausted.
options: By the collapse of the core of a very massive star after exhaustion of its fuel
By the merger of two giant planets
By the gradual cooling of a white dwarf
By the explosion of a comet at high speed

quiz.question: True or false: a black hole sucks in everything that passes nearby, even at a great distance.
quiz.explanation: A black hole does not suck up everything from a distance: its gravity depends on its mass and the distance, as with any other object.

quiz.question: What is the name of the supermassive black hole located at the center of the Milky Way?
quiz.explanation: The supermassive black hole at the heart of the Milky Way is called Sagittarius A*, with around 4 million solar masses.

quiz.question: What is the event horizon of a black hole?
quiz.explanation: The event horizon is the invisible boundary around the black hole: once crossed, no return is possible.
options: The invisible border beyond which nothing can escape
The name given to the light emitted by the black hole
The area where the accretion disk only forms
A synonym for the gravitational singularity

quiz.question: In what year was the first image of a black hole (M87*) published?
quiz.explanation: The first image of a black hole, that of the galaxy M87, was published in April 2019 by the Event Horizon Telescope project.

quiz.question: What did physicist Stephen Hawking show in 1974?
quiz.explanation: Hawking showed that due to quantum effects near the horizon, a black hole would emit very weak radiation and slowly lose mass.
options: That a black hole would emit very weak radiation and eventually slowly evaporate
That black holes don't really exist
That light can easily escape from a black hole
That all black holes have exactly the same mass

quiz.question: True or false: near a black hole, time passes faster for a distant observer than for someone close to the black hole.
quiz.explanation: It's the opposite: near a black hole, time passes more slowly, which appears slowed down to a distant observer.

title: The theory of relativity for everyone
description: In 1905 and 1915, Einstein changed our idea of space, time and gravity. And without his calculations, your GPS would be off by several kilometers.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: On what two ideas is special relativity, published in 1905, based?
quiz.explanation: Special relativity is based on two ideas: the laws of nature are the same for any observer at a constant speed, and the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for everyone.
options: The laws of nature are the same for any observer at a constant speed, and the speed of light is the same for everyone
Gravity does not exist and time is completely frozen
Space is infinite but time stops at each star
Light travels faster depending on the direction of movement

quiz.question: True or false: in 1905, when he published special relativity, Einstein was already a recognized university professor.
quiz.explanation: In 1905, Einstein was not a university professor: he worked as an examiner at the patent office in Bern, Switzerland.

quiz.question: What does time dilation describe?
quiz.explanation: Time dilation means that the faster an object moves, the slower time passes for it compared to someone at rest, an effect measured by atomic clocks.
options: The faster an object goes, the slower time passes for it compared to an observer at rest.
Time stops completely beyond a certain speed
Time only slows down in the vacuum of space
Time speeds up for any moving object

quiz.question: What does the formula E=mc² mean?
quiz.explanation: E=mc² shows that mass is a very concentrated form of energy: a very small mass can release colossal energy.
options: Mass is a highly concentrated form of energy
Energy can never be transformed into mass
The speed of light varies depending on the mass of the object
Only kinetic energy counts in physics

quiz.question: How does general relativity describe gravity?
quiz.explanation: Einstein proposed that gravity is a curvature of space-time: a mass like the Sun hollows this fabric, and objects follow this curvature.
options: Like a curvature of space-time caused by the presence of mass
Like an invisible force transmitted instantly
Like a magnetic field produced by the stars

quiz.question: Who verified in 1919, during an eclipse, that light is deflected by the Sun's gravity?
quiz.explanation: In 1919, Arthur Eddington observed during an eclipse that the apparent position of stars behind the Sun was shifted, confirming Einstein's theory.

quiz.question: Without relativistic corrections, how many kilometers per day could GPS be wrong?
quiz.explanation: Without relativistic corrections, the GPS position error could reach around 11 km per day.

quiz.question: True or false: Once the two relativistic effects are combined, the clocks on GPS satellites advance about 38 microseconds per day compared to those on the ground.
quiz.explanation: The speed effect slows the clocks by about 7 microseconds per day, while the gravity effect advances them by about 45 microseconds: the net result is an advance of about 38 microseconds per day.

quiz.question: In what decade were gravitational waves predicted by Einstein in 1916 first detected?
quiz.explanation: We had to wait until 2015 and the LIGO observatory to detect the gravitational waves predicted by Einstein in 1916.
options: In the 2010s, by the LIGO observatory
In the 1920s, just after their prediction
In the 1970s, thanks to the first satellites
They have never been detected before

title: How does lightning form?
description: Lightning is not magic: it is an enormous electrical discharge inside a storm cloud. Here is how it builds up, and then how it strikes.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Where do lightning bolts mostly originate?
quiz.explanation: Lightning occurs mainly in cumulonimbus clouds, which can reach heights of up to 15 km.
options: In the cumulonimbus, very large storm clouds
In the upper atmosphere, above 50 km

quiz.question: How do electric charges separate inside the storm cloud?
quiz.explanation: In the cloud, rising ice crystals and descending sleet grains collide and exchange electrical charges.
options: By collisions between rising ice crystals and descending sleet grains
By the friction of the cloud against the ground
By the rapid evaporation of water from the cloud
By the direct action of the Sun's rays

quiz.question: True or false: in a thunderstorm cloud, the top of the cloud becomes rather negative and the base rather positive.
quiz.explanation: It's the opposite: the top of the cloud becomes rather positive, while the base becomes rather negative.

quiz.question: Put these stages of lightning formation in order.
quiz.explanation: The charges first separate in the cloud, then the air ionizes, the returning arc illuminates the sky, and the sudden expansion of the heated air finally produces thunder.
items: Collisions between ice crystals and sleet separate electrical charges in the cloud
The air ends up ionizing under the effect of too much tension
The returning arc illuminates the sky from the ground to the cloud
The brutally heated air expands and produces thunder

quiz.question: Approximately what temperature does the air rise through the lightning channel, in degrees Celsius?
quiz.explanation: The air in the lightning channel rises to around 30,000°C, or about five times the surface temperature of the Sun.

quiz.question: Why do we hear thunder after seeing lightning?
quiz.explanation: Light arrives almost instantly, while the sound of thunder only advances at around 340 m/s: hence the lag.
options: Sound travels much slower than light
Thunder always comes from several kilometers further
The light of lightning takes time to pass through the clouds
Thunder is only produced several seconds after lightning

quiz.question: Which place in Venezuela is one of the most lightning-hit places on the planet?
quiz.explanation: Lake Maracaibo, Venezuela, experiences almost daily storms for much of the year.

quiz.question: True or false: in addition to being dangerous, lightning also helps to fertilize the soil.
quiz.explanation: Lightning helps produce nitrogen compounds that fertilize soils when they fall with rain.

title: What is the greenhouse effect (really)?
description: The greenhouse effect is not a problem in itself: it is the invisible blanket that keeps the Earth from freezing. The real trouble starts when we thicken it too fast.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What is actually happening to cause the greenhouse effect to warm the Earth?
quiz.explanation: The ground heated by the Sun radiates infrared heat; certain gases absorb it and return it in all directions, including towards the ground.
options: Gases absorb infrared heat returned from the ground and send it back to itself
The Sun directly sends more heat on certain days
The atmosphere blocks visible light from the Sun
The ground produces its own heat independently of the Sun

quiz.question: Without the greenhouse effect, to what average temperature would the globe fall?
quiz.explanation: Without a natural greenhouse effect, the average global temperature would drop to around -18°C, compared to around +15°C today.

quiz.question: True or false: nitrogen and oxygen, present in the majority in the air, play a major role in the greenhouse effect.
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen and oxygen hardly do this job: it is mainly water vapor, CO2 and methane that absorb infrared heat.

quiz.question: Which gas mainly explains the increase in the greenhouse effect since the industrial revolution?
quiz.explanation: Since the industrial revolution, the combustion of coal, oil and gas has released carbon into the air that has remained buried for millions of years.
options: CO2 from the combustion of coal, oil and gas

quiz.question: Approximately how many times more does methane heat up than CO2 over 20 years?
quiz.explanation: Raising and growing rice adds methane, about 80 times hotter than CO2 over a 20-year period.

quiz.question: How many parts per million (ppm) has the concentration of CO2 in the air risen today, compared to 280 ppm before the industrial era?
quiz.explanation: The concentration of CO2 increased from about 280 to more than 420 parts per million, a level not seen in about 3 million years.

quiz.question: What is the IPCC, mentioned in the course?
quiz.explanation: The IPCC synthesizes the work of thousands of climatologists and concludes that the warming since 1950 is unprecedented and of human origin.
options: The group that synthesizes the work of thousands of climatologists
A space agency that monitors the climate

quiz.question: Why does melting ice further accelerate warming?
quiz.explanation: When the white ice disappears, the dark soil and water absorb more sunlight: this is the decline in the Earth's albedo, which further accelerates warming.
options: Dark soil and water, revealed, absorb more sunlight than white ice
Melt water first cools the atmosphere and then heats it more
Glaciers emit methane as they melt

quiz.question: True or false: On Venus, the ground is hot enough to melt lead.
quiz.explanation: On Venus, an atmosphere of 96% CO2 brings the ground temperature to around 460°C, enough to melt lead.

title: Why do we sleep?
description: We spend a third of our lives asleep. It is not wasted time: sleep cleans the brain, repairs the body and etches memories into place.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Out of a 75-year life, approximately how many years do we spend sleeping?
quiz.explanation: In a life of 75 years, we sleep for almost 25 years: sleep is not a break, but work as vital as drinking or eating.

quiz.question: What did Randy Gardner's experience of going 11 days without sleep in 1964 reveal?
quiz.explanation: Randy Gardner has shown that a brain deprived of sleep collapses: hallucinations, paranoia and loss of bearings after several days.
options: The brain cannot stand without rest: hallucinations, paranoia, mind collapsing
The human body can do without sleep without consequences
Lack of sleep only affects memory, not emotions
After 5 days without sleep, the body automatically falls asleep

quiz.question: After his record, how many hours in a row did Randy Gardner sleep?
quiz.explanation: After his 11 days without sleep, Randy Gardner slept for 14 hours straight, before his sleep pattern returned to normal after several weeks.

quiz.question: True or false: in rats, a total lack of sleep can kill in 2 to 3 weeks, like starvation.
quiz.explanation: In rats, complete lack of sleep kills within 2 to 3 weeks, a time period comparable to that of starvation.

quiz.question: What does the hippocampus do during sleep?
quiz.explanation: During sleep, the hippocampus replays the events of the day and transfers the information to the neocortex, which explains why we learn 20 to 40% better after a good night's sleep.
options: It replays the day and sends the information to the neocortex for lasting storage
It blocks all brain activity to save energy
It destroys unnecessary memories of the previous day
It makes new neurons with each sleep cycle

quiz.question: What is the glymphatic system, mentioned in the course?
quiz.explanation: The glymphatic system is a cerebral drainage network ten times more active at night; it evacuates waste, including proteins linked to the risk of Alzheimer's.
options: A cerebral drainage network, approximately ten times more active at night, which evacuates waste from the brain
The name of the 90 minute sleep cycle
The area of ​​the brain that produces dreams
The system that regulates body temperature during sleep

quiz.question: True or false: Dolphins sleep with only one hemisphere of their brain active at a time.
quiz.explanation: Dolphins sleep with only one hemisphere at a time, to remain partially vigilant and continue to come up for air.

quiz.question: What happens after about 17 hours of continuous wakefulness?
quiz.explanation: 17 hours of wakefulness is equivalent to a blood alcohol level of 0.5 g/l; the brain then forces microsleeps, short breaks in consciousness.
options: Abilities drop to the level of a blood alcohol level of 0.5 g/l, with microsleeps
The body automatically enters deep sleep

quiz.question: Why do screens in the evening delay falling asleep?
quiz.explanation: Screens in the evening trick the circadian clock and delay the release of melatonin, the hormone that prepares the body for sleep.
options: They trick the internal clock and slow down the release of melatonin
They permanently increase the heart rate
They block the production of immune cytokines

title: How does the brain store memories?
description: Memory is not a library of drawers. It is a living network of neurons that strengthen, rebuild themselves and sometimes get it wrong.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What is a synapse?
quiz.explanation: A synapse is the point of contact between two neurons, where the signal that builds or reinforces a memory is transmitted.
options: The point of contact between two neurons
The central nucleus of a neuron
An area of ​​the cortex dedicated to memory
A protein that repairs the DNA of neurons

quiz.question: Approximately how many billion neurons are in the human brain?
quiz.explanation: The human brain has approximately 86 billion neurons and more than 100 trillion synapses.

quiz.question: What is long-term potentiation?
quiz.explanation: When information is repeated or linked to a strong emotion, the same neurons activate together and their link becomes easier to trigger: this is long-term potentiation.
options: Strengthening the link between two neurons which often activate together
The progressive destruction of unused synapses
The production of new neurons in adulthood
Slowing of brain activity during sleep

quiz.question: What role does the hippocampus play in the formation of memories?
quiz.explanation: The hippocampus receives and encodes memories, then redistributes them to the cortex: this transfer, called consolidation, occurs mainly during sleep.
options: It encodes memories then redistributes them to the cortex during consolidation
It definitely stores all the memories of a lifetime
It erases memories that have become useless

quiz.question: True or false: without a functioning hippocampus, we can no longer form new conscious memories.
quiz.explanation: Without a functioning hippocampus, we can live in the present moment, but we no longer hold new conscious memories.

quiz.question: What did the case of patient H.M., operated on in 1953, reveal?
quiz.explanation: Patient H.M. no longer formed new conscious memories, but progressed each day in drawing in a mirror: his memory of gestures, procedural memory, remained intact.
options: He was no longer forming new conscious memories, but was progressing in drawing in a mirror
He had lost all his old memories but was forming new ones normally.
He had only lost his memory of faces
He could no longer speak but kept all his memory

quiz.question: What did psychologist Elizabeth Loftus show?
quiz.explanation: Elizabeth Loftus has shown that false memories can be implanted with simple questions, which calls for caution when dealing with eyewitness testimony.
options: False memories can be implanted with simple questions
Human memory is always perfectly reliable
Old memories are more reliable than recent ones

quiz.question: True or false: Remembering an event is like replaying a faithful video from the past.
quiz.explanation: Recalling a memory is not like replaying a video: each recall makes the memory malleable, and the brain can modify it before re-recording it.

title: Why are some species immortal?
description: Some species seem to defy death. Jellyfish that grow young again, hydras that never age: the secret is cell repair.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Approximately how many years did the Ming clam, mentioned in the course, live?
quiz.explanation: The Ming clam lived 507 years, a striking example of extreme longevity among animals.

quiz.question: How does the Turritopsis dohrnii jellyfish escape aging?
quiz.explanation: Wounded or starved, Turritopsis dohrnii transforms its adult cells into virgin cells then becomes a polyp again, its starting stage: this is transdifferentiation.
options: It transforms its adult cells into virgin cells and becomes a polyp again
She clones herself identically before dying

quiz.question: What are telomeres?
quiz.explanation: Telomeres act like shoelace tips at the ends of chromosomes; with each cell division, they shorten, and if they are too short, the cell stops dividing.
options: Ends at the ends of chromosomes, which shorten with each cell division
Stem cells present only in invertebrates

quiz.question: True or false: the tardigrade can survive the vacuum of space and extreme radiation by drying out its body.
quiz.explanation: As it dries out, the tardigrade's metabolism drops to 99.99%, allowing it to survive the vacuum of space or extreme radiation.

quiz.question: How does the hydra renew its entire body without showing signs of aging?
quiz.explanation: The hydra, a small freshwater polyp, renews its entire body thanks to an almost unlimited stock of stem cells, without measurable aging.
options: Thanks to an almost unlimited supply of stem cells
Thanks to a shell that protects it from damage
By staying still to save energy
By absorbing the cells of other hydras

quiz.question: Approximately how many years can the bowhead whale live?
quiz.explanation: The bowhead whale can exceed 200 years, thanks to ultra-efficient DNA repair and strong resistance to cancer.

quiz.question: Why do lobster telomeres almost never shorten?
quiz.explanation: Lobsters make telomerase throughout their bodies, so their telomeres do not shorten; they grow all their lives.
options: They make telomerase all over their body
They never divide at the cellular level
Their shell directly protects their DNA
They replace their cells by transdifferentiation, like the jellyfish

quiz.question: What are the senolytic treatments discussed in the course aimed at?
quiz.explanation: Senolytics aim to eliminate zombie cells that accumulate and inflame tissues; in animals, this has already rejuvenated certain functions.
options: Eliminate zombie cells that accumulate with age
Accelerate the division of all cells in the body
Replacing shortened telomeres with new ones

quiz.question: True or false: Even a biologically immortal species can die from predators, disease, or disaster.
quiz.explanation: Biological immortality protects against the internal damage of aging, but not from predators, disease, or disaster.

title: Photosynthesis explained simply
description: Plants do something extraordinary: they cook sugar out of light, water, and air. And they hand us the oxygen as a gift.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Why do leaves appear green to us?
quiz.explanation: Chlorophyll mainly captures the blue and red of light; the green is returned, which gives their color to the leaves.
options: Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red, and returns green
Green is the only color in sunlight
Leaves reflect all colors except green absorbed by the air

quiz.question: Where does CO2 enter the leaf for photosynthesis?
quiz.explanation: CO2 enters through tiny pores called stomata, while water rises separately from the roots.
options: Through openings located only on the flowers

quiz.question: What does the light phase of photosynthesis produce?
quiz.explanation: The light phase breaks up water molecules, releases oxygen and stores the captured energy in two chemical cells, ATP and NADPH.
options: ATP and NADPH, breaking water molecules and releasing oxygen
CO2 intended to be released into the air
Fresh chlorophyll to replace that which is degrading

quiz.question: What is the Calvin cycle?
quiz.explanation: The Calvin cycle, named after chemist Melvin Calvin, uses the energy of ATP and NADPH to assemble carbon from CO2 into glucose.
options: The phase where the plant assembles carbon from CO2 into glucose, using the energy already stored
The phase where light breaks water molecules
The name of the pigment that captures blue and red light
The process by which oxygen is released into the air

quiz.question: Approximately how many billion years ago did the Great Oxidation take place?
quiz.explanation: Around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria began to massively release oxygen: this is the Great Oxidation.

quiz.question: True or false: for many organisms of the time, the oxygen released by cyanobacteria was poison.
quiz.explanation: During the Great Oxidation, the oxygen massively released by cyanobacteria was toxic for many organisms of that time.

quiz.question: Approximately how much of the earth's oxygen comes from phytoplankton in the oceans, and not from forests?
quiz.explanation: About half of Earth's oxygen comes from phytoplankton in the oceans, not just forests.

quiz.question: Approximately what percentage of the solar energy received does a leaf convert into biomass?
quiz.explanation: A leaf only converts 1 to 3% of the solar energy received into biomass, a modest but sufficient yield on a planetary scale.

quiz.question: What is special about the sea slug Elysia chlorotica, mentioned in the course?
quiz.explanation: The sea slug Elysia chlorotica goes so far as to steal chloroplasts from the algae it eats, to live somewhat on solar energy.
options: It steals chloroplasts from algae to live a little thanks to solar energy
She has been making her own chlorophyll since birth
It feeds exclusively on sugar produced by trees.
It transforms CO2 into oxygen through its skin

title: Why do leaves change color?
description: Autumn does not invent the colors. It removes the green that was hiding them. Behind the show sits a survival plan for getting through winter.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Why are the leaves green from spring to late summer?
quiz.explanation: As long as chlorophyll dominates, the leaf remains green, even if it already contains yellow and orange carotenoids, invisible under the green.
options: Chlorophyll dominates and masks the other pigments present in the leaf
The leaves contain no pigment other than chlorophyll
Summer light makes other pigments invisible

quiz.question: What is the real trigger for leaf color changing in fall?
quiz.explanation: It is not mainly the cold that triggers autumn, but the length of the nights, measured by the phytochromes of the trees.
options: The amount of rain that fell in autumn
The wind that tears away the leaves

quiz.question: True or false: yellow and orange pigments, carotenoids, are produced only in the fall.
quiz.explanation: Carotenoids are already present in summer, but invisible under the green of chlorophyll; autumn only reveals them.

quiz.question: What is the separation zone that forms at the base of the petiole?
quiz.explanation: The separation zone forms a plug at the base of the petiole: the sap rises less, the leaf isolates itself and degrades its chlorophyll more quickly.
options: A sort of plug which reduces the circulation of sap and insulates the leaf
A protective layer that prevents the leaf from falling
The point where chlorophyll is produced in the greatest quantity
The area where red anthocyanins form

quiz.question: Why does the tree produce anthocyanins, the red and purple pigments, just before losing its leaves?
quiz.explanation: Anthocyanins act as a solar filter that protects tissues while the tree recovers nitrogen and other valuable nutrients from the leaf.
options: To protect still active tissues during nutrient recycling
To attract pollinating insects in autumn
To replace the missing chlorophyll and continue photosynthesis

quiz.question: What conditions typically produce the most vibrant fall reds?
quiz.explanation: The most beautiful reds are born from sunny days and cool frost-free nights, which favor the transformation of sugar into anthocyanins.
options: Sunny days followed by cool, frost-free nights
A gray and rainy autumn from start to finish
Early frost at the start of the season

quiz.question: True or false: An early frost kills the leaves before they have time to change color.
quiz.explanation: An early frost kills the leaves before the color show, unlike sunny days and cool nights which favor vibrant reds.

quiz.question: What are tannins, mentioned at the end of the season?
quiz.explanation: In the end, all that remains is the tannins, brown substances typical of the autumn forest floor.
options: Brown substances that remain in the forest floor once other pigments have degraded
The pigments responsible for the brightest red
The molecules that protect the leaf from frost

title: What is dark matter?
description: No one has ever seen it. Yet without it, galaxies would come apart. Dark matter is the invisible glue of the universe.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: How much of the Universe is made up of dark matter?
quiz.explanation: Dark matter represents around 27% of the Universe, five times more than all ordinary matter.

quiz.question: What did astronomer Vera Rubin discover in the 1970s?
quiz.explanation: Vera Rubin measured that stars at the edges of spiral galaxies rotated as fast as those in the center, evidence of an invisible mass holding them back.
options: Stars on the outskirts of galaxies rotated as fast as those in the center
Spiral galaxies do not contain any stars in the periphery
The rotation speed of galaxies decreases over time
The Solar System rotates at the same speed as spiral galaxies

quiz.question: True or false: Vera Rubin faced obstacles because of her gender early in her career.
quiz.explanation: Princeton long denied Vera Rubin a doctorate in astronomy because she was a woman, a rule maintained until 1975.

quiz.question: What is WIMP, one of the avenues considered for dark matter?
quiz.explanation: The WIMP would be a heavy particle outside the standard model of physics, sought in particular by liquid xenon detectors buried underground.
options: A heavy particle that would exist outside the standard model of physics
An invisible star because it's too cold to shine
A type of galaxy never before observed

quiz.question: How does dark matter betray its presence by means other than the rotation of galaxies?
quiz.explanation: Dark matter bends space and creates gravitational lenses, which distort the image of galaxies behind it.
options: It curves space and distorts the image of the galaxies located behind it
It emits a very weak but detectable light
It completely blocks the light of the stars it surrounds
She changes the color of the stars she crosses

quiz.question: How does dark energy, discovered in 1998, act in the opposite way to dark matter?
quiz.explanation: Dark matter attracts, while dark energy accelerates the expansion of the Universe: galaxies move away from each other more and more quickly.
options: It accelerates the expansion of the Universe instead of attracting matter
It attracts matter even more strongly than gravity
It slows down the rotation of galaxies
It only concerns the interior of galaxies, never the space between them

quiz.question: Approximately how much of the Universe is dark energy?
quiz.explanation: Dark energy is estimated to make up about 68% of the cosmos; with dark matter, this makes 95% of the invisible Universe.

quiz.question: What could dark energy cause in the very distant future, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: In the very distant future, dark energy could push other galaxies away to the point of making them invisible from the Milky Way.
options: Move other galaxies away to the point of making them invisible from the Milky Way
Bringing all galaxies to a single central point
Gradually transforming dark matter into ordinary matter
Completely stop the expansion of the Universe

quiz.question: When was dark energy discovered?
quiz.explanation: Dark energy was discovered in 1998, observing that the expansion of the Universe is speeding up instead of slowing down.

title: How does electricity work in our body?
description: Thinking, a heartbeat, lifting an arm: all of it travels first as living electricity, carried not by electrons but by ions.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: In the body, what circulates to create electrical signals, unlike a wall outlet?
quiz.explanation: In a wall outlet, electrons circulate; in the body, these are ions, charged atoms, which enter and leave cells.
options: Ions, charged atoms that move in and out of cells
Free electrons circulating in the blood
Magnetic waves produced by the brain
Static electricity accumulated in the skin

quiz.question: Approximately what is the resting potential of a neuron, in millivolts?
quiz.explanation: Thanks to sodium-potassium pumps, a neuron at rest maintains a potential of around -70 millivolts, with the inside being more negative than the outside.

quiz.question: What is the action potential of a neuron?
quiz.explanation: When a stimulus arrives, sodium rushes in and the polarity flips: that's the action potential, an all-or-nothing signal that runs down the axon.
options: An all-or-nothing electrical signal that runs along the axon when sodium suddenly enters
The level of energy the neuron consumes at rest
The amount of neurotransmitters stored in the neuron
The time it takes for a neuron to regenerate after use

quiz.question: How does a neuron transmit its signal across the synapse, the space that separates it from the next neuron?
quiz.explanation: The electrical signal cannot jump the synapse: the axon releases neurotransmitters which attach to the next neuron like a key in a lock.
options: By releasing neurotransmitters which attach to the next neuron
By directly sending an electric current through space
By temporarily fusing its membrane with that of the next neuron
By releasing calcium ions which pass through space freely

quiz.question: Approximately how fast do certain nerve signals travel, in meters per second?
quiz.explanation: Some nerve signals travel at around 120 m/s, or more than 430 km/h, enough to respond almost instantly to a burn.

quiz.question: What is the sinus node in the heart?
quiz.explanation: In the right atrium, the sinus node generates its own electrical impulses, approximately 60 to 100 times per minute at rest.
options: The structure that itself generates the electrical impulses of the heartbeat
The valve that separates the atria from the ventricles
The main muscle that pumps blood to the lungs
The nerve that connects the heart directly to the brain

quiz.question: True or false: the heart needs a command from the brain for each beat.
quiz.explanation: The heart does not wait for an order from the brain for each beat: the sinus node itself generates its own electrical impulses.

quiz.question: How many volts can an electric eel produce?
quiz.explanation: The electric eel uses the same principle of excitable cells as the human body, but in series, up to 600 volts, enough to paralyze prey.

quiz.question: What does defibrillation do?
quiz.explanation: Defibrillation sends an external shock that resets all cardiac cells, so that the sinus node returns to normal tempo.
options: It sends a shock which resets all the cardiac cells so that the sinus node resumes the tempo
It directly stimulates the brain to revive the heart
It chemically replaces the heartbeat with a permanent artificial rhythm
It completely blocks the electrical activity of the heart

title: Why do some sounds give us chills?
description: Goosebumps, tingles, a racing heart: music can hijack the circuits we use for pleasure and for survival. Here is why.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: Approximately what proportion of people feel chills when listening to music?
quiz.explanation: About 55 to 70 percent of people experience chills to music, a phenomenon called aesthetic thrill.

quiz.question: What brain system is activated when a piece of music touches someone?
quiz.explanation: A touching piece activates the brain's reward system, the same as for food, sex or certain drugs.
options: The reward system, the same as for food or certain drugs
The immune system, to combat stress
The motor system, which controls voluntary movements
The digestive system, linked to strong emotions

quiz.question: What has the effect of naltrexone, a drug that blocks opioid receptors, shown?
quiz.explanation: Naltrexone, which blocks opioid receptors, can almost erase musical pleasure, evidence that the brain produces its own reward substances.
options: It can almost erase musical pleasure, proof that the brain produces its own reward substances
It greatly amplifies the pleasure felt when listening to music
It has no measurable effect on musical pleasure
It improves the memory of the melodies heard

quiz.question: Approximately what proportion of people feel no pleasure from music despite having normal hearing?
quiz.explanation: Around 5% of people experience no pleasure from music despite normal hearing: this is called specific musical anhedonia.

quiz.question: What often triggers a musical thrill, depending on the course?
quiz.explanation: The thrill often arises from a violation of musical expectation: the brain continually predicts the next note, and a harmonic surprise triggers the emotional alert.
options: A violation of musical expectation, such as an unexpected modulation
A perfectly regular tempo from start to finish
An identical repetition of the same note

quiz.question: Why do some songs give you goosebumps?
quiz.explanation: Goosebumps, or piloerection, is an old reflex that raises the hairs to appear taller or keep warm; the music triggers him by surprise.
options: It's an old reflex that raises the hairs to appear taller or keep warm
It is a sign that the body is lacking oxygen.
This is a reaction solely linked to the temperature of the room.
It is a direct side effect of low frequencies on the skin

quiz.question: What did researcher Matthew Sachs show about people who are highly sensitive to musical thrills?
quiz.explanation: Matthew Sachs showed that people prone to shivering often have more connections between the auditory cortex, the prefrontal cortex and the insula.
options: They have more connections between the auditory cortex, the prefrontal cortex and the insula
They have physically more sensitive hearing than average
They systematically listen to more music than others
They have a less active reward system than average

quiz.question: True or false: From an evolutionary perspective, musical thrill directly nourishes or protects the individual.
quiz.explanation: Musical thrill is an evolutionary paradox: it does not directly nourish or protect, but synchronizing a group's emotions may have promoted social cohesion.

title: Why do other planets have seasons?
description: On Earth, the seasons come from the tilt of the axis. Elsewhere the same rule gives winters that last 42 years, or almost no seasons at all.
subject: sciences

quiz.question: What is the obliquity of a planet?
quiz.explanation: Obliquity is the angle between the axis of rotation of a planet and the perpendicular to its orbit; the larger it is, the more marked the seasons.
options: The angle between its axis of rotation and the perpendicular to its orbit
The average distance between the planet and the Sun
The speed at which the planet rotates
The total length of a year on this planet

quiz.question: How many degrees is Uranus, the most extreme case in the Solar System, tilted?
quiz.explanation: Uranus is tilted about 98°, almost lying on its side, giving it extreme seasons.

quiz.question: On Uranus, approximately how many years does each period of continuous day last at a pole?
quiz.explanation: Uranus takes 84 years to circle the Sun; each pole therefore receives nearly 42 years of continuous day, then 42 years of total night.

quiz.question: Why do Jupiter and Mercury have almost no seasons?
quiz.explanation: Jupiter and Mercury have an almost straight axis of rotation, which creates almost no season, unlike Uranus or Earth.
options: Their axis of rotation is almost straight, very slightly inclined
They are too far from the Sun to feel variations
Their orbit is perfectly circular, without any possible variation
They do not rotate on themselves

quiz.question: On Mars, why are southern hemisphere summers shorter but warmer?
quiz.explanation: The Martian orbit is oval; In the Southern Hemisphere, summer falls near perihelion, resulting in shorter but hotter summers, sometimes with dust storms.
options: They fall near perihelion, the point where Mars is closest to the Sun
The Martian atmosphere traps heat like a giant greenhouse
The South Pole receives twice as much light as the North Pole
Mars changes rotation speed depending on the season

quiz.question: True or false: In 2018, a seasonal dust storm ended the Opportunity rover's mission.
quiz.explanation: In 2018, a seasonal Martian dust storm obscured the Sun and permanently stopped the Opportunity rover.

quiz.question: Why does the temperature of Venus remain almost constant everywhere, despite an extreme tilt of its axis?
quiz.explanation: Despite extreme tilt, Venus' monstrous greenhouse effect equalizes the temperature around 460°C everywhere, all the time.
options: Its monstrous greenhouse effect equalizes the temperature to around 460°C everywhere
Venus actually has no measurable tilt
Its very rapid rotation distributes heat evenly
Venus is too far from the Sun to feel variations

quiz.question: True or false: on Venus, a day, that is to say a complete rotation on itself, lasts longer than a year, that is to say a revolution around the Sun.
quiz.explanation: On Venus, a day lasts 243 Earth days, compared to 225 Earth days for a year: the rotation is longer than the revolution.

quiz.question: What role does the Moon play in the Earth's seasons?
quiz.explanation: Without the Moon, the Earth's inclination would oscillate chaotically between 0° and more than 80°; the Moon acts as a gravitational stabilizer.
options: It stabilizes the inclination of the earth's axis, avoiding chaotic oscillations
It directly warms the hemisphere which it illuminates at night
It accelerates the rotation of the Earth around the Sun
It blocks part of the sunlight in summer

title: The Odyssey, Homer
description: After Troy, Odysseus, king of Ithaca, takes ten years to get home. Monsters, gods and temptations mark out a voyage that invents the cunning hero of Western literature.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Which Greek hero took ten years to return home after the Trojan War?
quiz.explanation: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, takes ten years to return home after the end of the Trojan War: this is the subject of the Odyssey.

quiz.question: How does the Odyssey start, as a story?
quiz.explanation: Homer starts in the middle of the action: Odysseus is held by the nymph Calypso, and only later tells his earlier adventures in flashback.
options: In media res, in the middle of the action, while Odysseus is held by Calypso
With the story of Odysseus's birth
With the start of the Trojan War

quiz.question: True or false: Odysseus escapes the Cyclops Polyphemus without ever revealing his name.
quiz.explanation: Odysseus proudly shouts his real name after blinding Polyphemus, which lets the Cyclops call down his father Poseidon's vengeance on him.

quiz.question: How does Penelope repel the suitors who besiege her in Ithaca?
quiz.explanation: Penelope buys time by promising to remarry once the shroud is completed, which she undoes each night in secret.
options: She weaves a shroud by day and undoes it every night
She locks herself in an impregnable tower
She asks Athena to turn them into stone
She goes to hide in Crete with her son

quiz.question: Who recognizes Odysseus first when he returns to Ithaca, disguised as a beggar?
quiz.explanation: The dog Argos, very old, recognizes Odysseus before anyone else, followed by his nurse Euryclea.

quiz.question: True or false: Modern scholars believe that the Odyssey arose from a long oral tradition rather than from the pen of a single author.
quiz.explanation: The work of Milman Parry shows that the text comes from a tradition of singers, the bards, who composed with ready-made formulas.

quiz.question: About how many books (parts) does the Odyssey have?
quiz.explanation: The Odyssey has 24 books and about 12,000 lines.

quiz.question: Which 20th-century writer folded Odysseus's journey into a single day in Dublin?
quiz.explanation: In 1922, James Joyce published his novel Ulysses, which folds Homeric wandering into a single day in Dublin.

title: The Iliad, Homer
description: Not the whole Trojan War: 51 days of wrath. Achilles withdraws, Patroclus dies, Hector falls. Homer shows how glory can turn brutal, then human again.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: On how many days does the action of the Iliad mainly focus?
quiz.explanation: Homer focuses his account on 51 days of the tenth year of the war, not the entire conflict.
options: 51 days of the tenth year of the war
The complete ten years of the Trojan War
The twenty years of Odysseus' absence

quiz.question: What is the true first theme of the poem, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: The poem opens with the anger of Achilles, provoked by the humiliation inflicted by Agamemnon, even before the question of Troy.
options: The construction of the Trojan horse

quiz.question: True or false: Agamemnon humiliates Achilles by taking his captive Briseis.
quiz.explanation: Agamemnon takes Briseis from Achilles, which hurts his timè, the honor due to his merit, and triggers his anger.

quiz.question: Why does Patroclus borrow Achilles' armor?
quiz.explanation: Without Achilles removed from the fight, the Greeks fold; Patroclus borrows his armor to intimidate the Trojans led by Hector.
options: To scare the Trojans who threaten the Greek ships

quiz.question: Who kills Patroclus, with the help of the god Apollo?
quiz.explanation: Patroclus disobeys Achilles' orders and is killed by the Trojan prince Hector, aided by Apollo.

quiz.question: True or false: in the Iliad, the gods can also be harmed by mortals.
quiz.explanation: The warrior Diomedes wounds Aphrodite in the hand, and the god Ares must flee screaming: even the gods are not invulnerable.

quiz.question: How does Achilles treat Hector's body after killing him?
quiz.explanation: Achilles ties Hector's body to his chariot and drags it before the walls of Troy, before the eyes of his family, refusing the funeral rites.
options: He ties him to his chariot and drags him through the dust
He buried him immediately with honors
He immediately returns it to Priam
He burns it on a Greek funeral pyre

quiz.question: What drives Achilles to finally return Hector's body to Priam?
quiz.explanation: Faced with the old king Priam who came to beg him, Achilles thinks of his own father and returns his son's body to him.
options: He thinks of his own father when he sees Priam broken with pain
Zeus orders it directly on the battlefield
Hélène intervenes to ask for peace

quiz.question: Put these steps of the Iliad in order.
quiz.explanation: These four milestones structure the poem: the initial argument, the mourning which arms Achilles, the decisive duel, then the scene of rediscovered humanity.
items: Dispute between Achilles and Agamemnon
Death of Patroclus
Death of Hector
Meeting between Priam and Achilles

quiz.question: True or false: the Iliad ends with the episode of the Trojan horse.
quiz.explanation: The poem ends with Hector's funeral; the Trojan horse is not there.

title: Oedipus Rex, Sophocles
description: Oedipus wants to save Thebes from a plague. As he investigates, he discovers that he is the guilty man. Sophocles invents the tragedy in which knowing means destroying yourself.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What plague strikes Thebes at the beginning of the play?
quiz.explanation: Thebes is struck by a plague, and the oracle demands that the murderer of the former king Laius be punished.

quiz.question: What does Oedipus promise the city of Thebes?
quiz.explanation: Oedipus promises to find the murderer of Laius, without knowing that he will find him in himself.
options: Find and punish the murderer of Laius

quiz.question: True or false: Sophocles refines the tragedy inherited from Aeschylus by adding more characters and psychological tension.
quiz.explanation: Sophocles evolves the tragic genre by giving more space to the characters and their inner tension, the chorus remaining a commentator rather than a driving force behind the action.

quiz.question: Who does Oedipus question first in his investigation into the murder of Laius?
quiz.explanation: Oedipus first questions the soothsayer Tiresias, then his wife Jocasta, widow of Laius, before the clues close in on himself.

quiz.question: According to Aristotle, what are the two key effects that he admires in Oedipus Rex?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle admires the peripeteia, the sudden reversal of the situation, and the anagnorisis, the moment when Oedipus understands who he is.

quiz.question: What does Oedipus do when the truth completely comes out?
quiz.explanation: When the truth comes out and Jocasta commits suicide, Oedipus puts out his eyes, he who saw for the city now refusing to look at the world.
options: He immediately exiled himself without a word
He abdicates and appoints a successor

quiz.question: True or false: in Oedipus the King, the more lucidly the hero seeks the truth, the closer he comes to his own downfall.
quiz.explanation: This is the tragic irony of the play: Oedipus's desire to be just and lucid accelerates his loss rather than protecting him from it.

quiz.question: What does Oedipus mean for the city once the truth is known?
quiz.explanation: Oedipus becomes the pharmakos: the plague being the sign of an unpurified crime, he is expelled to purify the city.
options: The pharmakos, the one who is expelled to purify the community
A king who is celebrated as a savior
A judge responsible for punishing other culprits

quiz.question: Which 20th century thinker rereads the myth of Oedipus through psychoanalysis?
quiz.explanation: Freud sees in the Oedipus myth the complex that bears his name, one reading among others of the broader scope of the play.

title: Antigone, Sophocles
description: Antigone buries her brother against the order of King Creon. Between the law of the city and duty to family, Sophocles sets up a conflict that has never aged.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What does Creon refuse to grant to one of the two brothers who died killing each other?
quiz.explanation: Creon orders one of the brothers to be honored and the other to be left unburied, which Antigone refuses.

quiz.question: What does Antigone do against King Creon's order?
quiz.explanation: Antigone refuses Creon's decree and herself buries the body of her brother who remains unburied.
options: She demands arbitration from the gods at the temple

quiz.question: True or false: Antigone is the daughter of Oedipus.
quiz.explanation: Antigone belongs to Oedipus' cursed family, which weighs on the entire play.

quiz.question: What conflict of values ​​does Antigone oppose to Creon?
quiz.explanation: Antigone invokes a law older than the royal decree, while Creon defends the positive law he has just decreed.
options: The natural law of duties towards the dead against the positive law of the city

quiz.question: Who is Haemon in the play?
quiz.explanation: Haemon, son of Creon and fiancé of Antigone, begs his father in vain to renounce the sentence.
options: A guard who discovers Antigone's crime

quiz.question: What flaw in Creon does Sophocles highlight through his decision to be stubborn?
quiz.explanation: Creon persists despite pleas, embodying hubris, the excess which blinds and leads to catastrophe.
options: Hubris, the proud excess that blinds
Cowardice in front of the people

quiz.question: True or false: when Creon finally gives in and renounces his decision, there is still time to save everyone.
quiz.explanation: Creon gives in too late: Antigone, then Haemon and Queen Eurydice die despite his change of mind.

quiz.question: How does Antigone's sister, Ismene, react to Creon's decree?
quiz.explanation: Ismene hesitates in the face of the royal ban, while Antigone openly accepts her action.
options: She hesitates, unlike Antigone who chooses the act
She denounces her sister to the king
She buries the body in its place
She takes up arms against Creon

quiz.question: Which 19th century philosopher reads in Antigone a conflict between two equally legitimate rights?
quiz.explanation: Hegel analyzes the play as the confrontation of two legitimate rights, public order and family piety, without either being entirely wrong.

title: The Symposium, Plato
description: Around an Athenian dinner, the guests take turns defining love. Aristophanes tells the story of the androgynes, Socrates lifts desire toward the Beautiful. Plato turns a party into philosophy.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: In what context does the dialogue of the Banquet take place?
quiz.explanation: The Banquet takes place during a symposion, a citizen's meal where people drink, discuss and compete in eloquence.
options: A meal of Athenian citizens, a symposion
A temple during a religious ceremony

quiz.question: What theme should the guests of the Banquet address in their speeches?
quiz.explanation: The imposed theme of the evening is Eros, and each guest offers their own theory of love.
options: Death and the immortality of the soul

quiz.question: What do the androgynes say in Aristophanes' speech?
quiz.explanation: Aristophanes says that humans were once double and that Zeus cut them in two to punish them, each seeking their lost half ever since.
options: Humans were once double, before Zeus cut them in two
The gods created humanity from clay
Men are descended from a single immortal ancestor

quiz.question: True or false: Aristophanes' myth of androgynes gave French the expression "soulmate".
quiz.explanation: This story of humans cut in two inspired the French expression “soulmate”, designating the half that we are trying to find.

quiz.question: Who teaches Socrates the theory of love as an intermediary, or daimon?
quiz.explanation: Socrates reports the teaching of Diotima, a wise foreigner, that Eros is a daimon, a go-between who desires what he lacks.

quiz.question: According to the teaching of Diotima, through what stages does the lover progress?
quiz.explanation: The lover starts from the beautiful body, moves on to beautiful souls, then to beautiful actions, before reaching Beauty in oneself: this is the scale of Platonic Eros.
options: From beautiful bodies to beautiful souls, then to beautiful actions, until Beauty in itself
From friendship to hatred to forgiveness
From marriage to solitude then to wisdom
From wealth to poverty to virtue

quiz.question: Who bursts in, drunk, at the end of the Symposium to praise Socrates?
quiz.explanation: Alcibiades, a drunken ambitious young man, bursts in and praises Socrates as a troubling Satyr, showing that philosophical desire does not abolish trouble.

quiz.question: True or false: in everyday language, “platonic” love has the same meaning as for Plato himself.
quiz.explanation: In everyday language, “platonic” means without flesh, while in Plato the body remains a legitimate starting point, not a shame.

title: The Republic, Plato
description: To define justice, Plato imagines an ideal city and the myth of the cave. The Republic is not an election platform: it is an inquiry into the soul and into power.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What central question does Plato seek to resolve in the Republic?
quiz.explanation: The Republic starts from a simple question: what is justice? To answer this, Socrates imagines an ideal city.
options: What is the origin of the gods?

quiz.question: How does Plato divide the human soul in the Republic?
quiz.explanation: Plato distinguishes desire (Epithumia), courage (Thumos) and reason (Logos), which he puts in parallel with the three classes of the ideal city.
options: In three parts: desire, courage and reason
In two parts: body and mind

quiz.question: Who should govern the ideal city, according to Plato?
quiz.explanation: The ideal rulers are the philosopher-kings, long trained in mathematics and dialectics, living without excessive private property.
options: The philosopher-kings, who love truth more than power

quiz.question: True or false: Plato trusts Athenian democracy as the best possible regime.
quiz.explanation: Plato, on the contrary, is wary of Athenian democracy, which according to him condemned Socrates, a just man.

quiz.question: What do the chained prisoners see in the myth of the cave?
quiz.explanation: Prisoners of myth only see shadows on a wall, mistaking these illusions for the only reality they know.
options: Only shadows cast on a wall
Their own reflection in the water

quiz.question: What happens when a freed prisoner returns to warn the others, in the myth of the cave?
quiz.explanation: The freed prisoner who returns to announce what he saw to the sun is treated as crazy by those who remain in chains.
options: Everyone immediately follows him towards the exit
He is named king of the cave
The others thank him and go out with him

quiz.question: Which 20th century philosopher accuses the Republic of announcing totalitarianism?
quiz.explanation: Karl Popper accuses the Republic of opening the way to totalitarianism, while others see it more as an educational utopia.

quiz.question: Put these political regimes back in the order of degeneration described by Plato.
quiz.explanation: Plato describes a progressive degeneration of regimes, each one born from the vices of the previous one, from aristocracy to tyranny.
items: Aristocracy
Timocracy
Oligarchy
Democracy
Tyranny

quiz.question: According to the theory of Ideas, what is the sensible world we perceive?
quiz.explanation: For Plato, the world we sense is only a shadow of the world of Ideas — that's what the cave myth is getting at.
options: A shadow of the real world of Ideas
A perfect creation of the gods

title: The Apology of Socrates, Plato
description: In 399 BC, Athens put Socrates on trial. Accused of corrupting the young, he refused to plead for pity. Plato fixed the founding scene of Western philosophy.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: In what year was Socrates tried and sentenced to death in Athens?
quiz.explanation: Socrates was tried and convicted in 399 BC, a trial that became the founding scene of Western philosophy.

quiz.question: What is Socrates accused of during his trial?
quiz.explanation: Socrates is accused of not honoring the gods of the city and of corrupting the youth with his speeches.
options: Not to honor the gods of the city and to corrupt the young
For having insulted a magistrate in public

quiz.question: True or false: in court, Socrates pleads for mercy to obtain clemency from the judges.
quiz.explanation: Socrates refuses to play the repentant accused: he transforms the tribunal into an examination of the city itself rather than pleading for mercy.

quiz.question: What does the oracle of Delphi reveal to Socrates, according to his own account?
quiz.explanation: The Oracle of Delphi states that no one is wiser than Socrates, who then understands that his wisdom consists of knowing that he does not know.
options: That no one is wiser than him
That he must become a sophist

quiz.question: What is Socrates' method of dialogue called, compared to childbirth?
quiz.explanation: Socratic maieutics compares dialogue to childbirth: creating clearer thoughts in the other through successive questions.

quiz.question: What does Socrates propose as a punishment after being found guilty, angering the judges?
quiz.explanation: Rather than careful exile, Socrates suggests being fed to the Prytaneus, a provocation that causes the judges to vote for death.
