options: Being fed at the Prytaneum, an honor reserved for benefactors
A fine paid by his disciples

quiz.question: Who wrote the Apology of Socrates?
quiz.explanation: The Apology is written by Plato, a disciple of Socrates, who depicts the trial of his master.

quiz.question: True or false: depending on the course, Socrates is clearly distinguished from the sophists, although public opinion sometimes confuses them.
quiz.explanation: The sophists are paid teachers of rhetoric from whom Socrates stands out, even if Athenian opinion tends to mix them.

title: The Poetics, Aristotle
description: Aristotle analyzes Greek tragedy and coins words that are still everywhere: mimesis, catharsis, peripeteia. The Poetics is the first great instruction manual for storytelling.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What does Aristotle seek to analyze in the Poetics?
quiz.explanation: Poetics analyzes tragedy and seeks to understand how a story produces fear and pity, and why this effect makes us feel good.
options: How tragedy creates fear and pity, and why it makes us feel good
How to compose a political speech
How to found an ideal city
How to conduct a judicial investigation

quiz.question: How does Aristotle name the artistic imitation that he rehabilitates in the face of Plato's distrust of images?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle rehabilitates mimesis, artistic imitation, which he compares to the way a child imitates to understand the world.

quiz.question: True or false: for Aristotle, tragedy must above all respect the documentary accuracy of real facts.
quiz.explanation: For Aristotle, the criterion is not the true documentary but the probable and the necessary, what had to happen in this story.

quiz.question: What does catharsis mean according to Aristotle?
quiz.explanation: Catharsis refers to the way in which tragedy orders our affects of pity and fear, even if the exact meaning of the term remains debated.
options: A form of purification of the emotions of pity and fear
A memory exercise for the actors
A religious ritual before the performance

quiz.question: According to Aristotle, what constitutes the heart of the drama, more than the characters?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle places the muthos, the intrigue, at the heart of the drama, valuing the adventure and the recognition more than the characters themselves.

quiz.question: Which play does Aristotle cite as a star example of peripeteia and recognition?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle takes Oedipus the King as a star example: the hero discovers too late who he is, in an exemplary reversal.

quiz.question: What type of hero does Aristotle prefer for a successful tragedy?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle prefers an error, hamartia, to pure wickedness: the hero is neither perfectly good nor monstrous, which makes his fall logical and terrible.
options: A hero who makes a mistake, neither perfectly good nor monstrous
A perfectly virtuous hero punished without reason
A totally evil hero who receives his punishment
A hero absent from the main action

quiz.question: True or false: according to Aristotle, poetry says the particular while history says the general.
quiz.explanation: It's the opposite: for Aristotle, poetry speaks of the general, while history speaks of the particular.

title: Works and Days, Hesiod
description: Hesiod speaks to his brother Perses: work, be just, beware of excess. Between the myth of Pandora and a farming calendar, an ethic of labor is born.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: To whom does Hesiod address his poem Works and Days?
quiz.explanation: The poem is addressed to Perses, Hesiod's brother, accused of having cheated on the division of an inheritance.

quiz.question: True or false: unlike Homer, a vague figure, Hesiod portrays himself in his poem.
quiz.explanation: Hesiod speaks of his village, his father who came from Asia Minor and his trial against Perses, a personal voice which contrasts with the anonymity of the Homeric bard.

quiz.question: What does Prometheus do in the myth told by Hesiod to explain the harshness of life?
quiz.explanation: Hesiod relates that Prometheus steals fire, a gesture that results in divine punishment and helps explain the harshness of the human condition.
options: He creates the first men in clay

quiz.question: What does Pandora's jar release, according to the myth told by Hesiod?
quiz.explanation: Pandora's jar releases the evils that have since struck humanity.

quiz.question: According to the five ages of humanity described by Hesiod, what age are we living in?
quiz.explanation: Hesiod places his time in the Iron Age, the last and worst of the five ages, where justice falters.
options: The Iron Age, the worst, where justice wavers
The Silver Age, peaceful and long
The age of heroes, glorious and just

quiz.question: What other poem, attributed to Hesiod, tells of the birth of the gods?
quiz.explanation: The Theogony, another poem by Hesiod, tells of the birth of the gods, while Works and Days descend from heaven to the plow.

quiz.question: What moral opposition structures the heart of the poem?
quiz.explanation: The poem opposes Dikè, justice, to Hubris, arrogant excess: unjust kings are threatened by Zeus, while the honest peasant has a chance.
options: Dikè, justice, against Hybris, arrogant excess

quiz.question: Which Latin poet would later draw inspiration from Works and Days in his Georgics?
quiz.explanation: Virgil will remember Hesiod's poem in his Georgics, another great poetic text devoted to agricultural life.

quiz.question: True or false: according to Hesiod, any form of rivalry between neighbors is bad and should be avoided.
quiz.explanation: Hesiod distinguishes the good Eris, a useful rivalry which pushes one to work better, from the bad Eris, that of hatred and trial.

title: Medea, Euripides
description: Jason leaves Medea for a princess. She kills their children. Euripides creates a heroine who is terrifying, brilliant and foreign: passion turns into reasoning.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Why does Jason leave Medea in Corinth?
quiz.explanation: In Corinth, Jason abandons Medea to marry the king's daughter, which triggers Medea's vengeance.
options: To marry the daughter of the king of Corinth
Because she lost her magical powers

quiz.question: What did Medea bring to Jason before he divorced her?
quiz.explanation: Without Medea's spells, Jason would never have obtained the Golden Fleece: Euripides insists on the ingratitude of "civilized" man.
options: His magical help in obtaining the Golden Fleece

quiz.question: True or false: in the eyes of the Greeks, Medea is considered a Barbarian, foreign to the Hellenic world.
quiz.explanation: Medea comes from Colchis, outside the Greek world, and this status as a foreigner becomes central when Jason repudiates her.

quiz.question: How does Euripides represent Medea's decision to kill her children?
quiz.explanation: Medea hesitates, but her decision to kill her children is explained in a lucid speech: it is not a silent act of madness.
options: Like a lucid choice, presented in a thoughtful speech
Like a direct order from the gods
Like an act immediately regretted and canceled

quiz.question: How does the play end for Medea?
quiz.explanation: A deus ex machina allows Medea to escape on a winged chariot sent by her grandfather the Sun, without immediate punishment.
options: She escapes on a winged chariot sent by her grandfather the Sun
It is publicly executed in Corinth
She commits suicide like Jocasta in Oedipus the King
She is forgiven by Jason and remains in Corinth

quiz.question: True or false: depending on the course, Euripides is clearly trying to excuse Medea's action.
quiz.explanation: Euripides does not excuse infanticide, but he forces the audience to hear the voice of the person who commits it.

quiz.question: How is Euripides considered the most “modern” of the three great Greek tragedians?
quiz.explanation: Alongside Aeschylus and Sophocles, Euripides explores the interiority of characters who doubt and contradict themselves, which makes him read as a psychological genius.
options: It explores the interiority of characters who doubt and contradict themselves
He avoids any dialogue in favor of pure action
He abandons the chorus in all his pieces

quiz.question: Beyond personal vengeance against Jason, what does Medea also destroy by killing her children, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: By destroying her own lineage, Medea also harms the future of the city, a political cost that the course underlines.
options: The future of the lineage, with a political cost for the city

title: Les Misérables, Victor Hugo
description: Jean Valjean looks for redemption in a France that refuses to forgive him. Hugo mixes love story, historical chronicle and a plea for the outcast.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: For what crime was Jean Valjean sentenced to prison for nineteen years?
quiz.explanation: Valjean is convicted of stealing a piece of bread and spends nineteen years in prison before his release.
options: The theft of a piece of bread

quiz.question: Who offers Valjean a second chance by making him believe that he received his silverware as a gift?
quiz.explanation: Bishop Myriel offers Valjean a second chance by letting him believe that he received his silverware as a gift, rather than reporting him for theft.

quiz.question: Under what identity does Valjean become mayor and philanthropic industrialist?
quiz.explanation: Under the identity of Monsieur Madeleine, Valjean becomes a philanthropic mayor, before Javert ends up recognizing him.

quiz.question: True or false: Inspector Javert embodies in the novel a merciless justice who relentlessly hunts down Valjean.
quiz.explanation: Javert represents an inflexible justice, incapable of reconciling law and grace, which will lead him to suicide.

quiz.question: Why does Fantine sink into poverty?
quiz.explanation: Fantine becomes impoverished and sacrifices herself to pay the pension of her daughter Cosette, left in the hands of the Thénardiers.
options: To pay for her daughter Cosette's keep, entrusted to the Thénardiers
To pay off a gambling debt
To flee the police after a theft

quiz.question: What Parisian historical event structures the climax of the novel?
quiz.explanation: The story shifts to Paris with the insurrection of June 1832, led by the republican youth of the Friends of the ABC.

quiz.question: Who dies on the barricades, becoming a symbol of sacrificed innocence?
quiz.explanation: Gavroche, a street child, dies on the barricades and becomes the symbol of innocence sacrificed by the violence of History.

quiz.question: True or false: Inspector Javert ends up committing suicide, unable to reconcile law and grace after being saved by Valjean.
quiz.explanation: Saved by Valjean, Javert cannot reconcile his attachment to the law with the grace he has just received, and commits suicide.

quiz.question: Put these stages in the story of Les Misérables in order.
quiz.explanation: Hugo began the novel in 1845, took up the manuscript in exile after the coup d'état of 1851, before the book appeared in Brussels in 1862.
items: Hugo begins writing the novel under the title “Les Misères”
The coup d’état interrupts and then restarts writing in exile
The novel finally appears in Brussels

quiz.question: In what year was Les Misérables finally published, after seventeen years of work?
quiz.explanation: Les Misérables appeared in 1862 in Brussels, after seventeen years of work begun in 1845.

title: Madame Bovary, Flaubert
description: Emma Bovary confuses real life with the romantic novels she has read. Flaubert invents the modern novel, and the trial that makes it famous.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Who is the author of Madame Bovary?
quiz.explanation: Gustave Flaubert published Madame Bovary in 1857, marking the birth of modern realism.

quiz.question: Who does Emma marry at the beginning of the novel?
quiz.explanation: Emma marries Charles Bovary, an honest but dull provincial doctor, with whom she settles in Yonville.

quiz.question: What narrative process does Flaubert invent in this novel, mixing the voice of the narrator with that of a character without quotation marks?
quiz.explanation: Flaubert invents the free indirect style: the narrator's voice merges with that of Emma, ​​while maintaining an ironic distance.

quiz.question: True or false: Flaubert was convicted during his 1857 trial for Madame Bovary.
quiz.explanation: Flaubert was acquitted in 1857 of the charge of “offending public morals.”

quiz.question: What pushes Emma towards dreams and adultery, according to the novel?
quiz.explanation: Raised in a convent with sentimental novels, Emma confuses real life with the fiction she read, which fuels her dissatisfaction.
options: The sentimental novels she read at the convent

quiz.question: Who pushes Emma into debt by selling her goods on credit?
quiz.explanation: The merchant Lheureux pushes Emma to get into more and more debt, until the couple's financial ruin.

quiz.question: How does Emma kill herself at the end of the novel?
quiz.explanation: Emma commits suicide with arsenic that she steals from the apothecary Homais, unable to cope with her debts and her disillusionment.
options: She swallows arsenic stolen from the apothecary Homais

quiz.question: How many years did Flaubert spend writing Madame Bovary?
quiz.explanation: Flaubert isolated himself in Croisset and devoted five years, from 1851 to 1856, to writing this novel.

quiz.question: What term did the philosopher Jules de Gaultier coin to designate Emma's chronic dissatisfaction?
quiz.explanation: Jules de Gaultier coined the term “bovaryism” to designate the dissatisfaction of someone who prefers fantasy to reality.

title: The Red and the Black, Stendhal
description: Julien Sorel, a carpenter's son, wants to rise in a France that is closed to him. Stendhal invents the modern psychological novel.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Who is the author of The Red and the Black, whose real name is Henri Beyle?
quiz.explanation: Stendhal, whose real name was Henri Beyle, published The Red and the Black in 1830.

quiz.question: What is the social origin of Julien Sorel, the hero of the novel?
quiz.explanation: Julien Sorel, the son of a despised carpenter, has rare intelligence and dreams of rising in a society closed to him.
options: Son of a carpenter, he wants to rise in society

quiz.question: What do the red and black in the title symbolize?
quiz.explanation: The red of the military uniform and the black of church dress were, under the Restoration, the only paths to power for an educated commoner.
options: The military uniform and ecclesiastical dress, the only paths to ascension for a commoner

quiz.question: True or false: Stendhal calls his dry and unemphatic style “Beylism”.
quiz.explanation: Stendhal claims a dry style influenced by his military career, which he himself calls Beylism.

quiz.question: Who does Julien become a tutor for, in Verrières?
quiz.explanation: Julien entered the seminary then became tutor to the children of Mr. and Mrs. de Rênal, in Verrières.
options: At the Marquis de La Mole
At the home of a rich merchant

quiz.question: In Paris, who does Julien seduce into the service of the Marquis de La Mole?
quiz.explanation: Julien becomes secretary to the Marquis de La Mole and seduces his daughter Mathilde, a proud aristocrat who loves danger.

quiz.question: What causes Julien's final downfall?
quiz.explanation: As Julien prepares to marry Mathilde, a letter from Madame de Rênal reveals his past lies and breaks his rise.
options: A letter from Madame de Rênal denouncing her lies
A lost duel against a rival

quiz.question: What real news story inspired the plot of the novel?
quiz.explanation: Stendhal is inspired by the case of Antoine Berthet, a seminarian sentenced to death in 1827.
options: The Antoine Berthet affair, seminarian sentenced to death
The assassination of the Duke of Berry

quiz.question: In what year was The Red and the Black published?
quiz.explanation: The novel appeared in 1830, shortly before the Trois Glorieuses.

quiz.question: True or false: faced with death, Julien redoubles his efforts to escape the scaffold by trickery.
quiz.explanation: In prison, Julien stops calculating: faced with death, he refuses to save his head through intrigue and accepts his destiny.

title: Candide, Voltaire
description: Candide crosses a cruel world still believing that all is for the best. Voltaire demolishes the optimism of Leibniz with relentless irony.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Who is the author of Candide?
quiz.explanation: Voltaire published Candide ou l'Optimisme in 1759, a masterpiece of philosophical tale.

quiz.question: What real event in 1755 shocked Voltaire and fueled the writing of Candide?
quiz.explanation: The Lisbon earthquake of November 1, 1755, which killed around 60,000 people, shattered Voltaire's confidence in a perfectly ordered world.

quiz.question: What philosophical theory does Voltaire attack through the character of Pangloss?
quiz.explanation: Pangloss is a caricature of Leibniz: Voltaire attacks the idea that all evil is the condition of a superior good.

quiz.question: True or false: according to Pangloss, every event, even terrible, has a beneficial cause.
quiz.explanation: Pangloss claims that every event, no matter how atrocious, has a beneficial cause, going so far as to say that syphilis is essential for chocolate.

quiz.question: Why is Candide chased out of the castle at the beginning of the story?
quiz.explanation: Candide is kicked out of the castle for having loved Cunégonde, the baron's daughter, which triggers his wandering around the world.

quiz.question: What does Eldorado demonstrate in the story?
quiz.explanation: Eldorado, a rational South American utopia, proves that optimism can work, but Candide leaves it all the same to find Cunégonde.
options: That optimism can work in a rational society
That money always makes you happy
That religion is essential to happiness
That war is necessary for progress

quiz.question: What pushes the fate of the “Negro from Surinam”, a slave mutilated for European sugar, Candide to do?
quiz.explanation: Faced with this mutilated slave, Candide finally defines optimism as “the rage to maintain that everything is good when one is bad”.
options: Define optimism as “the rage to maintain that everything is good when we are bad”

quiz.question: What famous sentence concludes the tale?
quiz.explanation: The tale ends with “We must cultivate our garden”: Voltaire abandons metaphysical speculation in favor of concrete action.

quiz.question: In what year was Candide published?
quiz.explanation: Candide appeared in 1759, without author's name, four years after the Lisbon earthquake.

quiz.question: True or false: Candide is banned by the Parliament of Paris but still circulates clandestinely.
quiz.explanation: Despite the ban by the Parliament of Paris, the tale circulated underground, with more than 20,000 copies in the first year.

title: The Confessions, Rousseau
description: Rousseau tells his own life with an honesty nobody had risked before. The Confessions invent modern autobiography and open the way to Romanticism.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Who wrote The Confessions?
quiz.explanation: Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote The Confessions, published after his death between 1782 and 1789.

quiz.question: What literary genre did The Confessions invent?
quiz.explanation: The Confessions mark the birth of modern autobiography: the “me” becomes the object of literary investigation.

quiz.question: According to Rousseau's autobiographical pact, why does he tell his life story?
quiz.explanation: Rousseau writes: “I am forming a company which never had an example”; he tells his life for its own sake, not to glorify History.
options: For itself, not to glorify History through it
To obtain forgiveness from the Church

quiz.question: True or false: as in Augustine's Confessions, the judge of confession remains God in Rousseau.
quiz.explanation: Unlike Augustine, the judge is no longer God but the reader: Rousseau secularizes confession and invents authenticity as the supreme value.

quiz.question: What nickname does Rousseau give to Madame de Warens?
quiz.explanation: Rousseau calls Madame de Warens “Mama”, a relationship which profoundly marks his youth.

quiz.question: What does Rousseau confess about his five children?
quiz.explanation: Rousseau admits to having abandoned his five children to the Foundlings, a painful admission at the heart of his sincerity enterprise.
options: He abandoned them to the Foundlings
He sent them to study abroad
He entrusted them to his sister

quiz.question: Who publicly revealed, in an anonymous pamphlet, the abandonment of Rousseau's children?
quiz.explanation: Voltaire reveals in an anonymous pamphlet the abandonment of Rousseau's children, forcing him to make a public confession in Confessions.

quiz.question: What role does nature play in The Confessions?
quiz.explanation: For Rousseau, the landscape becomes the mirror of a new sensitivity, which will become the basis of romanticism.
options: It becomes the mirror of a new sensitivity, at the source of romanticism
It serves as simple, unimportant decoration.

quiz.question: True or false: The Confessions were published during Rousseau's lifetime.
quiz.explanation: The Confessions were published posthumously, between 1782 and 1789, after Rousseau's death in 1778.

title: The Stranger, Camus
description: Meursault does not cry at his mother's funeral. In 123 pages of stripped-down prose, Camus invents the absurd.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Who is the author of The Stranger?
quiz.explanation: Albert Camus published The Stranger in 1942, his first novel.

quiz.question: What is the job of Meursault, the narrator of the novel?
quiz.explanation: Meursault is an office worker in Algiers, whose indifference to conventions leads to his downfall.

quiz.question: What does Meursault refuse to do, at his mother's funeral and in his relationship with Marie?
quiz.explanation: Meursault refuses to lie about his feelings, living the present and his physical sensations more than the expected morality.

quiz.question: Under what circumstances does Meursault kill a man on the beach?
quiz.explanation: Dazzled by the sun on the beach, Meursault shoots a man in a gesture that the novel presents as a tragic coincidence, without hatred or revenge.
options: Dazzled by the sun, in a gesture without hatred or revenge
By accident, while handling a weapon

quiz.question: What does the prosecutor also accuse Meursault of during the trial?
quiz.explanation: The prosecutor accuses Meursault of having drunk café au lait in front of his mother's coffin and of going to the cinema the day after the funeral.
options: For drinking coffee with milk in front of his mother's coffin

quiz.question: True or false: Meursault is condemned only for the murder he committed.
quiz.explanation: Society especially condemns Meursault for refusing collective rituals, as if he had buried his mother "with the heart of a criminal".

quiz.question: What philosophical concept does the novel put into fiction?
quiz.explanation: The Stranger turns Camus's absurd into fiction: the split between our demand for meaning and the silence of the world.

quiz.question: True or false: for Camus, the absurd must lead to nihilism and renunciation.
quiz.explanation: For Camus, the absurd does not lead to nihilism but to revolt: it is about living despite the absence of meaning.

quiz.question: At what age did Camus receive the Nobel Prize for Literature?
quiz.explanation: Camus received the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1957, at the age of 44.

quiz.question: Which contemporary Algerian writer rereads The Stranger from the point of view of the anonymous victim, in “Meursault, counter-investigation”?
quiz.explanation: Kamel Daoud rereads The Stranger from the point of view of the anonymous victim in his novel “Meursault, contre-investigation”.

title: The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus
description: Camus starts from suicide in order to define the absurd. Sisyphus, condemned to roll a rock forever, becomes the hero of a clear-eyed joy.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Who is the author of The Myth of Sisyphus?
quiz.explanation: Albert Camus published The Myth of Sisyphus in 1942, a founding essay on the thought of the absurd.

quiz.question: With what famous statement does Camus open his essay?
quiz.explanation: Camus opens his essay by asserting that the only truly serious philosophical problem is judging whether life is worth living.
options: “There is only one really serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide”

quiz.question: Where does the absurd reside, according to Camus?
quiz.explanation: For Camus, the absurd is neither in the world nor in man alone, but in their confrontation: the mind aspires to order, the world remains silent.
options: In the confrontation between the human aspiration for order and the silence of the world
Only in the chaos of the outside world
In the total absence of reason in man

quiz.question: What, according to Camus, is the only authentic response to the absurd?
quiz.explanation: The only authentic response is absurd revolt: standing in the face of the silence of the world, without consolation or escape.

quiz.question: True or false: for Camus, philosophical suicide consists of fleeing towards faith or the irrational.
quiz.explanation: Philosophical suicide, or “leap” according to Kierkegaard, flees the absurd towards faith or the irrational rather than confronting it.

quiz.question: Why is Sisyphus condemned, in the Greek myth taken up by Camus?
quiz.explanation: Sisyphus, king of Corinth, is condemned to eternally roll a rock to the top, from where it always comes back down.
options: To roll forever a rock that always comes back down
To carry the world on his shoulders
To wander endlessly far from his kingdom

quiz.question: At what precise moment is Camus interested in the myth of Sisyphus?
quiz.explanation: Camus is interested in the moment of descent: Sisyphus is superior to his destiny because he is fully aware of it.
options: At the moment of descent, when Sisyphus is aware of his destiny
When Sisyphus pushes the rock upwards
At the time of his condemnation by the gods
At the time of his death

quiz.question: What famous sentence concludes the essay?
quiz.explanation: The essay concludes with “We must imagine Sisyphus happy”: a happiness that is born from lucidity and acceptance of the struggle.

quiz.question: Which playwrights of the theater of the absurd does Camus influence?
quiz.explanation: The Myth of Sisyphus influences the theater of the absurd by Samuel Beckett and Eugène Ionesco, where the characters rotate in a loop.

title: In Search of Lost Time, Proust
description: Seven volumes, 1.5 million words: Proust explores involuntary memory and makes time the main character of the novel.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Who is the author of In Search of Lost Time?
quiz.explanation: Marcel Proust wrote In Search of Lost Time between 1913 and 1927.

quiz.question: What type of memory, triggered by a sensation, does Proust place at the center of the novel?
quiz.explanation: Proust distinguishes voluntary, cold memory from involuntary memory, provoked by a sensation and which resurrects the past in its emotional entirety.

quiz.question: What food dipped in tea triggers the most famous memory in the novel?
quiz.explanation: The madeleine dipped in tea brings back to life in the narrator all the emotional memories of Combray.

quiz.question: Why does Proust line his room with cork?
quiz.explanation: Proust isolated himself after the death of his mother and lined his room with cork to protect himself from noise and pollen.
options: To protect against noise and pollen
To insulate your manuscripts from humidity

quiz.question: True or false: the first volume, On the Side of Swann, was immediately accepted by the publishers.
quiz.explanation: On the side of Swann suffered several refusals and had to be published independently in 1913.

quiz.question: Which writer later admits to having made a serious error by refusing Proust's manuscript?
quiz.explanation: André Gide, who had disdained the manuscript, would later admit to having made a serious error.

quiz.question: What does the seventh and final volume reveal to the narrator?
quiz.explanation: Time Recovered reveals to the narrator his vocation as a writer: to write the work that the reader has just read.
options: His vocation as a writer, that of writing the work that we have just read
A family secret hidden since childhood

quiz.question: How many volumes does In Search of Lost Time have?
quiz.explanation: The novel has seven volumes, published between 1913 and 1927.

quiz.question: Which character introduces hitherto taboo themes into the novel?
quiz.explanation: Monsieur de Charlus introduces themes that were previously taboo in literature in La Recherche.

quiz.question: What literary prize did Proust receive in 1919?
quiz.explanation: Proust received the Goncourt Prize in 1919 for In the Shadow of Young Girls in Flowers.

title: Père Goriot, Balzac
description: Goriot gives up everything for two ungrateful daughters. Rastignac learns Paris at the expense of an old man and a convict. Balzac invents The Human Comedy.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Who is the author of Père Goriot?
quiz.explanation: Honoré de Balzac published Père Goriot in 1835.

quiz.question: To which romantic group does Father Goriot belong?
quiz.explanation: Father Goriot is the pivot of the Comédie humaine, where Balzac introduces for the first time the return of recurring characters.

quiz.question: For whom does Father Goriot sacrifice all his fortune?
quiz.explanation: A former vermicelli maker, Goriot sacrificed everything for his daughters Anastasie and Delphine, who abandoned him once they got rich.

quiz.question: Where does Father Goriot live, while his resources are running out?
quiz.explanation: Goriot descends from floor to floor at the Vauquer pension as his resources become exhausted, up to the most modest room.

quiz.question: True or false: Goriot's daughters remained at his bedside until his death.
quiz.explanation: His daughters only come back to ask for money and go to the ball while their father dies alone at the boarding house.

quiz.question: Who is Vautrin, a character who proposes a cynical pact to Rastignac?
quiz.explanation: Vautrin, whose real name is Jacques Collin, is an escaped convict who offers Rastignac to make his fortune through murder.
options: An escaped convict, real name Jacques Collin

quiz.question: What does Vautrin offer in Rastignac to make a fortune quickly?
quiz.explanation: Vautrin offers Rastignac a cynical pact: to make a fortune by organizing a murder, which Rastignac ends up refusing.
options: Steal from the Vauquer pension fund

quiz.question: What does Rastignac say from the Père-Lachaise cemetery at the end of the novel?
quiz.explanation: From Père-Lachaise, after the death of Goriot, Rastignac launched his challenge to Paris: “Now it’s both of us!” »

quiz.question: What novelistic technique does Balzac inaugurate with this novel?
quiz.explanation: Father Goriot inaugurates in the Comédie humaine the return of the characters, who reappear from one novel to another.
options: The return of characters from one novel to another

quiz.question: How many characters does Balzac aim to create in the entire Comédie humaine?
quiz.explanation: Balzac wants to archive all the social types of his time through 90 novels and around 2,000 characters.

title: Les Fleurs du Mal, Baudelaire
description: Baudelaire draws beauty out of evil and out of everyday life in Paris. Condemned in 1857, Les Fleurs du Mal founded modern poetry.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Who is the author of Les Fleurs du Mal?
quiz.explanation: Charles Baudelaire published Les Fleurs du Mal in 1857 — the birth of modern poetry.

quiz.question: Why were Les Fleurs du Mal condemned in 1857?
quiz.explanation: The collection was condemned for “offending public morals,” a scandal that was not officially lifted until 1949.
options: For endangering the security of the state

quiz.question: In what year were the six condemned poems from Les Fleurs du Mal officially rehabilitated?
quiz.explanation: The six poems condemned in 1857 were not officially rehabilitated until 1949, 92 years later.

quiz.question: What is the albatross in the “Spleen and Ideal” section?
quiz.explanation: The albatross, majestic in flight but clumsy once it lands, is the poet in a world that does not understand him.
options: The poet, majestic in flight but ridiculous on the ground

quiz.question: Which section of the collection makes Paris a psychological landscape?
quiz.explanation: “Parisian Scenes” turns the city into a psychological landscape. The poet wanders there as a flâneur, watching Parisian life under Haussmann.

quiz.question: Which poem describes nature as a “temple” of signs linking scents, colors and sounds?
quiz.explanation: “Correspondences” describes nature as a temple of signs. The senses mix there: scents, colors and sounds answer one another.

quiz.question: True or false: Baudelaire entirely rejects classical poetic forms like the sonnet.
quiz.explanation: Baudelaire, on the contrary, links the classical form, such as the sonnet and the alexandrine, to a radically new poetic vision.

quiz.question: What poetic movement did Baudelaire's correspondences found, later taken up by Verlaine and Mallarmé?
quiz.explanation: This poetics of correspondences founded Symbolism, later taken up by Verlaine and Mallarmé.

quiz.question: Which American writer, described as a “soul brother”, did Baudelaire translate?
quiz.explanation: Baudelaire translated Edgar Poe, whom he considered a “soul brother” who shared his taste for the macabre.

quiz.question: How does Baudelaire summarize his poetic alchemy of extracting beauty from mud?
quiz.explanation: Baudelaire summarizes his project with this formula: “You gave me your mud and I made gold from it”.
options: “You gave me your mud and I made gold from it”

title: 1984, George Orwell
description: Published in 1949, 1984 invented Big Brother, Newspeak, and the Ministry of Truth. Orwell describes a society where surveillance and state lies grind down the individual until he loves the tyrant.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What is George Orwell's real name?
quiz.explanation: George Orwell is the pseudonym of Eric Arthur Blair.

quiz.question: What conflict did Orwell fight before writing 1984?
quiz.explanation: Orwell fought in 1936-1937 in the POUM militias during the Spanish Civil War, where he was injured.

quiz.question: What struck Orwell the most during this experience, beyond the violence?
quiz.explanation: What strikes Orwell the most is seeing newspapers rewrite the past and erase fighters, an obsession with state lies which fuels the novel.
options: The falsification of facts and the past through propaganda

quiz.question: What real totalitarian regime inspires the Oceania system?
quiz.explanation: The Oceania system is particularly inspired by Soviet totalitarianism as a model.

quiz.question: What is the name of the single party that runs Oceania?
quiz.explanation: Oceania is run by Ingsoc, which is based on four paradoxical ministries: Peace, Abundance, Love and Truth.

quiz.question: What does Winston Smith do for work at the Ministry of Truth?
quiz.explanation: Winston Smith works at the Ministry of Truth, where he erases the past to fit the Party-defined present.
options: He erases and rewrites the past to fit the Party's present
He trains new members of the Party

quiz.question: What do you call the ability to accept two contradictory truths at once, in 1984?
quiz.explanation: Doublethink refers to the ability to accept two contradictory truths at once, a pillar of the Party's mind control.

quiz.question: Why is the Party reducing vocabulary through Newspeak?
quiz.explanation: Newspeak reduces the vocabulary available to make critical thinking itself impossible to formulate.

quiz.question: Put these stages of Orwell's life and work in order.
quiz.explanation: These four stages mark Orwell's path: the Spanish Civil War (1936–1937), Animal Farm (1945), 1984 (1949), then his death in 1950.
items: Orwell fought in the POUM militias during the Spanish Civil War
He published Animal Farm
He published 1984
He died in Scotland shortly after the novel came out

quiz.question: True or false: at the end of the novel, Winston Smith ends up loving Big Brother.
quiz.explanation: Totalitarianism wins on a psychological level: Winston not only obeys, he comes to love Big Brother.

title: Animal Farm, George Orwell
description: In 1945, Orwell tells the story of a farm where the animals drive out the farmer, then watch the pigs take his place. A crystal-clear allegory of the Russian Revolution and of a revolution betrayed.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What historical event is Animal Farm an allegory of?
quiz.explanation: Orwell turns the main stages of the Russian Revolution and Stalin's betrayal into an animal fable.

quiz.question: Which animal stands for Stalin in Orwell's allegory?
quiz.explanation: Napoleon, the pig who seizes power by force after driving Snowball out, is modeled on Stalin.

quiz.question: True or false: Publisher T.S. Eliot refused to publish Orwell's manuscript, fearing that clever pigs would offend statesmen.
quiz.explanation: T.S. Eliot, then editor, actually rejected the manuscript for this reason.

quiz.question: What are Napoleon's dogs in the allegory?
quiz.explanation: The dogs Napoleon trains to chase Snowball and terrorize the farm are the Soviet secret police.

quiz.question: Which animal embodies the proletariat exploited to the point of exhaustion?
quiz.explanation: Boxer, a devoted and tireless workhorse, stands for a proletariat that works without ever questioning authority.

quiz.question: Put these steps from Animal Farm in order.
quiz.explanation: This sequence shows the gradual shift from the egalitarian revolution towards the dictatorship of the pigs.
items: The animals chase Farmer Jones
Napoleon chases Snowball with his dogs
Pigs secretly change the Seven Commandments
Pigs start walking on two legs

quiz.question: What final formula sums up, at the end of the novel, the betrayal of the egalitarian ideal?
quiz.explanation: This paradoxical formula, inscribed on the barn wall, reveals that the proclaimed equality has been emptied of its meaning.
options: “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others”

quiz.question: True or false: at the end of the novel, the other animals are no longer able to distinguish pigs from humans.
quiz.explanation: The pigs walk on two legs, dress and banquet with the farmers, completely blurring the line between them.

quiz.question: Approximately how many words does Animal Farm have, a deliberately very short text?
quiz.explanation: Orwell delivers his allegory in barely 30,000 words, which reinforces the effectiveness of the fable.

title: Hamlet, Shakespeare
description: Around 1601, Shakespeare wrote Hamlet, a prince who hesitates after his father's murder. Between revenge, feigned madness, and the question “To be or not to be,” the modern hero of conscience is born.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Who assassinates the king of Denmark, Hamlet's father?
quiz.explanation: Claudius kills his brother, the king, then marries Queen Gertrude and takes the throne.

quiz.question: Who tells Hamlet about his father's murder?
quiz.explanation: The ghost of the deceased king appears to Hamlet to reveal Claudius' crime.

quiz.question: What strategy does Hamlet adopt to investigate the crime without revealing himself?
quiz.explanation: Hamlet feigns madness to observe the court without arousing suspicion, a strategy that ultimately fails.
options: He goes into exile in Wittenberg

quiz.question: True or false: during the reign of Elizabeth I, female roles like Ophelia were played by women on stage.
quiz.explanation: Women were banned from the stage: the female roles were played by men, often teenagers.

quiz.question: What does Hamlet enact to trap Claudius and confirm his guilt?
quiz.explanation: Hamlet puts on a play reenacting his father's murder to observe Claudius' reaction.
options: A room within a room, the “Mousetrap”

quiz.question: Who does Hamlet kill by mistake, precipitating the tragic spiral?
quiz.explanation: Hamlet kills Polonius, the king's advisor, believing he is hitting a spy hidden behind a curtain.

quiz.question: According to the medicine of the time, what explains Hamlet's melancholy?
quiz.explanation: Elizabethan medicine attributed melancholy to an excess of black bile, making the subject bright but paralyzed.

quiz.question: What reading does Freud propose of Hamlet, several centuries after Shakespeare?
quiz.explanation: Freud interprets Hamlet's hesitation through the Oedipus complex, popularizing a psychoanalytic reading of the play.
options: He sees it as an expression of the Oedipus complex
He sees it as a criticism of emerging capitalism
He sees it as a religious allegory
He sees it as a plea for the monarchy

quiz.question: True or false: the monologue “To be or not to be” has remained the most famous existential question in Western theater.
quiz.explanation: This monologue has become emblematic of the existential question in the theater, opposing action and suffering.

title: Romeo and Juliet, Shakespeare
description: Around 1595, two lovers in Verona die in less than five days. Shakespeare compresses a romance into a social tragedy: clan hatred destroys the young.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What source did Shakespeare primarily rely on to write Romeo and Juliet?
quiz.explanation: Shakespeare draws inspiration from the Italian storyteller Matteo Bandello, but compresses the action over five days to intensify the tragedy.
options: A short story by Matteo Bandello

quiz.question: Over how many days does Shakespeare condense all the action of the play?
quiz.explanation: Shakespeare tightens the plot over five days, making the final catastrophe all the more inevitable.

quiz.question: What event shifts the tone of the play from comedy to tragedy?
quiz.explanation: The death of Mercutio, killed by Tybalt, removes the carelessness and definitively shifts the play into tragedy.

quiz.question: Who celebrates the secret marriage of Romeo and Juliet, hoping to reconcile the two families?
quiz.explanation: Brother Laurent secretly marries the lovers, hoping that their union will appease the hatred between the clans.

quiz.question: What prevents Brother Lawrence's message from reaching Romeo on time?
quiz.explanation: An epidemic of plague delays the messenger responsible for warning Romeo, precipitating the final double suicide.
options: A plague epidemic that delays the messenger
The arrest of the messenger by the Prince

quiz.question: True or false: in Bandello, Shakespeare's Italian source, Juliet wakes up before Romeo dies, unlike in the play.
quiz.explanation: Shakespeare deletes this farewell present in Bandello to make the end of the play more cruel.

quiz.question: Who kills Tybalt, causing Romeo to be banished from Verona?
quiz.explanation: Romeo kills Tybalt to avenge Mercutio, which results in him being banished from the city.

quiz.question: Which 20th century work transposes the conflict of the clans of Verona to the streets of New York?
quiz.explanation: West Side Story replaces the Montagues and Capulets with the Sharks and Jets gangs.

quiz.question: True or false: Dante was already talking about the Montecchi and Cappelletti families two centuries before Shakespeare.
quiz.explanation: Dante mentions these two Veronese families in his work, long before Shakespeare made them a universal tragedy.

title: Brave New World, Aldous Huxley
description: In 1932, Huxley imagined a happy, stable future where people give up freedom for pleasure. Soma, genetic castes, and endless entertainment: the other great dystopia of the 20th century.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: How does the domination imagined by Huxley differ from that of Orwell in 1984?
quiz.explanation: Where Orwell describes police terror, Huxley imagines voluntary submission obtained through pleasure and comfort.
options: It is based on pleasure and comfort rather than terror
It is based on organized famine
It is based on a permanent war
It relies on constant police surveillance

quiz.question: What industrial model did Huxley inspire to organize his future society?
quiz.explanation: Huxley transposes the logic of assembly lines and industrial standardization to human reproduction itself.

quiz.question: True or false: the original title, Brave New World, ironically quotes a Shakespeare play.
quiz.explanation: The title quotes Shakespeare's The Tempest, whose naive wonder here masks a dehumanized future.

quiz.question: How are social castes, from Alphas to Epsilons, determined in the novel?
quiz.explanation: The Bokanovsky process allows each caste to be produced and conditioned from conception, so that it likes its condition.
options: From design, thanks to the Bokanovsky process
By an exam taken as an adult

quiz.question: What role does the soma play in this society?
quiz.explanation: Soma is a drug with no side effects that instantly dissolves any frustration or pain.
options: It's a comfort drug that removes all frustration
It is a fuel reserved for industry
It is a compulsory vaccine for everyone
It is a rationed staple food

quiz.question: Who is Savage John?
quiz.explanation: John, born outside the system on a Reserve, embodies the humanist capable of pain and ecstasy, trained by reading Shakespeare.
options: A man born naturally on a Reservation, who read Shakespeare
A rebel Alpha raised in the capital

quiz.question: What does John claim against Mustapha Mond, the World Controller?
quiz.explanation: John refuses artificial comfort and claims the right to suffer, to create and to truly love.
options: The right to possess more soma
The right to rule the world
The right to live in the capital

quiz.question: True or false: at the end of the novel, John agrees to live in comfort in Brave New World.
quiz.explanation: John refuses the soma and the artificial paradise proposed by Mond: he kills himself, with no possible reconciliation.

quiz.question: In what year did Aldous Huxley publish Brave New World?
quiz.explanation: Huxley published this novel in 1932, having written it the previous year.

title: Frankenstein, Mary Shelley
description: In 1818, an 18-year-old Mary Shelley wrote the first great science-fiction novel. Victor Frankenstein creates life, then runs from his creature: a fable about science without ethics.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What climatic event forced Mary Shelley and her friends to remain locked up at Villa Diodati in 1816?
quiz.explanation: The eruption of Tambora plunged Europe into a year without summer in 1816, forcing the group to remain cooped up on the shores of Lake Geneva.
options: The eruption of the Tambora volcano, causing a year without summer

quiz.question: Who is running the Frankenstein Scary Story Contest?
quiz.explanation: It was Lord Byron who proposed this competition to relieve boredom during the bad weather of 1816.

quiz.question: How old was Mary Shelley when she wrote Frankenstein?
quiz.explanation: Mary Shelley was only 18 years old when she wrote this novel, at the crossroads of dark romanticism and the scientific debates of her time.

quiz.question: What scientific field does Mary Shelley draw inspiration from for the awakening of the creature?
quiz.explanation: Galvanism, which seemed to animate dead matter with electricity, directly inspires the creature's creation scene.
options: Galvanism, these electrical experiments on dead matter

quiz.question: Why does Victor Frankenstein seek the secret of life in Ingolstadt?
quiz.explanation: Victor is driven by the ambition to challenge the natural order and become a creator, a “modern Prometheus”.
options: To become a modern Prometheus, not to get rich

quiz.question: How does the creature learn human language and feelings?
quiz.explanation: The creature learns alone, in secret, by observing a peasant family and reading Paradise Lost.
options: By observing a peasant family and reading Milton's Paradise Lost
By taking courses at the University of Ingolstadt

quiz.question: What does the creature ask of Victor, who refuses it?
quiz.explanation: The creature asks for a companion so that it is no longer alone; Victor's refusal triggers his destructive revenge.
options: A public pardon for his crimes

quiz.question: True or false: In the novel, the name "Frankenstein" refers to the creator, while the creature itself has no name.
quiz.explanation: The creature never has a proper name, a sign of Victor's denial of paternity: calling the monster "Frankenstein" is therefore a misinterpretation.

quiz.question: Where does the novel end, between Victor's death and the creature's disappearance?
quiz.explanation: The novel ends in the ice of the Arctic, where Victor dies and the creature disappears into the mists.

title: Crime and Punishment, Dostoyevsky
description: In 1866, Raskolnikov kills a pawnbroker to prove that he is a superman. Dostoyevsky turns the crime into a laboratory of conscience and redemption.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What does Raskolnikov do to test his “superman” theory?
quiz.explanation: Raskolnikov murders an old loan shark to check whether he belongs to the “extraordinary” beings authorized to transgress the moral law.
options: He kills a loan shark who he considers useless to society
He robs a St. Petersburg bank
He reports an innocent man to the police
He challenges a noble to a duel

quiz.question: Who does Raskolnikov also kill, without having planned it?
quiz.explanation: Raskolnikov also kills Lizaveta, who arrived by surprise, which aggravates his crime of unpremeditated murder.
options: Lizaveta, the loan shark's innocent sister

quiz.question: According to Raskolnikov's theory, who has the right to transgress the moral law?
quiz.explanation: Raskolnikov divides humanity into “ordinary” and “extraordinary,” the latter of whom can transgress the law for a higher purpose.

quiz.question: True or false: after the murder, Raskolnikov took full advantage of the money stolen from the loan shark.
quiz.explanation: Raskolnikov does not benefit from the stolen money: he discovers that his conscience cannot bear the blood shed.

quiz.question: What personal experience transformed Dostoyevsky's worldview before he wrote this novel?
quiz.explanation: A member of the Petrachevsky Circle, Dostoyevsky undergoes a mock execution then goes to the Omsk penal colony, an experience that changes his vision of the world.
options: A mock shooting followed by a prison in Siberia
A long study trip to Western Europe
A duel that he narrowly loses

quiz.question: Who is Sonia Marmeladova in the novel?
quiz.explanation: Sonia, who sacrificed herself out of love for her family, opens to Raskolnikov a path to redemption through confession rather than pride.
options: A young woman sacrificed to feed her family, which pushes Raskolnikov towards confession
The investigating judge responsible for the investigation
A childhood friend of the loan shark

quiz.question: How does judge Porfiri Petrovich treat Raskolnikov, whom he strongly suspects?
quiz.explanation: A master of forensic psychology, Porfiri Petrovich lets Raskolnikov betray himself little by little through his own conscience.
options: He guesses his guilt but lets him accuse himself
He arrests him immediately without proof
He has him tortured to obtain a confession
He ignores it completely until the trial

quiz.question: True or false: Raskolnikov discovers that he easily supports the weight of spilled blood, confirming his superman theory.
quiz.explanation: On the contrary, Raskolnikov discovers that his conscience cannot bear the crime: he is not the superman he thought he was.

quiz.question: Which intellectual movement is Dostoyevsky fighting in particular through this novel?
quiz.explanation: Returning from exile, Dostoyevsky fights the nihilism that is sweeping Russian youth in the 1860s, showing how an idea cut off from life leads to crime.

title: The Trial, Kafka
description: Josef K. is arrested one morning without being told why. Kafka describes an endless trial and an opaque bureaucracy: the word “Kafkaesque” was born from this nightmare.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What happens to Josef K. at the very beginning of the novel?
quiz.explanation: Josef K. is arrested one morning without any explanation, opening a trial whose rules he will never really understand.
options: He is arrested one morning without being explained why
He is summoned to an ordinary civil trial
He suddenly loses his job as a banker
He is publicly accused by his neighbors

quiz.question: What double life did Kafka himself lead, alongside his work?
quiz.explanation: Kafka worked for an insurance company in Prague during the day, and only wrote at night.
options: Insurance official by day, writer by night
Lawyer by day, painter by night
Teacher by day, musician by night
Doctor by day, journalist by night

quiz.question: True or false: Kafka asked his friend Max Brod to burn his manuscripts after his death.
quiz.explanation: Kafka had asked Max Brod to destroy his manuscripts; Brod refused and published The Trial in 1925.

quiz.question: In what year was The Trial published posthumously, by Max Brod?
quiz.explanation: The Trial was published in 1925, a year after Kafka's death, thanks to Max Brod who guessed the order of the chapters.

quiz.question: Where do the court hearings take place in the novel?
quiz.explanation: The court sits in the attics of ordinary buildings, a sign of justice that is both omnipresent and elusive.

quiz.question: What does the priest tell Josef K. in the cathedral?
quiz.explanation: This parable from the Law illustrates the vain expectation and the impossibility of accessing a justice that remains out of reach.
options: The parable of a man who waits all his life in front of a closed door
The story of his own religious conversion
The story of the trial of another acquitted accused
A prophecy about the outcome of his own trial

quiz.question: True or false: in his professional life, Kafka was a mediocre employee, often reprimanded by his superiors.
quiz.explanation: Ironically, Kafka was a model employee, initiating safety measures such as helmets for workers.

quiz.question: Which philosophical movement recognizes Kafka as a major precursor?
quiz.explanation: Sartre and Camus see in the absurdity of The Trial a prefiguration of 20th century existentialism.
options: The existentialism of Sartre and Camus

quiz.question: How does Josef K.'s life end at the end of the novel?
quiz.explanation: Josef K. is executed without ever having understood his accusation, only murmuring “Like a dog!” ".
options: It is performed while whispering “Like a dog!” »
He was finally acquitted by the Court
He himself becomes a judge of the court

title: Don Quixote, Cervantes
description: Don Quixote charges at windmills, convinced he is fighting giants. Cervantes invents the modern novel out of generous madness, irony, and metafiction.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What does Don Quixote think he sees when he attacks windmills?
quiz.explanation: Don Quixote, carried away by his reading of chivalric novels, takes windmills for giants to fight.

quiz.question: What personal experience marked Cervantes' life before he wrote Don Quixote?
quiz.explanation: Cervantes was wounded at Lepanto in 1571 then captured and held captive for five years in Algiers, before experiencing relative poverty in Spain.
options: He was wounded at the Battle of Lepanto then captive for five years in Algiers.
He became a priest before converting to writing
He runs a traveling theater troupe
He inherits a fortune which he loses gambling

quiz.question: True or false: in 1614, another author published a false sequel to Don Quixote, which pushed Cervantes to write the true second part.
quiz.explanation: Furious at this false sequel, Cervantes published his own second part in 1615, where the heroes discover their own celebrity.

quiz.question: What emblematic duo does Cervantes invent to contrast the ideal and the real?
quiz.explanation: Don Quixote, dreamer of chivalry, and Sancho Panza, pragmatic and attached to the stomach, form a duo that has become universal.
options: Alonso Quijano and the Knight of the White Moon

quiz.question: What process does Cervantes use to blur the line between fiction and reality?
quiz.explanation: Cervantes pretends to be only the translator of an Arabic manuscript, which calls into question the very reliability of the story.
options: He claims to translate an Arabic manuscript found in a market
He writes only in the first person like Don Quixote
He inserts real letters from readers into the story
He refuses any form of conclusion to the novel

quiz.question: In the second part of the novel, how do certain nobles make fun of Don Quixote?
quiz.explanation: Having read his published adventures, nobles orchestrate stagings to entertain themselves at the knight's expense, further blurring the line between fiction and reality.
options: They organize scenarios to deceive him, having read the first volume
They lock him up in an asylum as soon as they meet
They denounce him to the religious authorities
They hire him as a true knight in their service

quiz.question: What does the term “quixotism” mean today?
quiz.explanation: “Quixotism” designates a generous idealism which persists despite failure, inherited from the character of Cervantes.

quiz.question: How does Don Quixote's life end at the end of the novel?
quiz.explanation: Defeated by the Knight of the White Moon, Don Quixote renounces chivalry, regains his reason and dies under his real name.
options: Defeated in a duel, he regains his sanity and dies under his real name, Alonso Quijano
He dies fighting one last windmill
He becomes governor of an island with Sancho
He disappears without us knowing his fate

quiz.question: In what year did Cervantes publish the first part of Don Quixote, with immediate success?
quiz.explanation: The first part of Don Quixote was published in 1605, meeting with immediate success with the public.

title: The Grapes of Wrath, Steinbeck
description: In 1939, the Joad family leaves a drought-stricken Oklahoma behind. Steinbeck tells the story of the Okie exodus and celebrates a solidarity that stands up to injustice.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Why is the Joad family driven from their land in Oklahoma?
quiz.explanation: The Dust Bowl drought and the replacement of sharecroppers with tractors pushed the banks to evict the Joads.
options: Because of drought and agricultural mechanization
Because of a local civil war
Because of an epidemic that decimates the region

quiz.question: How did Steinbeck collect the material for his novel?
quiz.explanation: Steinbeck immerses himself in the lives of migrants and lives in makeshift camps, the Hoovervilles, to capture their language and their despair.
options: He traveled with migrants and lived in Hoovervilles
He relied solely on government reports
He drew inspiration from his childhood in the Dust Bowl

quiz.question: True or false: the title of the novel comes from a line from a song, suggested to Steinbeck by his wife Carol.
quiz.explanation: The title is taken from a line in The Battle Hymn of the Republic, an idea suggested by Steinbeck's wife Carol.

quiz.question: What iconic route does the Joad family take to flee to the West?
quiz.explanation: The Joads take Route 66, nicknamed “the escape route”, in an overloaded truck towards California.

quiz.question: What do the Joads discover when they arrive in California?
quiz.explanation: The Californian reality contradicts the leaflets: crushed wages, unsanitary camps and private militias await the migrants.
options: Crushed salaries and unsanitary camps, far from the promised dream
Fertile land and well-paid jobs for all
An abandoned region empty of any inhabitants

quiz.question: Who helps Tom Joad develop political and collective consciousness?
quiz.explanation: Contact with Jim Casy, an itinerant preacher, transforms Tom, who was initially focused solely on his survival.

quiz.question: True or false: Jim Casy dies trying to organize a union among migrant workers.
quiz.explanation: Casy dies trying to organize migrant workers, which pushes Tom to understand the collective dimension of their struggle.

quiz.question: What gesture closes the novel as a symbol of absolute solidarity?
quiz.explanation: Rose of Sharon, whose child died of malnutrition, breastfeeds an old man dying of starvation, transforming an intimate tragedy into a symbol of sharing.
options: Rose of Sharon breastfeeds a starving old man
Ma Joad distributes all her savings to neighbors
Tom Joad joins the army to protect his family
The Joads return to Oklahoma to rebuild their farm

quiz.question: In what year was The Grapes of Wrath published, in the midst of the Great Depression?
quiz.explanation: The novel was published in 1939 and won the Pulitzer Prize the following year.

title: To Kill a Mockingbird, Harper Lee
description: Scout, six years old, watches the town of Maycomb, Alabama. Between children's games and an unjust trial, Harper Lee shows moral courage facing down racism.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Who tells the story in To Kill a Mockingbird?
quiz.explanation: The novel is told through the eyes of Scout, a six-year-old girl living in Maycomb, Alabama.

quiz.question: Whom does Atticus Finch defend in court, knowing he will lose?
quiz.explanation: Atticus agrees to defend Tom Robinson despite the certainty of losing, because in the segregationist South the skin color of the accused weighs more than the evidence.
options: Tom Robinson, a black man unfairly accused
His daughter Scout, accused of theft
A lawyer friend threatened with disbarment

quiz.question: True or false: Truman Capote, Harper Lee's childhood friend in Monroeville, inspired the character of Dill.
quiz.explanation: Truman Capote, future author of In Cold Blood, was Harper Lee's childhood friend and inspiration for Dill, the boy who visits the Finches every summer.

quiz.question: What is the mockingbird that Atticus tells you not to kill?
quiz.explanation: The harmless mockingbird is Tom Robinson and Boo Radley: two beings that society hunts or turns into monsters for no reason.
options: Innocent beings like Tom Robinson and Boo Radley

quiz.question: Who secretly saves Scout and Jem at the end of the novel?
quiz.explanation: Boo Radley, the hermit feared by the entire neighborhood, saves the children and proves to be a timid man rather than a monster.

quiz.question: True or False: Despite Atticus' evidence demonstrating the physical impossibility of the crime, Tom Robinson is convicted.
quiz.explanation: Although Atticus demonstrates that Tom could not commit the crime, he is convicted: justice fails in the face of the racism of the jury.

quiz.question: Which novel, published in 2015 shortly before Harper Lee's death, turns out to be a first version written before that of 1960?
quiz.explanation: Go Set a Watchman, published in 2015, is actually a draft written before the final 1960 version.

quiz.question: What teaching does Atticus pass on to his children after the trial?
quiz.explanation: Atticus teaches empathy: understanding others requires putting yourself in their place, and true courage consists of fighting even when you know you will lose.
options: You only really know someone by putting yourself in their shoes.
We must flee Maycomb as soon as possible

quiz.question: Put these stages of the novel's career in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: The novel appeared in 1960, received the Pulitzer in 1961, then was adapted for the cinema with Gregory Peck in 1962.
items: Publication of the novel
Pulitzer Prize awarded to Harper Lee
Release of the adaptation with Gregory Peck

title: The Great Gatsby, Fitzgerald
description: Jay Gatsby throws lavish parties to win Daisy back. Fitzgerald paints the Jazz Age and the corruption of the American dream.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Who throws lavish parties to win back Daisy Buchanan?
quiz.explanation: Jay Gatsby throws fabulous parties at his West Egg mansion with the sole aim of winning back Daisy Buchanan.

quiz.question: What does the green light that Gatsby contemplates every night at the end of the platform symbolize?
quiz.explanation: The green light at the end of the Buchanans' platform symbolizes the future that Gatsby pursues without ever being able to reach it.
options: The future he pursues, always out of reach
His childhood home in the Midwest
The lighthouse that guides boats from the port

quiz.question: True or false: When it was released in 1925, The Great Gatsby was a huge commercial success.
quiz.explanation: The novel only sold around 20,000 copies upon publication; it was only after Fitzgerald's death that it became a classic.

quiz.question: Where does the fortune of Jay Gatsby, born James Gatz, son of poor farmers, come from?
quiz.explanation: Gatsby built his fortune in the alcohol trade made lucrative by Prohibition, with the sole aim of winning back Daisy.
options: Stock market speculation on Wall Street

quiz.question: Who tells the story of Gatsby, observing him with fascination and disgust?
quiz.explanation: Narrator Nick Carraway, Daisy's cousin, observes this world with both fascination for Gatsby and disgust for the cruelty of the Buchanans.

quiz.question: Who is really responsible for Myrtle Wilson's death when she was hit by a car?
quiz.explanation: Daisy accidentally kills Myrtle while driving Gatsby's car, but she leaves him to take the blame for the accident.
options: Daisy Buchanan, who lets Gatsby take the blame
Jay Gatsby, who intentionally drove towards her
Tom Buchanan, jealous of his affair

quiz.question: True or false: Many friends and acquaintances attend Gatsby's funeral.
quiz.explanation: No one comes to Gatsby's funeral, revealing to Nick that his whole social life was just a mirage.

quiz.question: What are the eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg that watch over the Valley of Ashes?
quiz.explanation: These eyes painted on a billboard symbolize an absent god, indifferent to the moral corruption of this earth.
options: An absent god on a corrupt earth

quiz.question: What event allowed the novel, shunned upon its release, to become a classic after Fitzgerald's death?
quiz.explanation: Rediscovered after 1945 thanks to its distribution to soldiers during the Second World War, the novel finally became a classic.
options: Its distribution to soldiers during World War II
A new preface written by a famous critic
Its immediate adaptation to the cinema from 1926

title: The Lord of the Rings, Tolkien
description: Frodo must destroy the One Ring in Mount Doom. Tolkien invents Middle-earth and redefines modern fantasy.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What was J.R.R. Tolkien's profession before becoming the author of Middle-earth?
quiz.explanation: Tolkien was a professor of Old English at Oxford, and his specialty as a philologist is the basis of his entire universe.
options: Professor of Old English and philologist at Oxford

quiz.question: In what order did Tolkien build Middle-earth?
quiz.explanation: Tolkien first invents languages ​​like Quenya and Sindarin, then imagines the people who speak them.
options: He first invented languages, then imagined the people who speak them
He first drew a map, then invented languages
He wrote history first, then created languages ​​last
He translated already existing ancient languages

quiz.question: Who should destroy the One Ring at Mount Destiny?
quiz.explanation: Frodo Baggins, a simple hobbit with no ambition, is tasked with carrying and destroying the One Ring at Mount Doom.

quiz.question: Who forged the One Ring?
quiz.explanation: The One Ring was forged by Sauron, a fallen Maia who focused all his power on it.

quiz.question: True or false: The Fellowship of the Ring brings together nine representatives of the free peoples of Middle-earth.
quiz.explanation: The Fellowship of the Ring has nine members representing the various free peoples of Middle-earth.

quiz.question: Why is a hobbit presented as the ideal candidate to wear the Ring?
quiz.explanation: The Ring attacks the will of its wearer; a hobbit without political ambition is therefore the ideal candidate to resist his temptation.
options: Because he has no political ambition
Because he is the physically strongest
Because he is immune to magic
Because he is related to Sauron

quiz.question: What does the pity enjoyed by Gollum after his capture allow, unintentionally?
quiz.explanation: Gollum, spared out of compassion, unknowingly allows the final accomplishment of the quest when Frodo in turn fails to throw away the ring.
options: The final fulfillment of the quest, when Frodo himself fails to throw away the ring
Frodo's immediate destruction of the Ring
The capture of Sauron by the armies of Gondor

quiz.question: True or false: Tolkien intended The Lord of the Rings as an explicit allegory for World War II.
quiz.explanation: Tolkien refuses explicit allegory; rather, his work explores, more broadly, corruption by power.

quiz.question: Who fights battles as heir of Gondor, while Frodo advances alone towards Mordor?
quiz.explanation: Aragorn, heir of Gondor, fights battles while Frodo and Sam advance alone, exemplifying two forms of courage.

title: Fahrenheit 451, Bradbury
description: In this future, firemen burn books. Guy Montag discovers that culture dies of indifference as much as of censorship.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What do firefighters do in the world imagined by Fahrenheit 451?
quiz.explanation: In this future imagined by Bradbury, the firefighters' mission is to burn books deemed dangerous for social stability.
options: They put out fires like today

quiz.question: What does the title Fahrenheit 451 mean?
quiz.explanation: The title refers to the temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, at which the paper ignites.
options: The temperature at which paper ignites
The number of the Montag fire station

quiz.question: True or false: according to Bradbury, the disappearance of books comes solely from state-imposed censorship.
quiz.explanation: Bradbury nuance: the threat also comes from television and mass consumption, not just from political censorship.

quiz.question: Unlike 1984, where does the oppression come from in Fahrenheit 451?
quiz.explanation: Unlike 1984, here it is the citizens themselves who have given up books, out of comfort and fear of debate.
options: Citizens themselves, who have given up books for comfort
Of a single dictator who imposes his will

quiz.question: Who makes Guy Montag wonder about his job as a firefighter?
quiz.explanation: His young neighbor Clarisse reminds him that firefighters used to put out fires, which pushes Montag to doubt.

quiz.question: Why does Captain Beatty, who knows the classics, burn them with fervor?
quiz.explanation: Beatty believes that books create anxiety by revealing inequalities, which in his view justifies burning them.
options: Because according to him, books create anxiety by revealing inequalities
Because he never managed to read them himself
Because the government made them illegible

quiz.question: How do the intellectuals Montag meets preserve the forbidden culture?
quiz.explanation: The community of intellectuals that Montag joins each memorizes an entire book in order to transmit it orally.
options: Everyone memorizes an entire book to transmit it orally
They hide the books in underground bunkers
They translate the books into a secret code

quiz.question: True or false: the novel ends with the hope of a cultural rebirth after a nuclear war.
quiz.explanation: The novel ends with a nuclear war which destroys the city, but the resistance fighters leave: culture can be reborn if humanity agrees to think again.

quiz.question: In how many days did Ray Bradbury write Fahrenheit 451, on a typewriter rented from a library?
quiz.explanation: Bradbury wrote the novel in just nine days, on a typewriter rented ten cents for thirty minutes from a university library.

title: One Hundred Years of Solitude, García Márquez
description: Seven generations of Buendías in Macondo. García Márquez blends wonders and tragedy to tell the history of Latin America.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: How many generations of the Buendía family does the novel span in Macondo?
quiz.explanation: The novel traces seven generations of the Buendía family in Macondo, from the founder of the village to its last descendants.

quiz.question: What global literary movement did One Hundred Years of Solitude give rise to?
quiz.explanation: One Hundred Years of Solitude is the global birth certificate of magical realism, where the marvelous is told as an ordinary fact.

quiz.question: Who founded the village of Macondo in the jungle?
quiz.explanation: José Arcadio Buendía founded the village of Macondo in the jungle, the cradle of the entire family saga.

quiz.question: What happens to Colonel Aureliano Buendía after his thirty-two armed uprisings?
quiz.explanation: Colonel Aureliano Buendía leads thirty-two armed uprisings and loses them all, without ever overthrowing the power in place.
options: He died during the first uprising

quiz.question: What real historical event does the massacre of the workers in the novel transpose?
quiz.explanation: The episode of the massacre of the workers transposes the real massacre of the Colombian banana plantations of 1928, subsequently erased from collective memory.
options: The Colombian banana plantation massacre of 1928
The Colombian Civil War of the 19th century

quiz.question: True or false: when Remedios ascends to heaven by folding sheets, the narrator emphasizes the extraordinary nature of the event.
quiz.explanation: The narrator shows no surprise: the magical is told as an organic extension of reality, without the element of surprise.

quiz.question: What does the Melquíades manuscript, written in Sanskrit, reveal?
quiz.explanation: The Melquíades manuscript recounts in advance, in Sanskrit, one hundred years of the history of the Buendía family.
options: The complete story of the Buendía family, a hundred years before it happened
The map of gold mines in the region
A peace treaty between rival families

quiz.question: What does García Márquez do right after having his creative enlightenment while driving to Acapulco?
quiz.explanation: García Márquez turned around and isolated himself for eighteen months to write the novel, while his wife pawned their property.
options: He turned around and isolated himself for eighteen months to write the novel
He immediately leaves to present his idea to an editor
He begins to write the novel in English

quiz.question: True or false: time in Macondo is circular, with the Buendías repeating the mistakes of their ancestors.
quiz.explanation: Time in Macondo is circular: members of the Buendía family repeat, generation after generation, the mistakes of their ancestors.

quiz.question: In what year did García Márquez receive the Nobel Prize for Literature?
quiz.explanation: García Márquez received the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1982, fifteen years after the novel's publication.

title: The Metamorphosis, Kafka
description: Gregor Samsa wakes up turned into an insect. Kafka shows how a family, and a whole society, reject the person who can no longer work.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: How does The Metamorphosis begin, in one of the most famous incipits in literature?
quiz.explanation: The novel opens with Gregor Samsa waking up transformed into a monstrous insect, without any explanation of the phenomenon.
options: Gregor Samsa wakes up transformed into a monstrous insect
Gregor Samsa goes to work like every morning
The Samsa family learns of Gregor's death
Gregor Samsa leaves the family home

quiz.question: What was Gregor Samsa's profession before his transformation?
quiz.explanation: Before his transformation, Gregor was a traveling salesman and the sole financial support of his family.
options: Traveling salesman, sole financial support for his family

quiz.question: True or false: Kafka explains in detail, in the story, how and why Gregor transforms into an insect.
quiz.explanation: Kafka treats transformation with clinical realism, without ever explaining the phenomenon; the focus is on its consequences.

quiz.question: Why does Kafka forbid his publisher from depicting the insect on the cover of the book?
quiz.explanation: Kafka preferred that the reader imagine the horror of the transformation for themselves, rather than seeing it fixed by an illustration.
options: So that each reader imagines their own version of horror
Because the design cost too much to make
Because the censorship would have banned it
Because he wanted to keep the author anonymous

quiz.question: Who disobeyed Kafka's last wishes by publishing his manuscripts instead of destroying them?
quiz.explanation: Max Brod, Kafka's friend, disobeyed his last wishes by publishing his manuscripts rather than destroying them.

quiz.question: Who in the Samsa family feeds and cleans Gregor's room at the beginning of his metamorphosis?
quiz.explanation: At first, it is his sister Grete who feeds Gregor and cleans his room, before her devotion erodes over time.

quiz.question: What do the Samsa do to support themselves after Gregor's transformation?
quiz.explanation: To survive, each member of the family goes back to work, and they rent rooms to boarders.
options: They all work again and rent rooms to boarders
They ask for help from the municipality

quiz.question: How does Gregor's life end, once Grete declares that they must get rid of him?
quiz.explanation: Realizing that he no longer has his place, Gregor starves himself to death in his room.
options: He lets himself die of hunger
He is forcibly chased away by his father

quiz.question: True or false: Gregor's death is experienced by his family as a heartbreaking tragedy.
quiz.explanation: Gregor's death is, on the contrary, a deliverance for his family, who go for a walk already thinking about Grete's marriage.

quiz.question: In what year did Kafka write The Metamorphosis?
quiz.explanation: Kafka wrote The Metamorphosis in 1912, in a period of great creativity, before its publication in 1915.

title: The Master and Margarita, Bulgakov
description: The devil visits Stalin's Moscow while a writer tells the story of Pontius Pilate. Bulgakov's answer to censorship: manuscripts do not burn.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What three worlds does the novel The Master and Margarita interweave?
quiz.explanation: The novel weaves three worlds: Soviet Moscow in the 1930s, ancient Jerusalem and a fantastical space ruled by the devil.
options: Soviet Moscow, ancient Jerusalem and a fantasy world ruled by the devil
The Tsarist Past, the Stalinist Present and an Ideal Communist Future

quiz.question: Why did Bulgakov burn the first manuscript of the novel in 1930?
