quiz.explanation: For fear of searches by the Soviet political police, the NKVD, Bulgakov burned his first manuscript then began writing again from memory.
options: Because he considered the text unfinished
Because an accidental fire broke out

quiz.question: True or false: Bulgakov had his novel published in full during his lifetime.
quiz.explanation: Bulgakov died in 1940 without seeing his work published; the novel would not appear in full until 1967.

quiz.question: Who arrives in Moscow with his black cat Behemoth and sows panic among the literary caste?
quiz.explanation: Woland, who is none other than Satan, arrives in Moscow with his black cat Behemoth and sows panic among the corrupt literary caste.

quiz.question: What does the Master say in the novel he writes within the novel?
quiz.explanation: The Master writes the story of Pontius Pilate and Yeshua Ha-Nozri in Jerusalem, in parallel with the Muscovite intrigue.
options: The story of Pontius Pilate and Yeshua Ha-Nozri
Daily life in Moscow under Stalin

quiz.question: What does Marguerite do to save the Master, interned after the destruction of his manuscript?
quiz.explanation: Marguerite agrees to become a witch and preside over the devil's ball to save the Master, in a total loving sacrifice.
options: She becomes a witch and presides over the devil's ball
She denounces Woland to the authorities
She rewrote the lost manuscript herself
She goes into exile in Leningrad

quiz.question: Which vice does Woland present as the most terrible of all?
quiz.explanation: Woland reveals that cowardice is the most terrible of vices, that of Pontius Pilate as well as that of the Soviet critics.

quiz.question: What does the famous phrase “Manuscripts do not burn” mean?
quiz.explanation: This sentence affirms that the truth of art always ends up triumphing over repression and political censorship.
options: That the paper used by Bulgakov was non-flammable
That Stalin forbade the destruction of books

quiz.question: How did the novel circulate clandestinely in the USSR before its official publication?
quiz.explanation: In the USSR, the novel circulated in samizdat, clandestine typewritten copies exchanged between readers.
options: In the form of samizdat, clandestine typewritten copies
Thanks to an edition printed abroad and imported illegally

quiz.question: True or false: The Master and Margarita inspired the song “Sympathy for the Devil” by the Rolling Stones.
quiz.explanation: The novel inspired Mick Jagger to write "Sympathy for the Devil", after Marianne Faithfull offered it an English translation in 1967.

title: Moby-Dick, Melville
description: Ishmael signs on to the Pequod to hunt Moby Dick. Melville mixes sea adventure, the science of whales, and a meditation on obsession.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What personal experience did Herman Melville have before writing Moby Dick?
quiz.explanation: Melville sailed on whaling ships in the Pacific in the 1840s, even living among tribes in the Marquesas Islands.
options: He sailed on whaling ships in the Pacific and lived among tribes in the Marquesas
He was a British naval officer
He ran a whaling company in New Bedford
He studied marine biology at Harvard

quiz.question: True or false: Moby Dick enjoyed immense commercial success upon its publication in 1851.
quiz.explanation: The novel was a total commercial failure upon its release; Melville dies convinced that his name will disappear.

quiz.question: How does the novel begin, with one of the most famous sentences in American literature?
quiz.explanation: The novel opens with the phrase “Call me Ishmael,” one of the most famous incipits in American literature.
options: It was the best of times
In the beginning there was Moby Dick

quiz.question: Which ship does the narrator Ishmael embark on?
quiz.explanation: Ishmaël joins the Pequod in New Bedford, a ship which becomes a microcosm of American society.

quiz.question: Who is Queequeg, one of the Pequod's sailors?
quiz.explanation: Queequeg, son of a Polynesian chief, illustrates the diversity of origins brought together aboard the Pequod.
options: The son of a Polynesian chief

quiz.question: For Captain Ahab, what really is the white whale Moby Dick?
quiz.explanation: For Ahab, Moby Dick is not an animal but the mask of the cosmic malignancy he wants to destroy.
options: The mask of a cosmic malignancy, not a simple animal
The symbol of wealth to conquer
A creature invented by the legend of sailors

quiz.question: Why does Ahab dedicate his life to tracking down Moby Dick?
quiz.explanation: Having lost his leg in a previous encounter with the whale, Ahab now devotes his life to tracking down the evil that it embodies for him.
options: Because the whale made him lose a leg
Because she sank a friendly ship
Because it represents an inestimable fortune

quiz.question: What does the whiteness of the whale symbolize according to Melville?
quiz.explanation: Melville uses the white of the whale to emphasize the indifference of nature, a terrifying void to which the universe does not respond.
options: The indifference of nature, a terrifying void with no response from the universe
The old age of the animal

quiz.question: Who is the sole survivor of the final sinking of the Pequod?
quiz.explanation: Only Ishmael survives the shipwreck, floating on Queequeg's coffin before being picked up by the whaler Rachel.

quiz.question: True or false: when he died in 1891, Herman Melville was already recognized as a great American writer.
quiz.explanation: Melville was so forgotten when he died that the New York Times published his obituary under the incorrect name "Henry Melville."

title: The Little Prince, Saint-Exupéry
description: A little prince from a tiny planet teaches a stranded pilot that what really matters is invisible to the eye.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: Where and in what context did Saint-Exupéry write The Little Prince?
quiz.explanation: Exiled in New York while France was occupied, Saint-Exupéry wrote this desert story in the comfort of Long Island.
options: In exile in New York, during the occupation of France
In Paris, before the Second World War
In North Africa, during his Aéropostale missions
In Morocco, after his retirement as a pilot

quiz.question: Where does the Little Prince that the narrator meets in the middle of the Sahara come from?
quiz.explanation: The Little Prince comes from a tiny asteroid called B-612.
options: From an island lost in the desert
From a fantasy land called Maycomb

quiz.question: What must be removed regularly from the Little Prince's planet to save it?
quiz.explanation: On his asteroid, the Little Prince must uproot the baobab trees, otherwise their roots will burst his tiny planet.

quiz.question: Among the adults that the Little Prince meets, who finds favor in his eyes?
quiz.explanation: Only the lamplighter finds favor in the eyes of the Little Prince, because he lights the world for others and not for himself.
options: The lamplighter, who lights the world for others
The King, who reigns over all
The Conceited One, who likes to be admired
The Businessman, who counts the stars

quiz.question: What does the Fox teach him about taming?
quiz.explanation: The Fox teaches the Little Prince that to tame is to create bonds that make the other unique among all the others.
options: To tame is to create links that make the other unique
To tame is to dominate a wild animal
To tame is to forget someone gradually

quiz.question: True or false: according to the Fox, “the essential is invisible to the eyes”.
quiz.explanation: This sentence from the Fox sums up the idea that the truth of a being lies in the relationship we have with them, not in their appearance.

quiz.question: What element of the original manuscript was removed, at the suggestion of a friend, to leave room for the reader's imagination?
quiz.explanation: The original manuscript showed a sheep in the crate; a friend suggested Saint-Exupéry hide it to leave room for imagination.
options: The sheep visible in its crate
The snake that bites the Little Prince

quiz.question: True or false: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry lived long enough to experience the global success of his book.
quiz.explanation: Saint-Exupéry disappeared at sea in 1944 and never experienced the global success of his work.

quiz.question: What happened to Saint-Exupéry's plane on July 31, 1944?
quiz.explanation: On July 31, 1944, Saint-Exupéry's plane disappeared at sea; its wreck would not be identified until the year 2000, off the coast of Marseille.
options: It disappeared at sea, and its wreck was not identified until the year 2000.
He was shot down over Paris
He makes an emergency landing in the Sahara

quiz.question: Into how many languages ​​has The Little Prince been translated, making it the most translated French book in the world?
quiz.explanation: The Little Prince has been translated into more than 300 languages, making it the most translated French book in the world.

title: The Alchemist, Paulo Coelho
description: Santiago, an Andalusian shepherd, sets out for the Pyramids to find a treasure. Coelho turned the search for self into a worldwide phenomenon.
subject: litterature

quiz.question: What does Santiago, the Andalusian shepherd, dream of finding at the Pyramids of Egypt?
quiz.explanation: Santiago, an Andalusian shepherd, dreams of a treasure hidden near the Pyramids of Egypt.

quiz.question: What does Melchizedek, the King of Salem, teach him about his destiny?
quiz.explanation: Melchizedek teaches Santiago the notion of personal legend, the destiny that everyone desires to fulfill since childhood.
options: The personal legend, the destiny that everyone desires to achieve since childhood
The art of reading star charts

quiz.question: True or false: when it was first published in 1988, The Alchemist immediately became a huge commercial success.
quiz.explanation: A small Brazilian publisher only printed 900 copies in 1988 and refused to reprint; global success comes later.

quiz.question: Who, in the desert, teaches Santiago to read the signs of the universe?
quiz.explanation: It is the Alchemist, met while crossing the Sahara, who teaches Santiago to read the signs of the universe.

quiz.question: What is the Soul of the World in the novel?
quiz.explanation: The Soul of the World is the single energy that everything that exists is said to share, in the novel's philosophy.
options: A unique energy shared by everything that exists
The collective consciousness of Tangier merchants
A force reserved only for alchemists

quiz.question: What does the Arabic word “Maktub” mean, which Santiago often hears on his route?
quiz.explanation: Maktub means “it was written”: this expression refers to the Islamic idea of ​​a destiny already mapped out.
options: The name of an oasis in the Sahara

quiz.question: What did Paulo Coelho do before becoming a successful writer?
quiz.explanation: Before his fame as a writer, Paulo Coelho was a lyricist for the Brazilian rocker Raul Seixas.
options: He was a lyricist for Brazilian rocker Raul Seixas
He was a philosophy professor in Rio
He worked as a tour guide in Egypt
He was a monk in a Spanish monastery

quiz.question: What does Santiago finally discover when he arrives at the Pyramids?
quiz.explanation: At the Pyramids, Santiago finds nothing: the treasure was actually near its starting point, under a sycamore tree in Spain.
options: That he does not find any treasure there, it being in reality near his starting point in Spain
An immense treasure that makes him rich for life
A royal tomb unknown to archaeologists
A coded message left by Melchizedek

quiz.question: True or false: according to the novel, Santiago's material treasure ultimately matters more than the experience of the journey itself.
quiz.explanation: The novel affirms on the contrary that experience, the encounter with Fatima and listening to the heart are worth more than gold.

quiz.question: How many copies did the first Brazilian printing of The Alchemist have in 1988?
quiz.explanation: The first Brazilian edition had only 900 copies, and the publisher refused to reprint the book.

title: The Italian Renaissance
description: In two centuries, Italy reinvented painting, sculpture, and architecture, and changed the way we see the world.
subject: art

quiz.question: Which Florentine family financed Renaissance artists through banking?
quiz.explanation: The Medici, rich bankers of Florence, massively financed artists through patronage to establish their prestige.

quiz.question: Who invented linear perspective around 1420, in Florence?
quiz.explanation: Around 1420, the architect Brunelleschi developed the mathematical rules of linear perspective.

quiz.question: True or false: The fall of Constantinople in 1453 caused Byzantine scholars to flee to Italy with ancient Greek manuscripts.
quiz.explanation: This arrival of forgotten Greek manuscripts directly nourished humanism and the rediscovery of Antiquity in Italy.

quiz.question: In what year did Michelangelo finish the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
quiz.explanation: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel between 1508 and 1512, covering approximately 500 square meters.

quiz.question: Put these milestones of the Italian Renaissance in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four milestones (1420, 1453, 1504, 1512) span nearly a century, from the technical invention of perspective to the artistic peak of the High Renaissance in Rome.
items: Brunelleschi invents linear perspective
Fall of Constantinople
Michelangelo's David
The ceiling of the Sistine Chapel is completed

quiz.question: Which Raphael fresco brings together the great thinkers of Antiquity?
quiz.explanation: Raphael paints The School of Athens, which features Plato, Aristotle and other ancient philosophers in perfect harmony.

quiz.question: Which movement of thought affirms that human beings can understand nature through reason?
quiz.explanation: Humanist thinkers like Pic de la Mirandola place human reason at the center of understanding the world.

quiz.question: True or false: it was the King of France François I who invited Leonardo da Vinci and launched the French Renaissance.
quiz.explanation: Francis I attracted Leonardo da Vinci to France and launched the French Renaissance, visible in particular in the castles of the Loire.

quiz.question: What pictorial technique from Flanders allows chiaroscuro?
quiz.explanation: Oil paint, coming from Flanders, gradually replaced tempera and allowed the strong contrasts of chiaroscuro.

title: The birth of Impressionism
description: In 1874, painters rejected by the Salon put on their own show. A critic mocked Monet and accidentally gave **Impressionism** its name.
subject: art

quiz.question: Which critic invented the word “impressionists” while making fun of a painting by Monet?
quiz.explanation: Louis Leroy mocks Monet's title Impression, Sunrise, which accidentally gives the movement its name.

quiz.question: Which Manet painting scandalized the Salon des Refusés in 1863?
quiz.explanation: Manet shocks by mixing a female nude and two men in modern dress in The Luncheon on the Grass.

quiz.question: True or false: in 1863, the Salon jury refused more than 3,000 paintings.
quiz.explanation: This massive refusal pushed Napoleon III to authorize the Salon des Refusés in response.

quiz.question: What material innovation allowed the Impressionists to paint outdoors?
quiz.explanation: Transportable paint tubes free painters from the workshop and allow them to work outdoors.

quiz.question: Which chemist inspired the Impressionists in their use of complementary colors?
quiz.explanation: Chevreul's research on complementary colors pushed the Impressionists to ban black from shadows.

quiz.question: Where did the first impressionist exhibition of 1874 take place?
quiz.explanation: The group exhibits in the former workshop of photographer Nadar, due to lack of access to the official Salon.
options: In the studio of photographer Nadar
At the Academy of Fine Arts

quiz.question: What artistic influence from Asia inspired the asymmetrical framing of the Impressionists?
quiz.explanation: Japanese prints provide asymmetrical framing and bird's-eye views previously unheard of in Europe.

quiz.question: Put these stages of impressionism in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These three milestones span from 1863 to 1886, from the initial scandal to the end of the group's collective exhibitions.
items: The scandal of Manet's Déjeuner sur l'herbe
The first independent exhibition at Nadar
The last of the group's eight exhibitions

quiz.question: In what year did the Impressionists organize their first independent exhibition?
quiz.explanation: The group's first independent exhibition took place in April 1874 in the studio of photographer Nadar.

title: Caravaggio and chiaroscuro
description: **Michelangelo Merisi**, known as Caravaggio, changed painting forever with brutal realism and an extreme contrast of light and shadow: chiaroscuro.
subject: art

quiz.question: What is the real name of the painter known as Caravaggio?
quiz.explanation: Caravaggio's real name is Michelangelo Merisi, originally from the Milan region.

quiz.question: What is the extreme form of chiaroscuro invented by Caravaggio called?
quiz.explanation: Tenebrism plunges the scene into an opaque darkness from which bodies emerge with sculptural force.

quiz.question: True or false: Caravaggio chose his models from among beggars and common people to paint his saints.
quiz.explanation: He refused to idealize his religious characters and took his models from the street, which scandalized his contemporaries.

quiz.question: Which painting from 1600 astounds Rome with its sacredness to the face of the street?
quiz.explanation: The Vocation of Saint Matthew, painted for the Contarelli chapel, imposes a sacred personified by ordinary people.

quiz.question: Why did Caravaggio have to flee Rome in 1606?
quiz.explanation: During a brawl in 1606, he killed Ranuccio Tomassoni and was sentenced to death, forcing him into exile.
options: He kills Ranuccio Tomassoni during a brawl

quiz.question: What style did Caravaggio reject, considered too graceful and artificial?
quiz.explanation: He refuses the artifices of mannerism, this graceful and distorted style which preceded it.

quiz.question: Which Dutch painter later inherited Caravaggio's shadow poetry?
quiz.explanation: Rembrandt takes up and deepens the legacy of Caravaggesque chiaroscuro in his own style.

quiz.question: At what age did Caravaggio die, on the run, in Porto Ercole?
quiz.explanation: Hunted and injured, Caravaggio died at the age of 38, a few days before a papal pardon.

quiz.question: Put these events in Caravaggio's life in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: This trajectory covers his arrival around 1593, his triumph in 1600, his exile after 1606 and his death in 1610.
items: Arrival in Rome
The Vocation of Saint Matthew astounds the city
Murder of Ranuccio Tomassoni and escape
Death in Porto Ercole

title: Rembrandt and the Flemish school
description: **Rembrandt van Rijn** was the great painter of the Dutch Golden Age. Self-portraits, biblical scenes, and *The Night Watch*: he painted the human soul.
subject: art

quiz.question: In what political space does Rembrandt operate, driven by a bourgeois art market?
quiz.explanation: In the 17th century, the Dutch Protestant bourgeoisie ordered paintings for their homes, without going through the Church or the court.

quiz.question: What is Rembrandt's signature thick, raised painting technique called?
quiz.explanation: Impasto is this paint applied so thick that it creates a relief, going against the taste for smooth surfaces.

quiz.question: True or false: The Night Watch actually represents a daytime scene.
quiz.explanation: The title is a misinterpretation: the scene is diurnal, but centuries of dirty varnish have darkened the canvas to the point of suggesting night.

quiz.question: What is the painting known as The Night Watch really showing?
quiz.explanation: It is the company of Captain Frans Banning Cocq, a militia shown on the move instead of lined up as convention required.
options: A bourgeois militia company on the move

quiz.question: What financial event struck Rembrandt in 1656?
quiz.explanation: In 1656, Rembrandt's personal bankruptcy led to the auction of his house and collections.

quiz.question: Approximately how many self-portraits did Rembrandt paint during his life?
quiz.explanation: Rembrandt painted around 80 to 90 self-portraits over nearly forty years, a unique testimony to his evolution.

quiz.question: Which 17th century painter influenced Rembrandt's chiaroscuro?
quiz.explanation: Rembrandt reinvents the chiaroscuro inherited from Caravaggio by making it more interior and emotional.

quiz.question: True or false: Rembrandt softened his style at the end of his life to please fashion and save his fortune.
quiz.explanation: On the contrary, he refuses to soften his style despite his ruinous lifestyle, remaining faithful to his artistic vision.

quiz.question: Put these stages of Rembrandt's life in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones extend from 1631 to 1669, from his triumphal installation in Amsterdam until his death.
items: Arrival in Amsterdam
The Night Watch
Personal bankruptcy
Death of the painter

title: Romanticism in painting (Delacroix, Géricault)
description: Between 1810 and 1850, Romanticism revolted against the coldness of Neoclassicism. Color against line, passion against reason: **Géricault** and **Delacroix**.
subject: art

quiz.question: Against which movement did romanticism position itself in reaction?
quiz.explanation: Romanticism is opposed to the cold rigor of neoclassicism embodied by Jacques-Louis David.

quiz.question: What real event inspires The Raft of the Medusa by Géricault?
quiz.explanation: Géricault was inspired by the real-life sinking of the Méduse in 1816, where a captain abandoned around 150 sailors on a raft.
options: The sinking of the frigate Méduse

quiz.question: True or false: Delacroix painted Liberty Leading the People to celebrate the July Revolution of 1830.
quiz.explanation: The painting celebrates the Three Glorious Years, the revolutionary days of July 1830.

quiz.question: What journey transformed Delacroix's palette in 1832?
quiz.explanation: His trip to Morocco in 1832 revealed a new light to him and partly founded orientalism.

quiz.question: Which academic painter opposed Delacroix by defending line rather than color?
quiz.explanation: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, rival of Delacroix, defends smooth and precise line against emotive color.

quiz.question: To paint the truth of the bodies of the Raft of the Medusa, what does Géricault do?
quiz.explanation: Géricault studies corpses to realistically represent the agony of the shipwrecked.

quiz.question: Approximately how many sailors were abandoned on the raft of the Méduse in 1816?
quiz.explanation: A captain appointed by royal favor abandons around 150 sailors on a makeshift raft.

quiz.question: Who took the lead in the romantic movement after the premature death of Géricault?
quiz.explanation: After Géricault's premature death, Delacroix became the leader of the Romantic movement.

quiz.question: Put these works and events of Romanticism in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones range from 1816 to 1832, from the actual shipwreck to the transformation of Delacroix's palette by the Orient.
items: The sinking of the frigate Méduse
The Raft of the Medusa is on display
The July Revolution and Liberty Leading the People
Delacroix's trip to Morocco

title: Cubism: Picasso and Braque
description: Between 1907 and 1920, **Picasso** and **Braque** broke the object into facets seen from several angles at once. The most radical revolution since the Renaissance.
subject: art

quiz.question: Which painter advises treating nature through the cylinder, the sphere and the cone, influencing cubism?
quiz.explanation: Cézanne seeks the solidity of forms behind the light and directly inspires Cubist geometrization.

quiz.question: What discovery at the Trocadéro museum in 1907 marked Picasso?
quiz.explanation: Picasso discovered African and Oceanian masks at the Trocadéro which conceptualized the face rather than copying it.

quiz.question: Which painting from 1907 marks the starting point of Cubism?
quiz.explanation: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, with its sharp-faceted nudes, stunned even people close to Picasso.

quiz.question: True or false: in analytical cubism, color almost disappears in favor of grays and ochres.
quiz.explanation: Between 1908 and 1912, Picasso and Braque reduced color to force the eye on the construction of space.

quiz.question: What is the name for the technique that introduced newspapers and wallpaper into Cubist paintings around 1912?
quiz.explanation: Collage, which appeared with synthetic cubism, brings real materials such as newspaper into the painting.

quiz.question: Which cubist brought a particular mathematical rigor to the movement?
quiz.explanation: Juan Gris develops an approach to cubism marked by geometric and mathematical rigor.

quiz.question: What previous profession of Georges Braque explains his talent for imitating materials in his collages?
quiz.explanation: A former painter-decorator, Braque knew how to paint fake wood so perfect that it seemed more real than the wood that was actually glued.

quiz.question: Put these stages of Cubism in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones range from 1907 to 1912, from the initial breakup to the invention of collage.
items: The Young Ladies of Avignon
Analytical Cubism dissects the object
Collage and synthetic cubism

quiz.question: Around what year did Picasso complete Les Demoiselles d'Avignon?
quiz.explanation: Picasso completed this founding painting of Cubism in 1907.

title: Surrealism: Dalí and Magritte
description: Born in 1924, Surrealism set out to free the unconscious: dreams, desires, wild associations. **Dalí** raves, **Magritte** puzzles.
subject: art

quiz.question: Who founded surrealism with the Surrealist Manifesto in 1924?
quiz.explanation: The poet André Breton founded the movement with his Manifesto of Surrealism published in 1924.

quiz.question: What method did Dalí invent to paint his voluntary delirium?
quiz.explanation: Dalí invents the paranoid-critical method, a voluntary delirium combining heterogeneous elements.

quiz.question: True or false: surrealism is inspired by Sigmund Freud's theories on the unconscious.
quiz.explanation: Freud shows that the unconscious dominates the psyche, which directly inspired the surrealists.

quiz.question: Which Dalí painting shows soft watches in a Catalan landscape?
quiz.explanation: The Persistence of Memory, painted in 1931, shows soft watches in a landscape inspired by Port Lligat.

quiz.question: What sentence did Magritte write under a realistically painted pipe?
quiz.explanation: In The Betrayal of Images, Magritte reminds us that the image of a pipe is only a sign, not the object itself.

quiz.question: What movement precedes and directly influences surrealism?
quiz.explanation: After Dadaism, which destroyed meaning, Breton wanted to rebuild the mind by freeing thought.

quiz.question: True or false: André Breton nicknamed Dalí Avida Dollars and excluded him from the movement in 1939.
quiz.explanation: Breton judged that Dalí had commercialized himself too much and excluded him from the surrealist group in 1939.

quiz.question: What collective game did the surrealists invent to create without rational control?
quiz.explanation: The Exquisite Corpse is a game where everyone adds a sentence or a drawing without seeing the previous contribution.

quiz.question: Put these milestones of surrealism in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones range from 1924 to 1939, from the founding of the movement to the break between Breton and Dalí.
items: Breton's Manifesto of Surrealism
Dalí joins the surrealist group
The Persistence of Memory
Breton's exclusion of Dalí

title: Expressionism: Munch and The Scream
description: Expressionism puts inner feeling ahead of the outside world. With **Munch** and *The Scream*, modern dread became an icon.
subject: art

quiz.question: Which Norwegian painter was the pioneer of expressionism with The Scream?
quiz.explanation: The Norwegian Edvard Munch made modern anguish and solitude a universal symbol with The Scream.

quiz.question: Which two German groups structured expressionism at the beginning of the 20th century?
quiz.explanation: Die Brücke, more raw, and Der Blaue Reiter, more spiritual, structured the movement in Germany.
options: Die Brücke and Der Blaue Reiter

quiz.question: True or false: Munch lost his mother and sister to tuberculosis.
quiz.explanation: These early bereavements had a profound impact on Munch's work and fueled his existential anguish.

quiz.question: Where did Munch have the vision that inspired The Scream?
quiz.explanation: The origin of the Cri dates back to a walk on the hill of Ekeberg, where the sunset sky becomes a fire.
options: In a fjord in Northern Norway

quiz.question: What natural event is sometimes linked to the red sky at the origin of the Scream?
quiz.explanation: Ash from the 1883 eruption of Krakatoa is said to have tinted sunsets red around the world.

quiz.question: In what year was the word “expressionism” used for the first time, at the Berlin Secession?
quiz.explanation: The word appeared in 1911 at the Berlin Secession to distinguish artists refusing impressionist gentleness.

quiz.question: How many versions of The Scream did Munch paint in total?
quiz.explanation: Munch painted four versions of the Scream, in tempera, pastel and oil, proof that this motif haunted him for a long time.

quiz.question: True or false: in The Scream, the figure covers its ears because the cry comes from outside, from the landscape.
quiz.explanation: The cry is actually internal: the figure covers its ears in the face of the howl of the world, not the other way around.

quiz.question: What later artistic movement did Munch's audacity help to pave the way for?
quiz.explanation: This audacity to represent psychological truth rather than perfect anatomy paves the way for surrealism.

title: Abstract art: Kandinsky and Mondrian
description: For the first time, a painting represented nothing at all from the visible world. **Kandinsky** set forms free; **Mondrian** cut everything down to geometry.
subject: art

quiz.question: What ancient rule of painting does abstract art break?
quiz.explanation: Abstraction breaks mimesis, this ancient obligation to faithfully represent the visible world.
options: Mimesis, the obligation to represent the visible world

quiz.question: What event pushed Kandinsky towards abstraction around 1910?
quiz.explanation: Returning at dusk, Kandinsky is upset by a painting that he does not recognize: it is one of his own, placed upside down.
options: He is upset by one of his paintings placed upside down, unrecognizable
He visits an exhibition of African masks
He reads a treatise by Freud

quiz.question: In which book did Kandinsky theorize lyrical abstraction in 1911?
quiz.explanation: Kandinsky published Du Spirituel dans l'Art in 1911, where he theorized the emotional vibration of colors.

quiz.question: True or false: Mondrian arrives at abstraction by starting from series of representations of trees which he gradually simplifies.
quiz.explanation: Between 1908 and 1912, his series of trees show the trunk and branches disappearing in favor of a framework of lines.

quiz.question: What is the movement founded by Mondrian in 1917 called?
quiz.explanation: Mondrian founded the De Stijl movement in 1917 and theorized neoplasticism.

quiz.question: What colors and shapes does Mondrian's neoplasticism exclusively allow?
quiz.explanation: Neoplasticism reduces art to straight lines and three primary colors, to aim for the universal.
options: The straight line and the three primary colors

quiz.question: Which school founded by Walter Gropius in 1919 links abstraction to design and architecture?
quiz.explanation: At the Bauhaus, founded by Walter Gropius in 1919, Kandinsky taught and Mondrian's aesthetic inspired architects and designers.

quiz.question: Put these abstract art milestones in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones range from 1910 to 1919, from the beginnings of Kandinsky to the entry of abstraction into design.
items: Kandinsky shifts towards abstraction
Spiritual in Art is published
Mondrian founds De Stijl
Foundation of the Bauhaus

quiz.question: In what year did Mondrian found the De Stijl movement?
quiz.explanation: Mondrian founded De Stijl in 1917 and theorized neoplasticism there.

title: Pop Art: Warhol and Lichtenstein
description: Pop Art answers the consumer society head-on. **Warhol** and **Lichtenstein** turn advertising, comic books and movie stars into high art.
subject: art

quiz.question: In which country was Pop Art born, before exploding in the United States?
quiz.explanation: Pop Art was born in Great Britain with the Independent Group, before exploding in the United States in the 1960s.

quiz.question: Which artistic movement does Pop Art reject, deemed too introspective?
quiz.explanation: Pop artists opposed abstract expressionism, the introspective paintings then dominant.

quiz.question: What is the name of Andy Warhol's collective studio in New York?
quiz.explanation: Warhol's Factory functions like a factory where assistants and friends produce together.

quiz.question: What technique did Warhol use to reproduce an image like Marilyn Monroe dozens of times?
quiz.explanation: Screen printing allows Warhol to multiply an image, illustrating the idea that reproduction transforms the aura of a work.

quiz.question: What signature visual motif does Lichtenstein reproduce by hand in his comic book-inspired canvases?
quiz.explanation: The Ben-Day dot, a manual imitation of an industrial printing process, is Lichtenstein's visual signature.

quiz.question: True or false: Richard Hamilton described Pop Art in 1957 with adjectives like ephemeral, cheap and sexy.
quiz.explanation: In 1957, Hamilton thus summarized an art designed to be consumed as quickly as a magazine.

quiz.question: Which painting by Lichtenstein transforms an air combat comic strip into a monumental painting?
quiz.explanation: Whaam! transforms a diversion comic panel into a large format modern history painting.

quiz.question: In what year did a portrait of Marilyn by Warhol reach $195 million at auction?
quiz.explanation: In 2022, this portrait of Marilyn becomes one of the most expensive American works of art ever sold.

quiz.question: Put these Pop Art milestones in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones range from 1957 to 2022, from the definition of the movement to the consecration of its icons on the art market.
items: Richard Hamilton defines Pop Art
Warhol and Lichtenstein impose pop aesthetics in the United States
A portrait of Marilyn sells for $195 million

title: The birth of electronic music
description: From the theremin to the clubs of Chicago and Detroit, electronic music invents sounds without an orchestra and changes the way the world dances.
subject: art

quiz.question: Who invented the Theremin in 1920, an instrument played without contact?
quiz.explanation: In 1920, Russian inventor Leon Theremin designed a device played by moving the hands near electromagnetic antennas.

quiz.question: Who invented musique concrete in Paris after 1945?
quiz.explanation: Pierre Schaeffer and Pierre Henry invented musique concrete by recording and manipulating everyday noises on magnetic tape.

quiz.question: True or false: musique concrete is based on sounds created by oscillators, without any real acoustic source.
quiz.explanation: It's the opposite: musique concrete starts from real recorded noises, while pure Cologne synthesis uses oscillators.

quiz.question: Who miniaturized the synthesizer using transistors in the 1960s?
quiz.explanation: American engineer Robert Moog miniaturized the synthesizer with transistors, making it usable in the studio.

quiz.question: Which 1968 album proves that electronics can carry the complexity of classical music?
quiz.explanation: Switched-On Bach by Wendy Carlos demonstrated in 1968 that the synthesizer could perform complex classical works.

quiz.question: Which German group imposes cold and repetitive pop with albums like Autobahn and The Man-Machine?
quiz.explanation: The Kraftwerk group, founded by Ralf Hütter and Florian Schneider in Düsseldorf, sings about the highway, the robot and the city.

quiz.question: What inexpensive drum machine from the 1980s became a key tool in house and techno?
quiz.explanation: Initially a commercial failure deemed unrealistic, the TR-808 became the cheap weapon of Chicago DJs.

quiz.question: Which DJ refined house music in Chicago in the 1980s?

quiz.question: Which critical review, founded in 1951, became the laboratory of ideas for the New Wave?
quiz.explanation: The Cahiers du cinéma, founded in 1951 by André Bazin, brought together young critics who would become the directors of the New Wave.

quiz.question: According to the authors' policy defended by Cahiers du cinéma, who is the true creator of a film?
quiz.explanation: For the critics of Cahiers, the real creator is not the screenwriter but the one who directs the scene, just as a novelist has his own style.

quiz.question: Which François Truffaut film triumphed at Cannes in 1959 and launched the New Wave?
quiz.explanation: In 1959, The 400 Blows by François Truffaut triumphed at Cannes and put auteur cinema on the map.

quiz.question: True or false: Breathless by Jean-Luc Godard shocked people in 1960 with its abrupt cuts in the middle of gestures.
quiz.explanation: Godard cuts in the middle of the gestures in Breathless, as if he were editing the film with scissors, which was shocking in 1960.

quiz.question: What technical innovation allowed New Wave directors to leave the studios to film in the streets of Paris?
quiz.explanation: Lightweight cameras like the Éclair Caméflex and more sensitive films make it possible to shoot on natural settings, outside of studios.
options: Lightweight cameras like the Éclair Caméflex

quiz.question: Which Brazilian cinematic movement is directly inspired by the freedom of filming of the New Wave?
quiz.explanation: The freedom of filming of the New Wave then inspired Cinema Novo in Brazil, then Dogme 95 in Denmark.

quiz.question: True or false: New Wave directors mainly shot in studios, with sophisticated artificial lighting.
quiz.explanation: On the contrary, they film in cafes, apartments and the streets of Paris, often in natural light.

quiz.question: Which American directors of the 1970s were inspired by the freedom of the New Wave?
quiz.explanation: In the 1970s, New Hollywood, driven by Scorsese, Coppola and Spielberg, mixed American efficiency and French freedom.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the New Wave in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These three milestones (1951, 1959, 1960) show the transition from a critical review to a revolution in auteur cinema.
items: Founding of Cahiers du cinéma
The 400 Blows triumphs at Cannes
Release of Breathless

title: Kubrick and 2001: A Space Odyssey
description: In **1968**, **Stanley Kubrick** turned science fiction into a sensory experience. Few lines of dialogue, exact images, and one question: what becomes of humans when they face their own tools?
subject: art

quiz.question: What year was 2001: A Space Odyssey released in theaters?
quiz.explanation: 2001: A Space Odyssey was released in 1968 and redefined science fiction in cinema.

quiz.question: Which science fiction writer did Kubrick contact in 1964 to create 2001?
quiz.explanation: In 1964, Kubrick contacted the writer Arthur C. Clarke to invent a film and a novel together in parallel.

quiz.question: Which short story did Kubrick and Clarke start from to develop 2001?
quiz.explanation: Kubrick and Clarke start from the short story The Sentinel and build the film and the novel in parallel.

quiz.question: Who invented the slit-scan technique to film the final journey of the film?
quiz.explanation: Effects supervisor Douglas Trumbull invents the slit-scan, which creates hypnotic tunnels of light for the final journey.

quiz.question: What is HAL 9000 in the film?
quiz.explanation: HAL 9000, the onboard computer, chooses to kill the humans to resolve the contradiction in its mission.
options: The onboard computer that ends up killing the crew
An alien who came to warn humanity
The robotic clone of an astronaut
A simple voice assistant with no consciousness

quiz.question: True or false: HAL 9000 attacks the crew because it is caught in a contradiction between accomplishing its mission and hiding its true nature.
quiz.explanation: Caught in this contradiction, HAL chooses to eliminate humans to preserve the secrecy of his mission.

quiz.question: To film Barry Lyndon only by candlelight, which lenses did Kubrick adapt?
quiz.explanation: Kubrick had Zeiss lenses designed for NASA adapted to film Barry Lyndon by candlelight alone.

quiz.question: What piece of music accompanies orbiting space stations in 2001?
quiz.explanation: Johann Strauss's waltz The Blue Danube accompanies the space stations, while Thus Spoke Zarathustra marks the leaps of evolution.
options: The Blue Danube by Johann Strauss
Thus Spoke Zarathustra by Richard Strauss

quiz.question: What does the black monolith symbolize in 2001?
quiz.explanation: The black monolith is a silent presence that restarts human evolution at several points in the film.
options: A presence that restarts human evolution
An alien weapon destined to destroy Earth
A simple setting without narrative meaning

title: Hitchcock and suspense
description: **Alfred Hitchcock** invented modern suspense: give the audience information the characters do not have. In *Psycho*, *Vertigo* and *Rear Window*, he plays with where we look.
subject: art

quiz.question: According to Hitchcock, what is the difference between surprise and suspense?
quiz.explanation: Hitchcock explains to Truffaut that suspense shows the audience the bomb while the characters ignore it, which prolongs the tension.
options: Suspense shows the bomb to the audience before it explodes, surprise does not
Suspense scares, surprise makes you laugh
The surprise lasts longer than the suspense
There is no difference, they are synonyms

quiz.question: What is a MacGuffin in a Hitchcock film?
quiz.explanation: The MacGuffin is an item or secret that advances the plot, even if its precise nature doesn't really matter.
options: An object or secret that motivates the characters without its exact nature mattering
The name of the killer in Psycho

quiz.question: What technique does Hitchcock use in Rope (1948) to simulate a film shot in a single movement?
quiz.explanation: Hitchcock hides the cuts behind a back or a dark piece of furniture to fake a single long take in Rope.
options: A sequence shot with hidden cuts behind backs or furniture

quiz.question: What visual effect did Hitchcock invent for Vertigo in 1958?
quiz.explanation: For Vertigo, Hitchcock invented the Dolly Zoom: the camera moves back while the zoom advances, distorting space to make people feel dizzy.

quiz.question: True or false: in Rear Window, the spectator sees exactly what the hero sees thanks to the subjective camera.
quiz.explanation: Hitchcock uses the subjective camera: we see exactly what the hero sees, nothing more.

quiz.question: Who is the hero of Rear Window (1954)?
quiz.explanation: The hero is a photographer with a broken leg who spies on his neighbors from his window.
options: A photographer with a broken leg who spies on his neighbors
A private detective in charge of an investigation
A police officer on forced leave

quiz.question: True or false: for Psycho, Hitchcock forbade entry into the room after the start of the session.
quiz.explanation: Hitchcock bars entry after the session begins for Psycho, turning the secret of the plot into an event.

quiz.question: Which composer regularly collaborates with Hitchcock to heighten tension through music?
quiz.explanation: The collaboration between Hitchcock and composer Bernard Herrmann links music and editing to accelerate the viewer's pulse.

quiz.question: Put these Hitchcock technical innovations in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These three innovations (1948, 1954, 1958) mark the evolution of Hitchcock's style, from the illusion of the continuous plane to the optical distortion of vertigo.
items: La Corde simulates a single sequence shot
The Rear Window uses the subjective camera
Vertigo invents the Dolly Zoom

title: Gothic architecture: the cathedrals
description: From the 12th to the 16th century, Gothic cathedrals pushed stone toward the sky. Pointed arches, rib vaults, stained glass: a technical revolution in the service of light.
subject: art

quiz.question: Where and around what date was the Gothic style born?
quiz.explanation: Gothic was born in Île-de-France around 1140, with the choir of the basilica of Saint-Denis.

quiz.question: Who launched the construction of the choir of the basilica of Saint-Denis, at the origin of the Gothic style?
quiz.explanation: Abbot Suger carried the founding shock of the Gothic by wanting a more united, clearer and higher space in Saint-Denis.

quiz.question: What three innovations made it possible to lighten the walls of Gothic cathedrals?
quiz.explanation: The pointed arch, ribbed vault and flying buttress work together to free up the walls and allow for large windows.
options: The pointed arch, the ribbed vault and the flying buttress
The dome, the pediment and the colonnade
The dome, the pilaster and the lintel
The barrel vault, the massive buttress and the bell tower-porch

quiz.question: According to the theology defended by Father Suger, what role does light play in the cathedral?
quiz.explanation: For Suger, the colored rays of the stained glass windows help the soul to rise towards God, making the cathedral a cage of light.
options: It helps the soul to rise towards God
It is only used to illuminate religious services.
It marks the financial power of the clergy
It protects the stone from humidity

quiz.question: True or false: the construction of a Gothic cathedral often takes more than two centuries.
quiz.explanation: Wars, epidemics and lack of money caused construction sites to move forward in fits and starts, often over more than two centuries.

quiz.question: In what year did construction of Notre-Dame de Paris begin?
quiz.explanation: Notre-Dame de Paris began in 1163 and took shape around 1345, after around 180 years of construction.

quiz.question: True or false: only monks participate in the construction of cathedrals, without help from the city's inhabitants.
quiz.explanation: The whole town works on the site: stonemasons, carpenters and glaziers, which also makes it an economical machine.

quiz.question: Which unfinished Gothic cathedral was finally completed in the 19th century thanks to the Gothic Revival?
quiz.explanation: In the 19th century, Europe rediscovered Gothic and completed unfinished projects like that of Cologne, completed in 1880.

quiz.question: Put these stages of Gothic architecture in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones (1140, 1163, 13th century, 19th century) show the birth of the style, its diffusion, its classical apogee then its modern rediscovery.
items: Suger launches the choir of Saint-Denis
Start of construction on Notre-Dame de Paris
Chartres and Amiens impose the classic model
Europe rediscovers style with neo-Gothic

title: The Bauhaus
description: Between **1919** and **1933**, the **Bauhaus** school fused art, craft and industry in Germany. Closed by the Nazis, it still spread modern design across the world.
subject: art

quiz.question: Who founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919?
quiz.explanation: The architect Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919, with architecture as his ultimate goal.

quiz.question: Which principle of Gropius' manifesto abolishes the hierarchy between fine arts and applied arts?
quiz.explanation: Each Bauhaus workshop is led by an artist and a craftsman, with craftsmanship becoming the basis of all creation.
options: Each workshop has a master artist and a master craftsman, equally
Only architects can teach at Bauhaus
Art must remain separate from craft
Students choose a single art to master

quiz.question: What Dutch movement dialogues with the Bauhaus around the rectangle and pure colors?
quiz.explanation: The school dialogues with De Stijl, a Dutch movement obsessed with the rectangle and pure colors.

quiz.question: What slogan summarizes the philosophy of the Bauhaus after its installation in Dessau?
quiz.explanation: In Dessau, the Bauhaus turned to mass production under the slogan form follows function.

quiz.question: What industrial material does Marcel Breuer recycle to invent lightweight chairs?
quiz.explanation: Marcel Breuer recycles tubular steel from bicycles to create light and modern chairs.
options: The curved wood of old armchairs

quiz.question: True or false: the Nazi regime closed the Bauhaus in 1933, accusing it of cultural Bolshevism.
quiz.explanation: Deemed too modern and too left-wing, the school was closed by the Nazis in 1933, accused of cultural Bolshevism.

quiz.question: Who led the Bauhaus in Berlin just before it was closed down by the Nazis?
quiz.explanation: Mies van der Rohe directed the Bauhaus during his visit to Berlin, just before its closure in 1933.

quiz.question: True or false: the closure of the Bauhaus puts an end to its influence, which disappears with the school.
quiz.explanation: On the contrary, the exile of the Bauhaus masters in the United States, Great Britain and Palestine spread its ideas throughout the world.

quiz.question: Put these stages of Bauhaus history in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These three milestones (1919, 1925, 1933) retrace the founding in Weimar, the industrial shift in Dessau, then the closure which spread the Bauhaus throughout the world.
items: Foundation of the Bauhaus in Weimar
The Bauhaus settles in Dessau and aims for mass production
School closed by the Nazis

title: The Mona Lisa
description: Painted by **Leonardo da Vinci** between **1503** and **1519**, the *Mona Lisa* became the absolute icon of the Louvre. Technique, a mysterious smile, and a theft in **1911** that changed everything.
subject: art

quiz.question: Who painted the Mona Lisa between 1503 and 1519?
quiz.explanation: Leonardo da Vinci began the portrait around 1503 in Florence and retouched it until his death in 1519.

quiz.question: Who commissioned the portrait, and who would be the model?
quiz.explanation: The sponsor is the merchant Francesco del Giocondo, and the model is said to be his wife, Lisa Gherardini.
options: The merchant Francesco del Giocondo, whose wife Lisa Gherardini would be the model
King Francis I, whose sister would be the model
Pope Julius II, of whom a niece would be the model
The Duke of Milan, whose daughter would be the model

quiz.question: Which Leonardo painting technique, made of thin superimposed layers, erases the contours of the face?
quiz.explanation: Leonardian sfumato, very thinly layered glazes, erases harsh lines and makes the face melt into air.

quiz.question: Why does the Mona Lisa's smile seem to change depending on where you look?
quiz.explanation: When we stare at the eyes, the edges of the retina perceive the mouth in soft shadows, which makes the smile appear or disappear.
options: It plays with the peripheral vision of the human eye
The painting was repainted several times by Leonardo
It is an effect of the varnish applied to the painting
The smile changes depending on the brightness of the room

quiz.question: True or false: Leonardo da Vinci delivered the Mona Lisa to his sponsor shortly after completing it.
quiz.explanation: Leonardo never delivers the painting: he keeps it, retouches it for years and takes it with him to France.

quiz.question: Who stole the Mona Lisa on August 21, 1911?
quiz.explanation: Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian glazier working at the Louvre, stole the painting by hiding it under his blouse.

quiz.question: True or false: before the 1911 theft, the Mona Lisa was already considered the number one work in the Louvre.
quiz.explanation: In the 19th century the Mona Lisa was admired, but it was not yet the Louvre's most famous work; the theft is what made it world-famous.

quiz.question: In what year did the Mona Lisa, stolen in 1911, reappear?
quiz.explanation: The painting reappears in 1913 and returns to the Louvre transformed into a world celebrity.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Mona Lisa story in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones (1503, 1519, 1911, 1913) retrace the creation of the portrait, the death of Leonardo, then the theft which transformed the work into a world myth.
items: Leonardo begins the portrait in Florence
Death of Leonardo da Vinci in France
The theft of the Mona Lisa by Peruggia
The return of the painting to the Louvre

title: The Starry Night, Van Gogh
description: In **1889**, from the asylum at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, **Vincent Van Gogh** painted *The Starry Night*. The sky swirls: art stops copying the real world and starts speaking an emotion.
subject: art

quiz.question: Where did Van Gogh paint Starry Night in 1889?
quiz.explanation: Van Gogh painted The Starry Night from his room in the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum, near Saint-Rémy-de-Provence.
options: At the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum, near Saint-Rémy-de-Provence
In Arles, with his brother Théo
In the Netherlands, his native region

quiz.question: What event shortly preceded Van Gogh's internment in Saint-Rémy?
quiz.explanation: After the drama in Arles with Gauguin, which cost him part of his ear, Van Gogh was interned in Saint-Paul-de-Mausole.
options: The drama of Arles with Gauguin, which cost him part of his ear
The death of his brother Théo

quiz.question: True or false: the village depicted in Starry Night is an exact copy of the landscape visible from Van Gogh's window.
quiz.explanation: Van Gogh mixes observation and invention: he reconstructs the landscape and the village to serve emotion, rather than exactly copying reality.

quiz.question: What painting technique gives an almost sculpted appearance to the sky in Starry Night?
quiz.explanation: Van Gogh uses impasto, a thick, almost sculpted paint, to give relief to the swirling sky.

quiz.question: What Japanese work inspired the large swirls of the sky in Starry Night?
quiz.explanation: The swirls of the sky recall the dynamics of the Great Wave off Kanagawa, a Japanese print that Van Gogh admired.

quiz.question: True or false: Van Gogh was already famous and recognized during his lifetime.
quiz.explanation: Van Gogh died almost unknown in 1890; it was his sister-in-law Johanna van Gogh-Bonger who made his work known after his death.

quiz.question: Who saves Van Gogh's work after his death, by organizing exhibitions and publications?
quiz.explanation: Johanna van Gogh-Bonger, Van Gogh's sister-in-law, saved his work through exhibitions, sales and the publication of his letters.

quiz.question: At what age did Van Gogh die, in 1890?
quiz.explanation: Van Gogh died in July 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, at the age of 37, almost unknown.

quiz.question: Put these stages of Van Gogh's life in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones (1888, 1889, 1890) trace the crisis with Gauguin, the creation of Starry Night from the asylum, then the death of the artist.
items: The drama of Arles with Gauguin
Van Gogh paints The Starry Night in Saint-Rémy
Death of Van Gogh in Auvers-sur-Oise

title: Guernica, Picasso
description: After the bombing of Guernica, Picasso painted a black-and-white scream against war. The canvas traveled the world, then came home to Spain once Franco was gone.
subject: art

quiz.question: What event in 1937 pushed Picasso to paint Guernica?
quiz.explanation: On April 26, 1937, the Basque town of Guernica was bombed during the Spanish Civil War, which prompted Picasso to react with a huge canvas.
options: The bombing of the Basque town of Guernica
The start of the Second World War

quiz.question: Why did Picasso renounce color for this painting?
quiz.explanation: Picasso abandons color to stick to the urgency of the testimony, as if he were painting a newspaper front page in black and white.
options: To stick to the urgency of the testimony, like a newspaper front page
Because he ran out of colored paint
To comply with an order from the Spanish government

quiz.question: True or false: Guernica depicts a heroic battle with victorious soldiers.
quiz.explanation: Guernica shows a grammar of civil terror, disembowelled horse and mother with child, and not a heroic battle.

quiz.question: Which side supported the bombing of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War?
quiz.explanation: The saturation bombing of Guernica is carried out by Franco's nationalists, supported by the German Condor Legion.
options: Franco's nationalists, aided by the German Condor Legion

quiz.question: True or false: Picasso refused to allow Guernica to be sent to Spain as long as Franco remained in power.
quiz.explanation: Picasso in fact refused to allow the painting to reach Spain as long as Franco remained in power.

quiz.question: In what year did Guernica return to Spain after the death of Franco?
quiz.explanation: The painting returned to Madrid in 1981, after the end of the Franco dictatorship.

quiz.question: Where did the painting remain protected during much of the Franco dictatorship?
quiz.explanation: After the Universal Exhibition in Paris, the painting remained at the MoMA in New York for a long time, protected during the Franco dictatorship.
options: At the MoMA in New York
At the National Gallery in London

quiz.question: Put these stages of the story of Guernica in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: The painting was painted after the bombing of April 1937, shown at the Universal Exhibition in Paris the same year, then exiled to the MoMA before returning to Madrid in 1981.
items: The bombing of the Basque town of Guernica
The Paris Universal Exhibition presents the painting
The work is kept at the MoMA in New York
The painting returns to Madrid after the death of Franco

title: Liberty Leading the People, Delacroix
description: Delacroix painted the Three Glorious Days of July 1830: Marianne holding the flag, a mixed crowd, barricades. Political Romanticism walked into the museum.
subject: art

quiz.question: What event in 1830 pushed Delacroix to paint this painting?
quiz.explanation: In 1830, the Three Glorieuses chased away King Charles X and Delacroix immediately painted Liberty Leading the People.
options: The Three Glorious Girls who chased Charles

quiz.question: What artistic movement does this painting embody, mixing allegory and reporting?
quiz.explanation: Allegory and reportage mingle in this painting, it is romanticism in action.

quiz.question: What does the woman with the Phrygian cap in the center of the painting symbolize?
quiz.explanation: The woman in the Phrygian cap embodies Marianne, symbol of the French Republic.
options: The Marianne, allegory of the Republic

quiz.question: True or false: in the painting, Liberty is represented as a distant goddess, separated from the people.
quiz.explanation: Liberty, bare breasted, is not a distant goddess: she walks in the mud with the people.

quiz.question: What does Delacroix place at the forefront to show the price of insurrection?
quiz.explanation: Delacroix places dead bodies in the foreground: victory has a price.

quiz.question: True or false: Delacroix reportedly declared having undertaken “a modern subject, a barricade”.
quiz.explanation: Delacroix would have declared that he had undertaken a modern subject, a barricade.

quiz.question: Why was the painting removed from the picture rails after the Salon?
quiz.explanation: Exhibited at the Salon, the painting quickly bothered Louis-Philippe d'Orléans, the new king, who had it put away.
options: He bothers the new king Louis-Philippe of Orléans
It is considered too poorly painted
Delacroix himself removed it out of superstition
It is sold to a foreign collector

quiz.question: Which political regime has the Revolution of 1830 just overthrown?
quiz.explanation: The Bourbon Restoration, which had disappointed, was overthrown in three days of insurrection in Paris.

quiz.question: What social types mingle around Freedom in the composition?
quiz.explanation: Around Marianne, a worker, a bourgeois and a kid close to the future Gavroche mingle, uniting the classes in the insurrection.
options: A worker, a bourgeois and a kid close to Gavroche

title: The Creation of Adam, Michelangelo
description: On the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, Michelangelo painted God and Adam with their fingers almost touching. A masterpiece of fresco and of the Cinquecento.
subject: art

quiz.question: Who commissioned Michelangelo to paint the ceiling fresco of the Sistine Chapel?
quiz.explanation: Pope Julius II wanted a grandiose ceiling and imposed the order on Michelangelo.

quiz.question: True or false: Michelangelo, above all a sculptor, immediately and without hesitation accepted the commission for the ceiling.
quiz.explanation: Michelangelo, especially a sculptor, initially protested before accepting the order.

quiz.question: In what year did Michelangelo complete the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
quiz.explanation: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel between 1508 and 1512, completing the work in 1512.

quiz.question: What pictorial technique requires painting on a still fresh coating, like for this ceiling?
quiz.explanation: The fresco requires painting on fresh plaster, which imposes a grueling pace of work on Michelangelo.

quiz.question: What does the entire Sistine ceiling, of which The Creation of Adam is only one panel, say?
quiz.explanation: The entire ceiling tells the story of Genesis, and The Creation of Adam is only the most photographed panel.

quiz.question: What creates the central visual tension between God and Adam?
quiz.explanation: The space between the two index fingers creates tension: Adam almost touches God, but the gap remains.
options: The space that separates their two index fingers without them touching
An angel who separates them physically
A veil that hides their hands

quiz.question: How did Michelangelo's studies of anatomy influence his painting of bodies?
quiz.explanation: His anatomy studies, close to dissection, give the painted muscles a rare truth.
options: They give the muscles a rare truth, close to dissection
They push him to paint bodies always draped
They move it away from the representation of the human body
They have no influence on his pictorial style

quiz.question: True or false: the theory which sees in the mantle of God the shape of a brain is today scientifically proven.
quiz.explanation: This brain-shaped coat theory remains an attractive, but unproven, modern hypothesis.

quiz.question: Why was Michelangelo's work on this ceiling physically demanding?
quiz.explanation: Michelangelo worked lying under the vault for months, and his letters bear witness to this physical suffering.
options: He must paint lying down, with his back bent, for months
He must work at night by candlelight
He paints standing on a ladder without rest
He must transport the pigments from Florence alone

title: Impression, Sunrise, Monet
description: A seascape of Le Havre painted at speed, a mocking critic, and the word “impressionism” was born. Monet caught one bright, industrial moment.
subject: art

quiz.question: Where did Monet paint the scene in Impression, Sunrise?
quiz.explanation: Monet painted the port of Le Havre in the early morning around 1872.

quiz.question: Who, by making fun of the painting in 1874, involuntarily gave its name to Impressionism?
quiz.explanation: The critic Louis Leroy made fun of the painting in 1874 and despite himself baptized it Impressionism.

quiz.question: True or false: the painting was presented at the Official Painting Salon in 1874.
quiz.explanation: The painting was exhibited at Nadar in 1874, outside the official Salon.

quiz.question: What is Monet above all trying to capture in this painting?
quiz.explanation: The main thing is not the Documentary Haven, but the orange vibration in the gray mist.
options: The luminous vibration of a moment, more than the documentary detail of the port
An accurate historical reconstruction of the port
A tourist postcard from Le Havre

quiz.question: In what year was the painting exhibited at Nadar's, causing the scandal that gave the movement its name?
quiz.explanation: The painting was exhibited at Nadar in 1874, where Louis Leroy was ironic about its title.

quiz.question: Who supports Monet financially when the French public is still hesitant about his painting?
quiz.explanation: The dealer Paul Durand-Ruel supported Monet when the French public was still hesitant.

quiz.question: True or false: in 2014, an astrophysicist managed to precisely date the scene in the painting using tides and the position of the sun.
quiz.explanation: In 2014, an astrophysicist dated the scene to November 13, 1872 around 7:35 a.m., thanks to the tides and the sun.

quiz.question: What did Monet paint in the midst of the industrialization of the port, far from an idealized navy?
quiz.explanation: Monet painted chimneys, ships and fog of the port of Le Havre in full industrialization.

title: Nighthawks, Hopper
description: In a New York diner, Hopper painted American urban loneliness. Nighthawks became the icon of a country brightly lit and completely alone.
subject: art

quiz.question: What historical event shortly preceded the completion of Nighthawks in 1942?
quiz.explanation: The painting was completed shortly after the attack on Pearl Harbor, as the nation entered the war.
options: The end of the First World War

quiz.question: What does Hopper show of America at war, rather than battle scenes?
quiz.explanation: Hopper shows the emotional background: insomniacs, hot coffee, silence.
options: The emotional rear, made of insomnia and silence

quiz.question: True or false: The diner painted by Hopper has a clearly visible door that opens onto the street.
quiz.explanation: The diner has no visible door, making the space lit, exposed and secluded at the same time.

quiz.question: Who was Hopper a student of, before developing his personal style?
quiz.explanation: Hopper was a student of Robert Henri before painting motels, gas stations and windows with his cold clarity.

quiz.question: How does Hopper compose his scenes, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: Hopper constructs scenes like movie sets, with sharp angles and characters cut off from each other.
options: Like movie sets, with sharp angles and characters cut off from each other

quiz.question: True or false: Hopper was inspired by a real Greenwich Village restaurant to paint this diner.
quiz.explanation: Hopper said he took inspiration from a Greenwich Village restaurant, simplified down to the essentials.

quiz.question: Which directors later recycled the light and solitude of Nighthawks?
quiz.explanation: Ridley Scott and Wim Wenders, among others, recycled the neon light and solitude of the painting.

quiz.question: In what year did Hopper complete Nighthawks?
quiz.explanation: Edward Hopper completed Nighthawks in 1942, shortly after the United States entered the war.

title: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, Picasso
description: Five nudes built from facets and masks: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon breaks with imitation and opens the door to Cubism. Even Picasso's friends were scandalized.
subject: art

quiz.question: In which city did Picasso paint Les Demoiselles d'Avignon in 1907?
quiz.explanation: Picasso worked at the Bateau-Lavoir in Montmartre, where he completed the painting in 1907.

quiz.question: Where does the title Demoiselles d’Avignon come from?
quiz.explanation: The title refers to a street in Barcelona linked to prostitution.
options: From a street in Barcelona linked to prostitution
From a village in the south of France
From the name of the main model
From an order from the city of Avignon

quiz.question: True or false: the painting represents nudes according to the classical Greek ideal, soft and harmonious.
quiz.explanation: The nude is no longer the Greek ideal: it is frontal and disturbing, breaking classical mimesis.

quiz.question: What inspires the masked faces of the two figures on the right?
quiz.explanation: The faces on the right are inspired by early African and Iberian arts, in a primitivist logic.

quiz.question: True or false: Picasso painted this painting in one go, without any preparatory study.
quiz.explanation: Dozens of studies precede the canvas: Picasso hesitates, corrects and hardens his composition.

quiz.question: What artistic movement does this painting announce with its faceted shapes?
quiz.explanation: The facets of the painting announce analytical cubism.

quiz.question: How did those close to Picasso react upon discovering the painting?
quiz.explanation: Even those close to Picasso are shocked, because mimesis, the gentle imitation of reality, is dead.

quiz.question: Which painter, first stunned by the work, then joined Picasso in the Cubist deconstruction of space?
quiz.explanation: Braque, initially stunned, soon joined Picasso in the Cubist deconstruction of space.

quiz.question: In what year did Picasso complete Les Demoiselles d'Avignon?
quiz.explanation: Picasso completed the painting in 1907, in Montmartre.

title: The Persistence of Memory, Dalí
description: Soft watches on the Catalan coast: Dalí painted time melting. A surrealist icon that ended up at MoMA and in pop culture.
subject: art

quiz.question: Where is the setting of the painting, inspired by a real place where Dalí lived?
quiz.explanation: The setting recalls Cap de Creus and Port Lligat, in Catalonia, where Dalí lives with Gala.

quiz.question: What do the soft watches in the painting symbolize?
quiz.explanation: Watches illustrate slow time: the time experienced is not that of clocks.
options: Inner time, experienced, different from time measured by clocks

quiz.question: True or false: Dalí paints these impossible scenes with a deliberately crude and sloppy technique.
quiz.explanation: Dalí paints the impossible with a Renaissance finish, making the image believable and disturbing.

quiz.question: How does Dalí himself describe what he paints?
quiz.explanation: Dalí claims to paint “dream photographs”, mixing real and unconscious decor.

quiz.question: True or false: Dalí claimed to have been inspired by a too-made Camembert to imagine soft watches.
quiz.explanation: Dalí claimed to have been inspired by an overly made Camembert, somewhere between a joke and a method.

quiz.question: Which American institution acquired the painting, contributing to its worldwide fame?
quiz.explanation: The work was acquired by MoMA, which helped it enter popular culture.

quiz.question: Who was Dalí living with in Port Lligat, Catalonia, at the time of the painting?
quiz.explanation: Dalí then lived with Gala in Port Lligat, in Catalonia.

quiz.question: In what year did Dalí paint The Persistence of Memory?
quiz.explanation: Dalí painted the painting in 1931.

title: Greek tragedy and ancient theater
description: In Athens, Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides invented tragedy. Chorus, hubris, catharsis: a theater built for thinking about the city.
subject: art

quiz.question: Who finances the staging of Greek tragedies, through choreography?
quiz.explanation: A rich citizen finances the show: it's the choregy.
options: The high priest of the temple

quiz.question: In what religious and civic framework does the Greek tragedy take place?
quiz.explanation: The Dionysia, festivals of Dionysus, organize competitions where tragedy is born.
options: The Dionysia, festivals in honor of Dionysus

quiz.question: What is the name of the excess that pushes the tragic hero towards his downfall?
quiz.explanation: The tragic hero often gives in to hubris, the excess that defies order.

quiz.question: According to Aristotle, what effect does tragedy have on the spectator?
quiz.explanation: According to Aristotle, tragedy causes catharsis, a purification through pity and terror.
options: Catharsis, a purification through pity and terror
Simple entertainment with no moral effect
A lasting anger against the city

quiz.question: True or false: the Athenian public generally discovered a completely unknown plot, without knowing the myth in advance.
quiz.explanation: The public often knows the myth: the interest is not the twist, but the way of telling it.

quiz.question: What stage device allowed a god to be lowered by a crane to resolve the plot?
quiz.explanation: The deus ex machina brought down a god by a crane to resolve the plot.

quiz.question: What does the choir do during the performance?
quiz.explanation: The chorus sings, dances and comments on the action throughout the play.
options: He sings, dances and comments on the action
He chooses the winner of the competition

quiz.question: True or false: Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides each brought a different evolution to the tragedy.
quiz.explanation: Aeschylus adds actors, Sophocles refines psychology, Euripides disturbs certainties.

title: Shakespeare's theater
description: In London, Shakespeare wrote for the Globe. Hamlet, Macbeth, Romeo: popular theater that became the high point of the English language.
subject: art

quiz.question: For what audience did Shakespeare primarily write his plays?
quiz.explanation: Shakespeare wrote for the London stage, not for school, before a popular audience.
options: The popular audience of the London theater
The universities of Oxford and Cambridge

quiz.question: What is the name of the open-air theater where the Shakespeare troupe plays?
quiz.explanation: With the Lord Chamberlain's Men, Shakespeare plays at the Globe Theatre, an open-air circle.

quiz.question: Who are the groundlings at the Globe Theater?
quiz.explanation: The groundlings pay little and remain standing near the stage.
options: The less wealthy spectators, who remain standing near the stage
The main actors of the troupe

quiz.question: True or false: Shakespeare writes his plays in rhyming prose, without regular meter.
quiz.explanation: Shakespeare often writes in blank verse, an unrhymed iambic pentameter.

quiz.question: Thanks to which collection, published after his death, have several of Shakespeare's plays come down to us?
quiz.explanation: Several pieces have only come down to us thanks to the First Folio of 1623, published after his death.

quiz.question: Where does Shakespeare often get the material for his plots?
quiz.explanation: He recycles chronicles, Italian short stories and old pieces; its originality lies in the language and the characters.
options: From chronicles, Italian short stories and ancient pieces already existing
From a pure personal invention without any source
Of his own dreams, according to his notebooks
Orders from the King of England

quiz.question: True or false: Shakespeare often mixes the comic and the tragic in the same play, for example through the character of the madman who tells the truth.
quiz.explanation: Comedies and tragedies respond to each other in Shakespeare: the madman tells the truth, the king goes mad.

quiz.question: In what year did Shakespeare die?
quiz.explanation: William Shakespeare died in 1616.

title: Press freedom and photojournalism
description: From Cartier-Bresson to Nick Ut, news photography pins history down in a single image. Freedom, ethics, and media power in the same viewfinder.
subject: art

quiz.question: What does Henri Cartier-Bresson name his theory of right time, right place, right framing?
quiz.explanation: Cartier-Bresson theorizes the “decisive moment”: being in the right place, at the right time, with the right framing.

quiz.question: Who died covering the Spanish Civil War alongside Robert Capa?
quiz.explanation: Gerda Taro, alongside Capa, died covering the Spanish Civil War.

quiz.question: Which photo from the Vietnam War shocked public opinion by showing a little girl burned by napalm?
quiz.explanation: Nick Ut's photo showing a little girl burned by napalm shakes opinion during the Vietnam War.

quiz.question: True or false: Depending on the course, Nick Ut's photo alone and immediately ended the Vietnam War.
quiz.explanation: The image alone does not end war, but it makes the human cost impossible to deny.

quiz.question: What does the way dictatorships treat press photography reveal, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: Large democracies theoretically protect the press, while dictatorships control the viewfinder.
options: They control the viewfinder, unlike democracies which theoretically protect the press
They encourage total freedom for photographers
They generously finance independent photo agencies
They have no interest in the image

quiz.question: True or false: many of today's famous clichés were first censored or discussed before becoming historical evidence.
quiz.explanation: Many famous photos were first censored or discussed before becoming historical evidence.

quiz.question: In the digital age, what practices are required to verify the authenticity of a press photo?
quiz.explanation: In the digital age, verification is essential: metadata, reverse image search, context.
options: Metadata analysis and reverse image search
The only confidence in the reputation of the photographer
The total ban on digital photography

quiz.question: What does the appearance of illustrated magazines and photo agencies professionalize?
quiz.explanation: The appearance of illustrated magazines and photo agencies professionalized the profession of reporter-photographer.

title: The birth of the Greek gods
description: Before Zeus, his father Cronus devoured his own children. Here is how the void gave birth to the gods of Olympus.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: Who separates Heaven (Ouranos) from Earth (Gaia) by castrating his own father?
quiz.explanation: Kronos, the youngest of the Titans, uses the sickle forged by Gaia to castrate Ouranos and separate Heaven from Earth.

quiz.question: True or false: Cronus devours his own children for fear of one day being dethroned by one of them.
quiz.explanation: A prophecy tells Cronus that one of his sons will dethrone him: he therefore devours his children as soon as they are born to avoid it.

quiz.question: How does Rhea manage to save baby Zeus from his father Cronos?
quiz.explanation: Rhea deceives Cronus with a stone wrapped in cloths, while the real Zeus grows up in secret in a cave in Crete.
options: She makes Kronos swallow a swaddled stone instead of the baby
She sends Zeus directly to Olympus
She transforms Zeus into an eagle

quiz.question: What weapon do the Cyclops offer Zeus to defeat the Titans?
quiz.explanation: The Cyclops forge lightning, the decisive weapon that allows Zeus to win during the Titanomachy.

quiz.question: Put these stages of Greek mythology in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From this original void to the victory of Zeus, Greek mythology tells of a series of crises and family takeovers.
