He lives exactly 500 years like the Phoenix
He is reborn only from water, never from fire
It is the exclusive symbol of war

quiz.question: True or false: in Japan, the Hōō appears in particular on 10,000 yen notes.
quiz.explanation: The Japanese Hōō notably adorns 10,000 yen notes and the roofs of temples in Kyoto.

quiz.question: How did medieval alchemists reinterpret the myth of the Phoenix?
quiz.explanation: The Phoenix cycle reminds alchemists of the transmutation of metals, including the dark phase called nigredo: it is necessary to destroy in order to purify.
options: As a metaphor for transmutation, where one must destroy to purify
Like a simple tale for children
As proof of the existence of dragons
As a symbol of material wealth

quiz.question: Why does the city of Phoenix, Arizona have this name?
quiz.explanation: Named in 1867, the city of Phoenix stood on the canals and ruins of the Hohokam civilization, which had disappeared centuries earlier.
options: It rose on the canals and ruins of a vanished civilization, the Hohokam
It was founded by Greek immigrants
It burned to the ground and then was rebuilt identically.
It houses a temple dedicated to the god Bénou

title: The Titans vs. the Gods (Titanomachy)
description: For ten years, Zeus and the Olympians fight Cronus and the Titans. Their victory founds the order of the Greek world.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: Why does Kronos devour his own children as soon as they are born?
quiz.explanation: After dethroning his own father Ouranos, Kronos fears the same fate and therefore devours his children as soon as they are born.
options: He fears suffering the same fate as his father Ouranos, whom he dethroned
He obeys an order from his mother Gaia
He wants to punish his wife Rhea

quiz.question: How many years did the Titanomachy, the war between the Titans and Olympians, last?
quiz.explanation: The Titanomachy pitted Titans and Olympians against each other for ten years, before Zeus' victory.

quiz.question: What are the Cyclops forging to help the Olympians defeat the Titans?
quiz.explanation: Freed from Tartarus by Zeus, the Cyclops forge lightning, the trident and a helmet of invisibility, the decisive weapons of the three brothers.
options: Zeus's lightning, Poseidon's trident and an invisibility helmet for Hades
Golden armor for all the gods

quiz.question: What is the physical particularity of the Hecatonchires, decisive allies of Zeus?
quiz.explanation: The three Hecatonchires have a hundred arms and fifty heads, which allows them to tear off sections of mountain to throw at the Titans.
options: A hundred arms and fifty heads each
A single eye in the middle of the forehead
A body entirely of a snake

quiz.question: True or false: after their defeat, the Titans are chained in Tartarus, guarded by the Hecatonchires, their former companions in captivity.
quiz.explanation: The vanquished Titans are chained in Tartarus, where their jailers are now the Hecatonchires, yesterday prisoners in the same place.

quiz.question: How do Zeus, Poseidon and Hades share the world after their victory?
quiz.explanation: The three victorious brothers draw lots for their domains: the sky for Zeus, the sea for Poseidon, the underworld for Hades.
options: They draw lots: Zeus receives the sky, Poseidon the sea, Hades the underworld
Zeus imposes his choices by force on his brothers
They share the world without any distinction of domain
Everyone simply keeps the domain they already occupied

quiz.question: Which titanide escapes general defeat and keeps a place alongside Zeus in the new order?
quiz.explanation: Some Titans are spared: Themis, guarantor of divine law, thus remains at Zeus's side.

quiz.question: Which mortal must the gods call for help to defeat the Giants during the Gigantomachy, which follows the Titanomachy?
quiz.explanation: Gaia still gives birth to threats after the Titanomachy; to defeat the Giants during the Gigantomachy, the gods need the mortal Heracles.

quiz.question: True or false: the word “titanium”, named by the chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth in 1795, owes its name to the legendary strength of the Titans.
quiz.explanation: In 1795, the chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth named titanium after the Titans, in reference to its strength.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Titanomachy in order.
quiz.explanation: From the tyranny of Kronos to the division of the world between the three brothers, the Titanomachy follows a clear progression towards the Olympian order.
items: Kronos devours his children for fear of being dethroned
Zeus forces Cronus to regurgitate his brothers and sisters
Zeus frees the Cyclops and Hecatonchires from Tartarus
The defeated Titans are chained to Tartarus
Zeus, Poseidon and Hades share the world

title: Dionysus: the god of wine and excess
description: God of wine and ecstasy, Dionysus is also the patron of Greek theater. Born twice, he erases the border between order and chaos.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: Why do we say that Dionysus was “twice born”?
quiz.explanation: After the death of Semele, Zeus places the child in his own thigh until birth: Dionysus is therefore “twice born”.
options: Zeus carried the child in his thigh after the death of his mortal mother Semele
He was resurrected after being killed by the Titans
It is born first in men then in the gods

quiz.question: Why does Semele, Dionysus' mortal mother, die before he is born?
quiz.explanation: Hera, jealous, pushes Semele to demand that Zeus show himself in his true form: divine lightning then kills her.
options: Hera pushes her to ask Zeus to show himself in his true divine form, whose lightning kills her
She is punished by the gods for loving a mortal
Set kills her out of jealousy

quiz.question: Who are the followers of Dionysus who go into trance during his rites in the mountains?
quiz.explanation: The Maenads, or Bacchantes, leave the city for the mountains where dance, music and wine induce a trance.

quiz.question: True or false: the rites of Dionysus, called mysteries, reinforce the established social order of the city.
quiz.explanation: On the contrary, these rites overturn the social order for one night, before reason regains its rights.

quiz.question: According to legend, how did Dionysus take revenge on pirates who captured him to sell him?
quiz.explanation: Terrified by the oars that have become snakes and the vines growing on the mast, the pirates jump into the sea and become dolphins.
options: He turns the oars into snakes and makes vines grow on the mast
He turns the ship into stone
He summons a storm that sinks the boat
It makes pirates immortal and crazy

quiz.question: What art was born from the festivals in honor of Dionysus in Athens, during the Great Dionysia?
quiz.explanation: In Athens, this god of excess became the patron of the theater: the Great Dionysia organized dramatic competitions.

quiz.question: How is the theater actor “born”, according to the story of the evolution of the dithyramb?
quiz.explanation: The dithyramb, a choral song in honor of the god, gives birth to the actor when a singer breaks away from the choir to respond.
options: When a singer breaks away from the choir to respond
When a theater mask was first invented
When a poet composes the first dialogue
When Dionysus himself takes the stage

quiz.question: What two principles did the philosopher Nietzsche oppose in the 19th century, drawing inspiration from Apollo and Dionysus?
quiz.explanation: Nietzsche opposes Apollo, god of measure and clarity, to Dionysus, force of intoxication and creative chaos, to explain Greek tragedy.
options: Measurement and clarity against drunkenness and creative chaos

quiz.question: Put these stages in the life of Dionysus and his cult in order.
quiz.explanation: From its birth to the birth of theater, the myth of Dionysus follows a clear progression towards civic art.
items: Semele dies and Zeus completes the gestation of Dionysus in his thigh
The Maenads enter a trance during rites in his honor in the mountains
The song of the dithyramb is sung in chorus during festivals in his honor
The Great Dionysias give birth to theater in Athens

title: Aeneas and the founding of Rome (Virgil)
description: In the Aeneid, Virgil tells how Aeneas, a prince who escaped from Troy, crosses the Mediterranean to found the bloodline of Rome.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: Who is the author of the Aeneid, the founding epic of Rome?
quiz.explanation: Virgil composed the Aeneid over eleven years, to give Rome a past worthy of Homer.

quiz.question: Why did Emperor Augustus commission this epic from Virgil?
quiz.explanation: After civil wars, Augustus wanted to stabilize his power by linking it, via Aeneas, to a divine origin: this is Augustan propaganda.
options: To connect his power to a divine hero after the civil wars
To finance the construction of a large temple
To celebrate a military victory over Carthage
To replace the Homeric stories deemed too Greek

quiz.question: Who does Aeneas save while fleeing burning Troy, besides his father and son?
quiz.explanation: Aeneas carries off the Penates, gods protecting the home, a gesture that defines Roman pietas: duty to family, gods and destiny.
options: The Penates, gods of the hearth

quiz.question: True or false: In Carthage, Queen Dido commits suicide after Aeneas leaves and curses her lineage.
quiz.explanation: Called back to his mission by Jupiter, Aeneas leaves Dido, who commits suicide and curses her lineage: the myth thus explains the future hatred between Rome and Carthage.

quiz.question: Which Roman family, including Julius Caesar and Augustus, claims divine origin through the son of Aeneas?
quiz.explanation: The son of Aeneas, Ascanius, also called Iule, gives his name to the Julii family, to which Julius Caesar and Augustus claim credit.

quiz.question: Which Italian prince, supported by the goddess Juno, launches war against Aeneas in Latium?
quiz.explanation: Turnus, supported by Juno, a goddess hostile to the Trojans, opposes the union of Aeneas with Lavinia and starts the war.

quiz.question: What did Aeneas found after his victory over Turnus?
quiz.explanation: After defeating Turnus, Aeneas married Lavinia and founded Lavinium; his son will then found Alba the Long, from which Romulus and Remus will be born.

quiz.question: Put these stages of Aeneas' journey in order.
quiz.explanation: Aeneas' journey leads from the fall of Troy to the tragic love of Carthage, before the Italian victory which begins the lineage of Rome.
items: Fleeing burning Troy with father and son
Broken love with Queen Dido in Carthage
Victory over Turnus and founding of Lavinium

quiz.question: Which medieval poet uses Virgil as his guide in a great poem?
quiz.explanation: In the Middle Ages, Dante chose Virgil as his guide in the Divine Comedy, making the Latin poet an almost prophetic figure.
options: Chrétien de Troyes, in his novels

title: The Aztec gods and human sacrifice
description: For the Aztecs, the sun rises only if the gods are given blood. A harsh but coherent cosmology, right at the heart of their empire.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: According to the myth of the Five Suns, how many eras have already disappeared before the one we live in?
quiz.explanation: The Aztec myth has five suns: four eras have already perished in catastrophes before the current fifth sun, Nahui Ollin.

quiz.question: Why do the gods offer their own blood to Teotihuacán, according to the myth of the Five Suns?
quiz.explanation: After having thrown themselves into the blaze to become sun and moon, the gods notice that the sun remains motionless: they then offer their blood to set it in motion, a debt which men will inherit.
options: To set a still sun in motion
To punish men for their pride
To create the first Aztec warriors

quiz.question: Which Aztec god, associated with war and the midday sun, fights darkness every night?
quiz.explanation: Huitzilopochtli, god of war and the midday sun, fights every night against darkness to be reborn in the morning.

quiz.question: Which god controls rain, and therefore harvests or famine, among the Aztecs?
quiz.explanation: Tlaloc gives rain: depending on his mood, he brings good harvests or famine.

quiz.question: True or false: Flower wars (Xochiyaoyotl) aim to kill as many enemies as possible.
quiz.explanation: Flower wars aim to capture living warriors, worthy of being offered as sacrifice, and not to kill them on the battlefield.

quiz.question: With what tool does the priest extract the hearts of the victims at the top of the Templo Mayor?
quiz.explanation: The priest uses an obsidian knife, a sharp volcanic stone, to extract the heart at the top of the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlán.

quiz.question: What is the name of the precious blood offered to the Aztec gods?
quiz.explanation: The blood offered to the gods is called chalchihuatl, “precious water”; the extracted heart is thought of as a solar spark returned to the sky.

quiz.question: What event in 1519 precipitated the end of the Aztec sacrificial system?
quiz.explanation: In 1519, the arrival of Hernán Cortés and the Spanish conquistadors precipitated the end of this ritual universe.

quiz.question: Which rival god of Quetzalcoatl rules over night, destiny and magic?
quiz.explanation: Tezcatlipoca, the Smoking Mirror, is Quetzalcoatl's rival and reigns over night, fate and magic.

title: Quetzalcoatl
description: Quetzalcoatl, the Feathered Serpent, is the god of Mesoamerican civilization. His myth mixes creation, exile and a fatal meeting with Cortés.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: What does the union of the serpent and the feather symbolize in the name Quetzalcoatl?
quiz.explanation: The name associates the serpent (the earth) and the quetzal, a bird with green feathers (the sky), making Quetzalcoatl a bridge between the human and the divine.
options: The link between earth and sky
The duality between day and night
The transition from childhood to adulthood

quiz.question: What will Quetzalcoatl look for in Mictlán, the world of the dead, to create new humans?
quiz.explanation: Quetzalcoatl descends to Mictlán to recover the bones of humans from previous eras, to whom he brings back life with his own blood.
options: The bones of humans from past eras
The seeds of the original corn
The feathers of the sacred quetzal

quiz.question: True or false: among the Mayans and Aztecs, killing a quetzal was punishable by death.
quiz.explanation: The bird was so sacred that one could only take a few feathers from it before releasing it; killing him was punishable by death.

quiz.question: Who is Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl, historical face of the myth?
quiz.explanation: Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl was a king-priest of Tula in the 10th century who allegedly attempted to replace human sacrifices with offerings of flowers and butterflies.
options: A king-priest of Tula who would have wanted to abolish human sacrifices
An Aztec emperor conquering the Spanish
A Mayan priest who founded Chichén Itzá
The first Spanish explorer of Mexico

quiz.question: Why did the priest-king of Tula end up exiled to the east?
quiz.explanation: Tezcatlipoca pushes the king-priest to get drunk on pulque; humiliated, he exiled himself to the east, promising to return one year “A Reed”.
options: His rival Tezcatlipoca humiliates him by making him drink pulque
He loses a war against the Mayans
He is driven out by a popular revolt
He leaves to look for the lost corn

quiz.question: In what celestial form does Quetzalcoatl continue to exist after his departure, according to the myth?
quiz.explanation: After his exile, Quetzalcoatl sometimes becomes the Morning Star, the planet Venus: the god does not die, he changes form.
options: The Morning Star, the planet Venus

quiz.question: Why did the arrival of Cortés in 1519 particularly disturb Emperor Moctezuma II?
quiz.explanation: Cortés arrived in 1519, precisely the year “A Reed” of the Aztec calendar when the return of Quetzalcoatl was expected, plunging Moctezuma into hesitation.
options: It coincides with the year “A Reed”, that of the expected return of the god
It occurs on the day of a total solar eclipse.
It coincides with the annual corn festival
It follows a military defeat against the Mayans

quiz.question: Put these stages of the myth of Quetzalcoatl in order.
quiz.explanation: The myth follows a continuous thread: the creation, then the exile of the king-priest, and finally the resurgence of the legend during the Spanish conquest.
items: The creator god brings men back to life and offers them corn
The priest-king of Tula exiles to the east after his humiliation
Cortés' arrival revives the promise of a divine return

title: The Mahabharata
description: At 1.8 million words, the Mahabharata is the longest poem in the world. A war between cousins, a god as charioteer, and a lesson about duty.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: Who is traditionally referred to as the author of the Mahabharata, while also being a character in the story?
quiz.explanation: The Mahabharata is attributed to the sage Vyasa, who is both the legendary author and a character in the epic.

quiz.question: True or false: according to legend, the god Ganesha broke one of his tusks to serve as a stiletto for Vyasa.
quiz.explanation: Legend has it that Vyasa was dictating so quickly that Ganesha broke one of his tusks to continue writing without interruption.

quiz.question: What is the central issue of the Mahabharata War?
quiz.explanation: The war pits the Pandavas and the Kauravas, two branches of the same royal family, for the throne of Hastinapura.
options: The throne of Hastinapura, disputed between two branches of the same family
The conquest of a foreign neighboring kingdom

quiz.question: What ruins the Pandavas and sends them into exile for thirteen years?
quiz.explanation: A rigged dice game organized by the Kauravas caused the Pandavas to lose their kingdom and send them into exile for thirteen years.
options: A military defeat against the Kaurava

quiz.question: Who attempts mediation between Pandava and Kaurava before war breaks out?
quiz.explanation: Krishna, an ally of the Pandavas, attempts mediation before the war, but the Kauravas refuse it.

quiz.question: Why does the archer Arjuna drop his bow before the first battle of Kurukshetra?
quiz.explanation: Arjuna sees his uncles, his friends and his masters in the enemy camp and, upset, drops his bow before Krishna guides him.
options: He recognizes his uncles, friends and masters in the enemy ranks
He is injured by a poisoned arrow
He learns of his brother's death
He loses his sight due to a curse

quiz.question: What is the Bhagavad-Gita in the Mahabharata?
quiz.explanation: The Bhagavad-Gita is the dialogue of about 700 verses in which Krishna, Arjuna's charioteer, teaches him duty and selfless action.
options: Krishna's dialogue with Arjuna on duty and action
The list of laws of exile of the Pandavas
The story of the birth of the hundred Kauravas

quiz.question: What does Karma Yoga taught by Krishna to Arjuna mean?
quiz.explanation: Karma Yoga teaches to act according to one's duty, dharma, without clinging to the result or fruits of the action.
options: Act according to one's duty without attaching oneself to the fruits of the action
Completely renounce all action to meditate
Fight for revenge rather than duty

quiz.question: Put these steps of the Mahabharata in order.
quiz.explanation: The epic follows a logical spiral: ruin through gambling, the failure of mediation, then spiritual teaching just before the final confrontation.
items: The Pandavas lose their kingdom in a rigged dice game
Krishna attempts mediation refused by the Kauravas
Arjuna is taught the Bhagavad-Gita before the battle

title: Lancelot, Guinevere and the Round Table
description: Arthur, Lancelot, Guinevere: the greatest legend of the Western Middle Ages. An ideal of knighthood destroyed by a forbidden love.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: What do we call all the stories around King Arthur and his knights?
quiz.explanation: The Arthurian cycle is called the Matter of Brittany, mixing vague history, Celtic folklore and Christian morality.

quiz.question: What forbidden love ultimately brings down Camelot?
quiz.explanation: The forbidden love between Lancelot, the best knight, and Guinevere, Arthur's wife, becomes the poison that brings down Camelot.
options: The love of Lancelot and Queen Guinevere
The love of Merlin and Viviane
The love of Arthur and Morgane
The love of Gawain and Yseult

quiz.question: How does Arthur prove his legitimacy to become king?
quiz.explanation: Only the true king can pull Excalibur from the rock or the anvil: Arthur succeeds in this test and is crowned in Camelot.
options: By removing the sword Excalibur from the rock
By defeating Merlin in a duel
By building the Round Table alone

quiz.question: What does the circular shape of the Round Table symbolize?
quiz.explanation: The circular shape of the Round Table abolishes hierarchy: each knight is the equal of his neighbor, including the king.
options: Equality between knights, including the king
The strict hierarchy between the knights
The superiority of the king over his vassals

quiz.question: Why does Lancelot, the best knight in the world, fail in the quest for the Grail?
quiz.explanation: Only pure knights like Gilead, Percival and Bohort reach the Grail; Lancelot's love for Guinevere makes him unworthy of this vision.
options: His love for Guinevere makes him unworthy of the divine vision
He is too old to continue the quest
He refuses to participate in the quest
He is defeated in a duel by Mordred

quiz.question: True or false: Lancelot and Guinevere's affair is only a private matter, of no consequence for Arthur's kingdom.
quiz.explanation: The betrayal is not only marital: Guinevere being the wife of the overlord, it is also a feudal betrayal which tears the Round Table into civil war.

quiz.question: Who reveals Lancelot and Guinevere's affair to Arthur?
quiz.explanation: Mordred, Arthur's incestuous nephew or son depending on the version, reveals the affair between Lancelot and Guinevere.

quiz.question: What happens to Arthur after being mortally wounded at Camlann?
quiz.explanation: Wounded to death at Camlann, Arthur leaves for the island of Avalon: he becomes the sleeping king, “once king, future king”, who will return one day.
options: He leaves for the island of Avalon, the king who will return one day
He becomes a monk in a Breton monastery
He is buried in Camelot with Excalibur
He reconciles with Guinevere before dying

quiz.question: Put these stages of the Arthurian legend in order.
quiz.explanation: The Arthurian cycle follows a complete trajectory: glorious foundation, spiritual quest, betrayal revealed, then final fall of the kingdom.
items: Arthur removes Excalibur from the rock and founds the Round Table
The Quest for the Grail Reveals that Lancelot Is Not Pure Enough
Mordred reveals Lancelot and Guinevere's affair
The Battle of Camlann ends Arthur's reign

title: Merlin the Enchanter
description: Merlin, Arthur's counselor, prophet and magician: a figure born of a demon and a baptism, architect of Camelot, prisoner of his own love.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: What is the paradoxical nature of Merlin according to the poet Robert de Boron?
quiz.explanation: According to Robert de Boron, an incubus demon fathers Merlin to create an antichrist, but the child's baptism erases this curse.
options: He is the son of a demon, saved by baptism
He is a Celtic god disguised as a man
He is a fallen angel turned mortal
He is a knight cursed by a fairy

quiz.question: What do Merlin's powers remain despite his baptism?
quiz.explanation: Baptism erases the demonic curse, but Merlin retains the knowledge of the past, inherited from demons, and the gift of prophecy.
options: Knowledge of the past and the gift of prophecy
The power to fly through the air

quiz.question: How does Merlin allow Arthur to be born?
quiz.explanation: Merlin helps Utherpendragon to take the form of the Duke of Cornwall to join Duchess Igerne: from that night Arthur is born.
options: He helps King Utherpendragon take on the features of the Duke of Cornwall
He himself transforms Uther into an eagle
He kidnaps Duchess Igerne to marry her to Uther
He magically makes Arthur appear without parents

quiz.question: True or false: it is Merlin who leads Arthur to the Lady of the Lake to obtain Excalibur.
quiz.explanation: After raising Arthur in secret, Merlin leads him to the Lady of the Lake so that he obtains Excalibur, whose sheath protects against mortal wounds.

quiz.question: What is the Perilous Siege that Merlin places at the Round Table?
quiz.explanation: Merlin designs the Perilous Seat, a vacant place at the Round Table reserved for the purest knight, which will later be filled during the quest for the Grail.
options: A vacant seat reserved for the purest knight
The seat attributed to Merlin himself
A trap intended for the enemies of the kingdom

quiz.question: Who causes Merlin's disappearance, despite his love for him?
quiz.explanation: Merlin falls in love with Viviane and teaches her his most secret spells, knowing however that she will end up locking him away.
options: Viviane, the Lady of the Lake

quiz.question: What does Merlin know before he even falls in love with Viviane?
quiz.explanation: Merlin knows his end in advance and yet falls in love with Viviane, with full knowledge of the facts.
options: That he already knows his own end
That Arthur will betray him one day
That the Round Table will last forever

quiz.question: Which modern literary characters descend from the archetype of the wise old man set by Merlin?
quiz.explanation: Merlin stared at the image of the old wise man with the beard and staff: Tolkien's Gandalf and Rowling's Dumbledore are direct descendants of him.
options: Gandalf in Tolkien and Dumbledore in Rowling

title: One Thousand and One Nights (Scheherazade)
description: Scheherazade survives 1,001 nights by telling stories. A collection born between Persia, Baghdad and Egypt, now a myth the whole world knows.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: Why does Scheherazade tell stories to King Shahryar every night?
quiz.explanation: Scheherazade stops at the most tense moment of her story, forcing the king to postpone his execution to find out what happens next.
options: To delay his own execution until dawn
To distract the king from his melancholy
To win a story telling competition at court

quiz.question: What narrative technique does Scheherazade use to capture the king's attention?
quiz.explanation: Scheherazade piles up interlocking stories: one character tells another, who tells a third, constantly delaying the end.
options: Riddles that the king must solve
Stories always told in the first person

quiz.question: Where did the original core of The Thousand and One Nights come from?
quiz.explanation: The core of the collection comes from the Persian Hazār Afsāna (“A Thousand Tales”), themselves nourished by Indian traditions, before becoming Arabized in Baghdad.
options: A Persian collection, the Hazār Afsāna, nourished by Indian traditions
A Greek collection translated into Arabic in Baghdad
Spanish chronicles from the Middle Ages
A Chinese epic poem adapted into Persia

quiz.question: True or false: the tales of Aladdin and Ali Baba appear in the original medieval Arabic manuscripts of the Arabian Nights.
quiz.explanation: Aladdin and Ali Baba are orphan tales, absent from medieval Arabic manuscripts: they entered the corpus later, via Europe.

quiz.question: Who translated and popularized the Thousand and One Nights in France, between 1704 and 1717?
quiz.explanation: The French orientalist Antoine Galland published his translation between 1704 and 1717, adapted to the taste of the court of Louis XIV.

quiz.question: Thanks to whom did Antoine Galland add the tale of Aladdin to his translation?
quiz.explanation: Galland adds tales heard from Hanna Diyab, a passing Syrian, which brings Aladdin into the corpus.
options: Hanna Diyab, a passing Syrian who tells him stories
An Ottoman vizier met in Baghdad
A Persian princess exiled to Paris
A manuscript found in an Egyptian library

quiz.question: What change occurs in King Shahryar after listening to Scheherazade for a thousand and one nights?
quiz.explanation: After a thousand and one nights of listening, Shahryar changes: he finds empathy, and Scheherazade has thus repaired a tyrant through words alone.
options: He regains empathy and renounces killing his wives
He goes crazy and abandons his throne
He exiles Scheherazade to another kingdom

quiz.question: What modern narrative device is directly inherited from Scheherazade's technique?
quiz.explanation: The cliffhanger, this cut on the edge of the narrative precipice, is the direct heir of Scheherazade's technique.
options: The cliffhanger, which cuts the story at the most tense moment

title: Sinbad the Sailor
description: Sinbad the Sailor: seven voyages, monsters and treasure. Behind the wonders, a portrait of the merchant adventurer of the Islamic golden age.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: To whom does Sindbad the sailor tell his adventures, at the beginning of the story?
quiz.explanation: The story opens in Baghdad, where Sindbad, now old and rich, recounts his ordeals to a porter, also named Sindbad, in an immediate class contrast.
options: To a bearer also named Sindbad (or Hindbad)
To the Caliph of Baghdad himself

quiz.question: What mechanic repeats itself every time Sindbad travels?
quiz.explanation: Each journey follows the same mechanics: weariness of a sedentary life, shipwreck, survival in an unknown land, then return loaded with treasures.
options: Departure, shipwreck, survival, return loaded with treasures
A love quest in a distant kingdom

quiz.question: On which real and now extinct creature would the Roc, the giant bird of Sindbad, be based?
quiz.explanation: The Roc is probably inspired by the Aepyornis, an elephant bird from Madagascar that disappeared around the year 1000, whose eggs were gigantic.
options: The Aepyornis, elephant bird of Madagascar
The pterodactyl, a prehistoric flying reptile
The moa, giant bird of New Zealand

quiz.question: True or false: in the Arabian Nights, Sindbad is above all a warrior who sets out to conquer distant kingdoms.
quiz.explanation: Sindbad is not a warrior: he is a merchant-adventurer, a prestigious status in a society that values ​​commerce.

quiz.question: Which real stopover in the Indian Ocean inspires the trips to Sindbad, famous for its spices?
quiz.explanation: Serendib, present-day Ceylon, is one of the real stops mentioned in the travels of Sindbad, famous for its spices.

quiz.question: What is the main Western parallel evoked with Sindbad, but which describes Asia in facts rather than wonders?
quiz.explanation: Marco Polo is the Western parallel of Sindbad: he describes Asia in facts, where Sindbad paints it in wonders.

quiz.question: Why is the number seven central in the cycle of Sindbad's journeys?
quiz.explanation: The number seven, loaded with meaning in Islamic cosmology, gives the cycle of travels an initiatory dimension, from imprudence to wisdom.
options: It is loaded with meaning in Islamic cosmology and structures an initiatory journey
It corresponds to the exact number of seas crossed by the Arabs
It designates the seven caliphs who reigned over Baghdad
It comes from a purely commercial tradition with no religious significance

quiz.question: Who translated Sindbad's travels into French in the 18th century, making them known in Europe?
quiz.explanation: Antoine Galland translated the Arabian Nights, including the travels of Sindbad, in the 18th century, subsequently nourishing the European adventure novel.

title: The Titans vs. the Gods: the complete Titanomachy
description: After ten years of war, Zeus punishes Atlas, spares Prometheus, then faces the Giants. This is what came after the Titanomachy: punishments, the Gigantomachy, Olympian order.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: Who helps Zeus turn the war around after ten years without a winner?
quiz.explanation: On the advice of Gaia, Zeus frees the Cyclops, who forge lightning, and the Hecatonchires, giants with a hundred arms, finally bringing the Titans to their knees.
options: The Cyclops and the Hecatonchires, released on the advice of Gaia
The Muses, who sing to weaken the Titans
Poseidon alone, thanks to his trident
Prometheus, who betrays the Titans in the middle of battle

quiz.question: What happens to the Hecatonchires after the victory of the Olympians?
quiz.explanation: The defeated Titans are thrown into Tartarus, where the Hecatonchires become their jailers.
options: The jailers of the vanquished Titans, locked in Tartarus

quiz.question: What punishment does Zeus specifically reserve for Atlas?
quiz.explanation: Atlas, general of the armies of Cronus, is condemned to carry the celestial vault on his shoulders, so that Heaven and Earth no longer meet.
options: Carry the celestial vault on your shoulders
To be chained in Tartarus for eternity
Losing memory of your Titan past

quiz.question: True or false: Prometheus is sent to Tartarus with the other Titans after the Titanomachy.
quiz.explanation: Prometheus chooses to remain non-combatant during the war, which saves him from Tartarus and leaves him free, at the cost of lasting tension with Olympus.

quiz.question: Why does Gaia generate the Giants after the Titanomachy?
quiz.explanation: Furious at the fate of her Titan sons, Gaia breeds the Giants to overthrow Zeus, triggering the Gigantomachy.
options: To take revenge for the fate reserved for his sons the Titans
To help Zeus consolidate his power
To protect Atlas from his punishment
To replace the Titans imprisoned in Tartarus

quiz.question: What does the prophecy that accompanies Gigantomachy reveal?
quiz.explanation: A prophecy announces that the gods cannot defeat the Giants without the help of a mortal, which pushes Zeus to call on Heracles.
options: The gods cannot defeat the Giants without the help of a mortal
Zeus must ally with the Titans to defeat
Only Gaia can stop the Giants she created

quiz.question: Which mortal hero allows the gods to definitively defeat the Giants?
quiz.explanation: Heracles finishes off the Giants already struck down by lightning with his poisoned arrows, bringing the human courage necessary for the victory of the gods.

quiz.question: How are the three kingdoms ultimately divided between Zeus, Poseidon and Hades?
quiz.explanation: The Olympian edifice stabilizes with Zeus in the sky, Poseidon in the waters and Hades in the shadows, each master of his domain.
options: Zeus reigns over the sky, Poseidon over the waters, Hades over the shadows
Zeus rules the Earth, Poseidon the sky, Hades the waters
The three brothers rule together over a single common domain
Poseidon becomes supreme king of the three kingdoms

quiz.question: Put these post-Titanomachy stages in order.
quiz.explanation: The Olympian order is built in stages: military victory, then the distribution of punishments, before the final test of Gigantomachy.
items: The Cyclops and the Hecatonchires tilt the war in Zeus's favor
Atlas is condemned to carry the celestial vault
Gaia breeds the Giants to avenge the Titans
Heracles helps the gods defeat the Giants during the Gigantomachy

title: Ra and the creation of the world (Egypt)
description: Ra, the sun god of Egypt: he creates the world, crosses the sky each day, fights chaos at night, and punishes humanity with his Eye.
subject: mythologie

quiz.question: What is the Noun in the Egyptian cosmogony of Heliopolis?
quiz.explanation: Before time, there is the Noun: a dark, infinite water, full of germs, from which Atum emerges on the Benben Stone.
options: Dark and infinite water, full of germs, which precedes time
The name of the first deified pharaoh
The solar disk visible every morning

quiz.question: How does Atum appear according to the Heliopolitan cosmogony?
quiz.explanation: Atum, "the one who is completed", generates himself and emerges on the Benben Stone, the first solid point in the world.
options: He generates himself and emerges on the Benben Stone
It is born from the union of two primordial serpents
It is created by the god Amon on the orders of the priests
It arises from the blood of a defeated god

quiz.question: Which gods did Atum create first, before Geb and Nut?
quiz.explanation: Alone, Atum first creates Chou, the air, and Tefnut, humidity, before Geb (the Earth) and Nut (the Sky).

quiz.question: What force does Ra fight against every night during his passage through the Duat?
quiz.explanation: Every night, the boat of Re crosses the Douât in war against Isfet, the disorder, which the serpent Apopis seeks to impose.
options: Isfet, disorder, embodied by the serpent Apopis
The deceased pharaohs jealous of his power
The goddess Nut, who wants to prevent him from being reborn

quiz.question: True or false: Re is reborn every morning in the guise of the beetle Khépri.
quiz.explanation: Ra is reborn at dawn in the guise of Khépri, the scarab, a sign that Maat, balance, once again prevails over disorder.

quiz.question: Why does Re unleash his Burning Eye, the goddess Sekhmet, against humanity?
quiz.explanation: In the story of the Destruction of Men, the aging Ra learns that humanity is conspiring against him and unleashes his Eye, the lioness Sekhmet.
options: Men conspire against him as he ages
Men refuse to build temples for him
A solar eclipse made him furious
Men stole the sacred fire of Heliopolis

quiz.question: How does Re manage to stop the massacre of Sekhmet?
quiz.explanation: Ra brews jars of beer tinted with red ocher: Sekhmet, believing she is drinking blood, becomes drunk, calms down and becomes the gentle Hathor.
options: He makes Sekhmet drink beer tinged with red ocher which she mistakes for blood
He locks Sekhmet in the underworld
He transforms Sekhmet into a Khepri beetle
He asks Osiris to fight Sekhmet

quiz.question: Which god merged with Re in the New Kingdom to form Amon-Re?
quiz.explanation: In the New Kingdom, the Theban god Amon merged with Re: Amon-Re was born, “King of the Gods”, for whom the largest sanctuaries like Karnak were built.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the mythology of Ra in order.
quiz.explanation: The myth follows the creation of the world, then the birth of the gods, the crisis of human revolt, and finally the theological synthesis of the New Kingdom.
items: Atum emerges from the Noun on the Benben Stone
The great Ennead of the nine gods is born
Ra unleashes Sekhmet against rebellious humanity
Amon merges with Re to form Amon-Re

title: The birth of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict
description: One land, two peoples, and a British promise impossible to keep. How **1948** gave birth to the longest conflict in the Middle East.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: Who theorized modern political Zionism in 1897?
quiz.explanation: Theodor Herzl theorized political Zionism during the Basel Congress in 1897, in response to the rise of anti-Semitism in Europe.

quiz.question: In what year did the British government issue the Balfour Declaration?
quiz.explanation: The Balfour Declaration, issued in 1917, promised a “national home for the Jewish people” in Palestine.

quiz.question: What share of Palestine's population was Jewish in 1918, before the great wave of immigration in the 1930s?
quiz.explanation: The Jewish population of Palestine was approximately 8% of the total in 1918, before exceeding 30% by the late 1930s.

quiz.question: True or false: In 1947, Zionist leaders and Arab leaders both accepted the UN partition plan.
quiz.explanation: The Zionist leaders accept the UN partition plan, but the Arabs reject it: a civil war breaks out almost immediately.

quiz.question: Put these events in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four dates (1897, 1917, 1947, 1948) mark half a century, from the birth of political Zionism to the creation of the State of Israel and the Palestinian exodus.
items: Basel Congress
Balfour Declaration
UN Sharing Plan
Israeli independence and the Nakba

quiz.question: What do Palestinians call the 1948 exodus?
quiz.explanation: Nakba means “catastrophe” in Arabic: the term refers to the exodus of hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in 1948.

quiz.question: What organization did the UN create in 1949 to help Palestinian refugees?
quiz.explanation: UNRWA was created in 1949 to take care of Palestinian refugees, in a situation supposed to be temporary.

quiz.question: Approximately how many thousands of Palestinians fled or were driven from their homes during the 1948 Nakba?
quiz.explanation: Between 700,000 and 750,000 Palestinians fled or were driven from their homes during the 1948 war.

quiz.question: Who accepts the 1947 UN partition plan, unlike the Arab leaders?
quiz.explanation: Zionist leaders accepted the UN partition plan in 1947, while Arab leaders rejected it.

title: The China-United States rivalry
description: Two political models, two technological ambitions, one planet. Why the rivalry between **Beijing** and **Washington** shapes the whole century.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: Who launched the economic opening reforms in China from 1978?
quiz.explanation: Deng Xiaoping launched the “Four Modernizations” in 1978, breaking with communist orthodoxy to open China to capitalism supervised by the Party.

quiz.question: In what year did China launch its economic opening reforms?
quiz.explanation: Deng Xiaoping launched the opening-up reforms in 1978, a turning point that transformed China into the “factory of the world”.

quiz.question: Which city becomes the symbol of China's special economic zones?
quiz.explanation: Shenzhen becomes the symbol of special economic zones, attracting foreign companies with tax advantages and cheap labor.

quiz.question: Approximately how many billions of dollars of US debt does China hold?
quiz.explanation: China holds about $800 billion in U.S. debt, making a hard break ruinous for both economies.

quiz.question: In what year did China overtake Japan to become the world's second largest economy?
quiz.explanation: China overtook Japan in 2010 to become the world's second largest economy, nine years after joining the World Trade Organization.

quiz.question: What technology is at the heart of the “decoupling” between Washington and Beijing?
quiz.explanation: The Americans are seeking to isolate China from semiconductors, these chips essential to artificial intelligence and modern weapons.

quiz.question: True or false: US restrictions on Huawei and TikTok end after Donald Trump leaves the presidency.
quiz.explanation: This restrictive policy against Chinese companies continues after Trump's departure, proof that the rivalry goes beyond American political divisions.

quiz.question: Which project allows China to build a network of influence in more than 140 countries?
quiz.explanation: Xi Jinping is deploying the New Silk Roads, an investment project in more than 140 countries that secures Chinese supplies.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the China–United States rivalry in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From 1978 to the Trump-era trade war, these milestones show China's gradual transformation into a systemic rival to the United States.
items: Deng Xiaoping launches opening-up reforms
China's entry into the World Trade Organization
China becomes the world's second largest economy
Imposition of massive US tariffs on Chinese products

title: Tensions over Taiwan
description: An island of 36,000 km² makes most of the world's electronic chips. That is why **Taiwan** is one of the most dangerous places on the planet.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: Who led the Kuomintang nationalists who took refuge in Taiwan in 1949?
quiz.explanation: Chiang Kai-shek led the Kuomintang nationalists, crushed by the communist victory, who took refuge on the island of Taiwan in 1949.

quiz.question: Approximately how many millions of people does Taiwan have?
quiz.explanation: Taiwan has around 23 million inhabitants, a population that must deal with the island's diplomatic isolation.

quiz.question: What did Taiwan lose in 1971 to Beijing?
quiz.explanation: In 1971, the UN stripped Taipei of its seat as China's legitimate representative and gave it to Beijing, diplomatically isolating the island.
options: Its diplomatic recognition by the United States

quiz.question: In what year was TSMC founded in Taiwan?
quiz.explanation: TSMC was born in 1987 and became the heart of the global semiconductor industry.

quiz.question: How much of the world's most advanced electronic chips does TSMC make?
quiz.explanation: TSMC manufactures more than 90% of the world's most advanced electronic chips, creating a true "silicon shield."

quiz.question: What happened in Taiwan in 1996, marking a break with the Chinese authoritarian model?
quiz.explanation: In 1996, Taiwan held its first elections by direct universal suffrage, becoming one of the most liberal democracies in Asia.
options: The first elections by direct universal suffrage
Loss of seat at the UN

quiz.question: True or false: The United States officially recognizes Taiwan as an independent state.
quiz.explanation: The United States officially recognizes Beijing, but practices strategic ambiguity which nevertheless allows it to arm Taiwan.

quiz.question: What do you call the American policy that never specifies whether the United States would defend Taiwan militarily in the event of an attack?
quiz.explanation: Since 1979, the United States has practiced strategic ambiguity: it has been arming Taiwan without ever confirming direct military intervention.

quiz.question: Put these events in Taiwan's history in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the defeat of the Kuomintang to its first democratic elections, Taiwan built an identity distinct from mainland China in half a century.
items: Withdrawal of Kuomintang nationalists on the island of Taiwan
Chinese headquarters at the UN transferred to Beijing
Founding of TSMC
Taiwan's first elections by direct universal suffrage

title: The idea of a “multipolar” world
description: The world no longer has a single leader. **Multipolarity** is dealing out the cards of power again, and nobody yet knows who will write the new rules.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What term refers to the period of near-exclusive global domination of the United States after 1991?
quiz.explanation: Editorialist Krauthammer speaks of a “unipolar moment” to describe American domination without a credible opponent after the fall of the USSR.

quiz.question: For approximately how many years were international relations dominated by Cold War bipolarity?
quiz.explanation: Bipolarity lasted almost forty-five years, opposing the NATO bloc to that of the USSR until the fall of the latter in 1991.

quiz.question: Who theorizes the American “unipolar moment”?
quiz.explanation: The American columnist Krauthammer uses the expression "unipolar moment" to describe American supremacy after 1991.

quiz.question: In what year did the fall of the USSR put an end to the bipolar balance of the Cold War?
quiz.explanation: The USSR collapsed in 1991, paving the way for America's unipolar moment.

quiz.question: True or false: the American “unipolar moment” lasts more than thirty years.
quiz.explanation: The unipolar moment, located between 1991 and 2008, was one of the shortest empires in history, before the challenge from China and Russia.

quiz.question: What project allows China to weave an immense network of influence across the world?
quiz.explanation: Through the New Silk Roads, Beijing is investing massively abroad to build an alternative network of influence to the West.

quiz.question: Which organization brings together China, Russia, India and other emerging powers to influence the G7?
quiz.explanation: The BRICS allow emerging powers to collectively weigh against the G7 countries in international relations.

quiz.question: What do we call the concentration of economic exchanges between countries sharing the same interests, a symptom of selective deglobalization?
quiz.explanation: “Friend-shoring” refers to this concentration of exchanges between allies, a form of selective deglobalization born from multipolar tensions.

quiz.question: Put these stages of the march towards a multipolar world in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the balance of the Cold War to the rise of the BRICS, the world order has moved in a few decades from a rigid bipolarity to an uncertain multipolarity.
items: Cold War bipolar equilibrium
American unipolar moment after the fall of the USSR
China's economic rise
Affirmation of BRICS against the G7

title: Oil as a source of conflict
description: A black liquid has brought down prime ministers, started wars and made empires rich. Here is why **oil** is never just energy.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: In what year did engineer Edwin Drake drill the first commercial oil well in Pennsylvania?
quiz.explanation: Edwin Drake drilled the first commercial well in 1859, ushering in the era of industrial oil.

quiz.question: What is the name of the group of Western companies that controlled Middle Eastern oil before OPEC?
quiz.explanation: The “Seven Sisters” imposed disadvantageous contracts on producing countries for decades and maintained price control.

quiz.question: In what year did five producing countries found OPEC in Baghdad?
quiz.explanation: OPEC was founded in 1960 in Baghdad to allow producing countries to regain control of their resources.

quiz.question: By how much did the price of a barrel multiply during the oil crisis of 1973, in six months?
quiz.explanation: During the Arab embargo of 1973, the price of a barrel quadrupled in just six months.

quiz.question: True or false: the 1973 oil embargo was decreed by the Arab countries of OPEC against Israel's allies.
quiz.explanation: In the midst of the Yom Kippur War, the Arab countries of OPEC decree an embargo against Israel's allies, quadrupling the price of a barrel.

quiz.question: Who attempted to nationalize British oil companies in Iran in 1951, before being overthrown in a coup?
quiz.explanation: Iranian Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh nationalized British oil companies in 1951, before being overthrown in 1953.

quiz.question: Which country was invaded by Iraq in 1990, directly threatening the global oil market?
quiz.explanation: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990 threatened a huge share of the world's reserves and triggered the 1991 Gulf War.

quiz.question: What technology allows the United States to become a very large oil producer in the 2010s?
quiz.explanation: Thanks to hydraulic fracturing, the United States is massively exploiting shale oil, reducing its dependence on the Middle East.

quiz.question: Put these events in the history of oil as a source of conflict in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the first commercial well to the invasion of Kuwait, oil structures more than a century of geopolitical rivalries.
items: First commercial oil well in Pennsylvania
Founding of OPEC in Baghdad
Oil shock during the Yom Kippur War
Iraq's invasion of Kuwait

title: The Suez Canal: why it is strategic
description: A 193-kilometer water corridor carries 12% of world trade. One ship ran aground in 2021 and stalled the planet: welcome to **Suez**.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: How long is the Suez Canal, in kilometers?
quiz.explanation: The Suez Canal stretches 193 kilometers, connecting the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea.

quiz.question: In what year was the Suez Canal inaugurated?
quiz.explanation: The Suez Canal was inaugurated in 1869, after ten years of work carried out under the direction of Ferdinand de Lesseps.

quiz.question: Who is leading the drilling of the Suez Canal?
quiz.explanation: The French engineer Ferdinand de Lesseps led the drilling of the Isthmus of Suez between 1859 and 1869.

quiz.question: In what year did Egyptian President Nasser nationalize the Suez Canal?
quiz.explanation: Nasser nationalized the canal company on July 26, 1956, triggering the Suez Crisis.

quiz.question: True or false: the Suez Crisis of 1956 ended with a humiliating withdrawal by France and the United Kingdom, under pressure from the United States.
quiz.explanation: Under pressure from American President Eisenhower, France and the United Kingdom were forced into a humiliating withdrawal, consecrating Nasser's triumph.

quiz.question: How much of world trade passes through the Suez Canal today?
quiz.explanation: Around 12% of global trade passes through the Suez Canal each year.

quiz.question: Which giant container ship is blocking the Suez Canal in March 2021?
quiz.explanation: The giant container ship Ever Given ran aground across the canal in March 2021, blocking all traffic.

quiz.question: How many days will the Ever Given block the Suez Canal in 2021?
quiz.explanation: The Ever Given blocked the canal for six days, causing a traffic jam of more than 400 ships.

quiz.question: Which group attacks commercial shipping in the Red Sea from Yemen between 2023 and 2024, forcing diversions through southern Africa?
quiz.explanation: Houthi missile attacks from Yemen are forcing many shipowners to divert their fleets through southern Africa.

quiz.question: Put these events in the history of the Suez Canal in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From its colonial inauguration to the Houthi attacks, the Suez Canal remains a barometer of global balance of power.
items: Inauguration of the Suez Canal
Nationalization of the canal by Nasser
Blockage of the canal by the container ship Ever Given
Houthi attacks on ships in the Red Sea

title: NATO: what is it still for?
description: Founded against the USSR in 1949, **NATO** should have disappeared with the Cold War. It is now bigger and busier than ever.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: In what year was NATO founded?
quiz.explanation: NATO was officially born on April 4, 1949, in the middle of the Cold War.

quiz.question: How many countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in 1949?
quiz.explanation: Twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington in 1949, founding NATO.

quiz.question: Which article of the NATO treaty establishes the principle of collective defense?
quiz.explanation: Article 5 establishes that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all, deterring any Soviet offensive during the Cold War.

quiz.question: True or false: Iceland, a NATO member, does not have a standing army.
quiz.explanation: Iceland is the only NATO member country without a standing army: its contribution is based on radars, coast guards and the reception of allied planes.

quiz.question: Which war pushed NATO to intervene outside its territory for the first time in 1999?
quiz.explanation: The Kosovo War in 1999 marked the beginning of NATO interventions outside its home territory.

quiz.question: In what year did Russia invade Ukraine, pushing NATO to return to its territorial defense mission?
quiz.explanation: Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 ends any uncertainty about NATO's usefulness.

quiz.question: Which two long-neutral countries will join NATO after the invasion of Ukraine in 2022?
quiz.explanation: The shock of the invasion pushes Finland, which joins the alliance in 2023, and Sweden, in 2024, to abandon their historic neutrality.

quiz.question: How many members does NATO have today?
quiz.explanation: NATO now has 32 members, compared to 12 when it was founded in 1949.

quiz.question: Put these stages of NATO history in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From its founding against the USSR to the accession of Finland and Sweden, NATO has continued to expand and reinvent itself.
items: Signing of the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington
NATO intervention during the Kosovo War
Accession of the Baltic States to NATO
Accession of Finland and Sweden

title: The UN: powerful or powerless?
description: Created in 1945 to prevent war, the **UN** saves millions of lives every year, yet stays paralyzed in the face of the biggest conflicts.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: In what year was the UN founded?
quiz.explanation: The UN was founded in 1945, in the ashes of the Second World War, to replace force with law.

quiz.question: How many members does the UN Security Council have?
quiz.explanation: The Security Council has fifteen members, but only five of them have veto power.

quiz.question: Which two countries have veto power in the Security Council, alongside the United States, Russia and China?
quiz.explanation: The five permanent members with veto power are the United States, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom.

quiz.question: Which disease was eradicated in 1980 thanks to a specialized UN agency?
quiz.explanation: The eradication of smallpox in 1980, coordinated by the World Health Organization, is one of the greatest successes in human history.

quiz.question: Approximately how many millions of people does the World Food Program feed each year?
quiz.explanation: The World Food Program feeds nearly 100 million people affected by famine each year.

quiz.question: True or false: the mission of UN peacekeepers is to wage war against the belligerents.
quiz.explanation: The mission of the Blue Helmets is not to wage war, but to intervene between belligerents after a ceasefire.

quiz.question: What principle prevents the UN from intervening in the internal affairs of a state?
quiz.explanation: The principle of national sovereignty protects against arbitrary interference, but it also sometimes serves as a shield against dictatorships.

quiz.question: In what year did the concept of “responsibility to protect” (R2P) appear?
quiz.explanation: The concept of responsibility to protect appeared in 2005 to fill the gap left by the principle of national sovereignty.

quiz.question: True or false: the permanent members' veto power has been used more than 300 times since 1945.
quiz.explanation: The veto has been used more than 300 times since 1945, regularly blocking action in conflicts directly involving major powers.

quiz.question: Put these events in UN history in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the name invented by Roosevelt to the appearance of the responsibility to protect, these milestones show the successes and limits of the institution.
items: Franklin Roosevelt invented the name “United Nations”
Foundation of the United Nations
Smallpox eradication thanks to the World Health Organization
Appearance of the concept of responsibility to protect

title: Putin's Russia
description: In 25 years, a former KGB officer turned a country in crisis into an authoritarian power. A portrait of **Vladimir Putin** and his regime.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: In what year was Vladimir Putin first elected president of Russia?
quiz.explanation: Vladimir Putin was elected president in March 2000, after serving as interim president since the resignation of Boris Yeltsin.

quiz.question: In which secret services did Vladimir Putin make a career before joining politics?
quiz.explanation: A former KGB and then FSB officer, Putin cut his teeth in Saint Petersburg before joining Boris Yeltsin's entourage in Moscow.

quiz.question: By how much did Russian GDP multiply between 1999 and 2008, driven by the surge in oil prices?
quiz.explanation: Driven by soaring oil prices, Russian GDP increased eightfold between 1999 and 2008.

quiz.question: Which oligarch, boss of a large oil company, was arrested in 2003, a signal that the oligarchs were being brought into line?
quiz.explanation: The arrest of Mikhail Khodorkovsky in 2003 marks the beginning of the domestication of the oligarchs by Putin's power.

quiz.question: True or false: opponent Alexeï Navalny dies in a penal colony in February 2024.
quiz.explanation: After a poisoning in 2020 and his imprisonment upon his return to Russia, Alexei Navalny died in a penal colony in February 2024.

quiz.question: What are the representatives of the force structures, such as the army or the secret services, who dominate the Russian administration called?
quiz.explanation: The Siloviki occupy key positions in the administration and large public companies, merging security and financial interests.

quiz.question: In what year did Russia illegally annex Crimea?
quiz.explanation: Russia illegally annexed Crimea in 2014 and supported an armed insurgency in Donbass, marking the return of territorial warfare in Europe.

quiz.question: Until what year does the 2020 constitutional reform theoretically allow Putin to remain president?
quiz.explanation: The 2020 constitutional reform theoretically allows Putin to remain president until 2036.

quiz.question: Put these stages of Vladimir Putin's reign in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From his election to the invasion of Ukraine, this quarter of a century shows the gradual transformation of Russia into a bellicose authoritarian regime.
items: Putin becomes president of Russia
Arrest of oligarch Mikhail Khodorkovsky
Annexation of Crimea
Total invasion of Ukraine

title: The war in Ukraine explained
description: An invasion meant to last three days became the largest war in Europe since 1945. A look at the causes and the consequences of the conflict in **Ukraine**.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: In what year did Ukraine become independent, when the USSR broke up?
quiz.explanation: Ukraine became a sovereign state in 1991, upon the breakup of the USSR.

quiz.question: In what year did Ukraine sign the Budapest Memorandum, exchanging its nuclear arsenal for guarantees of territorial integrity?
quiz.explanation: By the Budapest Memorandum of 1994, Ukraine disarmed in exchange for guarantees of territorial integrity.

quiz.question: What 2014 event ousted a pro-Russian president and triggered Russia's annexation of Crimea?
quiz.explanation: The Maidan revolution ousted the pro-Russian president in 2014; in response, Russia illegally annexes Crimea.

quiz.question: In what year did Russia launch its full-scale invasion of Ukraine?
quiz.explanation: Russia launches its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, triggering the largest conflict in Europe since 1945.

quiz.question: True or false: the Russian army manages to take Kyiv and overthrow the Ukrainian government in the first weeks of the invasion.
quiz.explanation: The Battle of Kyiv ended in a crushing Russian failure in the spring of 2022, forcing Moscow to withdraw its troops from the north.

quiz.question: What did Volodymyr Zelensky respond when the United States offered him an evacuation at the start of the invasion?
quiz.explanation: Zelensky refuses evacuation, declaring “I need ammunition, not a taxi,” becoming the symbol of a nation that refuses to give in.

quiz.question: Which international banking system are Russian banks excluded from in 2022?
quiz.explanation: The exclusion of Russian banks from the SWIFT system and the freezing of central bank reserves mark a historic break in Western sanctions.

quiz.question: What percentage of Russian gas was Europe dependent on before the war?
quiz.explanation: Europe was 40% dependent on Russian gas before the war, which forced it to initiate a rapid energy transition.

quiz.question: Put these events of the war in Ukraine in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From independence in 1991 to NATO enlargement, these milestones trace three decades of tensions between Ukraine and Russia.
items: Independence of Ukraine
Maidan Revolution and annexation of Crimea
Full-scale Russian invasion
Membership of Finland and Sweden in NATO

title: How does the price of oil work?
description: No single seller sets the price of oil. It comes out of a **tug of war** between producing countries, financial markets and sudden crises, sometimes to the point of absurdity.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: In what year did the producing countries found OPEC?
quiz.explanation: OPEC was founded in 1960 to allow producing countries to influence the global oil market.

quiz.question: How much of the world's oil does OPEC+ control together?
quiz.explanation: Together, OPEC+ countries control around 40% of the world's oil.

quiz.question: Since what year did Russia join the alliance, forming OPEC+?
quiz.explanation: Russia joined the alliance in 2016, forming OPEC+.

quiz.question: What technique allows the United States to become the world's largest oil producer, overtaking Saudi Arabia?
quiz.explanation: Thanks to hydraulic fracturing, the United States became the world's leading oil producer in ten years.

quiz.question: What is the name of the reference oil extracted from the North Sea?
quiz.explanation: Brent, oil from the North Sea, is one of the two global oil price benchmarks, with WTI from Texas.

quiz.question: How many dollars below zero did the price of WTI oil fall in April 2020, in the midst of the COVID-19 crisis?
quiz.explanation: In April 2020, the price of WTI fell to minus $37 as sellers paid their buyers to dump their inventory.

quiz.question: True or false: In April 2020, oil sellers paid their buyers to clear their stocks.
quiz.explanation: Faced with full storage tanks, some sellers paid their buyers to get rid of their oil stocks in April 2020.

quiz.question: How many dollars will the price of Brent rise to in 2022, after the invasion of Ukraine?
quiz.explanation: Fearing a shortage linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Brent exceeds $130 in a few weeks in 2022.

quiz.question: How many liters are in a barrel of oil?
quiz.explanation: A barrel of oil contains 159 liters, which is as much energy as one person's manual labor for about a year.

quiz.question: Put these oil price events in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: From the founding of OPEC to the price surge in 2022, these events show the chronic volatility of the oil market.
items: OPEC Foundation
Russia joins the alliance to form OPEC+
Oil price collapse during COVID-19 pandemic
Brent price surge after Ukraine invasion

title: Tax havens explained
description: About 10% of the world's wealth escapes tax in secretive territories. How does the system work, and why does it survive so well?
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: How much of the world’s wealth is housed in tax havens?
quiz.explanation: It is estimated that around 8 to 10% of global wealth, or $10 trillion, escapes taxes in tax havens.

quiz.question: What tool allows a company to show its profits where taxes are lowest?
quiz.explanation: Transfer pricing consists, for a company, of setting itself the price of exchanges between its own subsidiaries, to move its profits to the country where the tax is lowest.

quiz.question: True or false: the French expression “tax haven” is a faithful translation of the English “tax haven”.
quiz.explanation: “Tax haven” means “safe harbor” for money (haven), not “paradise” (heaven): a confusion of sounds has changed the meaning of the word in French.

quiz.question: Put these events in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: The financial crisis of 2008 and then the Panama Papers of 2016 caused a wave of indignation which led to the 2021 international agreement on the minimum tax rate.
items: The global financial crisis
The publication of the Panama Papers
The international agreement on the minimum tax rate

quiz.question: Approximately how many billions of dollars do tax havens deprive states each year?
quiz.explanation: Tax havens deprive states of around $600 billion per year, money that could have financed hospitals or schools.

quiz.question: What is a shell company?
quiz.explanation: A shell company is a business that exists only on paper, with no office or employees, often created to hide the identity of the real owner of the money.
options: A company without an office or employee, which only exists on paper

quiz.question: Approximately how many thousands of businesses are registered in the Cayman Islands, which has a population of only 65,000?
quiz.explanation: More than 100,000 businesses are registered in the Cayman Islands, a territory smaller than Paris, making it the world's fifth-largest financial center for bank deposits.

quiz.question: If a company only pays 5% taxes in a tax haven, what does the 2021 international agreement now allow?
quiz.explanation: Since the 2021 agreement setting a global minimum rate of 15%, if a company pays only 5% in a tax haven, its home country can claim the remaining 10%.
options: Their country of origin can claim the remaining 10%
It is exempt from any tax audit
The tax haven automatically doubles its rate
Nothing, the agreement does not apply to this case

quiz.question: What are the three pillars on which a tax haven is based?
quiz.explanation: A tax haven is based on three pillars: taxes close to zero, great opacity, and little cooperation with other countries.
options: Taxes close to zero, great opacity and little cooperation with other countries
Strong growth, a stable currency and independent central banks
Low population, warm climate and beaches
A powerful stock market, developed industry and high exports

title: Tax avoidance by multinationals
description: The digital giants often pay tiny amounts of tax compared with their profits. It is not always illegal. It is the result of gaps in international law.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What does the acronym GAFAM mean?
quiz.explanation: GAFAM names Google, Apple, Facebook (Meta), Amazon and Microsoft, among the richest companies in the world.
options: Global Alliance For A Modern economy

quiz.question: On what notion was the international tax system, designed at the beginning of the 20th century for an industrial economy, based?
quiz.explanation: A company had to have factories or offices in a country, a permanent establishment, to be taxed there: a system designed for the industrial economy, not for the digital world.
options: The presence of a permanent establishment in a country
The total number of employees worldwide
The nationality of the company founder

quiz.question: How many billions of dollars in profits did Microsoft move to Puerto Rico in 2014 through intellectual property rights?
quiz.explanation: In 2014, Microsoft shifted $39 billion in profits to Puerto Rico, saving more than $6.5 billion in taxes.

quiz.question: According to the OECD, how much of the world's corporate taxes are lost each year to tax avoidance by multinationals?
quiz.explanation: According to the OECD, these practices cost between $100 billion and $240 billion a year, or 4 to 10 percent of all corporate taxes collected worldwide.

quiz.question: In what year did an international agreement establish the global minimum tax of 15% for multinationals?
quiz.explanation: In 2021, under the aegis of the OECD and the G20, a historic agreement established a global minimum tax of 15%.

quiz.question: What is the official corporate tax rate in Ireland, which has made it the European hub for tax optimization?
quiz.explanation: Ireland, with its official tax rate of 12.5% ​​and its secret agreements called tax rulings, has become the European hub of tax optimization.

quiz.question: True or false: the European Commission has obtained that Ireland immediately collects the 13 billion euros in taxes unpaid by Apple.
quiz.explanation: Ireland has long refused to collect these 13 billion euros, fearing that too strict rules would scare away head offices.

quiz.question: What turnover threshold must a company exceed to be affected by the 15% global minimum tax?
quiz.explanation: The global minimum tax targets companies whose turnover exceeds 750 million euros.

quiz.question: What must multinationals now publish, country by country, to help identify the most glaring tax discrepancies?
quiz.explanation: Multinationals must now publish, country by country, the location of their employees, their profits and their taxes.
options: Their employees, their profits and their taxes
The names of all their shareholders

title: The crisis of the welfare state
description: Born after 1945 to protect every citizen against illness, unemployment and old age, the welfare state is now shaken by aging populations and by globalization.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: Who published the founding report of the modern welfare state in 1942?
quiz.explanation: The British economist William Beveridge published the Beveridge Report in 1942, the founder of the modern welfare state.

quiz.question: In what year did France create Social Security?
quiz.explanation: France created Social Security in 1945, through a political compromise made within the National Council of the Resistance.

quiz.question: True or false: the welfare state was invented by socialist movements at the end of the 19th century.
quiz.explanation: The welfare state was invented by conservative German chancellor Otto von Bismarck in 1883, to appease workers and avoid revolution.

quiz.question: Which country invented the welfare state in 1883?
quiz.explanation: It was German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck who invented the welfare state in 1883, with a strategic aim of calming the workers.

quiz.question: Approximately how many assets finance the retirement of a single retiree in France today, compared to 4 in the 1960s?
quiz.explanation: In France, there were 4 assets to finance the retirement of a single retiree in the 1960s; this figure has fallen to less than 2 today.

quiz.question: What is the name of the Scandinavian model which allows for easy dismissals while offering generous unemployment benefits and strong support towards a new job?
quiz.explanation: Flexicurity, practiced in Sweden and Denmark, combines ease of dismissal for companies and strong social protection for employees.

quiz.question: How much of its GDP does Denmark spend on social protection?
quiz.explanation: Denmark spends around 32% of its GDP on social protection, one of the highest rates in the world.

quiz.question: To what age did the French reform of 2023 raise the legal retirement age?
quiz.explanation: The French reform of 2023 raised the legal retirement age to 64 years.

quiz.question: According to the Beveridge report, what are the five major risks against which the State must protect every citizen?
quiz.explanation: The Beveridge report aims to protect every citizen against five major risks: disease, ignorance, unsanitary conditions, idleness and poverty.
options: Disease, ignorance, unsanitary conditions, idleness and poverty
Unemployment, war, famine, exile and disease
Poverty, corruption, fraud, crime and disease
Inflation, unemployment, debt, war and famine

title: North-South inequality
description: The richest 10% of the planet take more than half of all world income. And yet extreme poverty is a quarter of what it was thirty years ago.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What share of global income do the richest 10% of the planet capture?
quiz.explanation: The richest 10% of the world's population capture more than 52% of global income.

quiz.question: What share of global income should the poorest 50% share?
quiz.explanation: The poorest 50% must share only 8% of global income, compared to more than 52% for the richest 10%.

quiz.question: What is the average life expectancy in Japan, one of the countries with the highest life expectancy in the world?
quiz.explanation: Life expectancy reaches 83 years in Japan, compared to 55 years in the Central African Republic.

quiz.question: What logic inherited from colonization pushes countries of the South to sell cheap raw materials while buying expensive manufactured products?
quiz.explanation: The terms of trade refer to the fact that countries in the South sell raw materials whose price varies greatly, while they buy manufactured products whose price only increases.

quiz.question: What share of the world's population lived in extreme poverty in 1990?
quiz.explanation: Extreme poverty affected 36% of the world population in 1990, compared to less than 10% before 2020.

quiz.question: True or false: the decline in extreme poverty in the world since 1990 is mainly explained by the growth of China and India.
quiz.explanation: This progress comes mainly from the meteoric growth of China and India, which has led to a spectacular reduction in absolute poverty.

quiz.question: What does economist Branko Milanovic's elephant curve show?
quiz.explanation: Branko Milanovic's elephant curve shows that the Asian middle classes have seen their incomes explode, while the working classes in rich countries have stagnated in the face of global competition.
options: Asian middle classes have seen their incomes explode, while working classes in rich countries have stagnated
All countries in the world are getting richer at the same rate
Poor countries are getting richer faster than rich countries

quiz.question: Why are countries in the South particularly vulnerable to climate change, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: The countries of the South, historically the least responsible for greenhouse gas emissions, are nevertheless the most exposed to droughts, floods and rising water levels.
options: They are historically the least responsible for emissions but the most exposed to climate disasters
They emit the most greenhouse gases in the world
They do not produce any agricultural resources
They are protected by more solid dikes than the northern countries

quiz.question: An American earns, in one hour of work, the equivalent of what a resident of Niger earns in...
quiz.explanation: An inhabitant of the United States earns on average, in one hour of work, as much as an inhabitant of Niger in an entire day.

title: Global debt
description: World debt has never been higher. Should we worry about it, or is it a normal tool for funding growth and getting through crises?
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What percentage of global GDP does global debt (states, businesses and households combined) exceed today?
quiz.explanation: Global debt today exceeds 300% of global GDP, an absolute record in economic history.

quiz.question: How much is Japan's public debt as a percentage of GDP?
quiz.explanation: Japan's debt is close to 260% of its GDP.

quiz.question: Why does Japanese debt, despite its very high level, not worry the financial markets?
quiz.explanation: Most of Japan's debt is held by its own banks and savers, sheltered from foreign markets.
options: It is owned by Japanese banks and savers themselves.
It is entirely borrowed in dollars
It was canceled by the IMF

quiz.question: In what year did the UK finish paying off debts dating back to the Napoleonic Wars and a 1720 financial bubble?
quiz.explanation: Only in 2015 did the United Kingdom finish repaying debts dating from the Napoleonic Wars and a financial bubble of 1720.

quiz.question: According to the price, what does the dangerousness of a public debt mainly depend on?
quiz.explanation: The real danger of a debt depends not only on its amount, but on the currency in which it is borrowed.
options: The currency in which it is borrowed
The color of the flag of the borrowing country
The exact date of its creation

quiz.question: What does a developing country that borrows in dollars risk if its own currency loses value?
quiz.explanation: If the national currency of a developing country loses value against the dollar, the amount to be repaid explodes overnight.
options: The amount to be repaid explodes overnight
The IMF doubles its financing without conditions
