Nothing, the amount to be reimbursed remains fixed

quiz.question: Which organization often intervenes in debt crises in developing countries, usually imposing strict savings policies?
quiz.explanation: The IMF often intervenes in these crises, but generally imposes strict savings policies which weigh heavily on the populations.

quiz.question: True or false: according to modern monetary theory, a government that borrows in its own currency can go bankrupt like any business.
quiz.explanation: Modern monetary theory states that a state cannot fail as long as it borrows in its own currency; the real limit is the level of inflation, not an arbitrary number.

quiz.question: What public debt threshold does the Maastricht Treaty impose in Europe?
quiz.explanation: The Maastricht Treaty imposes a threshold of 60% of GDP in Europe, considered arbitrary by supporters of modern monetary theory.

title: The platform economy (Uber, Airbnb...)
description: Uber, Airbnb and Deliveroo own almost nothing: no cars, no apartments, no employees. How did these platforms become global giants?
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What fundamentally distinguishes a digital platform like Uber from a traditional company?
quiz.explanation: A platform becomes a simple digital infrastructure that connects supply and demand, without producing anything itself.
options: It owns no factories, no vehicles, no employees
It employs more people than a traditional company
It only works in one country

quiz.question: What mechanism explains that the more users a platform has, the more new ones it attracts?
quiz.explanation: The network effect means that the more users a platform has, the more useful it becomes, which attracts even more users, almost always leading to near-monopoly situations.

quiz.question: Why has Uber invested billions of dollars in self-driving car research?
quiz.explanation: Uber has spent billions of dollars researching self-driving cars, ultimately aiming to get rid of its last big cost: the human driver.
options: Eventually getting rid of the human driver, its last big cost

quiz.question: What legal status do most platforms claim for their drivers and delivery people, in order to avoid paying social security contributions and minimum wage?
quiz.explanation: In the gig economy, the platform refuses employer status and presents its drivers and delivery people as independent, which avoids paying social security contributions, minimum wage or paid leave.

quiz.question: True or false: courts in several countries have started to reclassify driver and delivery worker contracts as real salaried jobs.
quiz.explanation: Faced with the algorithmic subordination suffered by independent workers, courts have begun to impose the reclassification of these contracts as real salaried jobs.

quiz.question: What effect has short-term tourist rentals via Airbnb had on cities like Paris or Barcelona?
quiz.explanation: Airbnb competes with hotels while reducing the number of homes available to residents, driving up rents in city centers.
options: An increase in rents and a drop in housing available for residents
A general decline in property prices

quiz.question: How much did the number of legal Airbnb listings drop in New York after strict 2023 regulations?
quiz.explanation: In New York, strict regulation against Airbnb in 2023 caused the number of legal listings to drop by 80% in a few months.

quiz.question: What do we call the situation where an independent worker nevertheless remains subject to the rules imposed by the application (rates, rating, sanctions)?
quiz.explanation: The worker alone bears the risks but often remains subject to the rules of the application: this situation is called algorithmic subordination.

quiz.question: What are some regulators proposing to improve the protection of platform workers without breaking the model?
quiz.explanation: The current debate concerns an intermediate status between employee and independent, with portability of rights, regardless of the number of platforms for which one works.
options: An intermediate status with portability of social rights
A compulsory return to traditional employment for all self-employed people

title: The role of data (the “oil of the 21st century”)
description: Data is often called the new oil. But unlike oil, it never runs out, and it grows more valuable every time it is combined with other data.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What fundamentally differentiates oil data, depending on the price?
quiz.explanation: Unlike oil, a resource that runs out, data is never consumed: it can be copied infinitely and becomes more valuable as it is combined with other information.
options: They are never exhausted and gain value when combined with other information.
They are more difficult to extract than oil
They do not bring any profit to the companies
They have been regulated longer than oil

quiz.question: What does researcher Shoshana Zuboff call the system that transforms humans into raw materials sold to the highest bidder?
quiz.explanation: Shoshana Zuboff calls this system “surveillance capitalism” where humans are no longer just a client, but the raw material of a system that sells predictions to the highest bidder.

quiz.question: What mechanism explains why digital giants are becoming almost impossible to compete with?
quiz.explanation: The data economy works in a virtuous cycle: the more data a company has, the better its service, which attracts more users, who generate even more data.
options: A virtuous circle: more data improves the service, which attracts more users and therefore more data
A law that prohibits them from any competition
A total lack of state regulation
The fact that they don't sell any paid services

quiz.question: What is the Chinese equivalent of the American GAFAM, cited in the course?
quiz.explanation: GAFAM in the United States has its equivalent in China with BATX, these giants who use their lead in data to expand into many areas.

quiz.question: When did the European Union introduce the GDPR?
quiz.explanation: The European Union introduced GDPR in 2018, a regulation that theoretically gives power back to citizens over their own personal information.

quiz.question: Up to what percentage of a company's global turnover can the GDPR fine?
quiz.explanation: The GDPR can impose fines of up to 4% of the global turnover of a company that does not comply.

quiz.question: Before the GDPR's requirement for clarity, how many working days would it have taken an ordinary person to read all the terms of service they agree to in a year?
quiz.explanation: Before GDPR, it would have taken an average person about 76 working days to read all the terms of service for the digital services they use in a year.

quiz.question: True or false: GDPR only applies to companies headquartered in Europe.
quiz.explanation: The GDPR applies to any company that handles the data of European citizens, wherever its head office is: it is this extraterritoriality that has made Europe a global regulator.

quiz.question: What do we call the risk, for a State, of depending on foreign technologies to protect the data of its citizens?
quiz.explanation: Countries unable to protect their citizens' data risk an attack on their digital sovereignty.

title: The global digital divide
description: 2.7 billion people still have no access to the Internet. In a world that is ever more digital, being offline has become a new form of exclusion.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: Approximately how many billion people around the world still do not have access to the Internet?
quiz.explanation: 2.7 billion people, or around a third of humanity, still do not have access to the Internet.

quiz.question: What share of the population in sub-Saharan Africa is connected to the Internet, compared to more than 90% in Europe and North America?
quiz.explanation: Sub-Saharan Africa remains at just 37% Internet connection, compared to more than 90% in Europe and North America.

quiz.question: Which language still largely dominates the content available on the web, hindering access to the Internet for many non-English speakers?
quiz.explanation: Around 70% of web content is in English, which constitutes an additional barrier for many Internet users.

quiz.question: Why did Kenya massively adopt an SMS payment system called M-Pesa in 2007?
quiz.explanation: Due to a lack of sufficient bank branches, Kenya massively adopted M-Pesa, a payment system by simple SMS, in 2007, beating Europe by ten years.
options: Lack of a sufficient number of bank branches
By order of the British government
To replace its own national currency

quiz.question: How many years before Europe did Kenya adopt widespread mobile payment thanks to M-Pesa?
quiz.explanation: Kenya adopted M-Pesa in 2007, beating Europe by ten years in this area.

quiz.question: What has Kenya dubbed its strategy of moving straight to modern technology without installing expensive and outdated infrastructure?
quiz.explanation: Kenya has dubbed this strategy technological leapfrogging, moving directly to a more modern and cheaper solution.

quiz.question: Which low-orbit satellite project promises to connect the most isolated villages, without having to lay cables?
quiz.explanation: The Starlink project sends thousands of satellites into low orbit, allowing rapid connection even in deserts or high mountains.

quiz.question: True or false: the cost of satellite Internet subscriptions like Starlink remains aligned with Western standards, which makes it difficult to access for the poorest rural populations.
quiz.explanation: The cost of the Starlink subscription and hardware remains aligned with Western standards, which makes these solutions inaccessible to the poorest rural populations without external assistance.

quiz.question: What risk does the rapid rise of artificial intelligence pose to the digital divide, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: Artificial intelligence requires immense computing and data power, concentrated in the hands of a few countries and companies, which threatens to deepen the digital divide.
options: It could make it worse, as it concentrates resources between a few countries and companies
It will reduce it automatically thanks to automatic translation
It has no connection with global connectivity
It makes the Internet free for everyone

title: Disinformation and fake news
description: False information spreads 6 times faster than the truth on social media. Why does it, and how can you protect yourself?
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: According to a 2018 MIT study, how many times faster does false information spread than verified information on Twitter?
quiz.explanation: An MIT study published in 2018 showed that false information spreads about 6 times faster than verified information on Twitter.

quiz.question: What is the mechanism by which social media algorithms are designed to maximize screen time called?
quiz.explanation: The attention economy refers to the fact that social media algorithms are designed to maximize screen time, focusing on emotion and shock rather than nuance.

quiz.question: What is a filter bubble?
quiz.explanation: A filter bubble locks Internet users in a space where algorithms only show them content confirming their already held opinions, making any correction difficult.
options: A space where algorithms only show content confirming opinions already in place
A fact-checking tool used by journalists
A social network specializing in fact-checking

quiz.question: For what purpose did the Russian Internet Research Agency create thousands of fake accounts to stir up tensions in Western democracies?
quiz.explanation: The Internet Research Agency did not seek to defend a specific side: the goal was often to create chaos and make people believe that “everyone is lying.”
options: Create chaos and make people believe that “everyone is lying”
Defend a single specific political camp

quiz.question: Why did young entrepreneurs in the town of Veles, North Macedonia, create fake news sites in 2016?
quiz.explanation: In Veles, young entrepreneurs created sensationalist sites without any political beliefs, only to make money from generated traffic.
options: Solely to earn money from traffic generated on social media
To support a Macedonian political party
By order of a foreign government

quiz.question: What journalistic discipline has developed to verify facts in the face of the deluge of disinformation?
quiz.explanation: Fact-checking, the verification of facts, has become a journalistic discipline in its own right, practiced in particular by agencies such as AFP.

quiz.question: True or false: deepfakes are videos doctored by artificial intelligence that make it increasingly difficult to distinguish between true and false.
quiz.explanation: Deepfakes make it possible to make a person say anything with disturbing realism, making the distinction between true and false difficult for the untrained eye.

quiz.question: What do we call the current era where objective facts sometimes weigh less than emotions and personal beliefs?
quiz.explanation: We are now talking about a post-truth era, where objective facts sometimes weigh less than emotions and personal beliefs.

quiz.question: What, according to the course, is the most robust response to misinformation?
quiz.explanation: The most solid answer remains media education: learning to verify a source, cross-referencing several pieces of information, and understanding how algorithms work.

title: The ozone hole (and its healing)
description: A giant hole spotted above Antarctica, a treaty signed by 197 countries, and a planet that is healing. This is **the only major ecological crisis** humanity has already solved.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: In which layer of the atmosphere is the ozone layer located, between 15 and 35 km altitude?
quiz.explanation: The ozone layer is found between 15 and 35 kilometers above sea level, in the stratosphere, where it absorbs most UV-B.

quiz.question: Which gases, invented in the 1930s and used in refrigerators and aerosols, are responsible for the destruction of the ozone layer?
quiz.explanation: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), invented in the 1930s, release chlorine under the influence of the Sun once they rise into the stratosphere, destroying ozone.

quiz.question: In what year did Mario Molina and Frank Sherwood Rowland warn about the link between CFCs and the destruction of ozone?
quiz.explanation: In 1974, chemists Mario Molina and Frank Sherwood Rowland warned that CFCs released chlorine which destroyed ozone; they will receive the Nobel Prize in 1995.

quiz.question: Why hadn't NASA satellites spotted the ozone hole before the British Antarctic Survey in 1985?
quiz.explanation: NASA satellites already had this data, but their software had dismissed it as too extreme to be true.
options: Their software had dismissed the data as too extreme to be true
NASA did not yet have satellites in orbit
The data was classified secret by the US government

quiz.question: How many countries signed the Montreal Protocol initially, in 1987?
quiz.explanation: The Montreal Protocol initially had only 24 countries; today it brings together 197, all the members of the United Nations.

quiz.question: True or false: the Montreal Protocol is the only treaty in the history of the United Nations ratified by every country in the world, without exception.
quiz.explanation: The Montreal Protocol is the only treaty in the history of the United Nations ratified by every country in the world, without exception.

quiz.question: Why is reducing CO₂ emissions much more difficult than banning CFCs, according to the course?
quiz.explanation: The ozone hole came from a small number of gases made by a small number of factories, easy to target, whereas CO₂ comes from almost everything our modern society does.
options: CO₂ comes out of almost all modern economic activity, while CFCs came from a small number of factories
CO₂ has no effect on the climate
There is no international climate treaty
CO₂ is easier to detect by satellite than CFCs

quiz.question: Approximately how many degrees Celsius of additional warming could CFCs have added to Earth by 2050, without the Montreal Protocol?
quiz.explanation: Without this treaty, CFCs could have added about 1°C of additional warming to the Earth by 2050, due to their greenhouse effect.

quiz.question: Put these steps in the story of the ozone hole in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These four stages mark the history of the ozone hole: the scientific alert of 1974, the confirmation of the hole in 1985, the signing of the treaty in 1987, then the measurable start of recovery from 2000.
items: Molina and Rowland's science alert
Confirmation of the hole by the British Antarctic Survey
The signing of the Montreal Protocol
The measurable start to healing the ozone layer

quiz.question: By what year should the ozone layer return to its 1980 state, if the treaty continues to be respected?
quiz.explanation: If the treaty continues to be respected, the ozone layer should return to its 1980 state around 2065-2070.

title: The biodiversity crisis
description: Wild animal populations have fallen by **69% since 1970**. We are living through the sixth mass extinction in the Earth's history, and the first one caused by a single species: us.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: Who publishes the Living Planet Index each year, which measures the state of animal populations around the world?
quiz.explanation: The WWF publishes the Living Planet Index each year, whose 2022 report revealed a 69% drop in animal populations since 1970.

quiz.question: According to the Living Planet Index, how much have wildlife populations fallen on average between 1970 and 2018?
quiz.explanation: Between 1970 and 2018, wildlife populations fell by an average of 69% worldwide.

quiz.question: What is the most destructive cause of biodiversity loss, according to scientists?
quiz.explanation: Land use change is the first and most destructive of the five causes identified by scientists, because it cuts natural habitats into fragments that are too isolated to survive.
options: Change in land use (deforestation, urbanization, intensive agriculture)

quiz.question: True or false: the 94% drop in animal populations observed in Latin America means that 94% of species there have disappeared.
quiz.explanation: This decline measures the size of populations, not the number of extinct species: species survive but in very small numbers, which makes them fragile in the face of total extinction.

quiz.question: How much of the world's food crops depend on pollinating insects to be fertilized?
quiz.explanation: About 75% of the world's food crops rely on insects to be pollinated.

quiz.question: What objective did the countries of the world set for themselves at COP15 in Montreal in 2022?
quiz.explanation: At COP15 in Montreal in 2022, countries set the goal of protecting 30% of land and seas by 2030.
options: Protect 30% of land and seas by 2030
Reforest half of the planet by 2050

quiz.question: What do we call the thresholds where an ecosystem suddenly and almost irreversibly collapses, like an Amazonian forest transforming into a savannah?
quiz.explanation: Ecological tipping points refer to those thresholds where an ecosystem collapses suddenly and in a way that is almost impossible to reverse.

quiz.question: According to IPBES, approximately how many animal and plant species are currently threatened with extinction?
quiz.explanation: According to IPBES, around a million animal and plant species are now threatened with extinction, sometimes in the coming decades.

quiz.question: What does the Dasgupta Review report remind us about the relationship between economy and nature?
quiz.explanation: The Dasgupta Review report reminds us that our economy depends on nature, not the other way around, while the services it provides (pollination, water regulation, fertile soils) are often invisible because they are free.
options: Our economy depends on nature, not the other way around
Nature has no measurable economic value
GDP already correctly reflects natural wealth
Biodiversity has no impact on agriculture

title: The circular economy
description: **Take, make, throw away**: that model is draining the planet. The circular economy proposes the opposite, keeping objects and materials in use for as long as possible.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What is the order of priority of the circular economy loops, from most to least desirable?
quiz.explanation: The circular economy always favors the shortest loop: eco-design, then reuse, then repair, and recycling as a very last resort.

quiz.question: What percentage of all the plastic ever produced by humanity has actually been recycled?
quiz.explanation: Only 9% of all plastic ever produced has been recycled; the rest ends up in nature or in landfill, where it can remain for 450 years.

quiz.question: How many years can plastic thrown into landfill last before it completely degrades?
quiz.explanation: Plastic in landfill can remain for up to 450 years before completely degrading.

quiz.question: What is the name of the traditional economic model that the circular economy seeks to replace?
quiz.explanation: The linear model, which consists of extracting resources, making products and then throwing them away, is the model that the circular economy seeks to overcome.
options: The linear model (extract, make, throw away)

quiz.question: True or false: Recycling aluminum uses more energy than extracting it from raw ore.
quiz.explanation: This is false: recycling aluminum consumes 95% less energy than extracting it from bauxite, the raw ore.

quiz.question: What does the “right to repair” implemented by the European Union in 2020 allow?
quiz.explanation: The right to repair requires manufacturers of electronic devices to provide spare parts for several years.
options: Oblige manufacturers to supply spare parts for several years
Prohibit the sale of any non-repairable product
Offer free lifetime repair for every device

quiz.question: What does Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) impose on manufacturers?
quiz.explanation: Extended Producer Responsibility makes manufacturers pay for the waste management of their products, which encourages them to design less polluting objects.
options: Pay for waste management of their own products
Take back all competing products for free
Reduce their sales prices by 10% each year

quiz.question: In the 3R rule (reduce, reuse, recycle), what is the first step, the one that has the greatest effect on the climate?
quiz.explanation: Reducing, i.e. asking yourself whether a purchase is really necessary, is the first step of the 3R rule and the one that has the greatest effect on the climate.
options: Reduce, asking yourself if the purchase is really necessary
Reuse an object for as long as possible
Repair an object before throwing it away

title: Why are bees vital?
description: Without bees, **75% of the world's food crops** would be at risk. These quiet little workers hold up our food supply, and their populations are collapsing.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: How much of the world's food crops depend, at least somewhat, on pollinators like bees?
quiz.explanation: Around 75% of the world's food crops depend, at least somewhat, on pollinators like bees, including coffee, cocoa and almonds.

quiz.question: What is pollination?
quiz.explanation: Pollination is the transport of pollen, the male cells of one flower, to the female organ of another flower of the same species.
options: The transport of pollen from one flower to the female organ of another flower of the same species
The production of honey by bees
The construction of a hive by a colony
The reproduction of bees among themselves

quiz.question: Since the 1990s, what percentage of their colonies have some beekeepers lost each winter?
quiz.explanation: Since the 1990s, some beekeepers have lost up to 30 to 50% of their colonies each winter, while natural loss should be around 10%.

quiz.question: True or false: the natural loss of bee colonies should normally be around 50% each winter.
quiz.explanation: Natural loss should be around 10% per winter; the losses of 30 to 50% observed since the 1990s are abnormal and worrying.

quiz.question: Which family of pesticides is particularly responsible for the decline of bees?
quiz.explanation: Neonicotinoids permeate the entire plant, including its nectar and pollen, disorienting bees and weakening their immune systems.

quiz.question: Approximately how many species of bees are there in the world, beyond just the honey bee?
quiz.explanation: The domestic bee is only one species among more than 20,000 in the world, including bumblebees and osmia.

quiz.question: Why can bumblebees pollinate certain flowers, such as tomato flowers, that the honey bee does not pollinate effectively?
quiz.explanation: Certain flowers, like those of the tomato, only release their pollen under a specific vibration; Bumblebees know how to do this through a technique called sonication, unlike honeybees.
options: They know how to make the flower vibrate using a technique called sonication

quiz.question: What did the European Union do in 2018 to protect pollinators?
quiz.explanation: The European Union banned three major neonicotinoids in open fields in 2018, to reduce their impact on pollinators.
options: It banned three major neonicotinoids in open fields

title: Rising seas
description: By 2100, the oceans could rise by **one meter**. For whole countries and for coastal megacities, that is no longer a distant guess. It is a planning problem.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: By 2100, according to the most pessimistic scenario, how much could the oceans rise at most?
quiz.explanation: According to the most pessimistic scenarios, the oceans could rise by up to one meter, or 100 centimeters, by 2100.

quiz.question: What are the two physical mechanisms responsible for sea level rise?
quiz.explanation: Sea levels rise for two reasons: the thermal expansion of water which heats up, and the melting of ice placed on dry land, such as in Greenland or Antarctica.
options: Thermal expansion of water and melting of land ice
Melting Arctic sea ice and tides

quiz.question: True or false: the melting of the Arctic sea ice, which already floats on water, is causing sea levels to rise.
quiz.explanation: The Arctic ice pack already floats on the water: its melting does not cause sea levels to rise, unlike the melting of ice placed on dry land, such as in Greenland.

quiz.question: How much of the excess heat generated by human activity since 1970 has been absorbed by the oceans?
quiz.explanation: The oceans have absorbed more than 90% of the excess heat generated by human activity since 1970, which is causing their volume to swell.

quiz.question: What is the current rate of sea level rise, in millimeters per year?
quiz.explanation: The rate of sea rise today is around 3.6 mm per year, compared to 1.4 mm per year in the 20th century, an acceleration of more than 150%.

quiz.question: What could a 50 centimeter rise in sea levels cause, depending on the course?
quiz.explanation: A rise of 50 centimeters can be enough to turn an expected once-in-a-century disaster into an almost annual event.
options: Turning a 100-year flood into an almost annual event

quiz.question: In Bangladesh, where 170 million people live, how much of the territory could be lost with a one meter rise in sea levels?
quiz.explanation: In Bangladesh, a one meter rise in sea levels could cause the loss of 17% of the territory.

quiz.question: Why is Jakarta particularly threatened by rising waters?
quiz.explanation: Jakarta combines rising water levels and land subsidence caused by excessive groundwater pumping, a double threat that has pushed Indonesia to build a new capital, Nusantara.
options: The city is sinking into the ground due to excessive pumping of groundwater, in addition to rising seas
It has been built entirely below sea level since its foundation
It is located on an active seismic fault

quiz.question: True or false: In 2009, the Maldives government held an underwater cabinet meeting to alert the world about rising sea levels.
quiz.explanation: In 2009, the Maldives government actually held a cabinet meeting underwater, in diving suits, before a major climate conference.

title: AI and jobs
description: Every technological revolution has frightened people about work. But generative AI is the first to reach **knowledge jobs**, not just physical strength.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: Who were the Luddites at the beginning of the 19th century?
quiz.explanation: The Luddites were British textile workers who, between 1811 and 1816, destroyed power looms threatening their craftsmanship.
options: British textile workers who destroyed power looms

quiz.question: After the transition from agriculture to industry, what percentage of the active population did the share of farmers fall to, compared to 40% a century earlier?
quiz.explanation: The transition from agriculture to industry reduced the share of farmers from 40% to 2% of the active population in a century, without causing permanent unemployment.

quiz.question: How does generative AI mark a real break from traditional computing?
quiz.explanation: Generative AI marks a real change because it no longer only follows rules set in advance: it creates original content, unlike traditional computing.
options: She creates original content instead of just following rules set in advance
It only works for physical tasks
It only replaces repetitive data entry tasks

quiz.question: Which professions are, according to recent reports, among the most exposed to generative AI?
quiz.explanation: Lawyers, editors and financial analysts are among the most exposed professions, because generative AI mainly affects white-collar workers whose main work tool is analysis.

quiz.question: What new profession has emerged with the diffusion of generative AI, consisting of formulating precise instructions to obtain the best result?
quiz.explanation: The prompt engineer is a new profession which consists of knowing how to formulate precise instructions to obtain the best from an AI.

quiz.question: True or false: Previous industrial revolutions have generally proceeded much more slowly than the current AI revolution.
quiz.explanation: Previous industrial revolutions took decades, allowing time to adapt, whereas the AI ​​revolution takes place in a few years.

quiz.question: Which idea is gaining ground in the debate over the redistribution of wealth created by automation?
quiz.explanation: The idea of ​​a universal basic income is gaining ground, not as a utopia, but as a real safety net in the face of automation.
options: Total abolition of taxes on work
The legal ban on artificial intelligence
The compulsory return to manual labor

quiz.question: What more optimistic view of AI is presented in the course?
quiz.explanation: A more optimistic view sees AI as an assistant rather than a replacement, automating less interesting tasks and leaving professionals more time for the human or strategic aspect of their work.
options: An assistant that automates repetitive tasks and gives humans more time for the strategic aspect
A tool that only serves to entertain
A technology reserved only for large companies
A system that completely replaces each profession without exception

title: Populism: why is it rising everywhere?
description: From the United States to India, and across Europe, populist leaders are shaking up the traditional parties. Why is this wave hitting **almost every democracy** at the same time?
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: According to political scientist Jan-Werner Müller, what is the central idea of ​​populism?
quiz.explanation: According to Jan-Werner Müller, the central idea of ​​populism is monism: there is only one “true people”, of which the populist leader would be the sole spokesperson.
options: There would only be one “real people”, of which the populist leader would be the sole spokesperson.
Populism is above all a protectionist economic program
Populism rejects any form of representative democracy
Populism is defined solely by opposition to immigration

quiz.question: How does populist discourse divide society?
quiz.explanation: The populist discourse divides society into two camps: a “pure people”, bearers of authentic values, and a “corrupt elite”, accused of betraying the general interest.
options: Between a “pure people” carrying authentic values ​​and a “corrupt elite”
Between young people and old people

quiz.question: What was the very first major modern populist party, appearing in the United States in 1892?
quiz.explanation: The People's Party, created in 1892 in the United States, is considered the very first major modern populist party; In particular, he called for the nationalization of the railways.

quiz.question: What did researcher Branko Milanović show about income between 1988 and 2008?
quiz.explanation: Branko Milanović showed that between 1988 and 2008, the Asian middle classes and the world's richest saw their incomes rise, while the Western middle classes stagnated, fueling a feeling of downgrading.
options: The Asian middle classes and the richest saw their incomes rise, while the Western middle classes stagnated
All social classes in the world have experienced the same increase in income
Only poor countries have seen an increase in income
Western middle classes have seen the biggest increase in income in the world

quiz.question: True or false: the 2015 migration crisis contributed to reinforcing a feeling of identity insecurity in Europe.
quiz.explanation: The acceleration of societal changes and the migration crisis of 2015 have created identity insecurity among many European voters.

quiz.question: What type of democracy has Viktor Orbán built in Hungary, where the election results justify a growing concentration of power?
quiz.explanation: Viktor Orbán has built an illiberal democracy in Hungary, where the results of elections justify an increasing concentration of power in his hands.

quiz.question: What strategy did Marine Le Pen pursue in France to expand her electorate?
quiz.explanation: Marine Le Pen pursued a strategy of demonization to broaden her electorate, while maintaining a discourse centered on national preference.

quiz.question: Once in power, what does a populist leader often do to maintain his rebellious image?
quiz.explanation: To maintain his rebel image once in power, the populist leader often appoints new enemies, such as judges or civil servants, accused of blocking his will.
options: It designates new enemies, such as judges or civil servants
He resigns to make way for a successor

quiz.question: Put these events related to the rise of populism in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: Three emblematic milestones: the birth of the first modern populist party in 1892, the European migration crisis of 2015, then the attack on the Capitol in 2021 after the contestation of an electoral result.
items: Creation of the People's Party in the United States
Migration crisis in Europe
Attack on the Capitol in Washington

title: Mental health as a social issue
description: Mental illness accounts for **20% of illness worldwide**, but gets only 2% of health budgets. Here is why a cause left aside for so long is becoming a major social issue.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: How much of the world's illnesses are linked to mental health?
quiz.explanation: Mental health accounts for around 20% of illnesses worldwide.

quiz.question: What share of global health budgets is devoted to mental health?
quiz.explanation: Despite its 20% burden of global diseases, mental health receives only 2% of health budgets.

quiz.question: Which disease is today the leading global cause of disability, ahead of heart disease or diabetes?
quiz.explanation: Depression is today the leading global cause of disability, ahead of heart disease and diabetes.

quiz.question: How many deaths by suicide are recorded each year in the world?
quiz.explanation: Suicide is responsible for 700,000 deaths per year worldwide, a figure greater than the number of victims of war and natural disasters combined.

quiz.question: What did the World Health Organization recognize in 2019 as a work-related phenomenon?
quiz.explanation: In 2019, the WHO recognized burnout as a work-related phenomenon, shifting responsibility from the individual alone to their work environment.

quiz.question: Around what year did the United States experience a marked turning point in the increase in anxiety and depression among 12-25 year olds, coinciding with the widespread use of smartphones?
quiz.explanation: This turning point took place around 2012, which corresponds to the generalization of smartphones and social networks.

quiz.question: What is “upward social comparison”, mentioned in relation to the impact of social networks on young people?
quiz.explanation: Upward social comparison involves comparing yourself to unrealistic standards of living seen on social media, which creates a deep feeling of inadequacy among young people.
options: Comparing yourself to unrealistic standards of living, which creates a feeling of inadequacy
Compare your salary to that of your colleagues
Compare your academic results to those of the previous year

quiz.question: How much is the annual cost of burnout and suffering at work estimated in the United States, in billions of dollars?
quiz.explanation: The annual cost of burnout and suffering at work is estimated at $300 billion per year in the United States alone.

quiz.question: True or false: Generalized anxiety affects approximately 300 million people worldwide.
quiz.explanation: Generalized anxiety affects approximately 300 million people worldwide, one of the most common mental health disorders.

title: The EU: how does it really work?
description: The European Union governs **450 million citizens**, yet the way it works often looks like a black box. Here is how a European law is really born, and who decides what.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: Approximately how many citizens does the European Union govern?
quiz.explanation: The European Union governs around 450 million citizens.

quiz.question: Which institution sets the main political guidelines of the EU during summits, without writing laws itself?
quiz.explanation: The European Council, made up of the heads of state of member countries, sets the main political guidelines at summits, without writing laws itself.
options: The Court of Justice of the EU

quiz.question: What is the only European institution elected directly by citizens?
quiz.explanation: The European Parliament is the only institution directly elected by citizens, which ensures the democratic legitimacy of the system.

quiz.question: Which institution is the only one able to propose a new European law?
quiz.explanation: The European Commission has a monopoly on legislative initiative: it is the only institution that can propose a new law.
options: The Court of Justice of the EU

quiz.question: What is the difference between a regulation and a European directive?
quiz.explanation: The regulation applies directly and equally in all countries, while the directive sets an objective but lets each country choose how to achieve it.
options: The regulation applies directly and identically everywhere, the directive sets an objective that each country achieves in its own way
The regulation concerns the economy, the directive concerns the environment
The regulation is temporary, the directive is permanent
The regulation is voted on by citizens, the directive by governments

quiz.question: True or false: the European Union can act in all areas, without any limits imposed by member countries.
quiz.explanation: This is false: the EU can only act in the areas that countries have entrusted to it, some belonging to it, others being shared or remaining national.

quiz.question: Which subjects remain almost entirely managed by each country and often require unanimity in the EU Council?
quiz.explanation: Sensitive subjects such as taxation, health or defense remain almost entirely managed by each country and often require unanimity in the EU Council.
options: International trade and the single currency

quiz.question: Approximately how many agents does the European Union administration have to manage the entire continent?
quiz.explanation: The European administration has around 60,000 agents to manage an entire continent, less than the city of Paris alone.

quiz.question: What did the Next Generation EU plan, launched after the 2020 pandemic, achieve for the first time?
quiz.explanation: For the first time, member countries agreed to borrow together on the financial markets with the Next Generation EU plan, marking a turning point towards a more united union.
options: Member countries to borrow together on financial markets
It's up to the EU to raise a common army
It's up to each country to freely leave the EU
It is up to the Commission to set national taxes itself

quiz.question: What does the European Citizens' Initiative enable?
quiz.explanation: The European Citizens' Initiative allows one million citizens to ask the Commission to study a new law.
options: One million citizens to ask the Commission to study a new law
It is up to each citizen to vote directly on European laws
For NGOs to block a European law
Companies to propose laws to Parliament

title: Press freedom around the world
description: Fewer than **10% of the world's people** live in a country with a truly free press. Between state censorship and economic pressure, this essential right is retreating almost everywhere.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What share of the world's population lives in a country where the press is truly free, according to 2024 data?
quiz.explanation: Less than 10% of the world's population lives in an area where the press operates unhindered, according to 2024 data.

quiz.question: Which organization publishes a reference report each year on the obstacles to the profession of journalism around the world?
quiz.explanation: Reporters Without Borders publishes each year a reference report on the obstacles to the profession of journalism around the world.

quiz.question: In 2023, how many journalists have, at least, lost their lives in the exercise of their profession?
quiz.explanation: In 2023, at least 79 journalists have lost their lives in the exercise of their profession, often targeted to silence embarrassing investigations.

quiz.question: What strategy did Viktor Orbán use in Hungary to weaken opposition media, rather than banning them directly?
quiz.explanation: Rather than banning opposition media, Viktor Orbán favored their takeover by those close to the government, gradually transforming the media landscape.
options: Promote their takeover by people close to the government
Impose systematic prior censorship on them

quiz.question: What does the term SLAPP mean in the course?
quiz.explanation: SLAPPs are abusive lawsuits that are proliferating to intimidate critical voices in journalism.
options: Abusive legal proceedings intended to intimidate critical voices
A type of censorship on social networks
A public subsidy for independent media

quiz.question: True or false: the historical economic model of the press, based on single-issue sales and advertising, has collapsed with digital technology.
quiz.explanation: The historical model of the press has collapsed with digital technology, with the large platforms now capturing the majority of online advertising.

quiz.question: What does the expression “information desert”, mentioned in the course, mean?
quiz.explanation: An “information desert” designates an area where the closure of many local newspapers means that there is no longer anyone to monitor the action of local elected officials.
options: An area where the closure of local newspapers means that there is no longer anyone to monitor the action of elected officials
A region of the world without internet access
A country where the press is completely censored by the state
A rural area without a post office

quiz.question: What new economic model, financed by donations or direct subscriptions, is cited as an example for independent and profitable journalism?
quiz.explanation: Mediapart in France and ProPublica in the United States prove that independent journalism, financed by donations or direct subscriptions, can also be profitable.
options: Mediapart in France and ProPublica in the United States
The New York Times and Le Monde only

quiz.question: In what year was the first printed newspaper in history, the “Relation”, launched in Strasbourg by Johann Carolus?
quiz.explanation: The “Relation”, the first printed newspaper in history, was launched in Strasbourg in 1605 by Johann Carolus.

title: Climate migration
description: The climate will force hundreds of millions of people to leave home, and no international law protects them yet.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What exceeded, for the first time in 2022, the number of people fleeing wars?
quiz.explanation: In 2022, climate disasters will cause 60 million internal displacements, surpassing the number of people fleeing war for the first time.

quiz.question: According to the World Bank, how many millions of people could climate change force to migrate by 2050?
quiz.explanation: The World Bank estimates that, without massive effort, climate change could force 216 million people to migrate by 2050.

quiz.question: In 2009, which country held a council of ministers underwater to warn of rising water levels?
quiz.explanation: In 2009, the government of the Maldives held a council of ministers underwater, in oxygen tanks, to alert the world to the possible disappearance of this archipelago.

quiz.question: What type of climatic event permanently transforms a territory, such as rising water levels or desertification?
quiz.explanation: Slow degradation, such as rising water levels or desertification, transforms a territory forever, unlike sudden disasters, which are more brutal but often temporary.

quiz.question: True or false: the term “climate refugee” has a recognized value in international law.
quiz.explanation: The term “climate refugee” has no value in international law: the 1951 Geneva Convention protects persecuted people, not victims of climate change.

quiz.question: What principle prohibits sending a person back to a place where their life would be in danger?
quiz.explanation: The principle of non-refoulement prohibits sending a person back to a place where their life would be threatened, but climate displaced people do not benefit from this, due to lack of recognized status.

quiz.question: Which country bought land in Fiji to prepare, if necessary, for the relocation of its entire population?
quiz.explanation: Kiribati has purchased land in Fiji to prepare, if necessary, for the relocation of its entire population.

quiz.question: In 2018, which international agreement began to discuss the environmental causes of forced departures?
quiz.explanation: In 2018, the Global Compact on Migration began to discuss the environmental causes of departures, without creating a legal status for climate refugees.

title: Blockchain and cryptocurrencies
description: The **blockchain** invented a ledger that no one can forge alone. That idea opened the way to a whole new digital economy.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What is a distributed ledger, at the heart of how blockchain works?
quiz.explanation: A distributed ledger means that thousands of computers on the network each keep an identical copy of all transactions, without a central server.
options: A copy of transactions kept by thousands of computers
A file stored on a single server

quiz.question: What is the name of the mathematical calculation that connects each block to the previous one, forming an unfalsifiable chain?
quiz.explanation: Each block is linked to the previous one by a hash, a unique digital fingerprint, which makes the chain almost impossible to forge.

quiz.question: In what year was Bitcoin launched by Satoshi Nakamoto?
quiz.explanation: Bitcoin was launched in 2009 by an anonymous person or group under the name Satoshi Nakamoto.

quiz.question: What is the maximum number of bitcoins that could one day exist, in millions of units?
quiz.explanation: The creator of Bitcoin has set a strict cap of 21 million bitcoins, to guarantee its scarcity.

quiz.question: What major innovation does the Ethereum blockchain, which appeared in 2015, introduce?
quiz.explanation: Ethereum introduces smart contracts, programs that run automatically as soon as a condition is met.
options: The first block of the chain

quiz.question: True or false: the annual electricity consumption of the Bitcoin network is today comparable to that of a country like Argentina.
quiz.explanation: The annual electricity expenditure of the Bitcoin network is today comparable to that of an entire country like Argentina, which fuels criticism of its environmental impact.

quiz.question: Why does the high volatility of Bitcoin prevent it from becoming an everyday currency?
quiz.explanation: The price of Bitcoin can vary by 10 to 20% in a few hours, an instability which currently prevents it from becoming a real everyday currency.

It is not accepted by any merchant

quiz.question: What is a stablecoin?
quiz.explanation: A stablecoin is a cryptocurrency whose price is stabilized thanks to a reserve of dollars or euros, serving as a bridge between classic finance and cryptocurrencies.

A digital currency issued by a central bank
The very first block of the Bitcoin blockchain

quiz.question: In 2021, which country became the first in the world to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender?
quiz.explanation: In 2021, El Salvador became the first country in the world to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender, alongside the US dollar.

title: The right of asylum explained
description: Since 1951, one rule has protected persecuted people all over the world. But it never anticipated today's migration crises.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What year was the Geneva Refugee Convention signed?
quiz.explanation: The Geneva Refugee Convention was signed in 1951, after World War II.

quiz.question: According to the Geneva Convention, what ground does NOT allow you to obtain refugee status?
quiz.explanation: The definition of refugee excludes victims of natural disasters or famine, which do not constitute persecution within the meaning of the Convention.

quiz.question: What principle prohibits sending a person to a place where they risk torture or death?
quiz.explanation: The principle of non-refoulement prohibits returning a person to a place where they would risk torture or death.

quiz.question: What share of the world's refugees are hosted by low- and middle-income countries?
quiz.explanation: Around 75% of the world's refugees are hosted by low- and middle-income countries located near conflict zones.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a refugee and an economic migrant?
quiz.explanation: An economic migrant leaves his country voluntarily to seek a better life, and the Geneva Convention, reserved for persecuted people, does not apply to him.
options: The economic migrant leaves his country voluntarily, without persecution to prove
The refugee never has the right to work
The economic migrant automatically benefits from the Geneva Convention
There is no legal difference between the two

quiz.question: In 2015, how many millions of people crossed the Mediterranean Sea to reach Europe?
quiz.explanation: In 2015, more than a million people crossed the Mediterranean Sea, mostly fleeing the civil war in Syria.

quiz.question: What are the criticisms of the Dublin Regulation, revealed by the migration crisis of 2015?
quiz.explanation: The Dublin Regulation requires the first country of arrival to process each request, which overburdened Greece and Italy during the 2015 crisis.
options: It requires the first country of arrival to process each asylum request
It prevents any European country from welcoming refugees
It gives refugees the free choice of their host country

quiz.question: True or false: the status of climate refugee is today recognized by the Geneva Convention.
quiz.explanation: The status of climate refugee does not exist in international law, because these people cannot prove persecution within the meaning of the 1951 Convention.

quiz.question: Put these stages of asylum in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These stages span from 1951 to 2024: the Geneva Convention, its universalization by the 1967 protocol, the migration crisis of 2015, the EU-Turkey agreement of 2016, then the European pact of 2024.
items: Signing of the Geneva Convention on Refugees
Protocol making the Convention universal
Large-scale migration crisis in Europe
Agreement between the European Union and Turkey
New European pact on migration

title: Global food security
description: The Earth produces enough food to feed every human being. So why do **800 million people** around the world still go hungry?
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What proportion of the world's population suffers from hunger today?
quiz.explanation: Around 800 million people suffer from hunger, or one in ten people in the world.

quiz.question: According to the course, world hunger is primarily a problem of...
quiz.explanation: Humanity produces enough food for everyone: hunger comes primarily from a problem of distribution and access, not quantity.

quiz.question: What does “hidden hunger” mean, which affects around 2 billion people?

quiz.question: True or false: since the 2010s, obesity and diseases linked to excess weight kill more people worldwide each year than undernutrition.

quiz.question: How much of the world's food production is lost or wasted each year?
quiz.explanation: About a third of global food production, 1.3 billion tonnes, is lost or wasted every year.

quiz.question: What share of global wheat exports do Ukraine and Russia account for together?
quiz.explanation: Ukraine and Russia together account for nearly 30% of global wheat exports, making many countries very vulnerable to the slightest blockage.

quiz.question: What does the concept of “food power” mean?
quiz.explanation: Food power refers to the voluntary use of food exports as a means of diplomatic pressure, or even as a sanction against an opposing country.
options: The use of food exports as a means of diplomatic pressure

quiz.question: What wave of agricultural techniques, launched in the 1960s, increased yields but increased dependence on chemical fertilizers?
quiz.explanation: The Green Revolution of the 1960s greatly increased agricultural yields, but also made farmers dependent on chemical fertilizers.

title: Water: the next source of conflict?
description: Less than 1% of the water on Earth is fresh and easy to reach. Some experts already see it as the next great source of conflict.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What proportion of all water on Earth is liquid, easily accessible fresh water (lakes, rivers, shallow water tables)?
quiz.explanation: Liquid and accessible fresh water represents less than 1% of all water on the planet, the rest being salty or frozen.

quiz.question: In 2024, how many billion people live at least one month per year in a situation of water stress?
quiz.explanation: In 2024, around 4 billion people live at least one month per year in a situation of water stress.

quiz.question: What is a transboundary river?
quiz.explanation: A transboundary river crosses several countries, creating a dependency between the countries located upstream and those located downstream.
options: A river that crosses several countries
A river used only for irrigation
A river whose source is artificial

quiz.question: Why does the GERD dam built by Ethiopia worry Egypt?
quiz.explanation: Egypt depends on the Nile for 95% of its water: every cubic meter held upstream by the GERD dam is seen as a direct threat to its security.
options: Egypt depends on the Nile 95% for its water
The dam produces electricity for Egypt
The Nile does not flow through Egypt

quiz.question: True or false: the Indus River Treaty, signed in 1960 between India and Pakistan, was broken in each of the three wars between the two countries.
quiz.explanation: The Indus Treaty has survived three wars between India and Pakistan without ever being broken, proof that water can also be a tool for peace.

quiz.question: How much of its drinking water does Israel produce using desalination plants?
quiz.explanation: Israel produces more than 80% of its drinking water through seawater desalination plants.

quiz.question: What does drip irrigation do?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to plant roots, reducing agricultural consumption by 30 to 70 percent.
options: Reduce agricultural water consumption by 30 to 70%
Completely eliminate the need for irrigation
Transform sea water into fresh water

quiz.question: What does the concept of “virtual water” mean?
quiz.explanation: Virtual water refers to the quantity of water necessary to produce a product: importing wheat also means importing the water used to cultivate it.
options: The amount of water needed to make a product

quiz.question: How many liters of water are needed to produce a single kilogram of beef?
quiz.explanation: It takes around 15,000 liters of water to produce a single kilogram of beef, compared to 1,500 liters for one kilogram of wheat.

title: American soft power
description: How can a country dominate the world without going to war? By simply making others want to look like it.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: In what year did political scientist Joseph Nye invent the concept of soft power?
quiz.explanation: Joseph Nye invented the concept of soft power in 1990, in his book Bound to Lead.

quiz.question: According to Joseph Nye, on which three pillars does a country's soft power rest?
quiz.explanation: According to Nye, soft power is based on three pillars: culture, political values ​​applied at home, and a foreign policy perceived as legitimate.
options: The army, economic sanctions and diplomacy

quiz.question: What share of global cinema revenues do American films capture, despite a lower number of films than Bollywood?
quiz.explanation: American films capture around 70% of global cinema revenues, proof that influence depends above all on the control of distribution networks.

quiz.question: What event in 2003 permanently damaged the image of the United States in the world?
quiz.explanation: In 2003, the invasion of Iraq, carried out without UN agreement and justified by false weapons evidence, permanently damaged the image of the United States.
options: The invasion of Iraq without a UN agreement
The signing of a peace treaty

quiz.question: True or false: the storming of the Capitol in January 2021 reinforced the image of the United States as a model of stable democracy.
quiz.explanation: The assault on the Capitol in January 2021, on the contrary, weakened the image of the United States as a model of stable democracy.

quiz.question: What is the “Brussels effect”?
quiz.explanation: The Brussels effect refers to the fact that the strict rules of the European Union, particularly on data or the environment, often become standards applied by companies around the world.
options: Strict EU rules become standards applied worldwide
The cultural influence exerted by Belgium
The decline of American soft power in Europe
A military treaty between European countries

quiz.question: What is the name of the South Korean cultural wave which is conquering a global audience (music, series, cinema)?
quiz.explanation: Hallyu refers to the South Korean cultural wave (music, series, cinema) which is conquering a global audience.

quiz.question: What power is investing in cultural institutes and huge infrastructure projects to offer an alternative model of development?
quiz.explanation: China is investing in cultural institutes and huge infrastructure projects across Asia and Africa, to offer an alternative development model.

quiz.question: On the Soft Power 30 rankings, who overtook the United States for first place during Donald Trump's presidency?
quiz.explanation: The United States was overtaken by France or Germany on the Soft Power 30 rankings during Donald Trump's presidency, proof of the link between foreign policy and a country's image.

title: GAFAM: power and overreach
description: Five companies are worth more than the combined GDP of several major European powers. Welcome to the age of **GAFAM**.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: In 2024, how many billions of dollars will the five GAFAM companies be worth together?
quiz.explanation: In 2024, the five GAFAM companies will together be worth more than $10,000 billion, an amount comparable to the combined GDP of several major European powers.

quiz.question: Which GAFAM company became the first to exceed $3,000 billion in valuation?
quiz.explanation: Apple became the first company to exceed $3 trillion in market valuation.

quiz.question: What is the “network effect”, a key mechanism of GAFAM domination?
quiz.explanation: The network effect means that the more users a service has, the more essential it becomes to be part of it, which discourages the arrival of competitors.
options: The more users a service has, the more essential it becomes to be part of it.
A network of submarine cables owned by Google
An algorithm that detects fake news

quiz.question: In 2012, how many billions of dollars did Facebook pay to buy Instagram?
quiz.explanation: Facebook bought Instagram for $1 billion in 2012, when the app had just a dozen employees.

quiz.question: In 2014, how many billions of dollars did Facebook pay to buy WhatsApp?
quiz.explanation: Facebook bought WhatsApp in 2014 for $22 billion, locking in a burgeoning competing threat.

quiz.question: How much of the world's undersea fiber optic cables does Google own?
quiz.explanation: Google alone owns about 10% of all submarine fiber optic cables in the world.

quiz.question: In 2022, which European text requires the largest digital platforms to be more open?
quiz.explanation: In 2022, Europe adopted the Digital Markets Act, which requires the largest platforms to be more open, such as messaging interoperability.

quiz.question: True or false: in 2024, the European Union will become the first organization in the world to legally regulate artificial intelligence.
quiz.explanation: In 2024, the EU will effectively become the first organization in the world to legally regulate artificial intelligence.

quiz.question: Why do large multinationals often apply European digital rules worldwide?
quiz.explanation: It is easier for a multinational to apply the strictest rule everywhere than to create a different version for each country, which explains the global reach of European rules.
options: It is simpler to apply the strictest rule everywhere than to create a different one per country
The European Union bans any activity outside its borders
American rules are stricter than European ones
GAFAM are legally based in Europe

quiz.question: Put these takeovers and regulations of the world of GAFAM in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These events span from 2012 to 2024: the takeover of Instagram, that of WhatsApp, the adoption of the Digital Markets Act, then the legal supervision of artificial intelligence by the EU.
items: Takeover of Instagram by Facebook
Takeover of WhatsApp by Facebook
Adoption of the Digital Markets Act in Europe
Legal framework for artificial intelligence by the European Union

title: The energy transition
description: The world is trying to replace fossil fuels with cleaner sources. A shift as necessary as it is difficult.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: What year was the Paris Climate Agreement signed?
quiz.explanation: The Paris Agreement was signed in 2015, setting a goal of limiting warming to below 1.5°C if possible.

quiz.question: What is carbon neutrality?
quiz.explanation: Carbon neutrality refers to a balance between greenhouse gases emitted by human activities and their absorption by forests, soils, oceans or capture technologies.
options: A balance between greenhouse gases emitted and their absorption
The total cessation of all CO2 emissions

quiz.question: How much did the cost of solar power fall between 2010 and 2020?
quiz.explanation: The cost of solar power fell 90% between 2010 and 2020, a faster decline than almost any other technology in economic history.

quiz.question: In 2023, what proportion of new electricity capacities installed worldwide already came from renewable energies?
quiz.explanation: In 2023, almost 90% of new electricity capacity installed worldwide will already come from renewable energies.

quiz.question: What is the main technical challenge of solar and wind power, which do not produce electricity continuously?
quiz.explanation: Solar and wind power suffer from intermittency, meaning they do not produce electricity continuously, hence the importance of storage batteries.

quiz.question: How much of the world's solar panels does China manufacture today?
quiz.explanation: China now manufactures more than 80% of the world's solar panels, making the Western energy transition dependent on its manufacturing chain.

quiz.question: Towards what new dependence is the energy transition shifting the world, replacing oil?
quiz.explanation: The energy transition is shifting the world from a dependence on oil to a dependence on rare earths and other metals such as lithium or cobalt.
options: Rare earths and metals such as lithium or cobalt

quiz.question: For which sectors does green hydrogen appear to be a key decarbonization solution?
quiz.explanation: Green hydrogen appears to be a key part of decarbonizing the most difficult sectors, such as steel production or aviation, where electricity alone is not enough.

title: The future of work
description: Artificial intelligence and new forms of employment are shaking a model of work inherited from the industrial age.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: In what year did Henry Ford introduce the 40-hour work week?
quiz.explanation: Henry Ford established the 40-hour week in 1926, a choice motivated by the idea that workers with free time also became customers.

quiz.question: According to economist John Maynard Keynes in 1930, how many hours per week did his grandchildren have to work thanks to technological progress?
quiz.explanation: In 1930, Keynes predicted that his grandchildren would only work 15 hours a week thanks to technological advances, a prediction that did not come true.

quiz.question: How many millions of workers in the United States today sell their services via digital platforms, in the gig economy?
quiz.explanation: More than 57 million workers in the United States now sell their services via digital platforms, outside of traditional employment.

quiz.question: What concept from the economist Joseph Schumpeter describes the fact that a technological revolution destroys old professions but creates new ones?
quiz.explanation: Schumpeter's creative destruction describes the fact that each technological revolution destroys old professions, but ends up creating new ones, often more qualified.

quiz.question: In 2023, a study showed that artificial intelligence performed better than what percentage of humans on a creativity test?
quiz.explanation: In 2023, a study showed that artificial intelligence performed better than 99% of humans on a creativity test.

quiz.question: What does universal basic income offer?
quiz.explanation: The universal basic income proposes to pay a fixed sum to each citizen, without conditions, to secure life courses in an economy where work becomes more intermittent.
options: Pay a fixed amount to each citizen, without conditions
Reduce working time to 4 days per week
Replace all jobs with artificial intelligence

quiz.question: Where does the word “work” come from, which originally referred to an instrument of torture?
quiz.explanation: The word “work” comes from the Latin tripalium, an instrument of torture with three stakes, an origin which recalls that it was long perceived as suffering.

quiz.question: True or false: according to the optimistic scenario mentioned in the course, AI could free humans from repetitive tasks thanks to an increase in productivity.
quiz.explanation: The optimistic scenario imagines an increase in productivity which would free humans from repetitive tasks, as opposed to the pessimistic scenario which fears massive unemployment.

title: China and its economic model
description: In forty years, China went from an isolated farming country to the second largest economy in the world.
subject: comprendreLeMonde

quiz.question: In what year did Deng Xiaoping launch the “reform and opening” policy?
quiz.explanation: Deng Xiaoping launched the policy of “reform and opening” in 1978, after the death of Mao Zedong.

quiz.question: Which city has become the symbol of the special economic zones created by China on its coast?
quiz.explanation: Shenzhen, a simple fishing village in the 1970s, has become the symbol of China's special economic zones and a technological megacity.

quiz.question: Between 1978 and 2018, what was China's average annual economic growth rate?
quiz.explanation: Between 1978 and 2018, China maintained an average growth of 9.5% per year, an exceptional pace.

quiz.question: In forty years, how many millions of people has Chinese growth enabled to escape extreme poverty?
quiz.explanation: Chinese growth has enabled more than 800 million people to escape extreme poverty in forty years.

quiz.question: How do we qualify the Chinese economic model, which combines a dynamic market and strict state control over strategic sectors?
quiz.explanation: The Chinese model is described as “state capitalism”: a dynamic market economy for consumer goods, but strict control over energy, telecommunications and finance.

quiz.question: In what year did Xi Jinping launch the Belt and Road Initiative, the “new silk roads”?
quiz.explanation: Xi Jinping launched the Belt and Road Initiative in 2013, one of the largest infrastructure investment projects in modern history.

quiz.question: What did the near-bankruptcy of real estate giant Evergrande reveal in 2021?
quiz.explanation: The near-bankruptcy of Evergrande in 2021 revealed the flaws of a Chinese real estate market boosted by speculation and considerable debt.
options: The flaws of a Chinese real estate market boosted by speculation and debt
The complete solidity of the Chinese financial system
The end of Communist Party control over the economy
A drop in Chinese public debt

quiz.question: True or false: China's population began to decline in 2022, after decades of a one-child policy.
quiz.explanation: China's population actually began to decline in 2022, a long-term consequence of the one-child policy imposed between 1980 and 2015.

quiz.question: Around which territory are tensions between China and the West concentrated, linked to access to semiconductors?
quiz.explanation: Tensions between China and the West are particularly focused around the status of Taiwan and access to semiconductors, essential to modern industry.

quiz.question: Put these stages of recent Chinese economic history in chronological order.
quiz.explanation: These milestones span from 1978 to 2022: reform and opening up, the Belt and Road Initiative, the Evergrande crisis, then the start of demographic decline.
items: Launch of the reform and opening-up policy
Launch of the Belt and Road Initiative
Near-bankruptcy of the Evergrande real estate group
Beginning of the demographic decline of the Chinese population
